en: Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika,
Autpattikasūtra; Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Anumāna (Chapter 4).
Msv 5.5 = Śabda;
Msv 5.6 = Upamāna (incomplete);
Msv 5.7 = Arthāpatti (incomplete).
Msv 5.8 = Non-existence;
Msv 5.9 = Citrakṣepa (? = unclear.
The Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, together with the commentary named Kāśikā composed by Sucaritamitra.
(Third Part:
"And because it is non-deviant from direct perception, whatever is well-known to have such characteristics—such as inference and so forth—that too need not be examined here. (Msv 5.4)

In this regard, at the conclusion of the discussion on the Vijñānavāda, the author of the Bhāṣya concludes that perception is non-erroneous by stating, "Therefore, perception does not deviate," and then formulates the definition of inference with the words, "Inference belongs to one who knows the relation," and so forth.
He demonstrates the intended meaning of that [definition] with the words beginning "pratyakṣa" (perception).
This is the meaning:

for in the text of the Vṛttikāra it is stated, "By that [instance], perception errs; and because inference and the rest are preceded by that [perception], they too err. Thus, it is declared that inference and the other means of knowledge must be examined because they are subject to error, following upon the error of perception.
In this context, once the non-deviation of perception has been established, a doubt regarding deviation was raised on the grounds that [perception] arises from causes subject to deviation;
at most, a deviation based on its own nature (*svarūpa*) might be possible.
However, even that is certainly not to be suspected in the case of those [types of perception] whose characteristics will be described below.
For one who possesses the vision of an awakened one, there can be no cognition of deviation that acts as an obstacle [to knowledge],
because that would entail the undesirable consequence of the total cessation of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
We shall explain this for the other cases as well in their respective contexts.
Therefore, even inference and the like, being well-established in the world, need not be further examined.

And this commentary, which explains the intended meaning of the definitions of all the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that are about to be described, has been composed by the author of the *Vārttika* as a general introduction.
For this very section is the common locus for the entire expansion of all the means of valid cognition that will be discussed hereafter.
And by means of this verse, the occasion for the commencement [of the work] having been established, the detailed exposition will now be explained specifically.
This is what is meant:

here, definitions have not been formulated to demonstrate the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as something supernatural, as is done by the Naiyāyikas and others; rather, [they are formulated] according to those means of valid cognition well-known in the world (*lokaprasiddha*).
Because [the definition] is subject to deviation for the Mīmāṃsakas;
however, the well-known nature [of perception] is presented here merely to reject the examination that might be prompted by suspected deviation.
Therefore, it should not be thought that there is a lack of consistency with the definition of perception and the other means of valid cognition. // 1 //
Now, at this juncture of explaining the commentary on the definitions, he will first address the definition of inference (*anumāna*).
In that context, it is stated: "of one who has known the relation" (*jñātasambandhasya*). Regarding this, we do not know what the meaning of the compound *jñātasambandha* is.
It is not, first of all, a collection related to a person,
because it lacks a basis of apprehension (*anupādāna*);
for a *bahuvrīhi* compound does not occur when its other referent is not apprehended.
[Objection: Is it not the case that the person (puruṣa) brought to mind through its connection with cognition, or the aggregate implied by the two members of the compound, is what is qualified?

For cognition, being understood from its own word, brings to mind its own substrate since it cannot establish itself without that which possesses it; thus, there is no fault of non-inclusion [of the self].
[Reply: This is not so.
Because there is no distinction in that which is being traversed.
Indeed, fire understood through its invariable concomitance with the object denoted by the word "smoke" is not qualified as "blazing.
And he will say:
"And no qualification is ever observed for an object that is currently being traversed.
This might be thought.
True;
that which is not appropriated is not qualified.
Here, however, the related term must necessarily be something that is appropriated.
For instance, the syntactical connection of the words here is as follows:
"Inference is the cognition [of one part] from the perception of another part.
Therefore, when there arises the expectation "of which part?", that very same part is specified as "that whose relation is known."
But surely, because it is subordinate to the act of seeing (*darśana*), a single constituent part cannot function as a qualifier;
for a word that is subordinate (*upasarjana*) cannot be connected with another word.
Indeed, in the case of "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*), the word *ṛddha* (prosperous) does not serve as a qualifier for the king who has become subordinate to the man.
It is said:
there is no lack of connection because it is subordinate (*upasarjana*).
For that which is expected and capable of fulfilling [the requirement] is indeed connected even with a subordinate element.
Here, when it is stated "from the perception of one part," there arises the expectancy (ākāṅkṣā): "Of what [entity] is this one part?
Even in the case of a semantic connection, expectancy alone is the cause.
As for the technical designation "subordinate" (upasarjana), it is governed by the rule: "The subordinate member is placed first" (Pāṇini 2.2.30).
It is solely for the sake of establishing the prior application (*pūrveprayoga*).
For this very reason, the linguistic usage "whose teacher's family" (*kasya gurukulam*) is possible;
for in that case, the word "whose" (*kasya*) is a qualifier specifically of the teacher (*guru*), who is subordinate to the family (*kula*).

Moreover, it is observed that even when one part of the object of the act of seeing— the visible— is primary, there can be a connection with another word for that which is secondary, even if it is dependent [on the primary], as in "the king's man is handsome. Therefore, it is logically established that [inference occurs] from the perception of one part of an object whose relationship [to the other part] is already known.
This is not tenable;

for the Teacher himself has stated: "A subordinate term (*upasarjana*) is not connected with another word [as its primary], just as in the case of 'the king's man' (*ṛddhasya rājapuruṣaḥ*). And yet, the status of being a subordinate term has not been refuted.

The knower is said to be one who has cognized the relationship, or it is stated that he is a part [of that relationship]; alternatively, according to the *karmadhāraya* interpretation, it is the state of being a part within the relatum.
For if there were qualifiers, the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) would distinguish the king.
As for what was said—that "expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is the cause of connection"—that is incorrect;
for it has been stated that even one who possesses expectancy may lack fitness (*ayogyatva*).

Now, it might be argued that this fault applies only if [the two statements] form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*). [In that case, one might say: "Inference is the cognition of one part [of an object] based on the perception of another part;

therefore, when the sentence is completed, since there arises an expectancy as to which part [is meant], the word 'part' (*ekadeśa*) occurring in the sentence is qualified by the phrase 'whose relation is known' (*jñātasambandhasya*).
This is not so.
Because the sentence expressing the desire is not heard,

that very thing constitutes the fault of the external referent (anyapadārtha) not being included. However, where there is such inclusion, its unsuitability has been stated due to its status as a subordinate element (upasarjana).
Moreover, the very fault here is the splitting of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
Furthermore, that which was stated— that perception has the object of perception as its primary focus— is also incorrect.
Because in a *tatpuruṣa* compound the meaning of the final member is predominant,
and no connection with another word is observed by relying on an actual relationship of subordinate and predominant; for such is not seen in the case of "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*).
Is it not the case that the predominance of one part [of the compound] is understood through grammar alone?
For this genitive in the sense of the object is characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix. No;
because it is not heard [in the text].
For in a compound, the genitive case is not heard;
nor does that which is not heard express its own meaning.
Rather, its meaning is understood through indication (lakṣaṇā), as in the case of "the Niṣāda chieftain" (niṣādasthapati).

However, by direct audition (śruti), it is perception itself as delimited by the object of sight that is understood as primary; for this very reason, there is the grammatical rule that the final member of a compound is predominant,
since it is understood as such from the compound itself.
Furthermore, actual predominance of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is not the cause for its connection with another word or for its being a *sāpekṣasamāsa* (compound involving expectancy).

In the case of "whose teacher's family" (*kasya gurukulam*), there is no fault of lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*) because the word "teacher" (*guru*) is inherently expectant (*nityasāpekṣa*). For the meaning of "teacher" cannot be understood without incorporating the correlative;
this is because it is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*).
Therefore, since this [word] enters into the function [of the compound] precisely by requiring another referent, there is no fault;
however, the word "ekadeśa" (one part) is not like this, which constitutes the difference.
Consequently, the meaning of the compound whose relationship has been understood is difficult to ascertain.
Therefore, he says: "the knower" (pramātṛ). The intention here is this: it is true that a single part [of the compound] does not constitute the meaning of the external referent (anyapadārtha).
However, it is the cognizer himself, presented through his connection with the intellect (*buddhi*), who is designated as "one whose relation is known.
Moreover, even that which is merely implied is indeed qualified when presented by an unfailing mark (*cihna*);
for there is no fault in the non-mention of the referent of the word "Pinākapāṇi" [Śiva] in the expression "namaḥ pinākapāṇaye."

Furthermore, regarding the statement "one draws the Aindravāyava cup," how could the deity-indicating secondary suffix (*devatātaddhita*)— which functions as the meaning of a *bahuvrīhi* compound— apply to the Soma juice that has not yet been brought forth? If it is argued that the Soma juice understood through the context— by way of the sequence "he buys the Soma, he presses it, he purifies it, he draws it with a stream"— is the referent of the other member of the compound (*anyapadārtha*), then here too it is not untenable for the cognizer, who is understood through an inseparable connection with the intellect (*buddhyavinābhāva*), to be the referent of the *bahuvrīhi*.

The argument put forward by some, who feel as though they have obtained something difficult to find—that which was stated by the author of the Vārttika while standing in the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie position), namely that "that which is implied (*gamyamāna*) is not qualified"—is to be disregarded as mere verbiage.

For in the *siddhānta* (the established conclusion), it is precisely the implied individual (*vyakti*) that will be qualified by case-endings (*vibhakti*), by other words, and by adjectives; as in the cases of "two cows" (*gāvau*), "cows" (*gāvaḥ*), "white cow" (*śuklo gauḥ*), and "the platforms are shouting" (*mañcāḥ krośanti*).
And it is said:
"No one indeed intends to speak of the existence or non-existence of the universal (jāti),
for those two [existence and non-existence] are qualifiers of the individual (vyakti) which is perceived as being eternal."
Thus,
it does not follow that "this smoke is burning," because such a thing is not expressed.
For the world cannot be subjected to logical censure;
however, we do not forbid one who, out of impudence, uses the word "smoke" to indicate "fire" and employs it accordingly.

But [one might object]: "In this way, since the relationship is known by the cognizer, the 'single part' (ekadeśa) would not be specified, and thus the recollection of the pervaded (vyāpya) upon seeing the pervading single part (vyāpaka-ekadeśa) would result in mere inference."
But this is not accepted;

for inference is the knowledge of the pervader (vyāpaka) from the pervaded (vyāpya). Since it is said that "for one who knows the relation, [it arises] from a part (ekadeśa)," there might indeed be the apprehension of a specific part in the case of a relation.
For in that case, by the genitive in the phrase "of one part whose relation is known" (*jñātasambandhasyaikadeśasya*), it is precisely the pervaded (*vyāpya*) that is presented as the relatum;
for everywhere, the genitive is observed only in reference to the pervaded.
It is replied:

We have already stated that we are not describing some extraordinary nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Rather, their well-known nature in the world is merely restated for the purpose of demonstrating that they are not subject to critical examination. For it is well known in the world that inference is the knowledge of one part of the regulator (*niyāmaka*) based on the perception of one part of the regulated (*niyāmya*).
Indeed, even in the absence of an explicit qualifier, the "one part of the qualified" (*viśiṣṭaikadeśa*) is understood.
Moreover, he says that memory has as its object an entity not present to the senses (*asannikṛṣṭa*).
And memory does not have as its object an unperceived thing merely through the concomitance of what is seen with the pervader (*vyāpaka*);
for memory has as its object nothing more than what was already the object of a previous means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

However, it is precisely because of the pervaded (*vyāpya*)—due to the restriction of what has been previously experienced—that the mountain and so forth are understood as qualified by the pervader (*vyāpaka*).
Therefore, the attainment of the qualified single locus (*viśiṣṭaikadeśa*) is logically established.
As for the statement that the genitive case in the phrase "of one part whose relation is known" (*jñātasambandhasyaikadeśasya*) expresses a specific distinction: [this is explained as follows].

That is incorrect, because the genitive case can arise even from that which is coextensive (*vyāpaka*). For there is indeed the conventional usage: "being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is the reason for impermanence (*anityatā*)," and impermanence is coextensive with being produced.

Therefore, even when the term is mentioned without qualification, it is not untenable to obtain a specific relation or a specific portion [of that relation] through interpretation. For it has been well said: "The understanding of the specific [meaning] comes from interpretation, but a definition is not [invalidated] by doubt"; thus, it is correctly stated that the knower is one who has known the relation.
Alternatively, when two things whose relationship is known have been perceived together,
the members of that aggregate are expressed by means of words denoting one part of them.
He states another explanation: "the proponent of a partial view" (*ekadeśī*).
For two parts (*ekadeśau*) cannot exist without a whole (*ekadeśin*); thus, it is logical that the implied whole serves as the referent of the compound.
[Objection: But if it is stated in this way—"from the perception of a part belonging to a whole whose relation [to the other part] is known"—then...

Because that very [relation] is subordinate to the act of seeing, it follows that there is either a "relation" between a part and the whole, or else the fault of compounding (samāsadoṣa) arises for that which depends on a specific correlate.
This might be so.
Even if that [identity] were one, it would still belong to the proponent of a partial identity (ekadeśin), just as in the case of "the sacrificial post of the Vājapeya.
But who here is the proponent of a partial identity? Is it the subject (*pakṣa*), the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), or the known relation (*jñātasambandha*)?
It cannot be the subject, for the subject is not something graspable through a single observation of a relation that is currently being known.

However, through repeated observations, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is ascertained by means of the mere presence of smoke—distinct from all previously perceived places and times—as being characterized by the presence of fire;
it is not, however, ascertained here and now that "this [specific place] possessing smoke possesses fire.

Therefore, even for one who perceives only a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśin*), the relation conditioned by the general property of possessing smoke is known; thus, that alone constitutes the "known relation" (*jñātasaṃbandha*).

It should be understood that even when the location and so forth are apprehended in a general way, it is intended that the "part" (ekadeśin) and the "part" (ekadeśa) are the locus and the located; however, they are not to be regarded as the part and the whole (avayava-avayavin). //1//
Or, he says that this is a *karmadhāraya* compound: "it is a *karmadhāraya*.
The meaning is this: since it is both "known" (*jñāta*) and "the relation" (*saṃbandha*), this is a *karmadhāraya*.
And in this view, when the related object (*saṃbandhin*) is to be understood, both the indicator (*gamaka*) and the indicated (*gamya*) possess the status of being a single part (*ekadeśatā*).
How can the two relata be parts of the relation which has the substratum as its correlate?
For the mountain is not a part of the smoke whose substratum is the mountain.
But it is argued that smoke is indeed the thing to be contained (ādheya), yet it is regarded as a part of that [locus] because it occupies a portion of it.
To this it is replied: the expression "a part" is indeed applicable even to the locus (ādhāra).
Just as it is in the case of the parts which are the substrata of the whole, and in the case of the collections [of those parts], so it should be stated without objection. //2//
Or rather, he says that "the two" constitute the meaning of the other word—namely, "or the two.

At the time of grasping the relationship, the pair consisting of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*), which has been perceived as mutually related, is called "that whose relationship is known"; and its two constituent parts are the members of that aggregate.
And how this is so has already been stated earlier.
Furthermore, what is the object of cognition (*prameya*) in the case of a *karmadhāraya* compound or when there is a meaning distinct from the two members?
It is certainly not the relation (*sambandha*) or the aggregate (*samudāya*) alone.
Because these three have already been understood previously,
and because they are not currently understood through the distinction between property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmī*),
nor is there any other partial proponent (*ekadeśin*).
Because it does not grasp that [object],
nor is there an implication by way of its two parts,
since the relationship and the whole are free from expectancy.
Nor is inference the cognition of one independent part from the perception of another independent part, because [the latter] is already established;
for he will say later that it is not merely a property (*dharma*).
"Because it is established.

To this, it is replied: What is the meaning here? From the observation of one part of two things—either a relation (*sambandha*) that is already known or a related thing (*jñātasambandha*) whose relation is known—an inferential cognition arises regarding the other part in that very same locus; from where is this [established]?
Because of the inclusion of the term "not in contact" (asannikṛṣṭa).
For a single part of an independent [object] is not "not in contact";
rather, it is only in certain cases, such as with a mountain and the like, that a single part becomes "not in contact."
In that case, since it has not been previously understood, what is untenable?
Furthermore, what kind of relationship is intended here as a constituent factor (*aṅga*) of inference?
Some maintain that it is inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), based on identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*).

For it has been stated by them as follows: "The restriction of inseparable concomitance (avinābhāva) is determined either by the relation of cause and effect or by essential nature as the regulator; it is not [determined] by non-observation, nor by observation."
Thus [it is said]:
for the establishment of an inseparable connection (avinābhāva) does not result from the non-perception or perception of the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) and similar instances (sapakṣa);
because it is possible for even an indefinite [reason] to occur therein.
Furthermore, because the exclusion of all opposing factors cannot be established through the exclusion of just some opposing factors,
and because it is impossible to apprehend all opposing factors simultaneously, rather,

when it is known that smoke and the like exist when fire and the like are present and do not exist when they are absent— and thus smoke and the like have a nature dependent upon them— their invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is established.
Because that effect cannot attain its own existence without it [the cause], therefore,
in this case, the perception [of the effect] in fire and the non-perception [of it] elsewhere is the reason for its arising from that;
from this, the establishment of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) follows.
Even if there were identity (*tādātmya*), that [identity] would not be established, because for you, identity is untenable without that [invariable concomitance].
Now, one might object: "In this way, color, taste, and so forth—which lack such positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with smell—would not be inferred from it;
moreover, color is certainly not the very nature (*ātman*) of smell."
And since it is not the cause [of taste], how can that [color] be established from it?
Listen to how it is established:

for when taste itself is inferred from its own cause—just as fire is inferred from smoke—the cognition of color occurs through the transformation of the fuel within the same causal complex; thus, there is no logical inconsistency.
As it has been said:
"The cognition of form and so forth, which depend upon the same causal complex,
occurs through the inference of a property of the cause, just as [fire is inferred] from smoke, which is a transformation of fuel."
Thus [it is said].
Now, one might object: "In the case of the transformation of fuel, there is indeed an understanding [of causality] because both that [fuel] and the smoke have the single cause of fire;
however, color and taste do not have a single common cause."
For the tastes of the causes indeed initiate taste in the effect, and the forms of the causes [initiate] form in the effect. Therefore, how can there be identity of cause?
It is not by virtue of having a single cause that there is dependence on a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

However, from taste, that which causes taste is inferred; it is inferred as being accompanied by a material cause (upādānakāraṇa) whose nature is the power to produce the form [of the subsequent taste].
Since only such a thing possesses causality, and since form is produced by a cause that possesses the power of activity (pravṛtti), the establishment of form [is achieved].
This, however, is untenable: as for the claim that an effect does not exist without a cause, and therefore the knowledge of that [cause] was stated.
That is incorrect.
For how can it be determined that an effect simply does not exist without its cause? If it were to exist without that [cause], it would have to be either eternally existent or non-existent.
Consequently, its very nature as an effect would be lost;
for it has been said by them:
"Eternal existence or non-existence [follows] from a cause’s independence from anything else."
"For it is through dependence that the occasional occurrence of entities is possible.
Thus, through dependence there is occasionality; however, that which is independent must be either eternally existent or non-existent.

If it is argued that [the relation] is like the sky, the hare’s horn, and so forth—if this were so, then this restriction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaniyama*) would be something other than the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), such that "whatever is independent is either eternal or existent or non-existent.
And as for what was stated: that the cognition of color from taste is due to their dependence on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatvāt*).
That too has been stated:

although the cause of taste is understood from its own effect as being accompanied by the material cause (upādānakāraṇa) in the form of the power of manifestation, from what is color (rūpa) understood?
If it is argued that this is because of the causal capacity for activity (*pravṛtti*), [we reply:
surely sound (*nāda*) is not the effect or the essence of form (*rūpa*); so how could its disappearance be a cause [for the disappearance of form]?
If it is argued that this is because the cause, which possesses the power of activity, is never dissociated from its effect, we say: no.

If it is argued that the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) belongs only to the effect and its own nature, and that it might also exist in the case of the cause, we say no; for this would lead to the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) of inferring fire from smoke.
If it is argued that "let it be so," then it would follow that being an effect is irrelevant to inference;
for the inference of a cause's form does not arise from the capacity for purposeful action.
Rather, taste is produced by the cause of taste acting in conjunction with the cause of form, which possesses form;
since even a cooperative cause is indeed a cause when qualified [by its association], the entire causal cycle, mutually supported by taste and the other [sensory objects], is to be inferred.
That is not so;
because cause and effect are not simultaneous, it is impossible for the metaphorical cause (*rūpakāraṇa*) to possess that [quality].
By the method of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*), [it must be the primary cause].
It must be stated that form alone is the auxiliary cause;
and in that case, the labor of inferring its cause is useless.
This applies even to the claim that "form is the auxiliary cause."
An inseparable relation whose nature and color (form) have not been ascertained cannot be experienced;
how much less so when that [relation] has already been ascertained, for then the assumption of the form and its cause acting as concomitant causes is useless.
Here, "connection" is intended as "pervasion" (vyāpti), which is the relation of the property of the mark (liṅga) with the possessor of the mark (liṅgin). //3//
Moreover, this is indeed contrary to experience;
for ordinary people do not perceive color by means of inferring its cause after having perceived taste.
Rather, because of the rule of the constant association between taste and color, color is inferred from taste immediately and spontaneously.

Moreover, since the practical application of inference is seen most frequently to occur only between things that stand in the relation of cause and effect, the fact of being an effect need not be disregarded in the absence of deviation.
Likewise, identity (*tādātmya*) must also be rejected, as it would entail the consequence that there is no object left to be measured (*meyābhāva*);
for once the nature of the *śiṃśapā* tree is known within the essence of "tree," what remains to be measured?
The object is partless, because the apprehensions of its parts, though appearing distinct in terms of location and so forth, are not sublated and are thus correct; furthermore,
since inference relies upon conceptual distinctions, actual oneness is not a factor for it.

If it is argued that the conventional usage of "tree" is inferred [from the term "śiṃśapā"], how then can the conventional usage of "non-self" be inferred from "being a śiṃśapā"? For if there were identity (*tādātmya*) between them, it would follow—just as with the case of "tree"—that no inference could occur.
This argument applies equally to the suitability for conventional usage; therefore, this [objection] is trivial.
In the same way, it should be understood that even the modes of relation established in systems such as Vaiśeṣika—such as the relation of cause and effect—are not applicable;
for they too are indeterminate and do not serve as the cause for the arising of inference.
[Objection: "Then let restriction (niyama) be a constituent of inference. [Reply: No.

Since there is an absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the object] remains uncomprehended. First of all, perception arising from a mere superficial encounter is not capable of determining this [object]. Indeed, with eyes wide open, one suddenly perceives smoke in the kitchen accompanied by fire.
But one does not know with certainty that "this [result] is determined by this [cause]," for the determination of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is difficult to grasp;
even the great are not able to deduce it instantaneously.
For conceptual construction is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to that which is not within the scope of non-conceptual [cognition],
because it is preceded by that.
This might be so.

"The restriction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaniyama*) is determined because there is no deviation across differences of place and so forth. By whom is this determined? Since all perceptions function only with respect to the mere presence of a common feature (*anvaya*).

Now, the final [perceptual] cognition, accompanied by the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) produced by each preceding cognition, becomes a discerning awareness (*ālocanājñāna*) such that "this is restricted by this."
"Therefore, conceptual constructions will not arise"—
this is not so;
for perception is dependent upon the activity of the sense faculties.
Nor is there any operation of the external sense-faculties elsewhere than in the perception of coexistence;
nor does the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) function with regard to the cognition of external objects independently of them.

Furthermore, since even entities whose forms have been determined are experienced as becoming otherwise when there is a difference in place and so forth, it is not proper for those who rely on valid means of knowledge (prāmāṇika) to resort to a fixedness of intrinsic nature (svabhāvaniyama).
Regarding this, they say: “Since the potencies of entities differ due to differences in place, time, and other such factors,
the establishment of those entities through inference is extremely difficult.”
The pervaded is held to be the means of cognition, and the pervader is the object of cognition.
Whatever [object] may be equal to or even inferior to another in terms of place and time,
it is pervaded by that [other], whether the latter is equal to or superior to it.
Therefore, when the object to be pervaded (vyāpya) has been apprehended, its pervader (vyāpaka) is apprehended;
for otherwise, this relationship of pervaded and pervader between those two would not exist.
Therefore, the "relation" (sambandha), which constitutes a constituent part of inference, must be stated.
Hence he says: "the relation. For pervasion (vyāpti) indeed indicates the necessity of concomitance (sāhityaniyama).

For when one who perceives that [connection] sees one part, a cognition arises regarding another part; therefore, although the word "relation" (*sambandha*) expresses a generality, it here— in this section of the treatise defining inference— refers to a particular, due to its association with the subsequent context.
Furthermore, the proof for this restriction will be stated later. //3//

If inference belongs to one who has cognized the relation, then that relation—being dependent on two relata—is the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for the inference of both; therefore, he says: "The pervaded... (verse 4).
Regarding this, he states the reason in two verses beginning with "yo yasya" (that which belongs to which).
For that which is equal, not inferior, [and not superior] in terms of place and time is what is pervaded (*vyāpya*).
First, there is the case where both properties possess the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakatva*).
As will be illustrated further on;
the latter, however, is like smoke and so forth,
for it generally exists at the same place and time as fire.
That which does not pervade all of its [the object's] places and times is the non-pervasive;
the pervasive, however, has more extensive place and time.
Here too, the "prior" is exactly as previously described.
But the subsequent [reason] is like fire itself in relation to smoke; for it indeed pervades its [smoke's] space and time.
Even if it were to exist in the absence of smoke, it would still be designated as being superior to those [specific] space and time.

Since these two possess such an essential nature—that is, they consist of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader—for that reason, when the pervaded is apprehended, there occurs the apprehension of the pervader; for the latter does not exist even in the absence of the former.
Indeed, unlike fire [in relation to smoke], it does not exist by transcending the space and time of the fire.
For if it were [the cause], it would not fail to indicate that [fire] even in its absence;
however, since fire is not of such a nature, it does not serve as an indicator of smoke.
But surely this distinction is not understood from a word whose relationship [to the object] is unknown?

Even if that which is grasped as the pervader is in fact the pervaded, it would not establish the pervaded because there is no contradiction even when [the former] is greater [in extension]. (Msv 5.4.7)
This has been clearly observed in the cognition of "cow" and "hornedness":
because of pervasion, cows are the signifiers, while hornedness is not the pervader.
For he shows that the mere knowledge of the relationship is a contributing factor (*aṅga*), and not the state of being pervaded (*vyāpyatā*); so how is a specific distinction gained?
To this it has been said: this commentary is intended to establish non-investigation (*aparīkṣā*) by way of restating the worldly definition.
And in the world, it is established that inference is the knowledge of the pervader belonging only to one who perceives a part of what is pervaded; for it is not otherwise.
Having extracted the phrase "nahyanyathā" and joined it with what precedes, it should be explained as "tena," meaning by depending upon that [perception]. //6//
But surely, the cognition of the pervaded is also seen from the pervader;
for example, as that of "producedness" from "impermanence.
For indeed, there occurs the inference of "producedness" from the "impermanence" of entities.
Furthermore, impermanence is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of being produced (*kṛtakatva*).

Therefore, the pervader is the object to be known (*gamya*), while the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is the means of knowledge (*gamaka*). Since [the opponent] has stated this incorrectly, [the author] says "by being the pervader" (*vyāpakatvena*).
This is the intended meaning.
It is true that what is pervading possesses the capacity to indicate [the probandum], but not that which is grasped merely as being pervading.
For when it is grasped in that form, it does not contradict its status as a pervader even when there is an excess of space and time.
But surely it also possesses pervasiveness (*vyāpyatā*). Let it be so; however, since its nature as a non-entity is not grasped, how can it possess the capacity to indicate [the probandum]?
Once that nature is understood, its capacity to indicate is due to that very [nature], and not by way of being the pervader (*vyāpakatā*).
Therefore, it is well said that pervasion alone (*vyāpyatā*) is a constituent factor of inference, and not pervasiveness (*vyāpakatā*). //7//
It is shown by way of an unambiguous example that being the pervaded (vyāpyatva) is the essential factor, not being the pervader (vyāpakatva):
"Just as the pervaded is the indicator (gamaka) and the pervader is the indicated (gamya).
For between "cowness" and "having horns," it is indeed cowness that is the pervader.

In the context of inference (*mitau*), the meaning is that this distinction between the cognized (*gamya*) and the cognizer (*gamaka*) is observed between "cowness" (*gotva*) and "horns" (*viṣāṇitva*). //8//
Therefore, even where two properties are considered to stand in a relationship of the pervaded and the pervader,
it is only the state of being pervaded that serves as the logical reason (*aṅga*) for the inference, not the state of being the pervader.

Therefore, regarding other subjects of the dharma, whatever [connection] of whichever kind has been previously determined for someone by means of something, in whatever place or at whatever time it extends; Msv_5.4.10.

Thus, since there is no confusion when the distinction between the signifier (*gamaka*) and the signified (*gamya*) is maintained, even in cases where a confusion of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs, it is established that "the state of being the pervaded (*vyāpyatva*)" alone is the cause for being a signifier. He states this with the words "Therefore" (*tena*). //9//

Now, it has been stated that pervasion (vyāpti) is a constituent factor of inference. But to what does this [pervasion] belong? Is it to that which is conjoined (saṃyogin), or that which is inherent (samavāyin), or that which is related through a relation (sambandhisambandhin)?
For we do not perceive any fixed rule in this regard.
Because all [of these] are inferential indicators;
for if that which is conjoined were the pervader,
there would be no inference of color from taste.

Now, one must demonstrate that there is inference of fire from smoke based on essential identity (*samavāyin*), and the inference of a son’s Brahminhood from the Brahminhood of his parents based on a connection with a related entity (*sambandhisambandhin*), and so forth.
Furthermore, "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) is defined as positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
This means "contact.
And such contact is not possible between fire established on the ground and the tip of smoke situated in the sky;
nor does the rising of stars in the heavens perceive the shadow of a gnomon standing upon the earth.
Furthermore, the pervasion (vyāpti) of one thing by another occurs either spatially or temporally.
In the former case, because the rising of the sun that is yet to occur would be identical to the rising of the present sun, no inference could take place after eight watches (yāma) have passed.
In the latter case, one must raise an objection regarding such things as the inference of fire from smoke.
Therefore he says: "by that," which refers to two things;
namely, by whatever cause (yena kāraṇena) and by whichever one among those [factors] such as conjunction (saṃyoga), etc., and by whichever one among them.
Whatever nature of pervasion was previously understood— whether by means of conjunction with the other [the probandum] or otherwise— that alone serves as the cause for inference;
for non-conjunction is not pervasion.
For it has been said: “This is the restriction of the relation.
And that [relation] occurs even with that which is not directly contiguous;
for when X exists, Y comes to be.
And since [the effect] does not exist when [the cause] is absent,
it is said to be "determined" by that;
what is the use of [physical] contact here?

And here there is no intention to specify any particularity regarding place and so forth; for in whatever place or at whatever time a given thing exists, or in relation to which its pervasion has been previously established,
that pervaded portion remains exactly as it was when existing in that same extent of place and time, by means of the pervading factor that occurs throughout that extent of place and time.

In another locus of properties (dharmin) such as the sky, that which has been observed in the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin) in relation to the example-locus becomes a means of proof. To that extent, being of such a nature, it is observed again in another locus;
thus, the pervaded aspect is a means of proving the pervading aspect in exactly that same way. (Msv 5.4.11)
And the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between two general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) is understood through repeated observation;
it is also known in some cases between two particulars (*viśeṣa*), by means of abandoning their distinctions.
For restriction (niyama) is indeed a constituent part of inference, and that is certainly common to all [inferences] without distinction; what is the use of internal subdivisions?

By stating "as much as exists in a place," it demonstrates the pervasion (vyāpti) even of smoke and the like when they have risen only slightly, as well as of a river's flood situated at a great distance.
And by the rising of the stars situated at an extreme distance from the shadow of the gnomon;
for as long as that time.
And it demonstrates pervasion even in cases such as the inference of the rising of the sun that is yet to occur. //11//

Now, it was argued that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this pervasion (*vyāpti*); therefore, he says: "by repeated observation" (*bhūyodarśana*). But how can pervasion be understood through repeated observation?
For what [is there] in that case?
Is it that each individual observation is itself the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or rather is it that which arises from the observations?
In this regard, it has already been established that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not something to be apprehended through individual observations alone;
for indeed, when one suddenly beholds fire and smoke in a kitchen, the cognition does not immediately arise that "smoke is pervaded by fire."
Furthermore, that which has not been experienced by non-conceptual [perception] cannot be made an object even by conceptual perception.
Nor is there any such thing as a "collection of perceptions" (*darśana-samudāya*) composed of multiple perceptions, because it does not exist apart from those individual perceptions.

Furthermore, because past, future, and present [moments] cannot be integrated into a single whole, one must consider which among them is the valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*): is it the final perception, aided by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the various preceding perceptions?
It cannot, first of all, be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For that [cognition] is divided into two types:
non-conceptual sensory perception (*ālocanājñāna*) and the conceptual cognition (*vikalpasambhinna*) arising from it.
Of these, the former is not capable of ascertaining pervasion (*vyāpti*), because it lacks synthetic synthesis (*apratisandhāna*).

Because this [inference] consists of the synthesis that "this [reason] is connected with the pervasion," it does not attain its own nature as a conclusion without depending upon that [pervasion]. And as for this accumulation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),...
This too is not tenable;
for mental formations (saṃskāras), whose nature consists in the possibility of apprehending the form of a particular object, produce merely a memory with respect to that very object.
Furthermore, they are not capable of apprehending another object.

And when perception is the means of valid cognition for pervasion (*vyāpti*), how can there be an inference of Vedic rituals from those specific persons who possess results other than that [perception]?
Nor is the restriction of each respective ritual to its particular result, such as cattle and so forth, perceived directly, because it is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).
Furthermore, that inference of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) from the subsidiary and principal elements of the Veda during the extended sacrifice would also not be possible,
because there is a lack of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for ascertaining the invariable concomitance (*vyāpti*).
Furthermore, one must demonstrate such things as the inference of the absence of rain from the absence of clouds;
therefore, pervasion (vyāpti) is neither perceptual nor inferential.
Because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that [entity] which depends upon such a means for its own acquisition of existence is untenable.
Furthermore, verbal testimony (*śabda*) has as its object things that have not yet arisen or are yet to be produced; it is not capable of establishing a well-established pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Analogical cognition (*upamāna*) also has as its object merely the similarity to a thing already established by another means of valid cognition; it does not cognize the actual existence of a thing.
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) also has as its object a fact that cannot otherwise be accounted for, and it arises from perception;
yet, when two things have been perceived together, nothing at all can be said to be unaccounted for in the absence of a pervasion (*vyāpti*).
But surely, the status of being an effect is not established.
For how can there be an effect when a cause is absent?

Moreover, since the status of being an effect is to be understood through repeated observation, the establishment of the pervasion by the cause is based on the means of valid cognition consisting in the impossibility otherwise (anyathānupapatti) of the comprehension of the status of being an effect as produced by repeated observation.
How, then, will pervasion (*vyāpti*) be established between things that stand in neither a causal nor a non-causal relationship?
If it is argued that numerous observations themselves would not be possible in the absence of pervasion, [we reply:
for what is impossible regarding their own nature (*svarūpa*) without pervasion?
And for that long, the causal totality is indeed established;

even the self-illumination of its own object, insofar as the poison is determined by its own means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we see nothing at all that is untenable. Nor is this contradicted by another means of valid cognition.
That which is not logically tenable: it is not correct to say that a pervasion consisting of the essential nature of an entity is cognized by means of non-existence;
for in that case, such [pervasion] could never be established by the means of valid cognition known as non-apprehension (abhāva-pramāṇa).

It might be thought: "What is this other pervasion (*vyāpti*) of smoke by fire, [which consists] in the exclusion of non-fire? And since it is of the nature of a non-entity (*abhāva*), it is rightly cognized by means of non-apprehension (*abhāva*).
That is not so.
Because it has the nature of a real entity (*vastu*).
For the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of smoke and so forth, being of the nature of a real entity, is restricted by something;
otherwise, since this [nature] would indeed be excluded even from the absence of a rabbit's horn, it would be restricted by the rabbit's horn as well.
If it is asked, "How can that which is non-existent be restricted? what is the fault?
For restriction is indeed exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
If it is argued that "it exists," what is the point of [discussing] the existence or non-existence of a rabbit's horn?
If it is thought that the counter-example (vipakṣa) is an obstacle because it is excluded from the opposite side,
and that the absence of smoke— which is absent where fire is absent— is pervaded by the rabbit's horn just as "non-fire" is, then the absence of that [fire] would also be a counter-example.
Furthermore, because all contrary instances (*vipakṣa*) are incapable of being perceived, their exclusion from them cannot be understood through non-existence (*abhāva*).
For it will be stated that the absence of a capable means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the means of valid cognition for non-existence.
Therefore, there is no proof whatsoever for pervasion (*vyāpti*).
If it is argued that [the cognition] is mental, we say no, because the mind lacks independence regarding external objects.

In this regard, it might be thought: although the external sense-faculties are incapable of grasping the pervasion by means of various categories of entities such as the past and the future, [the mind can].

"But the mind, whose capacity is restricted to being common to the discernment of all objects—past, present, and future—is dependent on something else; therefore, pervasion will be grasped by a perception that arises through its power.
This is not so, because the mind lacks independence regarding external objects.

Furthermore, it has been explained that the mind is not independent in its cognition of external objects; for instance, in the passage beginning "the mind [requires] an object" (*sārtha*). For if the mind were held to be independent, everyone would be an all-seeing seer.
If it is argued that its establishment is by way of conditioning (*saṃskāra*), we say no, because it is the cause of memory.
In this regard, it might be thought: even if the mind is not independent in the determination of external objects, [it still functions as such].

Nevertheless, accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by successive prior experiences, it will function even with respect to external objects, just as the eye and other senses do with respect to form and so forth;
therefore, there is no lack of stability.
And yet, that is not the case.
Because it is the cause of memory.

For the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), which are produced by previous experiences and are the causes of mere memory, are capable of providing assistance toward the external apprehension of the mind;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that other objects of memory would also be apprehended.
For even in that case, there exists the *saṃskāra* (mental impression) which is the cause of memory.

If it assists the mind in the act of apprehension in some instance, why does it not also apprehend other objects of memory? Thus, this [objection] is trivial. As for the one who says: "The concomitance (*sāhitya*) of fire and smoke is their relation (*sambandha*)."
And that [relation] is indeed cognized at the very moment of its first apprehension;
furthermore, the relation between fire and smoke appears as being uninterrupted by space and time.
For there does not arise the thought, "The relation between these two exists only now" or "here."
Rather, it is only the space and time of those two things which are present and currently manifesting as "this-ness" that serve as their qualification, such that one says,
"these two are connected," or "there is no connection here [at this time]."
Thus, in this way, an intrinsic relation (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) of an uninterrupted nature is established;
and since it is intrinsic, the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is not possible.
Is it then the case that repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) is entirely irrelevant?
It is not a non-member [of the syllogism];
rather, it is a member by way of dispelling doubts based on adventitious conditions (*aupādhika*). For fire, even when perceived as conjoined with smoke, is sometimes seen to be without smoke.
In that case, it is determined that the adjunct consisting of wet fuel and so forth enters [into the relationship],
but the connection of fire with smoke is not intrinsic;
and because of that observation, [the same is concluded] regarding smoke as well.
A doubt arises: "Perhaps its connection with fire is merely adventitious (aupādhika). That doubt is removed by repeated observation (bhūyodarśana).
Even when smoke is observed many times, no limiting condition (upādhi) is found to exist in its connection with fire;
and although sought with great effort, since no such condition is seen, it is certain that none exists.
Thus, it is established that fire is invariably concomitant with smoke alone.
Furthermore, since there can be no suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding that which is unconditioned (*anaupādhika*), he must be asked:
"Is mere concomitance (*sāhityamātra*) now the constituent factor of inference, or is it the necessary restriction (*niyama*) between them?

If it were mere concomitance, then since that is already apprehended at the very first observation, there would be inference even for one who perceives smoke again but has not yet known the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Now, if it is argued that this very restriction (niyama) is established by following this means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), from what does it arise? For no such notion as "this [object] is restricted by this [cognition]" is seen to appear for one who perceives for the first time.
A relation that is understood as being unrestricted by space and time is considered to be inherent (svābhāvika).
If it is argued that there is a necessary rule (*niyama*) [between fire and smoke],
then since such a rule would have been understood at the very first instance, one would not require repeated observation.
Furthermore, even for fire seen in such a manner, its connection with smoke is subject to deviation.

And from seeing that [separation], a suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) arises even regarding smoke. If it is argued that repeated observation is required to dispel that suspicion, then [we reply]: if even for that which is not delimited by space or time, a separation from something is ever observed in some case; [then the rule is not universal].
What, then, is the assurance regarding other cases as well?
Is it not said that this suspicion is dispelled by repeated observation? How is it dispelled?
When fire has been understood to possess smoke hundreds of times, yet it is seen to be smokeless,
no such restrictive rule [of concomitance] is established by this many observations alone as to how non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) is proven.
Now, just as no *upādhi* (limiting condition) is perceived for the connection of fire with smoke, so too none is perceived for the connection of smoke with fire.
Therefore, how could this [invariable concomitance] not exist even when smoke is present? No;
for it is precisely because factors such as place (*deśa*) and so forth are suspected to be limiting conditions (*upādhi*) that one suspects this.

Having observed a deviation in the connection between fire and smoke, one suspects: "Perhaps, even in the case of smoke's connection with fire, there might be some limiting condition such as place, time, and so forth."
For it is observed that in certain regions, date palms produce the *piṇḍakharjūra* fruit,
and the sting of a scorpion causes death;
yet these do not occur in other regions.

In the same way, those who suspect that smoke might occasionally arise even without fire—thinking it could happen somewhere—do not determine its necessary concomitance with fire even by a hundredth part.
Since the suspicion of its exclusion from the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) obstructs the arising of inference, what kind of valid cognition is this:
"Fire, being free from adventitious conditions (anaupādhika), is invariably concomitant with smoke alone"?
It is not, first of all, perception, because it is exhausted by mere concomitance;
nor is it inference.
Because that [inference] is impossible in the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*),
and because there would be the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) if one were to postulate further and further inferences for the sake of establishing that pervasion;
furthermore, other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have already been refuted previously.
Therefore, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for ascertaining the relationship that is a constituent of inference must be explained;
that is now being explained. First of all, the proponent of the non-existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāvavādin*) must be addressed.
Is it indeed that a cognition whose object is pervasion (vyāpti) does not arise at all, or does it arise as doubtful, or does it arise erroneously?
For invalidity has been analyzed by investigators into three types, since no other possibility exists. First of all, it is not the initial position.
Because the cognition [of pervasion] is not incompatible with practical activity (*vyavahāra*).

For it is frequently observed that one who perceives smoke in relation to fire first ascertains, "This [smoke] is invariably concomitant with this [fire]," and having then inferred the fire from that, engages in corresponding practical activity.
This would not be possible if there were no cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Doubt and error must be eliminated simply by the observation of worldly practice (*vyavahāra*), because such practice is impossible in the presence of those two states;
therefore, there is no lack of validity [in cognition] for the time being.
Validity, however, is divided into six types;
we shall establish each according to its suitability within a particular instance of pervasion-cognition (*vyāpti-saṃvitti*).
For example, first, there is the case of perception regarding the pervasion of smoke by fire.
For it has already been explained that no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are possible here.
Now, it might be argued that since [the universal] is not apprehended at the first sight, the impossibility of perception has also been stated.
For this very reason, it is understood through repeated observation (bhūyodarśana).
But surely those [alternatives] have also been refuted by way of analysis, because neither individually nor collectively are they possible?
True;
it is simply that pervasion is not understood to exist in each [alternative] individually.
Furthermore, the individual perceptions do not coalesce;

rather, it is in the final perception, aided by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding multiple perceptions, that the smoke’s nature as being invariably concomitant with fire shines forth in the mind,
just as the true quality of a jewel appears to one who is examining it.
It is like the reality of sound for one refined by the grammatical tradition;
it is like Brahminhood for one assisted by the recollection of the relationship with mother and father;
it is like clarified butter melted and distinct from oil for one whose sense organ is assisted by taste and smell.
For it is not the case that because all this has not appeared at first glance, it must later appear otherwise;
nor does it establish the status of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Now, was it not said that mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) do not operate elsewhere than in memory?
Or rather, why is it maintained that the mental formations (*saṃskāras*) have a function other than memory?

Indeed, while they are themselves merely causing one to remember the previously understood connection with fire, they act as auxiliaries for the sense organ that is engaged in producing the cognition of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of smoke.
And it has been explained that perception, following upon the contact of the sense organ, persists even when interrupted by intervening acts of memory.
This is because there is a manifestation of direct perception following from the connection with the sense faculties as its result.
Furthermore, that which does not manifest immediately does not lose its status as direct perception when it manifests later,
just as in the case of the Brahmin cited in these very examples.
But has it not been stated that perception arising from a mere first impression (*āpātaja*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding pervasion (*vyāpti*),

and since determinate perception (*savikalpaka*) is preceded by that [indeterminate perception], how can the latter also possess validity? Or rather, is there, in the case of the perception of a Brāhmaṇa and so forth, an appearance of a form distinct from other persons during the state of indeterminate perception, as is seen in the case of elders and others?
By means of which [conceptualization] a subsequent determinate cognition proceeds;
for instance, when one perceives merely the physical form there, but possesses a memory-based connection [to its class], the direct perception "This is a Brāhmaṇa" arises.

Likewise here too, for one who has repeatedly observed fire and smoke, at the final observation there arises a perception whose object is the very nature of smoke— namely, that "this [smoke] is necessarily connected with fire"— characterized by the non-conceptual occurrence of the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of smoke.

This much alone constitutes the state of being preceded by the non-conceptual for one's own conceptualization, namely, that its activity is preceded by the arising of that [non-conceptual perception].
For that [perception] is first sought for the purpose of recollecting the name and so forth;

and since that is accomplished here simply by the perception of the individual (vyakti), due to the awakening of prior latent impressions (saṃskāra), it is not necessary that these two have the same object.

For this very reason, in the case of one who mistakes melted butter (ājya) distinct from oil for oil, thinking "this is oil," [the perception of the butter does not require the same object as the erroneous conceptualization].
The establishment of conceptual perception for a sense faculty assisted by odor [is as follows]:
for in that case, there was no unmixed cognition of the form of ghee.
Because of the error [thinking] "this is oil," immediately thereafter,

by the power of auxiliary conditions, there arises a conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) directed toward the individual entity presented by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*), namely, "this is ghee.
Since it is the same in this case as well, there is no fault.
But what, then, is made an object here by conceptual cognition?
"Niyama" (restriction) means "this [fire] is restricted to this [smoke].
For one who frequently perceives smoke in fire and observes its absence in the absence of fire, there eventually arises a reflection: "Could it be that this [smoke] is pervaded by this [fire]?"

Otherwise, how could it be that [the cognition] disregards the various locations distinguished by differences such as "jāṅgala" and so forth, and the various times distinguished by differences such as "evening" and so forth,

yet pursues fire alone— without regard for the specific conjunction of fuel such as grass, wood, or cow-dung— and does not occur when there is no fire? Furthermore, beyond that, just as fire [is pursued] even while setting aside qualities such as being smokeless or luminous...
Just as heat residing in a potter’s wheel and the like remains constant without abandoning its nature, so too does smoke remain invariably concomitant with fire;
thus, an immediate certainty arises that "there is smoke because of fire.
As for the objection regarding deviation in other locations and so forth—
That [objection] does not even enter as a doubt, because it has never been seen before nor heard of.
Nevertheless, for one who suspects in this way, there would be a lack of confidence in all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since deviation is observed in some cases.

As for the claim that even when the restriction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaniyama*) has been determined, it occurs otherwise in other places and so forth, as in the case of scorpions and the like—[this is not so].
That is not so, because of the distinction between intermediate species (*avāntarajātibheda*).
For that which is understood as necessarily connected with something else, and is uncontradicted, cannot become otherwise.
However, the determination of the effect is brought about by the presence or absence of power due to the distinction between intermediate species; thus, there is no deviation anywhere.
But why is it not accepted as inference itself?
That which is conditioned by adventitious properties (aupādhika) is inconstant,
like fire [is inconstant] with respect to smoke.
And it is not the case that smoke is invariably concomitant with fire without a limiting condition (*anupādhika*).
Let this be so;
however, the lack of a fixed rule (*avyavasthā*) remains present.
In that case, let it be presumption (*arthāpatti*).

It is precisely this—namely, the observation [of smoke] in fire and the non-observation in the absence of fire—which, being otherwise inexplicable, establishes the necessary connection (*niyama*) with fire.
What is it here that is inexplicable?
It is established by this much alone that perception occurs there;
for it is not the case that because something exists in one place, it must not exist elsewhere.
If it is argued that "it is impossible for there to be non-perception of something that exists elsewhere," we say no.
Because it is possible for other distant things not to be seen due to a lack of proximity;
if it is argued that non-perception is impossible in the case of fires that are nearby, [we reply] that it is possible because of their absence—
for in those cases, that [fire] simply does not exist.
How is this to be understood? In that case, if it must not exist elsewhere even though it exists [here], what is the proof for this?

Therefore, it should be established as follows: the direct determination of the intrinsic nature of a thing arises precisely through the sense faculty when it is assisted by both perception and non-perception.
But surely we do not know this very thing:
what kind of nature of the object is being determined?
It has been stated more than once that smoke is invariably concomitant with fire.
This is what is meant: whenever there is smoke, there is fire.
Now, one might object: "Let it be that perception consists only in a connection with a present location and time that is currently present;
but how can there be a connection with the future and so forth?"
For in that case, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). No;
because only the immediately present form is perceived. It is simply the nature of smoke and such things that it is inferred in this manner.
The form of walls and such things appears as if stable;
for in them there exists a manifestation of a form that persists through a period of time, being distinct from [forms] such as lightning.
However, because the proximate intermediate relation is not perceived, that form remains unperceived.
For if that [silver] were not perceptually present, there would be no sublation of the previously experienced silver by the cognition "this is not silver," because the objects would be different.

Indeed, at its own time, the silver was made an object by the prior cognition, and it is not present at the moment of the future sublating cognition; how then could that which was never presented there be sublated?

Even though it is connected with another time, that form—having been determined by the previous cognition—pervades even the time of the future cognition; thus, having attained identity of object, there occurs sublation (*bādha*).
[Objection: But surely, the nature of a thing is understood as independent of anything else, just as heat is the nature of fire.
And since the nature of smoke is not understood by one who has not grasped its relation [to fire], how can it have the nature of a real entity?
Do not say so; for this is indeed a relation.
How can it be determined that the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are not understood?
As he said:
"Now, according to our own view, what is called 'restriction' (*niyama*) is stated to be a relation (*sambandha*)."
Thus,
what is there that is untenable in the fact that this positive necessity of smoke with respect to fire is apprehended through perception?
And how it is that the absence of non-fire is not the [sole] rule has already been explained.

However, by way of the exclusion of the contrary (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*), the investigator explains and demonstrates to others that the restriction (*niyama*) is indeed of a positive nature (*vidhirūpa*), just as one determines the proximity of Rohiṇī upon observing the rising of Kṛttikā.

[Objection: But surely "being restricted" (*niyamyatva*) is also a status of being an object (*karmakārakatva*), and since that is of the nature of a capacity (*śaktirūpa*), how can it be perceived? [Reply: No.
Because it is established as being like the perception of other causal factors;
for even the potencies of other causal factors are not perceived.
Therefore, since the perception of potency does not exist, the causal factor itself must be accepted as perceptible.
In the same way here as well, what is there that is untenable in saying that [the object] will become perceptible once it has been restricted?
Therefore, its status as a perceptible object is established.

Regarding matters derived from scripture, it is understood from the treatise that this specific fruit is pervaded by this specific action, because each respective fruit is associated with its corresponding action to be known through the Veda, and because no connection with another action is perceived;
this is due to the understanding that the result is invariably produced by that specific means.
Furthermore, the nature of space appears like an independent absence in relation to the absence of clouds and the absence of rain;
and what is called the "absence of rain" is simply the state of the earth being dense, hard, pale, and so forth.

And since that form [of the reason] is to be apprehended through direct perception (pratyakṣa) by both parties, that alone is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the pervasion (vyāpti) therein. This should be demonstrated in other cases as well. Let us set this aside for now; we shall explain the rest later. Thus, the nature and the means of valid cognition regarding pervasion have been established.
But this must be considered:
of what is there pervasion by what?
For two specific instances of fire and smoke, known together in one place, are not seen again in another location.

Since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between those two must be apprehended through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) by means of one [of them], the locus of that pervasion must be stated;
therefore, he says: "The universal," etc.
It is true that there is no pervasion between two particulars; rather, it is only between two universal natures that the form of smoke is necessarily concomitant with the form of fire.
Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever.
This [rule], however, is general; for pervasion does indeed sometimes occur even between two particular permanent entities. Thus he says: "In some cases" (kvacit). //12//
Regarding this very point, he provides an example: "The rising of Kṛttikā.
For in that case, having observed the rising of Kṛttikā, the proximity of Rohiṇī is stated as: "Rohiṇī will rise immediately after.
In that inference, there is a pervasion (vyāpti) of a particular [effect] by a particular [cause].
For there is no commonality among them,
because there is a lack of evidence for any difference between the individual instances;
indeed, this very Kṛttikā is recognized as being the same.
"This very one is Rohiṇī;
how could it be another?
Therefore, it is established that the pervasion here exists only between two particulars."
If, then, pervasion (vyāpti) is the basis for inference,

and since such a pervasion indeed exists between the quality of being violence (hiṃsātva) and the quality of being unrighteousness (adharmatva) in the case of external acts of violence, it follows that in the context of a sacrifice as well, unrighteousness is inferred from the quality of being violence.
And in that regard:
And since pervasion is being observed, some property is the effective cause.
"It must exist when this exists" is determined by way of capacity;
others are dependent upon pervasions established by another.
Even when these [faults] are observed, the ascertainment of the pervading factor is not desired;
yet those who confidently employ even such [faulty reasons] for the sake of establishing their thesis— [they are to be censured].

Lest it follow that the killing of the sacrificial animal (*daikṣapaśu*) and similar acts would be unrighteous (*adharma*), he says [in response] with the pair of verses beginning "Because of pervasion" (*vyāpteśca*). The intended meaning is this: when there is a superficial appearance, an error arises; for instance, the misconception that the mere quality of being violence (*hiṃsātva*) is invariably connected with unrighteousness.
But this is not so;
for the nature of violence is pervaded by the fact that it is known as non-dharma (*adharma*),
and no means of knowing that [non-dharma] is possible apart from the scripture (*śāstra*).

Nor is there any scriptural authority stating that the mere fact of being violence is a means to an undesirable end; for specific forms of violence are prescribed by rule, and a prohibition has no scope regarding an object already encompassed by a mandatory injunction.

And because there is no means of knowing that [an action] is a cause of misfortune (anarthasādhanatva) except through a prohibition, one applies the general rule (utsarga) only after setting aside its exceptions (apavāda). Thus, the prohibition "one shall not harm" (na hiṃsyāt) applies to other forms of violence.

And so, although the coexistence of the nature of violence (hiṃsātva) and unrighteousness (adharmatva) has been understood in the case of external acts of violence, [the same does not hold for internal ones].
Nevertheless, being an act of violence (*hiṃsātva*) is not the determinant of its being unrighteous (*adharmatva*);
rather, it is its being prohibited (*niṣiddhatva*).
For even in the absence of violence, the status of being unrighteous is established for drinking liquor and the like solely by virtue of its being prohibited.

Therefore, that very property which is determined in this form— namely, that its existence is possible only when this [other property] exists, meaning it is understood as being pervaded— is called the "probans" (*prayojaka*).
However, properties such as "being violence" (*hiṃsātva*) depend upon a pervasion established by others;

therefore, one cannot determine through them a pervading factor such as "unrighteousness" (*adharmatva*), because sacrificial animal-sacrifices (*daikṣapaśu*) and the like, though involving violence, are prescribed [by scripture] and thus do not possess unrighteousness. //14//
But those who employ such non-conclusive reasons (hetus) as these will wander for a long time due to the easily available defects of counter-reasons (pratihetu) and so forth;
for it is indeed possible to demonstrate a counter-reason.
"The killing of the sacrificial animal is a dharma because it is prescribed, like the Agnihotra and other such rites.
For when a reason is *prayojaka* (essential), defects of this kind find no footing; however, when a reason is *aprayojaka* (non-essential), such defects are easily found.
This is what he says with the words "yetu" (let them go).
"Visrabdham" (confidently) is an adverbial modifier;
the meaning is that they employ [the means] in such a way that confidence arises. //15//
They wander for a long time, easily beset by faults such as counter-arguments and the like;
in those [systems], there is contradiction with scripture and the self-subversion of their own intended goals.
Therefore, those who rely on logic must avoid such worldly disputes;
for it is by way of being prohibited that the unrighteousness of acts of violence is established.
In the absence of that [cause], there is no establishment of that [result], because "being violence" is not a probative reason;
and since falsity in all cognitions is produced by two causes.
The property of being a knower, the property of possessing origination, and so forth,
are not the causal factors [for such status];
rather, the fact that sacrifices and the like cause heaven is established by the three castes.
It was stated that [the opponents] wander due to defects such as counter-reasons (*pratihetu*); he now sets forth those very defects with the words "In these...
First of all, the counter-reason has already been stated by us. Furthermore, for those who speak in this manner, a contradiction with scripture (*āgamavirodha*) necessarily follows.
Since dharma and adharma have scripture alone as their authority, there is in some cases the subversion of what is desired, and in other cases dispute regarding the non-worldly. //16//
He first states the example of contradiction with scripture (āgamavirodha) with the words "by virtue of being prohibited.
This has already been explained by us previously according to the principle of anticipating what follows. //17//
He states an example of a contradiction with what is desired [by the opponent] in the words "hetudvaya" (the two reasons).
For in all cases, the falsity of false cognitions depends upon either a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) or a defect in the cause (*kāraṇadoṣa*);
it does not depend on being a cognition (*jñānatva*) or on arising (*utpattitva*).
It is applied because these two are common to both truth and falsity;
for the Buddhist who seeks to prove its falsity on the grounds of its being a cognition, this reason functions as a *iṣṭavighātakārī* (one that subverts what is intended).
Because the intrinsic natures and specific qualities of both the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin) are also rejected,

and because the earth and other elements well-known to the entire world are denied, it is precisely here that even non-worldly disputes must be demonstrated; for worldly people do not tolerate a dispute such as "all cognitions are false."
For indeed, a sudden agitation arises in those who hear such a dispute,
as in the case of "the moon is not the moon" (*acandraḥ śaśī*) and so forth;
therefore, this is an extraordinary dispute (*alaukika-vivāda*).
And so it has been said:
"In this case, your thesis is certainly sublated by what is well-known to the whole world. //18//
He provides another example of contradiction with scripture (āgama-virodha) in the verse beginning with "traivarṇaka":
indeed, there exist rituals such as the Soma sacrifice, enjoined by such injunctions as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice.
In these [rituals], what...
Perishability is not applied merely by virtue of being human or by being a Śūdra;
rather, perishability is conditioned by factors such as having parts that are produced.
It is not employed with [words] similar to those whose cognition follows immediately after effort.
