When there arises a doubt as to whether the entitlement (*adhikāra*) belongs to the four castes or only to the three excluding the Śūdra, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it belongs to all four.
For all four castes indeed desire heaven, and thus they are designated by the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*).

Since it was initially argued that one who desires heaven is understood here as the qualified candidate (*adhikārin*), it was stated [in response]: "The qualification belongs to those other than Śūdras.
For those sacrifices are to be accomplished through both knowledge (*vidyā*) and fire (*agni*).
The last caste is without fire and without knowledge;

how, then, can he be entitled to perform rituals involving the sacred fires (*vaitānika-karman*)? But surely, by the very force of his entitlement as understood from the meaning of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), the Śūdra’s possession of fire and knowledge will be implied. No.
Because they are not prescribed [for him].

Since the knowledge of the fire-rituals is ordained for one belonging to the three higher castes alone by such injunctions as, "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age," and "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in the spring," it cannot be asserted that these will apply to a Śūdra as well without restriction.

For who, having obtained the connection with the fire of knowledge (*vidyāgni*) through the entitlements established for the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), would venture to prescribe initiation (*upanayana*) or the laying of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*)—which are restricted to specific times—for one of the lowest caste (*jaghanyavarṇa*) when there are scriptural injunctions regarding desires (*kāmaśruti*)?
Therefore, the status of sacrifices and other rites as causes of heaven is conditioned solely by being a member of the three higher castes;
it is not applied to a *śūdra* merely by virtue of his being human.

Now, if someone skilled in inference were to employ [the following argument]: "A sacrifice performed by a Śūdra is a cause for heaven, because it is performed by a human being, like a sacrifice practiced by those of the three higher castes," his [inference] would contradict scripture (*āgama*). But has not a contradiction with scripture already been illustrated?
What, then, is the purpose of that example?
It is said:
previously, the direct contradiction with scripture (*āgama*) regarding the inference of non-dharma (*adharma*) in the case of Vedic injury (*hiṃsā*) was described.

It is clearly understood that the slaughter of the sacrificial animal (*daikṣapaśu*), because it is enjoined by scripture, is a means to a purpose; how then could this be unrighteousness (*adharma*), given that only that which is characterized by a Vedic injunction (*codanā*) as being for a purpose is considered dharma?

In this case, however, the fact that sacrifices and the like performed by a Śūdra are not causes for attaining heaven is not directly refuted by scripture; rather, the distinction is that because the entitlement of the three higher castes is established, the exclusion of others follows by implication. //19//
Now, under the guise of an irrelevant example, he demonstrates other examples for the purpose of censuring the opponent with two verses beginning with "kṛta":

[The opponent] intends that properties such as being produced immediately after effort, being similar to cognition, not persisting, and so forth, which are the objects of those [words], do not entail the perishability of sound;
for that [perishability] is indeed entailed by [the property of] being produced and so on.
Furthermore, it is not possible to establish the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) solely by means of its observation immediately following effort,
because of the deviation [of the reason] from space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.
If, then, perishability is necessitated by the state of having parts (*sāvayavatva*), [then...]
Being born, possessing a sense faculty, and so forth, are bound solely by the existence of a real entity.
Who that is not a logician would fail to speak for the sake of establishing the impermanence of sound?
Therefore, whatever meaning is observed by someone through the power of the means of proof, [that is what he intends].
Only that [reason] is indicative of it, and not even one accompanied by a logical consequence;
furthermore, in this context, the subject (dharmin) is also "possessing a part" because it is grasped by means of two parts.
Are the worlds and the structures of the worlds— such as the earth, mountains, oceans, and so forth— now impermanent? Truly,
everything that possesses parts is subject to the nature of destruction.
Even the earth, mountains, and so forth, having attained the specific conjunctions and disjunctions of their own parts, certainly perish part by part;
however, we do not admit the destruction of anything that is without residue (*niranvaya*).
In this way, the destruction of the great earth itself should be demonstrated through the process of addition, subtraction, and differentiation.
Likewise, that which has been inferred by the Vaiśeṣikas— the non-eternality of sound on the grounds of its possessing a genus (jāti) and its being perceptible by the senses—
is also incorrect;
for this possession of a genus and so forth is based merely on the existence of a real entity and is common to both eternal and non-eternal things.
By this, impermanence is not being established. What is meant by "based solely on that which exists as a real entity"?
It is said to mean "based on that which exists in the ultimate sense."
Objects such as a jar, space, and the self are indeed ultimately real,
being the objects of the senses and possessing genus,
unlike things such as a hare's horn which are known through delusion. //21//
Thus, he concludes the statement that what is not a causal factor (aprayojaka) is not a prover (asādhaka): "Therefore" (tasmāt).

The meaning is this: whatever object, such as "being prohibited" (niṣiddhatva), is understood to possess the capacity for proving a property such as "non-dharma-ness" (adharmatva); that is to say, it is determined by such a capacity as "when this [reason] exists, this [property] must necessarily exist."

For the power of the object to be regulated is indeed designated as the power of the means; for it is only when the [object] is known with certainty that one is able to [lead to] the regulator, and not otherwise. (He) [says].
Only that which is restricted [to the subject] is a signifier, not "the state of being violence" (*hiṃsātva*) when it is accompanied by a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*).

For since "the state of being unrighteousness" (*adharmatva*), which is set out to be connected [with the subject] by virtue of its being prohibited, follows as a consequence, the "state of being violence" is also connected by that consequence; thus, the "state of being violence" accompanied by a consequence does not become a signifier of "the state of being unrighteousness.
In this way, the category of "relation" (*sambandha*), which constitutes a limb of inference in every respect, has been explained.
Now, it must be explained that cognition regarding another part [of an object] arises from the perception of one part.
In this regard, the following must first be stated:
it would follow that inference is the knowledge of another part occurring in such a manner based on the perception of an independent single part.
That is incorrect;
for that is memory— how could it be inference?
Furthermore, since smoke and the like do not possess a single nature in relation to their distinct aspects, they cannot occupy a single location;
thus, this very entity, being of a dual nature, must be either the object to be known or the means of knowledge itself.
It is claimed that the object of inference consisting in a single substratum (ekadeśin) distinguished by another part [of itself] is the seeing of one part;
but that is not so,
because it has not been established.
For here, the "partial proponent" (ekadeśin) is not expressed by any word;
therefore, suspecting that the definition is deficient because of this non-expression, he says: "is expressed.

Although the partial proponent is not expressed by his own specific term, nevertheless, he is implied by the force of the meaning through the two words "part" (ekadeśa); thus, there is no fault of deficiency. //23//
He states the reason for the implication of the meaning: "not for the sake of another" (*aparārtha*).
For the mere nature of smoke and so forth does not become the locus of the term "one part" (*ekadeśa*) when it is intended for another;
nor is the expression "one part" tenable through mutual dependence.
For no one has the cognition that "smoke is a part of fire.
Nor can smoke be understood as being a part of fire if the fire itself is not apprehended;
and once that [fire] is apprehended, there is no longer anything left to be inferred.
Therefore, it is established that because the existence of a "single part" (ekadeśa) is untenable, some single entity as its substratum must be understood. //23//
Surely, by means of the two terms "one part" (*ekadeśa*), the possessor of the parts (*ekadeśin*) may be implied;
however, from what is that unity [of the whole] understood? For this reason, one might not have an inference of the possessor of the parts upon seeing smoke in only one particular place.
However, co-occurrence in a single substratum (*aikādhikaraṇya*) between two parts is not established because [the whole] is not being mentioned; therefore, he says: "that very same.
By "that very same," he refers back to the previously mentioned possessor of parts (*ekadeśin*), intending it to have a singular number.
Indeed, that very single entity is of the nature of both the cognized and the cognizer, because it possesses a dual nature;
for it has those two selves which are about to be described, by virtue of which it is capable of having a twofold form.
But has it not been stated that unity is not obtained when the "one part" (ekadeśin) is not explicitly mentioned? No;

for it is included by the very use of the singular number in the phrase "of one who knows the relationship" (jñātasambandhasya). For in the case of the "one part," the referent of the other word (anyapadārtha) [is indeed singular].
The state of being a part (*ekadeśatva*) is expressed by a single word;

likewise, even in the case of the locus of the cognizer (*pramātṛpakṣa*), when the locus (*ekadeśin*) is implied by the word "part" uttered first, that very same [locus]— revolving in the mind— is understood as the substratum at the moment of requiring a second [part],
and not anything else.
Because there is no reason to abandon that [notion],
and because such linguistic usage is observed;
just as when Devadatta has a bracelet on one hand and a ring on another hand, the two hands are not understood to be distinct substrata.
Nevertheless, Devadatta is indeed one and the same;
therefore, it is established that the single entity itself possesses the dual form of both the mover and the moved. //24//
The unestablished part is that which is to be understood; the established part is the means of understanding.
It is taken by speakers as either distinct or non-distinct, according to their intention.

Since that which is produced is impermanent, as in the case of "that which possesses smoke possesses fire," the selection of the subject (*dharmī*) is non-different [from the property], whereas the distinction here is such that "fire" is the predicate.
It has been stated that [the reason] is both the object to be understood and the means of understanding.
He demonstrates those two aspects of being "both" with the words: "by the unestablished," etc.
For if it were established only for one party (the proponent), it would be established.
Or rather, in that case, it does not possess a dual nature.

However, because it is established by perception in its form as smoke and so forth, yet unestablished in its form as possessing fire and so forth, it possesses a dual essence; thus, both [theories] are tenable.
He says: "Let it be that one part is included by implication."

And that [inference] is both the object to be known (*gamya*) and the means of knowing (*gamaka*). However, how it is to be apprehended by cognizers has not been stated by the author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakāra*) in any manner whatsoever.
Since there might again be the charge of deficiency [in the definition], he says: "ātta" (taken up).
In that case, indeed, the mention of a specific [quality] is resorted to where there is an intention to express a particularity.
No specific distinction is intended here.
For that [part] may be presented by the two terms "one part" (*ekadeśa*) either as distinct or non-distinct, depending on the intention of the proponent (*ekadeśin*);
this is because the practice of inference is seen to occur in both ways. //25//
He demonstrates that very same twofold conventional usage with the words "impermanent," etc. The text is explained by its own reading. //26//
It has been shown that the object of cognition and the means of cognition are apprehended through both difference and non-difference.
However, a doubt arises as to how far the operation of inference extends;
for even when there is the cognition of a qualified object, a means of knowledge may terminate in the qualifier alone.
Just as with the word "cow":

it indeed produces a cognition of an individual qualified by its form, yet through the methods of agreement and difference (anvaya-vyatireka), it is determined that the word's denotation culminates in the form alone.

Therefore, here too, if it is maintained that the means of valid cognition terminates in the qualifier alone, just as in that previous case, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*).
For at the time of knowing the relation, fire in its mere generality is indeed already established.
What, then, is the use of inference?
If, however, it is maintained that inference has as its object only that which is qualified— just like words such as "two-piece-stick-holder" (dvikhaṇḍa-daṇḍin) and the like—
then [inference cannot occur] because of the absence of the apprehension of a relation (*sambandha*) therein.
[The reason] possesses the property of being the object of inference (*numeyatva*).
For smoke is not observed to be invariably concomitant with a specific fire-possessor such as a mountain (*parvata*),
nor is it common to all fire-possessors.
And it is the subject (dharmin) itself, as qualified by one part [of its properties], that is inferred here;
for without dependence on that [subject], the status of being an object of inference is not possible.
Neither the property alone, nor likewise the subject, nor both—
whether separate or combined— is inferred independently, because they are already established.
The status of being a logical mark (liṅga) belongs to a single part, and its concomitance with the probandum (sādhya) would likewise belong to that same part;
thus, these two [requirements] would not exist as intended in these various positions, respectively.
There exists some kind of universal;
even if that were the case, it would still result in proving what is already established.
For this very reason, they say:
“In this mire of the members of inference, the elephants of the disputants are submerged:
there is a lack of positive concomitance (anugama) in the particular, while in the universal there is the proving of what is already established.”
To this he says: "In one part," etc.
The intention is as follows: inference has only a qualified object as its domain, just like words such as "staff-bearer" (daṇḍin) and the like;
nor is there an absence of the apprehension of the relationship [between the sign and the signified].
We have stated that this occurs because, by abandoning all specific adjuncts (*upādhi*), one understands the connection of mere "smoke-possessing" with "fire-possessing.
Even in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*), the relationship of infinite entities is indeed grasped through some single adjunct.
Although it is understood in a general sense that "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire," [the specific relation is established through a particular condition].

Nevertheless, it has already been stated that its status as an object of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is established because of recognition (pratyabhijñāna) in a specific form, such as "this is that very same [thing].
Why, then, is it not accepted that the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) terminates solely in the qualifier?
To this he says: "For not... (na hi) //27//
He demonstrates the impossibility [of such an inference] with the words "not the property" (*na dharma*).
For you yourself have stated that at the time of grasping the relation, it is merely the property (*dharmamātra*) that is established.

In the same way, one should demonstrate the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) in the case of an inference of the locus alone (*dharmimātra*), or in an independent inference of both [property and locus]; thus he says: "likewise" (*tathā*). //28//

He states further refutations, corresponding respectively to the three cases where the property, the substratum, or both are the objects of inference, beginning with the words "of a single part" (ekadeśasya). //29//
Dharmas such as impermanence and so forth are not [identical to] properties such as being unproduced;
nor is there a concomitance of these with sound, nor a concomitance of both with both.
Furthermore, because there is no basis for it, neither a genitive relation nor even a sixth case-ending is found in the cognition [of the name];
nor is the concomitance of the logical mark (liṅga) with that [name] demonstrated here.
He explains this very point: "impermanence and so forth.

For a logical mark (liṅga) must be a property of one part of the subject (pakṣaikadeśa). Now, since the property called impermanence has been made the independent subject, how can "being produced" (kṛtakatva)—which is a property [of that subject]—be a logical mark that is not a property of the subject? It could not be.

Thus, even in the case of sound alone as an independent [subject], the restriction that "sound" occurs here and there cannot be established by the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*). Likewise, there is no connection between the two—consisting of the nature of sound and non-eternality—and the two [reasons] consisting of the presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and positive concomitance (*anugama*). Therefore, one must explain the word "connection" (*sambandha*), which appears later, by connecting it with the preceding and following terms through a distributive construction (*tantra*).

Thus it has been established that the property to be proven (*sādhya*) does not reside in the property (*dharma*), the substratum (*dharmin*), or both, whether taken individually or collectively. //30//

Now, why is it that the relationship between the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*) alone does not constitute the probandum? To this he says: "The relationship. He indicates that the statement of proof (*sādhana-vākya*) is limited [to the probandum]. Indeed, in the statement of proof, an investigator does not employ a relationship expressed by some name denoting a connection, nor by a genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*).
For one does not employ the reasoning in this way:
"There is a connection between fire and the mountain because of the presence of smoke," nor does one say, "The fire belongs to the mountain."
Rather, people are seen inferring a specific location itself as qualified by fire and so forth;
when they formulate it thus: "The mountain possesses fire."
The relationship is also not inferred as being "with the past"; thus,
it is not only not included in the proposition (*pratijñā*),
but in the example (*udāharaṇa*) as well, the concomitance of the logical mark (*liṅga*) with that [past] is not indicated.
For there is no perception [of the form] "wherever there is smoke, there is a connection with fire";
rather, there is the perception "whatever possesses smoke, that possesses fire," where the location itself serves as the illustration.
He says this very thing with the words "nor even" (*na cāpi*).
The word "here" (*iha*) refers back to the cognition (*miti*).

What is meant is this: in a statement of proof (*sādhanavākya*), the relation is not presented as the probandum (*sādhya*), nor is it indicated as an example (*dṛṣṭānta*); furthermore, it is not proper for investigators to state something that does not accord with how it appears [in cognition].
Nor can it have two aspects that function as the probandum and the probans;
therefore, because the meaning of the possessive suffix (*matup*) is already grasped by the object itself, it is to be understood [by implication].
It should not be considered independently, as in the case of words such as "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*);
when there is the cognition of a qualified object, the relationship [between the qualifier and the qualified] is necessarily implied.
Moreover, when this relation is being established, is it established as mere existence (*sanmātra*), or as qualified by some particular property (*dharma*)?
First of all, the mere existence of a thing is not the object of inference.
Furthermore, a relation does not possess two forms— one established and one to be established— such as those found in a mountain and so forth,
by virtue of which it could become the object of inference.
Therefore, he states "nor" (na ca) to show that a relation can in no way be the probandum (*sādhya*).
In the case of a relation that is already established, it is impossible to prove [the subject] as being qualified by that [relation].
There is no such possibility wherein a mountain, while not itself being related to fire, could become qualified by it; therefore, he says "therefore" (tasmāt) up to the end of the passage.
[Objection: It is true that if there were no relation, there could be no qualified [subject];
however, this much does not establish that the relation itself is what is to be proven (*sādhya*).

Rather, the fact that the relation—the sense of the possessive suffix (*matup*)—is to be proven is grasped through the force of the meaning (*arthagṛhīta*), because the establishment of the qualified subject would otherwise be impossible; it is not, however, [proven] as something independent.
Right here he provides an illustration, beginning with "just as":
for words such as "staff-bearer" (daṇḍin), while denoting the person qualified by the staff and so forth, imply the relationship through the force of the meaning, but they do not denote it directly.

Similarly here as well, when the object "the mountain possesses fire" is being established, the connection with fire is already grasped through the meaning [of the inference], and it is not that very same connection which is being established anew.
Just as when a qualified object is cognized from words such as "staff-bearer," the connection [between the staff and the bearer] becomes an invariable concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*).
Thus, here too, the meaning is that when the qualified [object] is being established, [the property] follows as a byproduct.
However, this must be considered:
how is it that words such as "staff-bearer" (daṇḍin) denote the qualified [object]?
The suffixes expressing possession (*matvarthīya*) are taught in the sense of "beneficial" (*hita*).
Furthermore, that [suffix] is traditionally recorded in the context of a relationship as meaning "this belongs to him" or "it exists in this";
therefore, in this case, the meaning of the suffix is precisely the relationship itself.
And that [suffix] is the principal [element], because of the traditional rule (smṛti): "The base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together, with the suffix being predominant.
For this statement is intended to demonstrate predominance precisely when both [the base and the suffix] denote their meanings separately.
Furthermore, the primary meaning is the word-meaning itself;
therefore, it is logical that words such as "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) are indeed expressions of a relationship.
Moreover, since it is said that "no cognition of a qualified object arises without the qualifier being apprehended," it is necessarily the case when one intends to express a qualified entity.

First of all, the expression of the qualifier must occur; since the comprehension of the qualified object is established from that very [expression], it is not possible to assume that the word has the power to denote [the qualified] until then.
For this very reason, the theory that the individual qualified by the form (ākṛti) is denoted will be refuted in the Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa.

Furthermore, the traditional authority states: "In the case of primary derivatives (kṛt), secondary derivatives (taddhita), and compounds, there is the expression of a relation by means of the suffixes -tva and -tal."

And how is the relationship expressed by those two in a secondary derivative formation (*taddhita-vṛtti*)? If it were not something to be denoted by the secondary suffix, then there would be no recollection of those two when the denotable object is extracted.
"For when a word is applied to a substance because of the presence of a certain quality, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used to denote that [quality]. Therefore,
if the relation between the staff and the person is the denotation of the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*), [then the suffix would denote that relation].
That being the case, when that [relation] is extracted, the grammatical rule for the suffixes *tva* and *tal*—namely, *daṇḍitvam* and *daṇḍiteti*—is justified.

Just as the universal denoted by the word "cow" is extracted by the suffix *tva* as "cowness" (*gotvam*), it follows that the relation alone is what is denoted by words such as "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*). Therefore, how can it now be said that the relation is merely "inseparable" (*nāntarīyaka*)?
To this it is replied: First of all, it is not possible to determine that the relationship [between word and meaning] is denotable by following the *Smṛti* (Pāṇinian grammar).
For the rule "tadasyāstyasmin" (Pāṇini 5.2.94) is merely an instruction regarding words (*śabdānuśāsana*), and not an instruction regarding meanings (*arthānuśāsana*).
Moreover, the relationship between the subordinate and the principal is seen to vary according to whether it is a compound (*vṛtti*) or an analytical expansion (*vigraha*).
For example, in the compound *citragu* ("one who has brindled cows"), Devadatta or another person qualified by the brindled cows is understood as the principal element in the compound;
however, in the analytical expansion "those whose cows are brindled" (*citragāvo yasya*), the cows themselves are the principal element.
Devadatta and others are subordinate as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), while those [sacrifices] are the primary elements (*pradhāna*).
This is also seen in the Veda: "The Soma sacrifice has the *Rathantara* as its *Sāman*."

Therefore, although the author of the *Smṛti* has indicated [the compound] by means of the genitive case in the analysis (*vigraha*) as "that of this" (*tasyeda*), thereby making the relationship the predominant factor,
nevertheless, in a secondary derivative formation (*taddhitavṛtti*) such as *gomat*, it is the possessor of that very thing (*tadvān*) who becomes the predominant element.
Likewise, when it is understood:
for the word "cow-herd" (gomaccha) appears as having the person as its primary referent, not the relationship as its primary referent.
Even for the Blessed One Pāṇini, it was intended to establish that the denotation is indeed qualified by means of expressing the relationship.
When the compound is being analyzed (*vigṛhyamāṇā*), the use of the genitive case is indeed unavoidable;
and because the meaning of that [genitive] is indicated as the primary thing to be expressed (*vācya*), an illusion arises.
Therefore, the relation is not the expressed meaning according to the traditional grammatical rule (*smṛti*).
As for the claim that the qualifier must be denoted first:
this is true;
however, in this context, the relation is not the qualifier.
For the staff is a qualifier of the staff-bearer, not a relation;
and that [staff] is already expressed primarily by the base form itself.
For this very reason, there is no fault of postulating multiple denotative powers.
For in the case of indivisible words such as "cow" (*go*) and the like, even though a qualified cognition arises, it is logical that only the qualifier is denoted;
for in that case, the fault of postulating two denotative powers for a single word would indeed occur.
Words such as *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer), however, possess constituent parts;
within them, there exist two distinct elements— arising from the distinct base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*)— which have attained the relationship of qualifier and qualified.
However, some maintain that the relationship of subordinate and principal (aṅgāṅgibhāva) between the two is optional.
In every respect, the property of the subject is understood by means of another property;
yet, in the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified, no distinction is perceived.
What is untenable about the qualified object being denoted?
Therefore, the person qualified by the staff—which is denoted by the base [of the word *daṇḍa*] and understood even earlier—is denoted by the word *daṇḍin*.
But surely, in the absence of a relation, the staff is not even able to qualify the man.
True;
however, by this much alone, the relation does not become denotable.
For it is not reasonable to assert that because cows not standing on the earth do not qualify their possessor, the earth itself must therefore be denoted.
Precisely because a specific cognition is untenable in the absence of a relation,
the relation itself is included by implication;
however, it is not directly denoted.
As for the argument that the grammatical rule prescribing the suffixes -tva and -tal would be untenable if a relation were not denotable, that is incorrect;
for the rule prescribing the abstract suffixes in words such as *gomattva* is not intended to extract the specific denotation [of the relation].

Nevertheless, while the rule *yasya guṇasya hi bhāvāt* serves to extract the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*), the present recollection is for the very purpose of not extracting the expressed meaning. Otherwise, since the matter would already be covered by that [previous rule], the statement *kṛttaddhitasamāseṣu* would become unnecessary.

Therefore, when one related element (*sambandhin*) qualified by a single cause has been previously perceived, and the other related element is subsequently expressed, the relationship is grasped through the sense-meaning (*arthagṛhīta*) and is not relegated to the category of the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*).
This same direction should also be shown for all derivative (yaugika) words;
and it has been said:
"In every case, by means of derivative words, only the substance (dravya) is denoted."
For it is not possible for the relation itself to be the expressed meaning, because that would entail excessive complexity.

Thus, since no other object of inference is possible, it follows that the property (dharma) and the property-bearer (dharmin), standing in the relation of qualifier and qualified, are precisely what are to be understood through inference. //32-33//

He summarizes [the argument] with the passage ending in "viśeṣaṇeti gamyau. Furthermore, this relationship of subordinate and principal (aṅgāṅgibhāva) has been accepted by some as being optional; for they think as follows:

For in every respect, if a mere phenomenon (*dharma*) or a phenomenon as a self-sufficient substratum (*dharmin*) were being cognized independently, faults such as proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) would arise; however, this is not the case when there is a cognition of something qualified (*viśiṣṭa*).
As for the state of being qualified, let it belong to whatever thing, in whatever way, according to one's intention—it does not cause any defect whatsoever.
In every respect, first of all, the property (dharma) such as fire belonging to a subject (dharmin) such as a mountain must be understood through that very property, such as smoke.
Regarding whether that property is the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) or the qualified (viśeṣya), others here offer this answer: if the subject is the qualifier...
The connection with the causal factor is unclear because of its lack of predominance.
For because of its primacy, the connection with the property (dharma) arises from the sentence;
since that is impossible there, it must subsequently be inferred in relation to the property-bearer (dharmin).

There is no distinction [to be made] as to whether it must be understood [in one way or another], because in either case there is an absence of independent inference (*svatantrānumāna*). Thus he says: "The word *aṅga* is determined by the end [of the sentence]. (34–35)
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "In this regard" (*atra*).

The intention is as follows: indeed, even by the authors of definitions (*lakṣaṇakāra*), worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be followed exactly as they are found in the world; they must not be treated contrarily.

For people do not understand that "fire is qualified by the mountain," but rather that "the mountain possesses fire. Likewise, when ordinary people, having themselves understood an object through inference, seek to communicate that very same object to another, they are seen to employ a reason (hetu) that is indeed qualified by the locus (dharmin).
Just as in the inference of fire, "this [place] possesses fire because it possesses smoke," that same [inference] is not tenable when fire is being inferred as qualified by a location.

For when fire qualified by a mountain is taken as the subject (*dharmin*) by virtue of its being a qualification, the connection of that [subject] with the property of the reason— "because of possessing smoke"— is not clearly manifested.
The status of being a logical reason belongs to that which is understood as possessing both the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*).
Furthermore, a substratum that has been subordinated as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*) cannot admit of a connection with the property of the reason,
because subordinate factors are not connected with one another.

Therefore, from this very specific application of the reason for the sake of others, it is inferred that worldly people themselves also understand the subject as qualified by the property, and not otherwise. // 36 //

If, then, the connection between the subject (*dharmī*) and the property of the reason (*hetudharma*) is not clear, by what [connection] would it follow? To this he says: "Because of its primacy" (*pradhānatvāt*). When it is stated that "impermanence as qualified by sound [is proven] because of being produced," the reason such as "being produced" would be connected with the property called impermanence alone—which, as the probandum (*sādhya*), is primary—and not with sound, which is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*).
For it is logical that everything contained within a single sentence should be connected only with the primary subject;
and when there is a connection with the primary subject, the reason lacks the property of being a characteristic of the locus (*apakṣadharmatva*).
Indeed, "the state of being produced" [is not a property of the subject].

Alternatively, according to the view of Anavaya, it is not a fault for a property that has been presented as a distinction to function as a subordinate element (guṇabhāva) within the manifestation of the suggested meaning (dhvani).
Eternality is not a property [of the word];
rather, it belongs to the sound.
Therefore, it is the substratum itself, as qualified by its property, that is apprehended by the cognizers themselves.
Thus, it is logical that [the reason] is presented for the sake of another.
However, if it is argued: "It is true that, primarily, the connection of the reason with the property (*dharma*) is understood from the sentence," [we reply:]
However, by virtue of the superior strength of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), the sentence will be sublated, and a connection with the subject (*dharmin*) alone will be postulated.
For it is the property of the reason (*hetudharma*) that is capable of being connected with the subject, not with [another] property;
therefore, due to the absence of a connection with a property, the connection will be with the subject alone. To this, he says: "In that case" (*tatra*).
This is the intended meaning: it is true that the connection with the property (*dharma*) is established in this way;
however, this very thing—that there is a disruption of the natural flow of the sentence—is itself a flaw.
For this reason, he says: "That [connection] must be postulated."
The fault lies solely in the conceptualization of something as being other than it is for one who has apprehended it otherwise; thus there is no contradiction. //37//
Alternatively, the reason (*hetu*) should be qualified by the inclusion of the subject (*dharmin*), as in "because sound is non-artificial" (*dhvaneḥ akṛtakatvāt*).
However, with the intention that one does not observe practitioners formulating the argument in this way, [the author] says: "of sound" (*dhvaneḥ*).

As for the one who argues that even when the subject is qualified, at the time of demonstrating the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), when it is stated, "wherever there is artificiality... [the following applies].

To refute the objection that "only the sound (dhvani) should be connected as the primary element, and not impermanence (anityatva), because the latter is subordinate," he says: "of the positive concomitance" (anvayasya).

For at the time of demonstrating positive concomitance, one indeed adopts the property (dharma) as distinct [from the subject]; namely, "wherever there is the state of being produced (kṛtakatva), there is impermanence. In that case, there is no suspicion of a connection with the primary element [as the subject].

Therefore, since the subordinate status of the quality (guṇabhāva) existed when the subject qualified by its property was being established during the stage of the thesis (*pratijñāvasthā*), that [status] does not become defective in the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭāntavākya*).
However, it has been stated that logicians employ the reason (*hetu*) as something unqualified;
thus, when it is employed without qualification, there arises the suspicion of a connection with the primary property (*pradhānabhūtadharma*).
As for the one who says that impermanence is qualified by the word ending in the genitive case— as in "the impermanence of sound"— in this way,
the connection of the term "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*) with "sound" itself, whose case-ending remains unchanged, becomes clear; otherwise,
the connection with the property (*dharma*) would only occur through a corresponding modification of the case-ending.
And since that [position] is unjust, it must be refuted;
this very position has already been rejected by the author of the Vārttika himself:
"The relation [between word and meaning] is not established either by the name [of the object] because it is not mentioned, nor even by the genitive case-ending in the cognition."
Thus,
for if there were an indication by the genitive case, the relation itself would be the probandum;
and its status as a probandum has already been refuted.
Abiding precisely within the subject (*pakṣa*) as qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhya*), the property (*dharma*) is now characterized by its relation to the locus (*dharmī*).
This is not the definition of the subject (*pakṣa*) itself; rather, its qualification by the location would be of this nature: "The fire is qualified by a specific place. (Msv 5.4.39)
That fire exists somewhere in a certain place where it has been seen,
or it is the fire previously experienced, conjoined with the mere location.
Either that fire is conjoined with this [pillar], or else that which was seen by him is [conjoined with it];
or this [fire] is conjoined with this [pillar] merely by way of location, or even this [pillar] is conjoined with the former [fire].
Or, if it is this fire here that is qualified by a specific location,
then in the former cases there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established, while in the latter cases there would be contradiction.
Pervasion by this [single] location is not possible for all fires;
nor does this fire qualify [itself] with respect to all [locations]. (Msv 5.4.43)
It is refuted.
Why is the point that the relationship is to be established being proposed again here?
Enough of this talk like that of a child! //38//

Moreover, he states "of fire" (*agner*) because if it were being proved that fire is qualified by a location, there would be an impossibility of all the types of subjects (*pakṣa*) that will be mentioned later. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to conjoin this with other refutations. The word "this" (*etat*) is a reference back to the definition that is about to be stated.
He makes a concise promise to state those very types of positions. //38//
Now he shows those very [alternatives] by dividing them, ending with the words "the fire which...
This passage is explained by its own reading (*nigadavyākhyāta*). However, the distinction between the positions is understood by those who have applied their minds [to the matter].
Furthermore, in the first two positions, there is the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
For fire is indeed established in some place;
even if it has been previously perceived as residing in a former location, it remains established—so what is the point of establishing it again?

Regarding the other five positions, however, he states that there is a contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntaravirodha*) in the words "But here... (*iha tu*). The fact that [the argument] proves what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) is indeed very clear. //40–42//
He elaborates on the contradiction: "Pervasion" (*vyāpti*).
First of all, that which was stated—that whatever is fire is conjoined with this [place]—is incorrect.
For not all fires are pervaded by this place, because the place is not all-encompassing (*avaibhava*) and because all fires are not present here.
For its existence is indeed contradicted here by non-existence. //42//
Nor can it be specified by its location, for how could it be said that "this [object] is distinguished by this particular location"? (MSV 5.4.44)
When fire is independent of location and is not determined as "this," then in this case,
the location itself is determined prior to the fire.
Furthermore, at the time of that cognition, "the mountain" would not be a qualifier for the fire;
for the nature of the mountain and such things exists independently of the fire.
He refutes what was stated [in the verse], "that which has been seen by him, or else [that which is seen] by this [person]," with the words "nor even by the former.
The meaning is that even for fire that has been seen, there is no pervasion (vyāpti) by this particular place.
Regarding the statement "this [fire] by the mere place," he states the refutation with the words beginning with "nor even" and ending with "by places."
For this fire standing before one is not qualified by all locations, because it is absent everywhere [simultaneously].
Regarding the phrase "or by the eastern [direction]," he states the contradiction: "by the eastern.
There is simply no qualification of this fire by the eastern location.
Because the eastern region does not exist here, and this [fire] exists there; furthermore,

the connection of previously experienced fire with mere space has already been refuted— by the same logic— as being equivalent to the refutation of the fire standing before one having a connection with all places, and thus it is not mentioned separately.
"Corrupted," thus [it is said]. //43//
Thus, when seven positions have been refuted, the eighth position remains: namely, that this fire is qualified by this particular location. He refutes that with the word "this" (*etad*).
One must state how this fire standing before one is established as being qualified by this location.
Since it is only that which exists at its own time and place that can be made an object of memory, how can this [fire] be qualified by this location?

Thus, one who speaks in this manner has not even considered that [the cognition] belongs to the previous [moment]. Furthermore, even in the case of an uninterrupted memory, it is not established by logic that a property (*dharma*) is a qualifier of its substratum (*dharmin*), because properties are always perceived only as qualifiers of the substratum; therefore, enough of this.
However, with the intention that it is the location (*deśa*) itself, already previously apprehended, that ought to be the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), he says: "of the fire" (*agner iti*). //44-45//
Furthermore, if fire were the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), then this would be its very first moment of cognition,
because a well-known thing is qualified by something unknown;
however, in this case, the mountain itself is cognized first.
He asks: how does this become a qualification of the fire that is to be brought back later? He says: "by the knowledge of that.
He points to the fire by means of its non-occurrence [at that time].
For at the time of knowing the fire, that very place is already perceived.
Since fire is not [previously] grasped, for what would the subsequent cognition of fire as qualified [by its locus] not be faulty?
Therefore, it must be that the substratum (dharmin) as qualified by its property (dharma) is the object of knowledge (prameya).

Is it not the case that a qualification, such as "fire-endowed" in the case of smoke or other things imagined by others, would be cognizable through a logical mark (*liṅga*) just like the word itself? Msv 5.4.48.
It is not so; for in this case, there is no assumption of multiple powers in the logical mark (liṅga), nor is it the object of inference, and the qualificand has already been ascertained.
The location serves as a qualifier;
for an object already cognized is sought to be cognized through an un-cognized property, such as "What kind of property does this possess?
In that case, it is that very location which is what is to be cognized.
And it is cognized [as fire], but not as "fire" [in itself].
Now, one might object: "Since the location too is indeed apprehended through perception, how can it become the object of inference? To this, he says: "Of the location..."

For in perception, only the locus (deśa) in its own nature is apprehended, whereas by inference, its being qualified by fire and so forth is inferred; thus, there is no grasping of what has already been grasped.
Therefore, he says "tasmāt" [therefore], meaning that the object of cognition (prameya) is the locus itself as qualified by its property, not the property as qualified by the locus. //46-47//
And thus, it is the location itself as qualified by fire that remains the object of cognition;
for that [location] is the locus (dharmin), since fire has it as its substratum.
But fire is not [the object], because the location does not have that as its substrate; thus he says: "That [inherence] belongs to the location.
Others, however, consider even previously perceived smoke—when qualified by fire—to be the object of inference (*prameya*).
With the intention that this too is indeed correct, he says: "And by others, [it is] imagined as smoke.
The connection is with the word "that" (sā), meaning "that is the object of knowledge" (*prameyatā*). Here, he raises an objection: "But surely... (*nanu*).
It has been stated that the object of inference is the qualified [entity].

According to the maxim that "that which has not grasped the qualifier [cannot grasp the qualified]," it is logical that the inferential mark (liṅga) also, like the word, should terminate in the qualifier alone.
For it will be explained in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* that a word indeed functions only with respect to the qualifier. //48//
He refutes [the objection] with "not so.
He states the reason: "for not...
Indeed, it is because of the fear of postulating multiple powers that it is desired that the word's function terminates in the qualifier alone.
The logical mark (liṅga), however, by the force of a previously apprehended invariable concomitance (pratibandha), brings about the cognition of that which is so conjoined.

Since it is understood that the state of possessing smoke is conjoined only to such an extent as the state of possessing fire is conjoined, it leads to the inference of fire itself; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

Furthermore, with the intention of stating that it has already been said that the mere qualifier cannot be the object of inference because it would involve proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatva), he says:
And because it is not known as being qualified, that [fire] alone is the object of inference.
But if smoke were the qualificand, would the reason not then reside in only a part of the subject?

This is not so; for when a specific [property] is to be proven by means of a general reason, there is the assumption of the validity of the smoke, its cognition, the recollection of their relationship, and the [resulting] inference. (Msv 5.4.51)
The identity of the object with its result was previously stated to be due to the operation of that [cognition];
however, the author of the Bhāṣya considers the cognition of the object of knowledge (prameya-dhī) itself to be the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

He says "the qualificand" (viśeṣya) [in verse 49], meaning that even the qualificand—such as a mountain and so forth—is not the object of inference, since it has already been determined in its own specific form.
Therefore, because it is known only in its qualified form, that very [qualified object] is what is to be inferred; thus he says: "by way of being qualified.
Here, an objection is raised: "But surely... It has been stated that even smoke is inferred as qualified by fire.
That is incorrect because it is a part of the very meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*).
He refutes this, saying: "This is not so."

For smoke consists of both the universal and the particular; therein, that which has been made the subject (*pakṣa*) by way of its particular nature possesses the status of a reason (*hetu*) by way of its universal nature, and thus it is not a mere part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśa*).
Thus much has been established: that the object of inference is indeed the qualified [particular].
It is not known what its own nature (svarūpa) actually is.

If, therefore, smoke, the cognition thereof, and so forth, are intended to be the inference itself, then there would be a difference in the object between the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and its result (phala); and that is untenable.

For this very reason, the Bhikṣu (Dharmakīrti), having stated that in perception cognition alone takes the form of both the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*), extended that same principle to inference as well by saying, "its result is as before" (*pūrvavat phalam asya*).
If, however, the cognition of the object to be inferred were itself intended to be the means of knowledge, then there would likewise be no result distinct from it.
Therefore, the nature of inference must be stated; thus he says: "From smoke and the cognition thereof... (*dhūmatajjñāna...*).

As for the claim that the result is indeed the result of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because they share a single object, which [the opponent] has relied upon, that must be refuted here just as it was in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For ordinary people do not consider the means of accomplishment and the object to be accomplished to be non-different;
who indeed would maintain the identity of the axe with the act of cutting the tree?
As for the avoidance of the objection regarding the difference of objects, that which was stated in the context of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) should be applied here as well.

For just as in the case where the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and so forth are considered the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it was established that there is identity of object (*samānaviṣayatva*) because the result is produced through the operation upon that very object;
so too here, in the case where smoke and so forth are considered the means of valid cognition, this aforementioned identity of object must be accepted as resulting precisely from their operation.
Therefore, let either the smoke or its cognition be the means of valid cognition, or else the relationship or the recollection thereof.

This is because the relationship between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) is dependent upon the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). Furthermore, the statement that there is no fixed rule regarding perception as a means of valid cognition for the intellect (*buddhi*) applies everywhere.
Because that which is grasped by inference is established by that very same [inference].
One who desires to speak to others should state the initial position (pakṣa) exactly as it has been formulated;
therein, having pointed out the subject (dharmin), the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is predicated.
It has been stated that if [cognition] were the result, there would be no result [distinct from the means].
For the author of the Bhāṣya demonstrates that cognition itself is the means of valid knowledge, since he states the reason: "Cognition [arises] regarding an object not in contact [with the senses].
And yet, there is no absence of a result.
Because only diminution (*hāna*) and so forth constitute the fruit;
nor is there any royal decree that the fruit must be of the same genus (*sajātīya*).
For through utility, a fruit—whether of the same genus or of a different genus—indeed arises.

Or rather, let the result be of the same genus; it will be the cognition of abandonment and so forth, or the recollection of assistance and so forth—with this intention, he says: "the cognition of the object of knowledge" (prameyadhīḥ). //52//

If the author of the Bhāṣya considers validity to belong only to cognitions that are themselves valid, how then can smoke and the like be accepted as means of valid cognition? To this he says: "perception," etc.
We have already stated that validity depends upon the speaker's intention.
Thus, when it is understood that smoke and the like alone possess the status of being the most excellent means [of knowledge],

then that alone is the valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). By the Commentator as well, through the passage beginning with "either cognition or birth," while demonstrating the restriction to perception, he has shown that in all cases there is indeed no such restriction, by means of an equal [argument].
Therefore, there is no contradiction with the Bhāṣya in accepting the validity of smoke and other such [inferential signs]. //52//
The Buddhists divide this inference into two types: for oneself (svārtha) and for others (parārtha). As it has been said:
"Inference is of two kinds; that for oneself is the perception of an object through a mark possessing the three characteristics."
Inference for the sake of others, however, is that which illuminates an object already perceived by oneself.
Thus, with the intention that this twofold division is untenable, he says: "by inference," etc.
The meaning of this is: [the testing] of an object grasped through inference by means of others—such as teachers, disciples, fellow students, adversaries, or opponents.
By one who desires to establish [the object] through that very inference, it must be stated how the subject— the qualified locus (*viśiṣṭo dharmī*)— is cognized, as we have previously established.
This is the underlying intention here.
To communicate to another a matter grasped by oneself through inference, one employs only a formal argument (*sādhana-vākya*).

The other person, however, having reflected upon the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpa-liṅga*) from that statement, understands the object to be proven for themselves; thus, this is inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) alone.
For the speaker as well, who has himself understood the object, it is simply an inference for oneself;
we do not know which among these two is an inference for others.
If you say that speech is for others, no.
Because it is not an inference.
We accept, however, that "speech is for the sake of others.
As for what he says, namely, "because seeing is for the sake of others," [we do not agree].
But that is not inference,
because it is produced from a mark (liṅga) lacking the three characteristics and is a perception of what is not the [intended] object;
for our established tenet is that "inference is the perception of an object through a mark possessing the three characteristics."
Therefore, how can speech be inference?
If it is argued that speech is metaphorically called "inference for others" (parārthānumāna) because it has the purpose of communicating an object already made the domain of inference,
then speech that conveys even an object apprehended by direct perception (pratyakṣa) would also be "for others," and thus direct perception itself would result in being "for others."

If, however, it is argued that perception is not for the sake of others because perception has the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) as its object, and that [particular] is not within the domain of words,
then that is incorrect; for in that case, it would be illogical to state a refutation of contradictions by those who express things contrary to what is grasped by perception.
For if someone asserts a matter contradicted by direct perception— such as "fire is not hot"— he is refuted by having that object of perception established through his own statement.
However, that [refutation] would not be possible in the case of an object of perception that lies beyond the range of words.

Therefore, one must admit that a word expresses even that which is an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). And in this way, since the statement of an object of direct perception is for the sake of another, who could prevent the fact that direct perception is for the sake of another? Thus, the two-fold division [of means of knowledge] is untenable.
Consequently, he stated that only the position as previously described should be maintained.
But this must be stated: what is this so-called "proposition" (pakṣa)? It is said in reply:
the meaning of the thesis (pratijñā) is the "proposition."
What is the proposition (*pratijñā*)? It is the statement that presents the probandum (*sādhya*). As they say:

Regarding the statement "the indication of the probandum (sādhyanirdeśa) is the thesis (pratijñā)," one must say that we call the "probandum" the "subject" (pakṣa); thus, it is stated that "the subject is what is to be expressed. He now introduces that very statement with the word "therein" (tatra).
In that context, having first pointed out the locus (*dharmin*) within the subject (*pakṣa*), the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), such as fire and so forth, is predicated;
thus it is said: "This mountain is possessed of fire.
However, some do not accept this statement of the subject, which is synonymous with the proposition (*pratijñā*).

And they say: "What is the use of this useless [member]? Even without the statement of the thesis (pakṣavacana), that which is required is indeed established; for it is the reason (hetu) that proves the probandum."
It is not a statement of the thesis;
for this is not a matter of scriptural authority, as that would entail the consequence of the uselessness of stating the reason.

If the determination of the chariot were to follow from the statement of the thesis (pakṣavacana) alone according to the authority of a reliable person (āpta), then the statement of the reason (hetu) would be useless;
the opponent would merely be intent on ascertaining the virtues and faults of the speaker.
However, since the final ascertainment depends upon the reason, it is appropriate to examine the capacity of that very reason.

What is the purpose of the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*)? Furthermore, the efficacy of the reason (*hetu*) is established solely by demonstrating its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the probandum (*sādhya*).

Therefore, since the probandum is established merely through the example (*udāharaṇa*) and the application (*upanaya*)—namely, "whatever is produced is impermanent, and sound is produced"—the proposition is useless.
However, it is the three-fold nature of the reason (*hetu*) itself that must be demonstrated;

and since that is stated by means of the two examples and the application (*upanaya*), enough has been said on this point at great length. If, on the other hand, it is said that the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is intended to announce the dispute (*vivāda*).
That is not so, because it is not universally applicable (*avyāpakatvāt*).

For one who thinks: "When this person asserts the thesis that sound is eternal, the other, the proponent of non-eternality, becomes provoked, and from that, debate (*jalpa*) proceeds"—[that is incorrect].

And that is not so, because it is not universally applicable. For one might think: "When this person asserts the proposition that 'sound is eternal,' the other, who maintains the doctrine of non-eternality, becomes opposed; from that, debate proceeds. [But this is incorrect.]
And that is not so,
because it is not all-pervasive;
this purpose does not pervade the statement of the thesis.
Because that [investigation] is impossible in a formal debate;
for it concerns the disciple,
and he must be made to understand reality itself.
Therefore, it is logical that reality is made known only after the power of the reason has been established;
why then take heed of dispute?
For one should not dispute with that [reality].
If it is argued that this may occur in the context of *jalpa* (wrangling), we say no;
for it is established otherwise.
In this regard, one might think: "In *jalpa*, indeed, one who desires to engage in debate formulates a proposition (*pratijñā*)."
But that is not so; for it is established otherwise,
since even in the absence of the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*), it is indeed observed [that one understands], "He infers sound to be impermanent."
Having stated, "Whatever is produced is impermanent, like a jar," one applies the property of being produced to sound by saying, "And sound is produced.
Thereafter, debate (*jalpa*) will certainly proceed.
As for cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), it proceeds in whatever manner once debate has been demonstrated.
For the caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*) has nothing to be established other than the refutation of another;
thus, when some matter is being established by means of a statement of a thesis (*pratijñā*), he—deeming it a proof of the opposite of his own position and becoming agitated—would engage in debate.
Therefore, they object that the statement of a thesis, being of no use in any of the three types of discourse, should be disregarded.
To this it is replied: You yourselves have stated that inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is the communication of an object perceived by oneself.
And since one has personally understood something qualified by some property due to a particular reason, it is logical that it should be communicated to another in exactly that same way.
For if the proposition (*pratijñā*) were absent, the reason and other members would be without a basis, as if fallen into space.
[Objection: But surely, since he did not previously know the probandum by means of a statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*), how can he communicate it thus to another?
[Response: Not so.

Although the words "sound is impermanent" were not uttered during his own cognition, nevertheless, because this cognition is conceptual (*savikalpaka*), there certainly exists for the cognizer here a specific conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Since utterance is for the sake of another, it did not exist for one's own comprehension;
however, because another cannot be made to understand by means of a word that has not been uttered, it is uttered so as to be communicated—thus, the mere utterance of the word is what is additional.
As for that which is of no use in debate:
This has been stated, but that is not so,
because it is extremely useful.

For since debate (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) proceed between two parties desiring victory, the statement of a proposition (*pratijñā*) would not be employed [by one party] merely to delude the other.

But since there is no dispute that a disciple must not be led astray, the proposition and its restriction are indeed quite clear; and while a contrary assumption is possible, one that is not contradictory is not.
Furthermore, by the expression "that which is not present to the senses" (asannikṛṣṭa), two things are here intended to be abandoned.
It is logical that [the goal] is accomplished by means of speech;
for it is not a lack of verbal skill that we should weary one who has approached us with a desire to know reality by means of indistinct words.
Nor is it the case that there is no utility in the formal statement (*jalpa*).
This has already been stated: for if the proposition (*pratijñā*) were not uttered, the reason (*hetu*) and other members would have no basis and could not function.
For they are subordinate elements that connect themselves only when there is a dependence upon the primary element, the probandum (*sādhya*).
And that [statement] is not tenable as a presentation of the probandum (*sādhya*).
For when the probandum has been presented, the reason (*hetu*) is connected to it in response to the expectation "Why? (i.e., "How is this established?").
Then, when the expectation arises, "In what way is this the prover of this [probandum]?", the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is given.
Otherwise, however, due to the absence of a single purpose, even the status of being a single sentence would not be established.
For instance,
when it is stated that "whatever is produced is impermanent," it is restated that the property of being produced is connected with impermanence.
Furthermore, in the statement "sound is produced," the connection of sound with its state of being produced is restated;
however, there is no means of valid cognition for a mutual connection [between the two].
One might suspect that these two sentences are unrelated.

A doubt might arise that for both [proponent and opponent], the statement "that which is produced is impermanent; sound, too, is produced" is merely a restatement of the nature of the thing itself, or that it would result in a different meaning altogether— namely,
that just as the property of being produced is impermanent, so too is the essence of sound.

In this case, it would follow that all produced things (*kṛtaka*) are identical in nature to sound (*śabda*); thus, the proposition (*pratijñā*), which is a constituent part of the primary statement, would be rendered as something well-established. Therefore, for anyone other than the nihilists (*nāstika*) who advocate the denial of everything, the repudiation of that proposition is not appropriate;
for it is indeed the very essence of all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*).
As it has been said:
"The thesis is declared to be the very essence of legal proceedings;
when that is abandoned, the proponent loses the case, and the opponent becomes victorious."
Thus, the manner of the proponent’s statement is well-expressed: having indicated the subject (*dharmin*), the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is predicated. //53-54//

But surely, if the subject (dharmin) is thus predicated as qualified by the probandum (sādhya), there would be an exclusion of other properties because only the connection with the probandum is understood.

Consequently, when it is said "sound is impermanent," due to the restrictive implication that it is *only* impermanent, properties such as being a quality of space (ambara-guṇatva) and so forth would also not be its attributes.
And in this way, since even the logical reason (hetu) is rejected, the establishment of the probandum becomes impossible.
If there were no restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), then [the entity] would also be eternal; thus, the desired conclusion would not be established.
Now, how is it that by the sense [of the statement], "one [entity] is both eternal and non-eternal," the opposing view is rejected?

True; for this very reason, when the restrictive emphasis is applied to exclude that [opposing view], there might also be the exclusion of the other [two possibilities]. Therefore, he says: "restriction" (*niyama*).
The restriction is postulated solely with reference to the intention to express the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), and not from other properties even if they are non-contradictory.
Therefore, when "possessing fire" is being proven as the thesis, only the mere absence of fire is excluded.
It is not, however, another distinct property (*dharmāntara*).
Just as when one says "a white cloth," there is the exclusion of its opposite— the absence of whiteness itself—
and not of non-opposing properties such as subtlety (*sūkṣmatva*) and so forth.

And here, it is said that inference has as its object "that which is not in close proximity" (*asannikṛṣṭa*). What is the meaning of this? If it means that inference takes as its domain an object that has never been previously cognized, that is not so;
for at the very time of knowing the relation, the connection between fire and the like with smoke and the like is already cognized precisely by virtue of their coexistence.
Otherwise, the restriction itself would not be determined.
Nor should it be said that the connection with place and time is something additional here;
for while the connection of smoke with place and so forth appears, that of fire does not.
Because the determination of the connection occurs precisely at the time of comprehending the connection of the smoke with all locations;
for this very reason, some have explained the term "non-proximate" (*asannikṛṣṭa*) for the purpose of dispelling the misconception that it is a memory.
For memory generally consists of a reflection that is delineated by the apprehension of something proximate.
For that [cognition] proceeds with the thought "it is that"; however, inference does not function in this way.
Therefore, this is not recollection.
[Objection: But surely memory arises even when there is no such representation [of the object], as in the case of a lapse of memory.
[Response: Not so.
For it is established that in such cases, even though cognition proceeds in the form of an experience, it is classified as memory because of the absence of a cause for apprehension [of the object].

Indeed, it is impossible for the sense organs—which function by reaching their objects—to be the cause for the manifestation of non-present silver and the like. However, since the impression (*bhāvanā*) produced by a prior experience exists as the cause of memory, it is maintained that this is indeed memory, merely with its reflective awareness (*tad-avamarśa*) obscured.

However, this inferential cognition (*laiṅgika-jñāna*), which arises by the power of causes such as the present mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, proceeds in the form of an experience (*anubhava*); it cannot be separated from that state of being [an experience].
And experience is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, inference is designated as a "means of valid cognition."
If that is so, then let this indeed be the purpose of the term "not proximate" (asannikṛṣṭa). No;

for it would follow that [the cognition] lacks authority due to the absence of a result. A means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is that which has the result of determining what was not previously determined.
If, however, mere determination were the result, then it would follow that memory (smṛti) is also [a valid means of knowledge], for that too arises as having the nature of determining its own object.
It might be argued: "Indeed, that which is not independent is not a means of valid cognition."
And since recollection depends upon grasping,
it is therefore not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
that is not so.
[This is] because it follows as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) from the *Liṅgika* [section].
For that too indeed depends upon the perception of a part (*ekadeśadarśana*) and so forth.
If it is argued that memory does not depend on the apprehension of its own object, we say no.
Here too, it is because of that dependence;
for even inferential knowledge depends precisely upon a prior cognition of fire.
Indeed, for one who has not cognized fire and does not know the [invariable] relation, the cognition "fire is here" does not arise.
Nor is it a royal decree that apprehension must be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone; for this would lead to the absurd consequence that even error would be so.
Even a mistaken apprehension is indeed an apprehension.
Nor is it invalid;
rather, we have already stated that it does not fail to exist when we explained the distinction between knowledge that accords with reality and knowledge that does not.
Furthermore, by the author of the Sūtra himself, who composed the aphorism "when the object is not perceived," [it is implied].
When an object has been cognized both through its own nature and by the exclusion of its opposite,
there arises no further dependence upon a means of valid cognition for that which has already been measured.
When an object has been determined through its specific form, a further means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is fruitless;
for it has been stated in the Sūtra that every means of valid cognition has as its object only that which has not yet been apprehended.
This point, too, has already been explained during the occasion of commenting upon that [Sūtra].
Therefore, the term "apprehension of an object not in contact" (*asannikṛṣṭārthagrahaṇa*) must be explained; hence he says: "not in contact" (*asannikṛṣṭa*).
Its meaning is as follows: for an object in contact is of two kinds—either cognized as it truly is (*tadrūpapramita*) or determined as its opposite (*viparītanirūpita*).
This expression "not in contact" is intended to exclude both of these.
What, then, is the refutation of that [objection]? To this he says: "Of what has been cognized" (*pramitasya*).

For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is required for the sake of practical activity (*vyavahāra*), specifically for the determination of what was previously uncognized, and not out of mere whim.
And since that [determination] is accomplished by the operation of the means of cognition just once, there is no requirement for another means of cognition. //55,56//
But why would there not arise a dependence on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that which has already been cognized?
To this he says: "by way of being of that same nature" (*tādrūpyeṇa*).
This has been explained: for that which is cognized is twofold—either by way of being of that same nature or by way of its opposite.

In that regard, first of all, no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is fruitful for the determination of identity (*tādrūpya*), because that object is already established by the preceding determination itself. Furthermore, regarding the determination of the opposite, there is simply no room for another means of valid cognition. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "not proximate" (*asannikṛṣṭa*) is meaningful for the purpose of excluding both of these [possibilities].

But surely it has already been stated that inference is indeed not a means of valid cognition because its object is something proximate? No; for [that objection applies] only to the specific subject matter under discussion.
Although the property (*dharma*) previously cognized is the object of memory, and the locus (*dharmī*), such as the mountain, is established through direct perception,
it has nevertheless been described more than once that it is the qualified [locus] that is made the object by inference.
But surely, even the [mountain] qualified by fire was already cognized at the very time of the convention regarding the relationship;
for in this way, at the time of grasping the pervasion, he understood that "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire.
Thus, his requirement is satisfied by the mere possession of smoke alone.
But when that [fire] is known, the state of possessing fire is experienced as having been previously cognized.
True;
however, even though the possessor of smoke was previously cognized as possessing fire, it is now recognized through a counter-inference (*praty-anumāna*).

And this recognition is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like perceptual recognition. For previously, a location was known as possessing fire by way of its form characterized by the presence of smoke;
that it is now specifically recognized through inference as "this possesses fire"—a cognition identical to the former—is what is not unreasonable?
This must necessarily be accepted;
otherwise, how could one proceed with practical activity after having cognized "there is fire"?
For we observe that this person, desiring to cook, infers the presence of fire and then runs toward the fire.
But when [an object] has been determined as the opposite, there is no room for another [cognition].
For when its root has not yet arisen, the object is seized by the former;
thus, the objects of the sixfold group beginning with direct perception are not at all determined.
By that very [reasoning], there would be a sublation of the subsequent [position], because alternatives and the like are impossible;
however, the ungraspability of sound and so forth is contradicted by direct perception.
For what reason?
Because if there were no distinction today from previous experience,
one would indeed not have understood that "this place possessing smoke possesses fire."
And it is not the case that one says "he runs for the sake of fire.
If it is asked, "How can one employ the term 'fire' when fire has not been apprehended as having a substratum? We say:
no, because even prior [to the perception of the fire], its status as a substratum is understood just as it is in the case of smoke.

If it is argued that one now acts toward fire by specifically apprehending the mountain through direct perception, what use has this seeker of fire for the perception of the mountain? Therefore, one must admit that this cognition of the mountain as possessing fire is distinct from the previous cognition.

Since a specific linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) is established by that [object], inference must be stated to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because its object has not been previously apprehended.
This very point is expressed by the inclusion of the term "not proximate" (*asannikṛṣṭa*).
As for those who say that the purpose [of this term] is merely to eliminate the suspicion that it might be memory (*smṛti*), [that is incorrect].
For them, even inference would result in having its object sublated;
