indeed, no refutation of that [sublation] is found to have been made by means of another member [of the syllogism] in the *Lakṣaṇagrantha*.
Therefore, the inclusion of the term "not proximate" (*asannikṛṣṭa*) alone serves to exclude both kinds of proximate objects; thus, this is the correct interpretation. //57//
It was stated that there is absolutely no room for [the objection] when [the object] is determined through its opposite.
He states the reason for this in the phrase "at the root":
for the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth is indeed the root of inference.

To the extent that a subsequent [cognition] is delayed by being occupied with its respective operation, the very production of that remote means of knowledge is obstructed by the prior [cognition], which occurs swiftly and seizes the object; this will be explained immediately below. How, then, can inference be sublated? For how can even that [inference], being a valid means of knowledge, be sublated by another means of knowledge?
Or, if there were sublation, there would be no confidence anywhere.
If it is argued that "it is the appearance that is sublated," how can it be an appearance?
If it is argued that there is mutual dependence because of sublation, then let it be that inference is sublated by perception, the senior means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
however, it is not sublated even by other [means] which are inferior to it.
For what reason? To this he says: "of perception and so forth," ending with the word *syāt*.
This is the intended meaning: that which is called a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is never sublated.

For a means of valid cognition is a cognition whose nature is precisely ascertainment (*avadhāraṇa*). Therefore, sublation would be predicated of a cognition—whether already arisen or yet to arise—only in a case where there is an ascertainment of some object in some particular form.
For that sublation (bādha) is of two kinds: sublation by what has been reached (prāptabādha) and sublation by what has not been reached (aprāptabādha).

Sublation by what has been reached is, for example, in the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl; for there, the subsequent [cognition] acquires its own nature precisely by the destruction of the preceding one, and thus it is the sublater of that [preceding cognition].

Furthermore, even when there is a difference in place and other factors, the subsequent [cognition], being uncontradicted and valid by its very nature, causes the preceding [cognition] to appear as a mere semblance.

Thus, regarding the case where the former is sublated by the latter, the word "ascertained" (*avadhārita*) excludes all three types of invalidity on the part of that subsequent cognition by which the object has been so determined.
For an object that is unknown, doubtful, or erroneous cannot be ascertained; thus, it is implied that there is no threefold invalidity in such a case.
Therefore, since the object was previously made manifest by the cognition itself, it is only that manifestation which is sublated, and thus there is no over-extension of the principle.

But when there is no sublation prior to attainment, as soon as a tainted means of inference begins to operate within its own domain, or as soon as a general rule (sāmānyaśāstra) begins to operate toward some particular object,

[the matter] is already determined by that very means— whether it be perception, inference, or scripture— which has all its constituent parts established and which arises more rapidly regarding that particular object.

By that very fact, there occurs a sublation (*bādha*) characterized by the obstruction of the arising of the subsequent [cognition]. For a [subsequent cognition] whose mouth of arising has been blocked by a stronger, more swiftly occurring means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot arise.

Thus, in this way, when there is no actual sublation because [the subsequent cognition] has not been reached, it is merely said to be "sublated" due to the possibility of its reaching [the object], just as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is [said to be sublated] by direct audition (*śruti*). Therefore, there is never an actual sublation of a means of valid cognition.
As for the claim that it is not proper for the primary [means of knowledge] to be sublated by the secondary,
that is not so;
for there is no rule of relative weakness among perception and the other [means of knowledge] as there is among the means of application (viniyoga-pramāṇa).
However, we declare that only that which arises more quickly, or which establishes itself by subverting the former, is the sublater (*bādhaka*);

and the other is the sublated (*bādhyam*). For this very reason, we speak of the sublation of the latter by the former—just as in the case of perception being sublated [by inference]—and specifically, the sublation of a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) by a particular rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*), where the former has its constituent parts established by that very same inference which possesses its own constituent parts as the probandum.
Therefore, we shall state a thesis that is indeed not contradicted by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
and there is no lack of confidence [in it],
because it is not sublated by fallacious appearances (*ābhāsa*).

Because it is by means of its own valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which consists of a determinative nature (*avadhāraṇātman*), that [the latter] is rendered as something else; this very point is expressed by the word "determined" (*avadhārita*).
Now, one might object: even by a stronger [cognition], a weaker one is not necessarily sublated.
For when there is no possibility [of contradiction], sublation occurs;
therefore, the determination of the object will be established through either alternation (*vikalpa*) or combination (*samuccaya*), without resorting to an absolute [exclusionary] understanding.
Hence he says: "from alternation and so forth" (*vikalpādeḥ*).
No such alternatives as these are possible here;
for two mutually contradictory forms cannot be combined in a single locus,
just as something cannot be both audible and inaudible.
It is possible that [the object] is both eternal and non-eternal;
yet this is not a conceptual construction (vikalpa),
because such a construction pertains to the domain of affirmation and negation, and is impossible with respect to an established reality.
Nor is there a fixed distinction regarding the objects [of inference],
because it is precisely those things whose nature is color that are proven to be either eternal or non-eternal.
Therefore, we state that there is sublation (bādha) simply because [the opponent's position] is impossible.
Thus, sublation (bādha) established in this manner should be demonstrated through examples.
Among those, he first demonstrates sublation by perception (pratyakṣabādha) with the words "ungraspability" (agrāhyatā). However, we do not understand this sublation by perception.
For them, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that has an object contrary to its own domain is contradicted by inference, such as [the claim] that sound is not audible;
for audibility is certainly not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This is understood through both positive and negative concomitance among those who are deaf and so forth.
There are three kinds of contradiction regarding words, categorized according to the divisions of the thesis and the other members of the syllogism.
It is logical that [the object] is sublated by perception;
however, "ungraspability" is not an object of perception, because the object of that [perception] is the relationship between the grasped and the act of grasping,
and that [relationship] falls within the scope of perception.
For sound is indeed perceived, yet it is not [inherently] graspable;
for this very reason, it will be stated that even the position that sound is not audible is not contradicted by perception.
To this, it is replied:
True; it is not the case that being an object of apprehension is the objective domain of the sense faculty;
rather, it is that which is apprehended that is its domain.
Thus, here it is shown that the denial of the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) itself contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);

that is to say, this applies to the inference [claiming] that there is no objective support (*nirālambana*). However, the cognition (*pratyaya*), being established by virtue of its not being the object of another's apprehension, declares the very non-existence of that [inference].
And what is the nature of the apprehended other than existence?
For this non-apprehensibility of a rabbit's horn consists simply in its not being an existent thing;
it is precisely because of that non-existence that there arise the designation and the cognition of "non-apprehensibility" in its regard.
Thus, by this method, it has been demonstrated that the position denying the existence of sound is indeed contradicted by perception; therefore, nothing is untenable. //58,59//
He states an example of contradiction by inference (*anumānavirodha*) with the words "of these" (*teṣām*).

For one who intends sound and the like— which are precisely those [objects]— as the subject (*pakṣa*) while asserting that they are inaudible or impermanent, is sublated by a counter-inference (*viparyayānumāna*) that arises immediately.
Others, however, consider this to be a contradiction with perception; he refutes them with the words "Not so.

For sound is indeed perceived, yet its "audibility" (śrāvaṇatā) is not [itself] perceived; for by the suffixes *tva* and *tal*, what is expressed is the relationship between the apprehended and the apprehender belonging to the sound and its audibility.
Because of the traditional rule (smṛti): "In the case of primary derivatives, secondary derivatives, and compounds, the relation [of the base] is denoted by the suffixes -tva and -tal";
and that [relation] cannot be apprehended through direct perception;
moreover, the sense of hearing is beyond the reach of the senses.

How could the relation of that [word] with the object be perceptible? For a relation whose substrata are both sensory and non-sensory is not perceptible, just as in the case of air and a tree. Therefore, this is not a contradiction of perception. //60//
What, then, is the measure of audibility?

To this he says: "That [is it]. Positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) are observed, since sound is perceived by those who are not deaf and the like, but is not perceived by those who are deaf and the like.
For instance, when there is merely an impairment of the ear, the cognition of sound is not observed in a deaf person who otherwise possesses the eyes and other faculties;
yet when the ear is intact, the apprehension of sound is observed even in the absence of the eyes and other faculties.
Therefore, by these two methods of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), this property of audibility (śrāvaṇatva) is understood.
But if this is so, how can there be a contradiction with inference?

For inference does not consist merely of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); rather, it is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of "non-audibility" that arises from such [concomitance].
Therefore, someone who is deluded might think that this [cognition] is indeed mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*); he should be told:
"It has been stated more than once that the mind is not independent in the cognition of external objects.
It is established in the case of all effects that whatever follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of something must have that as its cause."
And auditory perception conforms to the cognition of sound; thus, it has that [sound] as its respective cause.
This alone constitutes the audibility of sound.
As for the fact that the cognition is produced by hearing, this is therefore simply an inference.

[Objection: But how can it be understood that something else is the cause of another thing when it follows its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), if mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) is not relied upon? [Reply: Listen!
For we indeed perceive the relation of cause and effect with the eye itself, as we observe the production of a jar immediately following the activity of the potter.

For this being-a-product-of-that (tatkāryatva) of the jar is simply its arising immediately after that [cause]; and both that jar and its arising are purely visible. What, then, is the use of the mind here?
Therefore, when something exists, another comes to be...

And since [the effect] does not exist when [the cause] is absent, it is produced by that specific cause; thus, because the pervasion (vyāpti) is known through direct perception, inference is indeed established. And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "Sound is manifested by the means of valid cognition consisting of hearing; in that regard..."
Because it is perceived only when [the sense organ] exists;
for whatever is thus [perceived only when something else exists] is illuminated by that, just as a jar is illuminated by a lamp.
And this is an inference preceded by perception and preceded by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), which establishes its non-audibility.
And this [inference] is stronger than the inference of inaudibility based on the established fact of being omnipresent;

for as long as the pervasion of "quality-ness" by "inaudibility" is intended to be grasped, the inference of inaudibility— producing its result rapidly— obstructs the cognition of that pervasion, thereby preventing its very arising.

In the same way, even the inference of impermanence—though based on reasons such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*)—does not arise quickly due to defects such as being unestablished (*asiddha*) or inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*). Therefore, it is sublated by inferences of permanence that possess established members and arise rapidly;

for example, cognitions of the word "cow" (*gośabda*) occurring at different times and places have the same object because they arise as the cognition "cow," just like the current cognition of the word "cow," [proving] that the word "cow" uttered yesterday still exists today.
"By means of [arguments] such as 'like the word "cow" uttered today," and so forth. //60//"
He now announces the manner of contradiction by words with the term "threefold.
For contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*) and so forth are well known as contradictions by words; thus they are designated in that way.
However, these are not [inherently] contradictions by words.
For when a subsequent proposition is sublated by a word established in some particular meaning, there is a contradiction of the word (*śabdavirodha*).
However, in the case of a contradiction with one's own words (*svavāgvirodha*), there is no establishment of the word in any meaning whatsoever, because the expression is self-contradictory.
Even when there is a contradiction with a prior statement, the determination must follow the relative strength or weakness of the logic of what precedes and what follows;
for the prior statement, the initial declaration, and universal worldly consensus prevail.
By the mere utterance, "I shall remain silent for as long as I live," [the subsequent vow] is sublated.
"Since all speech is false, my own self is subverted by the very statement of a fact;
for by the statement of a fact, 'I am born from her,' she who is my mother must be barren."
Thus, there is no contradiction with the verbal testimony (śabda),
for in that case the object is not established by the authority of words alone, since it is to be understood through reasoning (nyāya).
Furthermore, worldly convention (lokaprasiddhi) is neither "word" (śabda) nor a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Rather, since [the contradiction] is already included within perception and the other means of knowledge, it is demonstrated precisely by showing a position contrary to that; therefore, it is not appropriate to include it within the category of contradiction with verbal testimony (*śabdavirodha*).

For the thesis "the moon is not the hare-marked one" does not contradict verbal testimony. Indeed, the word "moon" does not express the absence of a relationship between itself and the hare-marked one, such that there would be a contradiction with verbal testimony regarding a thesis that denies its denotation. For if the word expressed the relationship itself, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

Because there is designation from a relationship, and a relationship from designation; therefore, these are not contradictions of words (*śabdavirodha*). However, by reflecting on the capacity of preceding and succeeding words, one abandons the former and adopts the latter; thus, they are well-known as contradictions of words. The distinction of contradictions of words according to what is established in other systems (*tantrāntara*) is threefold.
Thus it is said.
But from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha), it is precisely the proposition of a meaning contrary to the statement of the Veda’s intent that must be refuted by means of words;
and we shall explain this immediately hereafter. //61//
He demonstrates those very three types by saying "the proposition" (*pratijñā*).
Among them, he states that the contradiction of the proposition alone is divided into three ways, using the verse beginning with "as far as" (*yāvat*) for one and a half verses.
The meaning is this: the contradiction of the proposition is indeed a contradiction with one's own words.
And that [vow] is divided into three types based on the distinction between the act of utterance, the property, and the possessor of the property:
the position that "I shall remain silent for as long as I live."
It is sublated by the very thesis itself;
for a thesis does not exist unless it is stated.
Since sublation occurs through the mere act of stating it, there is sublation by the thesis.

The position that all speech is false is, however, sublated by the very statement of a property (*dharma*). For if everything were false, the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) would itself be false, and thus nothing else could be true. Conversely, if that [statement] were not false, then since the statement of the proposition would also be false, one must consider the impossibility of its connection with the property; thus, there is a sublation of the thesis. This is what is meant by the designation "contradiction with the statement of a property."

In the previous case, however, it was stated "by mere assertion" because silence contradicts only an unqualified assertion. Regarding the phrase "sublation of the self," the meaning is "sublation of dharma."
This means that this very property (dharma) is said to subvert itself; for instance,
the thesis "my mother is barren" is subverted by the statement of its own property (dharmyukti),
since the status of being a mother is not established merely by being indicated.
The Buddhist [position] that words are eternal is sublated by what has been stated previously,
for it is he who denies that the hare-marked one (the moon) is denotable by the word "moon."
He is refuted by the knowledge of the moon established for all the world— [that person] who would attempt to prove this against one who has already recognized the forms of the cow and the gavaya.
The similarity between a cow and a gavaya does not invalidate that [perception] through comparison;
for instance, when Caitra, whose non-existence in the house has been ascertained, is alive and yet outside.
It would result in the status of being barren;
nor should it be said that the word "mother" is used figuratively, because of the qualification:
"from whom I was born."
Thus, when the subject (*pakṣa*) is qualified in this way, it is stated that there is a contradiction with the statement regarding the substratum (*dharmī*).
And this has been said by way of a concession (*abhyupagamavāda*);
however, the words of mere chatterers, which exceed the authority of *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, cannot be reconciled [with them] through such means as figurative interpretation (*gauṇatva*), and so forth.
Because it would follow that all criticisms are eliminated;
for criticisms arise only from negligence or ignorance. If these are somehow resolved, there would be no such thing as a criticism at all. //62,63//
He provides an example of contradiction with a prior statement (*pūrvasañjalpavirodha*) as follows: "Of the Buddhist.

When the Buddhist has stated, "Sound is impermanent," and is questioned by the opponent, "How can there be a cognition of the object from something momentary whose relationship [to that object] has not been grasped?", he replies, "In that case, it must be permanent. At that point, there is a contradiction of his own prior admission.

Although in this case the relationship between the sublated and the sublator follows the relative strength or weakness of the logical principles (*nyāya*), nevertheless, a proposition (*pratijñā*) that is internally contradictory in this manner does not even attain its own existence; thus, it does not require the application of logical principles.
For it is only when a matter is already plausible within a proposition that it is established by means of logic.
But when something is impossible, there is no need for logical reasoning at all, because it perishes by its own inherent nature;
therefore, contradiction with scripture alone subsumes such a case.
For their intention is that such a composition of words alone destroys a position that is contradictory to what precedes and follows it.
He provides an example of contradiction with what is well-known to all the world, beginning with the word "candra" (the moon).

In this case as well, the connection with a word whose meaning is contrary to common consensus is set aside by its own inherent nature, rather than depending on any formal means of valid cognition; thus, this is cited as an example of sublation by verbal testimony (*śabdabādha*). //64//
He states an example of contradiction with comparison (*upamāna*) as follows: "Known," etc.

For one who has previously seen the form of a cow in a city and now sees the form of a *gavaya* in the forest, the thesis that "the cow is not similar to the *gavaya*" is contradicted by comparison (*upamāna*).

If it is to be proven that [fire] does not exist, there would be a sublation [of the proof] by means of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti); likewise, when fire is to be proven as non-burning, or sound as not denoting its own form.
Furthermore, when the non-existence of the auditory faculty and so forth is established, and the impermanence of sound is being proven,
there is here a sublation by "presumption based on what is heard" (śrutārthāpatti) regarding that which has been refuted by the word of an authoritative person (āpta).
The eating at night is prohibited by means of the reason "one who eats during the day," while the similarity [of the cow] is to be understood through inference when the cow is out of sight;
however, when it is directly perceived, it is indeed perception itself.
For this very reason, the sequence "having perceived the forms of the cow and the gavaya" is intended [by the author]. //65//

Now, intending to explain the contradiction by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti-virodha*), [the author] first provides an example of that which is preceded by non-existence (*abhāva-pūrvikā*) in accordance with the Bhāṣyakāra: "In the house... (verse 66).
He provides an example based on perception: "In fire... and so forth.
"Non-burning" means being devoid of that capacity.
He provides an example of that which is preceded by inference: "and [the claim] that the word is non-expressive.

Having inferred the cognition of the object immediately following the hearing of the word through its [resultant] activity, it is concluded that the word is the cause thereof. Therefore, because all causal factors are invariably concomitant with an action, the operation is designated as "expression" (*abhidhā*).
And by the non-occurrence of that [otherwise inexplicable fact], the existence of that capacity is established through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). //67//

Likewise, he states that the position which denies the existence of the sense organs (*indriya*) is also contradicted by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) preceded by perception, using the words "the auditory organ," etc.

Although an example of presumptive testimony preceded by perception has already been cited, the author—intending to show that this same fault applies to the position denying the sense organs under the guise of pointing out a flaw in that specific position—has stated the contradiction once again.

Furthermore, by means of the word "etc. (*ādi*), the contradiction with presumptive testimony preceded by comparison (*upamāna*) is to be demonstrated: namely, that when a cow is compared to a *gavaya*, one denies its capacity to be grasped by the cognition produced by that [comparison].

He illustrates contradiction preceded by presumption (*arthāpatti*) with the words "In the case of sound," etc. For, having first ascertained the expressive power of a word through presumption based on the fact that its denotation of meaning would otherwise be inexplicable, one subsequently understands the eternity of the word through another presumption based on the inexplicability of that [expressive power] itself. //67//
He illustrates the contradiction involving presumptive testimony (*śrutārthāpatti*) with the phrase "contradiction by presumptive testimony" (*śrutārthāpattibādha*).
But why is presumptive testimony illustrated here at such length?
For the demonstration of its contradiction would indeed be established even by a single instance of it.
And thus, no detailed exposition has been shown regarding contradictions with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
or rather, like the case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the contradiction with other means of valid cognition should also be stated in detail.
True;
it is precisely by means of these sixfold distinctions that the Vārttikakāra intends to demonstrate the contradiction here,
and it is for the sake of illustrating that very point [that this is stated].

It has been stated that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) arises from the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). By that same method, the detailed exposition should be shown for the other means of valid cognition as well;
for instance:
Annulment by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) alone is divided into six types, excluding the sixth [type of invalidation].

For a proponent who is perspiring, the thesis "fire is not hot" is contradicted by a perception residing in direct experience (*anubhava*). However, for one who is not near the fire, that same thesis is contradicted by a perception residing in memory (*smṛti*).
When, at the time of debate, one asserts that fire is not hot, the other reminds him: "Do you not remember the heat of fire previously experienced, such that you speak thus?
Having remembered that, he desists from his position based on that perception; this is "sublation by perceived memory" (*smṛtapratyakṣabādha*).

As for "sublation by inferred perception" (*anumitapratyakṣabādha*), it occurs when, upon seeing a particular movement in the mouth of a trustworthy person, one promises to ward off tastes such as bitterness that were understood [by the opponent] through that [movement].

For, by the deformity of his mouth, his experience of bitterness is inferred; therefore, there is a sublation of the inferred [proposition] by perception (*anumitapratyakṣabādha*) on the part of the contrary position.

As for sublation by verbal perception (*śrutapratyakṣabādha*), it occurs where someone denies a certain matter, and it is called sublation by the perception of witnesses when it is said, "This matter was seen by the witnesses";
this is not a sublation by verbal testimony (*śabdabādha*).
For in this case, no object is denoted by them;
rather, it is the vision [of the object].
Therefore, the determination follows precisely that vision.
Since "seeing" (*darśana*) is conveyed by its own specific term, this is indeed a contradiction with the perception established by verbal testimony.

As for analogy (*upamāna*), however, its object is merely the similarity to a thing already established through another means of knowledge; thus, it takes as its domain the similarity of that which has been established elsewhere. For example, in the recognition of a sickle or similar tool, having observed one's own activity regarding it, one perceives it in another person and forms an analogy: "Just as my own recognition of the sickle and so forth arose as a direct perception, so too has such a recognition arisen for this person."
Otherwise, how could one proceed on the following day to complete a task that was only half-finished on the previous day?
Furthermore, in this case, having inferred through observed activity a corresponding object in another's domain, one draws an analogy based on its similarity to one's own cognition.
Although it might be possible here to demonstrate a contradiction of perception by means of inference, [the point remains as stated].
Nevertheless, since it is possible to demonstrate the determination of similarity with one's own cognition, the sublation of perception by that [cognition] is stated.
It is the very existence of the object of perception that is cognized through analogy (*upamāna*).
However, the sublation of perception by what is understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) should be demonstrated as follows:

For when many people seeking water are traveling and one among them, having set out to fetch it from a pond, delays, then his perception of water is inferred through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), since that delay would otherwise be inexplicable. In that case, the contrary position— that the pond is devoid of water— is sublated by the perception established through that presumptive testimony.

However, since direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in its positive form cannot be apprehended through non-existence (*abhāva*), the contradiction with unapprehended direct perception is not cited here as an example.

Hereafter, we shall investigate the sixfold division of sublation by inference (*anumāna-bādha*): first, the sublation of inference preceded by direct perception (*pratyakṣapūrvānumābādha*) occurs when there is a negation of fire already cognized through smoke.
When the heat of fire is inferred from the very inference of its existence based on smoke, the contrary position is sublated by that inferential inference (*anumitānumāna*).

However, where a specific application (*viniyoga*) of a mantra is understood from the scriptural injunction, "He offers [the oblation] with the mantra *devasya tvā*," and a contrary position is subsequently grasped regarding the remainder of that mantra, there is sublation by scriptural inference (*āgamānumāna*).

However, when an obligatory rite (*nitya-karman*) has commenced and there is a deficiency of rice (*vrīhi*), and wild rice (*nīvāra*)—which is similar to it—is substituted, the injunction "one should sacrifice with rice" is inferred to have the wild rice as its object.
For the parts of the rice, having their relationship [to the rite] already known through their being the intended objects, lead to that inference.
Indeed, the rice grains do not become the objects of that injunction in their own essential form (*svarūpeṇa*).
The parts of that [rice], however, are like the powdered grains of rice mentioned in the Vedic injunction;
since these parts also exist in *nīvāra* grass, the injunction regarding rice is inferred as applying to the *nīvāra*, which is analogous by virtue of possessing those common rice-parts.
Thus, in this case, the position that [the injunction] does not have that [rice] as its scope is sublated by an inference preceded by analogy (*upamāna*).
The sublation by inference preceded by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) has indeed already been stated regarding the position that sound is audible (*śrāvaṇatva*).

Where one perceives the absence of a tree from a distance and then infers the absence of its shadow, there the position asserting the existence of the shadow is sublated by an inference preceded by non-existence (*abhāva*). Furthermore, sublation by perception and by verbal testimony has already been shown to be threefold.
Others as well must be demonstrated by means of both Śruti and Smṛti.

Furthermore, the position that the Aṣṭakā and other such rites are not dharma has been shown in the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa* to be contradicted by the commonality of performers, by consent, and by the word [of scripture].
For it is possible that the Aṣṭakā and others...

One might infer [the authority of the Smṛti] on the grounds that it is rooted in the Word (śabda), established by scripture, and composed by inhabitants of Āryāvarta, just like the Agnihotra and other rites.

However, there is sublation by scriptural word (āgamika-śabda-bādha) in cases where, in a dispute concerning the subject matter of a Śruti found in another recensional branch (śākhā), the existence of the Śruti is ascertained by the statement of the authors of the Smṛti compendiums; for in such a case, a contradiction with the eternal scripture known through the authoritative tradition (āpta-āgama) is possible for the opposing position.

As for the contradiction with the term "upamitā" (inferred), when it is assumed— on the basis of the *arthāpatti* (presumption) arising from the *smṛtis* of Manu and others— that there exists some Vedic source [for them], then the assumption of a source similar to the Smṛti texts is sublated by the word "upamitā" in the case where the view that [the *smṛtis*] are based on *arthavādas* is held.

However, regarding the view that the Viśvajit sacrifice has no fruit, since its operation lies in the ascertainment established through *śrutārthāpatti*, there is an absence of operation in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma, where the entirety of the injunction has been ascertained and the acquisition of the archetypal (*prakṛta*) procedure is already established.
It is contradicted;

as he will state: "Because it is prescribed in its entirety, the Soma is not [replaced] by something else. However, the position that *nīvāra* grains may be taken when *vrīhi* rice is unavailable would contradict both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and analogy (*upamāna*).

An example of sublation by analogy preceded by inference (*anumānapūrvakopamānabādha*) is as follows: when one has inferred the motion of the sun from its arrival at another location, and then [proposes] that "the sun's motion during the middle or end of that period is such [as observed] at the end of the year," the position regarding the dissimilarity of that motion is sublated by analogy preceded by inference.
However, the position that "pūtīka plants are not similar to *soma*" is contradicted by analogy preceded by verbal testimony (*śabda*).

For the similarity between the *sāman* chant and the *pūtīka* plant is not perceived by direct perception; nor is there any contradiction in the possibility of a rabbit's horn and the like, since they are simply unperceived.
Thus, the sublation of the connection with the property has been illustrated;
as well as [the sublation] of the essential nature and specific qualities of both the property and the substratum.

Furthermore, by means of the word itself, which establishes that the *pūtīka* plants are produced from the rays of the *soma*, their similarity (*sārūpya*) is established through the natural fitness of cause and effect.

Thus, because the *pūtīkas* originate from a cause and effect as understood through the word, the comparison of the *pūtīkas* to the *soma* based on that [similarity] is contrary to its opposite— the comparison preceded by the word [which actually subverts it].
In the position that the ritual properties (*dharma*) belonging to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* do not apply to the *Satra* and *Ahīna* sacrifices, this is sublated by an analogy based on comparison:
for they reach the *Dvādaśāha* by means of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* as the standard of comparison, and the *Satra* and *Ahīna* [reach it] by means of the *Dvādaśāha* as the standard of comparison.

However, when the sense organs of another person—qualified by their similarity to one's own sense organs—are being compared, the negation of that [similarity] is sublated by an analogy based on presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

The thesis that the non-existence of the knower and the cause is not like the non-existence of a rabbit's horn and so forth is sublated by the comparison based on the prior non-existence [of the object].
When the non-existence of both is understood through their absence, similarity is then compared.
Furthermore, the sixfold contradiction with presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) has already been described.
However, we shall explain the contradiction regarding non-existence immediately hereafter. //68//
Now he illustrates contradiction with non-existence (abhāvavirodha) with the words "from a hare's horn," etc.
This is a contradiction with the non-existence of perception (pratyakṣābhāvavirodha).

When it is being considered whether or not the sun has gone to such-and-such a constellation, a person skilled in calculation understands through the inference of calculation that the sun has not gone; yet a deluded person says, "It has gone."
In that regard, [the claim] contradicts the absence of inference;
the position that [acts such as] bowing to a *caitya* constitute Dharma contradicts the absence of scriptural authority (*śruti*) and other traditional sources;
and the statement "the *darvī-homa* oblations are like those previously mentioned" contradicts the absence of analogy (*upamāna*).

Likewise, since the perception of sound is possible merely by the arrival of the sound-wave at the ear— without the sound reaching the location of the ear, nor the ear reaching the location of the sound— one must,

through the necessity of the facts (*arthāpatti*), assert that one sound initiates another sound, which is then gradually perceived by the ear until the final one is grasped; such an assertion is contradicted by the absence of any *arthāpatti* (i.e., no such explanatory necessity exists).

The absence of absence is to be demonstrated in this way: for when the absence of defects in the Vedas is understood through the absence of an author, then there is a sublation of the position that they possess defects by means of the absence of that absence. //69//

Thus, the sixfold sublation of the connection between the property (*dharma*) has been elaborated. Hereafter, we shall explain the sublation of the nature of the property, the substratum (*dharmin*), both together, as well as their own specific qualifications. To summarize this for the sake of easy comprehension and to ensure the concentration of the listeners' intellects, it should be stated that in a sentence, both the expressed meaning and that implied by the literal sense are subject to all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Just as [the presence of] fire is established from grass and other things that serve as causes for action.
In this case, however, there is a sublation arising from a specific quality of what is perceived through direct perception:
"Unrighteousness, when practiced, produces only slight suffering."
Because it has been prescribed, there is a sublation of the very nature of unrighteousness;
likewise, its specific quality of being a cause of suffering is sublated.
And he provides a summary of what has been discussed and what is about to be discussed with the verse beginning "In this way" (evam).
Regarding the phrase "of those implied by the direct statement and the meaning":
first of all, the essential nature [of the means] is everywhere indeed that which is directly stated by the sacred text.
Its specific qualification is also implied by the sense;
for it implies that particular qualification by which the essential nature of the property and the subject is pervaded,
and that will be explained immediately hereafter.
And the analysis [of the compound] is: "the meaning of the Veda and that which is implied. //70//

In this regard, the sublation of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the property (*dharma*) has already been described; therefore, without performing that [sublation], he provides an example of the sublation of its qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), beginning with "grass and so forth.

For one who seeks to prove that snow possesses fire based on the observation of transformations such as grass and the like, there is indeed a sublation of the essential nature of the property by the non-existence [of fire].
Furthermore, its qualification—namely, heat, which is implied by the context—is sublated by the coldness perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Nor should it be argued that fire is seen to be non-hot in its rays, and therefore how can the specific property be implied by the object;
for even in the rays, the fire is indeed hot,
but its touch is not perceived because it is overwhelmed.
Furthermore, it never abandons its heat,
for that is its inherent nature;
nor should it be said that there is no perception of it even in ice because it is overwhelmed [by cold].
This is because its opposite, coldness, is perceived.

As for the presentation of the reason (*hetu*), it is intended merely to demonstrate that it lacks a seed at the time of stating the faults of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*); thus, this is "sublation of a specific property by means of non-existence" (*abhāvena dharmaviśeṣabādha*). //71//

Since both types of sublation (*bādha*) regarding the subject (*dharmin*) have not yet been mentioned, he provides an example of such sublation in two ways with the verse beginning "Adharma... (along with its half-verse).
For it is generally understood that "violence (*hiṃsā*) is indeed unrighteousness (*adharma*).

When that very unrighteousness—namely, the violence toward the sacrificial animal (*daikṣapaśu*) which is enjoined—is restated as "it does not produce suffering" and then proven to be "insignificant," [that constitutes sublation].

Even then, by virtue of being enjoined (*vihitatvena*), non-dharma itself is sublated; its specific characteristic—namely, being a cause of suffering, which was implied for that purpose—is likewise sublated by that very same fact.
For nothing that is enjoined can ever become a source of suffering, because an injunction has as its sole purpose the accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
Thus,
when it is stated that "all cognitions are unreal," there is a sublation of both [the self and external objects],
because that cognition is proven to be false by virtue of its own nature and its lack of distinction [from other cognitions].
In this context, the two specific points—momentariness and absolute falsity—are refuted by the statement: "Because [the Buddha] has seen a portion [of it]. (Msv 5.4.75)
Where there is doubt, uncertainty, or error regarding either one or both [of the two criteria], [the inference fails]:
for example, that fire is not hot because it is cold, or that sound is impermanent because it is visible.
In cases such as "of the word" (*śabdasya*) and so forth, however, the contrapositive is unestablished for both [parties].
There is a sublation of the specific nature of the subject (*dharmin*) by means of scripture (*āgama*).
Nor should it be urged here that the specific property (*viśeṣa*) is only that which is directly expressed by the word (*śruti*).
Because it is a restatement for the purpose of enjoining that which is implied by the sense, due to its being minimal. //73//
He illustrates the contradiction of both [premises] with respect to both [conclusions] by saying "ayathārtha" (unreal).

For when it is established that all cognitions are false, then because the two cognitions grasping the property (*dharma*) and the locus (*dharmī*) are themselves false, and because the two cognitions grasping their respective qualifiers are also false, there occurs a sublation of both [premises] by both [conclusions].

And since this contradiction of both [the word and the fact] through the statement of a property (dharmokti) must be subsumed under the contradiction of the word itself, it is thus established that "contradiction of both" refers to a contradiction regarding their essential natures (svarūpa). //74//
But what, then, are those two specific [properties] implied by the sense of the word "viśeṣa" that are sublated?
To this he says: "momentary" (kṣaṇika).
It should be shown that the connection is to be understood by modifying the word "are sublated" (bādhyete) [to "sublate"].
And in that case, it is said "because of the perception of one part"; however, the inclusion of the term "perception" (darśana) is redundant; one should simply say "from one part" (ekadeśāt).
For that [mark] is indeed the sign (liṅga), not the perception itself; therefore, it must be explained as "from the perception of one part. To this he says: "from perception" (darśanāt).
The meaning is this:
a part is not a sign merely by its existence.
However,
he is able to take both [the root] *grah* itself, because the mention [of the form] is common to both the presence and absence of the causative suffix *ṇic*.
In the case of one's own realization (*svapratipatti*), the meaning is that the cognition arising when a single part [of the object] is perceived is inference (*anumāna*).

In the formulation for the sake of others (*parārthaprayoga*), however, it is stated that the cognition which arises after having shown a single part by means of the word "showing" (*darśana*) in its causative form (*ṇijanta*) is inference;
thus, this word "showing" uttered therein is to be explained in two senses.

And by this [definition], that which is called an "unestablished" (asiddha) fallacy of reason— wherein, in a certain respect, there arises for one or both of the proponent and the opponent doubt, uncertainty, or error— is excluded. For such a [reason] cannot be demonstrated to another,
as in the case of "being produced" or "being a quality" when stated by another to a ritualist.
And regarding the aforementioned type [of reason], it may be unestablished for one or the other;
or, when there is doubt as to whether it is vapor or something else, it is unestablished for both or for one of the two.
Thus, smoke may likewise be unestablished in three ways by way of its own nature;
these same modes would also apply when there is the conceptualization of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).
For even when its own nature is known, that which does not possess that property cannot be a cause;
or rather, it must be perceived by itself—
meaning that there is no cognition of it [as such].
Regarding that, he provides an example of the "twofold perversion" (dvayaviparyasta), stating: "Because of coldness" (*śaityāt*).
Since both the terms "fire" and "sound" are [respectively] cold and visible, they are unestablished (*asiddha*) due to the perversion of both the proponent and the opponent. //75-76//
He states an example of the "unestablished for one of the two parties" (anyatarāsiddha): "Regarding the property of being produced," etc.
When a Vaiśeṣika employs a reason such as "sound is impermanent because it is produced" or "because it is a quality" against a Mīmāṃsaka, that reason is unestablished for him in its essential nature.
But when one states such a reason to another person on one's own authority, then it is unestablished (*asiddha*) for that person.
For example: "Sound is eternal because it is a substance, like space.
For the Vaiśeṣikas do not accept sound as a substance, since they accept it as a quality (*guṇa*).
"Of such a kind" means "of a kind not established for the opponent. //77//
He illustrates the "doubtful-unestablished" (*sandigdhāsiddha*) with the passage ending in "bāṣpādi":

for when smoke is doubted as being vapor or the like— by both [possibilities] or by one of them, such as "Is this a rising of dust, or vapor, or smoke?"— then it is doubtful-unestablished for both or for either one of the two.
Thus far, the lack of proof (*asiddhatā*) has been illustrated by way of the absence of doubt and error;
however, it must also be shown through the employment of words whose meanings are not established due to ignorance.
It is threefold.
"There are three types [of unestablished reasons] for both the proponent and the opponent.
Thus, it has been stated that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) by way of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*); this is what he says with the word "evam" (thus). //78//

He states that the fallacy of the unestablished substratum (*āśrayāsiddhatā*) is also divided into three types by these very same factors—knowledge and so forth—which depend on both the proponent and the opponent: "These very [factors]," etc. (79).

"Is it not the case that a reason (hetu) would be defective due to its own nature being unestablished (svarūpāsiddhi), whereas what defect could there be for it due to its locus being unestablished (āśrayāsiddhi)? To this he says: 'Even when known'.
The intended meaning is this: the reason is not a prover by its own nature alone; rather, [the argument is] "the self is omnipresent because its effects are observed everywhere."
For a Buddhist, [the reason] is unestablished with respect to its substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*); for those such as worldly people, however, there is doubt.
This is because linguistic practice is not established merely by the non-establishment of a mere verbal expression.
That speech which is known by both [parties] as being devoid of a sentient being is considered a refutation;
however, the other would be a proof if it is established by the proponent.
It is known as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
Furthermore, it is not possible to know something as a property of that [subject] if its locus (*āśraya*) is unestablished.
Even in the cases of coldness and visibility, their status as non-reasons is due precisely to the failure to establish them as properties of the subject.
For coldness is established by its own nature in water, and visibility is established in color, the possessor of color, and that which inheres in the same object as color.

However, since these two [the substratum and the property] are unestablished in the case of sound and so forth due to the lack of their presence as properties of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), this is called the "unestablished nature of the form of the property" (*taddharmarūpāsiddha*).

Therefore, it is indeed logical that even in the case of the "unestablished substratum" (*āśrayāsiddhi*), there is no status as a valid reason because the property is not established as a property of the subject. //79//
He now illustrates this fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*): "In all cases" means according to the [opponent's] non-tenet.
For when the Mīmāṃsakas prove to a Buddhist that the self is omnipresent because an effect is perceived everywhere, then the reason has an unestablished locus for one of the two parties.
"Because the self (ātman) is not established for a Buddhist.

However, someone in the world who, being ignorant of the way of valid cognition (pramāṇa), has doubts regarding the self—when that very same reason is stated, he says that the reason is "uncertain with regard to its substratum" (saṃdigdhāśraya). [The author] says "of the worldly person, etc.
The meaning is: there is doubt regarding the self.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), those fellow-sectarians who also harbor doubts regarding the self are included.

Thus, the non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) has been stated by way of doubt and error; it should also be shown that the non-establishment of the locus occurs through ignorance when employing a term whose referent is not established.

For indeed, against one for whom the word "pakṣavacana" (the statement of the thesis) is not well-known, when such a reason is stated, there is a failure of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) due to ignorance. //80//
Now, if a reason is defective due to being unestablished for one of the two parties,
then in that case, even such reasons as "the self is inactive because it is formless" would not function as valid reasons, since for the Digambaras the formlessness of the self is unestablished;
for they consider the self to be material, consisting of the transformation of the body.
Furthermore, for the Buddhists, the claim that "the Veda is eternal because it has no author" is not a valid reason, as that [authorlessness] is unestablished.
For the Mīmāṃsakas, the argument "sound is impermanent because it is produced" is unestablished. Thus, there is no such thing as a "reason" (hetu) that remains definitively established.
Therefore, he says: "merely words" (*vāṅmātra*).

The meaning is this: a reason does not become unestablished (*asiddha*) merely because of the words, "It is not unestablished for me. If that were the case, no practice of inference (*anumānavyavahāra*) could be established at all.
However, when the non-existence [of the reason] is established by both the proponent and the opponent, the refutation belongs to the opponent;
and here, the reasons of doubt and contrariety are also excluded.
Because of the statement that "the relationship [of the reason] must be known," there are three causes of doubt.

When [the reason] is determined, it becomes unestablished (*asiddha*); the statement of its unestablished nature regarding such a subject constitutes a refutation for the proponent, not merely the fact that it is unestablished.
"Merely from the activity of speech," [it is said]. // 81 //
Now, what is this "unestablished for both"?
For there can be no agreement between two disputing parties on a single point;
indeed, even in a thousand lifetimes, a Buddhist would not accept the authorlessness of the Vedas.
Even a Mīmāṃsaka, though his very life-breath be at his throat, cannot admit the produced nature (kṛtakatā) of sound.
Thus, because there is no agreement between both parties regarding such matters, it does not function as a valid reason (hetu).
Therefore, he says: "the other."
The intended meaning is this: it is not the case that proof and refutation are rendered impossible merely because there is no agreement between the two parties.
Rather, if the proponent employs a proof and the opponent points out its unestablished nature (*asiddhatva*), and the proponent subsequently establishes that proof, then it becomes a valid proof.
If, however, the opponent refutes [the argument] by means of a statement supported by ultimate reasoning (*paramārtha*), then his refutation is established.

In this case, it is the establishment [of the reason] through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone that is relevant, not the acceptance by both parties. Even the statement, "that which is known by both to be non-existent," was spoken with the intention of establishing it through valid cognition.
It is not based merely on what is accepted [by others];
for it is generally observed that regarding whatever is established or sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is agreement between both parties.
The term "other" refers to that which is not known [as existent] by the knower;
or rather, when something is known as existent by the proponent but is known in the opposite way by the opponent, that which is being established by the proponent constitutes a proof (*sādhana*).
And this was stated while remaining within the framework of informal debate (*jalpa*);
however, in formal debate (*vāda*), there is indeed agreement between both parties. Nor does it follow that "unestablished for one of the two" (*anyatarāsiddhi*) is not a fault in such a case.

However, as long as the proponent does not establish the proof, he is defeated due to the non-establishment of one of the two [premises]; but once that has been established, the refutation becomes averted. //82 1/2//

Having thus shown the purpose for excluding [the cases of] "non-proximate" (*asannikṛṣṭa*) and "single part" (*ekadeśa*), he now shows the purpose for excluding [the case of] the term "known relation" (*jñātasambandha*) by means of the words ending with "doubt" (*sandeha*).
For, in the case of a cause that is either doubtful or contrary, the relation is not known.
For it cannot be said that "knowability" (*prameyatva*), being a common cause of doubt, has its relationship with permanence known;

for its relationship with impermanence is also known in the case of jars and the like. Nor can "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) be said to have its relationship with permanence known, since its connection with impermanence is perceived in those very same things.
Therefore, since both of those [types of inference] do not involve a known relation (*jñātasambandha*), the author excludes them by means of the term "known relation.
And here, starting from the word *asannikṛṣṭa* (not present),
the author of the Vārttika has stated, in reverse order, the purpose for including each qualification in the definition-text.
It exists in the probandum and in its absence, and it is excluded from both.
Two properties connected with contradictory meanings that reside in one and the same locus—
the subject— are the uncommon [inconclusive] reasons for both, such as the properties of being cognizable, impermanent, and formless.
For what reason?
Because it follows the sequence of cognition;
for the cognizer first cognizes the subject (*pakṣa*).
Thereafter, one considers the reason (*hetu*);

thereafter, the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Thus, for the purpose of refuting an invalid position (*asatpakṣa*), the term "not present to the senses" (*asannikṛṣṭa*) has first been explained. Thereafter, the term for the reason is "from the perception of a part" (*ekadeśadarśanāt*).

By the phrase "of one who has known the relationship," even the defects of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*), such as its being devoid of the probandum (*sādhya*) or the reason (*hetu*), are refuted by this;
for even when those are lacking, the relationship itself can be personally known and explained to another.
Furthermore, how many are the causes of doubt?
Therefore, he says: "The three. //83 1/2//
He shows those same three types [of reasons]: "existent" (*san*).
That which is non-existent (*asan*) in both the probandum (*sādhya*) and its absence (*tad-abhāva*) is called "common" (*sādhāraṇa*).
For example, "knowability" (*prameyatva*) [is common] to both the eternal and the non-eternal.
The "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) [reason] is that which is excluded from both the probandum and its absence; for example, the possession of odor belongs only to earth.
For that [odor] is excluded from all other substances—whether of the same class or a different class—as well as from their qualities and actions.
Thus, there are two connections with contradictory objects.

Those two which have been described by others as "the non-erroneous contradictories" (viruddhāvyabhicārin) should be illustrated immediately hereafter; therefore, they are not explained here. //84 1/2//
Therein, he first elaborates upon the common [inconclusive reason] by means of examples—beginning with "the object of cognition" (*prameya*).
The meaning is that these properties (*dharma*) are common to both the probandum (*sādhya*) and its absence (*tadabhāva*). //85//
In response to the question, "With regard to which unestablished [reasons] do these [fallacies] have commonality?", he says: "In the eternal," ending with that word.
But how, given the disparity in number, is there a correspondence according to order? To this he says: "The term 'non-eternality' occurs twice. Non-eternality is to be read twice in its own place.
Therefore, the correspondence [of the terms] is established as follows:
the meaning is this—that because "what is seen by both" is common to both, it is capable of being non-exclusive;
hence it is called "non-exclusive" (*anaikāntika*).
For this very reason, it is a cause of doubt;
for doubt arises from the perception of a general property, the non-perception of specific properties, and the recollection of specific properties—
as when there is the perception of the commonality of height and girth in a post and a person, yet the distinguishing [features] are not perceived.
The earth would be eternal because it possesses odor; however, this [reason] is an inconclusive (asādhāraṇa) one.
Because it lacks one of the factors of certainty, this is a cause of doubt;
and because there is no ascertainment of the property (*dharma*), it depends upon the recollection of specific features.
A doubt, which consists of a cognition that does not ascertain—"Is this a post, or rather a person?"—thus arises.

In this way, for one who knows that "knowability" (*prameyatva*) is a common property (*sāmānya*) of both the eternal and the non-eternal, there arises—dependent on the non-recollection of its specific [distinguishing] features—a cognition characterized by non-determination regarding those very two; this is what is called "doubt" (*saṃśaya*). Thus, knowability is a cause of doubt, and this is a cause of doubt that pervades both sides in their entirety.
Likewise, the reason "sound is produced by effort because it is impermanent" is also exclusively common (sādhāraṇa).
This is because it occurs in some things not produced by effort, such as lightning and the like, and it also exists in all things produced by effort, such as jars and the like.
Therefore, it should be understood that this [reason] pervades the entire dissimilar class (vipakṣa) while occurring only in a portion of the similar class (sapakṣa).
Likewise, in the case of the argument "sound is non-eternal because it arises from effort," non-eternality is observed in all things that arise from effort;
yet it is also observed in some cases, such as clouds, even in the absence of such effort.
It does not [exist] in space and so forth; therefore, it should be understood that this is a "common" (sādhāraṇa) reason which pervades the entire sapakṣa but exists only in a portion of the vipakṣa.
An example of one that exists in a portion of both is: "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal."

For incorporeality (*amūrtatā*) does not pervade all eternal things, because it exists in space (*vyoman*) and so forth, yet is absent in atoms (*aṇu*). Nor does impermanence pervade its own locus, because it is absent in jars, walls, and the like, yet present in actions (*karman*) and so forth. In this context, the reason (*hetu*) functions in both ways across all cases; however, although the aspect of its presence in the cause of doubt exists, it is not the operative factor and is therefore irrelevant. For this very reason, those who assert a fourfold division of the "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) reason find that such a classification is useless for proof or refutation. Thus, the aspect of its non-existence in some instances is what is actually utilized.
For even if it exists in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) by the slightest degree, a reason (*hetu*) must indeed be abandoned.

Even for the proponent of the refutation (*dūṣaṇavādin*), it is sufficient to state merely that [the reason] occurs in the dissimilar instance; so what is the point of resorting to its specific sub-varieties?

The author of the *Vārttika* also demonstrated an elaborate range of examples in order to show that, among those [reasons] common to all [fallacies], the very fact of occurring in both [the similar and dissimilar instances] is the cause of doubt.
Furthermore, it does not depend upon the fourfold classification,
as it has been said:
"But there is no utility for a single [type of fallacy] with respect to the pointing out of a refutation."
And thus, in the case of a means of proof, it is abandoned because of its commonality with [the probandum], especially so. (85½)

Having explained the "over-elaborated" (*prapañcita*) uncommon [reason], he now provides an example of an uncommon reason that causes doubt: "Earth is eternal. For odor is the specific quality (*asādhāraṇo guṇaḥ*) of earth.
Because it does not abandon that [object] to resort to another entity, whether permanent or impermanent, it is called "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa).
An example of the "common" (sādhāraṇa) is that which is observed as the cause for two cognitions.
And because contradictory [reasons] cannot both be established, they are considered a cause for doubt;
however, where there is no uncommon [reason], it is by way of the non-existence of that [doubt].
And because it contradicts the non-existence of both [alternatives], it is considered a cause of doubt.
He says: "Let the possession of odor (*gandhavattva*) be uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*); but how is it a cause of doubt?"
For it is logical that a common [reason], which relies on both sides and produces the cognition of non-settlement for both parties, is a cause of doubt;
however, since an uncommon [reason] is excluded from both and is thus unable to generate a cognition regarding either one, how can it be a cause of doubt?
To this, he says: "Because of the absence of certainty... and so forth.

For when producing certainty, both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are auxiliary factors for a reason; if either one is absent, the reason is not sufficient for certainty.

Just as a common (*sādhāraṇa*) reason, even if accompanied by positive concomitance, is incapable of producing certainty when deprived of negative concomitance, so too an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason, failing to provide even one of the two members known as positive concomitance, becomes a cause of doubt. //86 1/2//

[Objection: But was it not already stated that a common [reason], which goes to both sides and generates a cognition in both, is the cause of doubt; whereas an uncommon [reason] informs nothing at all, and thus it is not logical to say that it is a cause of doubt merely by being deficient in one factor? To this he says: "The common [reason]," etc., with two [verses]. The intention is this: even a common [reason] is not a cause of doubt simply because it generates a cognition in both [sides].
However, by way of presenting two contradictory [reasons],
when both contradictories have been presented, doubt arises precisely because of the contradiction, since their coexistence in a single locus is impossible;
and this is no different even in the case of the "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) reason.
Even a unique [reason], by excluding [the subject] from both [possibilities], brings about doubt precisely because the non-existence of both is impossible;
for it is not possible that a thing should neither be eternal nor non-eternal,
since the entire world of living beings is established through pairs of properties such as eternality and non-eternality.
Therefore, the absence of both is contradicted;
nor is there the presence of both, precisely because of that contradiction.
Nor can one of the two alternatives be accepted, because there is no distinction [between them].
Having encountered this dilemma, the authoritative person hesitates.
And here is the meaning of the individual components: just as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth, when observed as common [to both sides], serve as the cause for two distinct cognitions.
The compound *saṃśayanimitta* is a *bahuvrīhi*, meaning "that which has two cognitions as its cause.
By using the word *nimitta* (cause), it indicates that the two cognitions are merely the causes [of doubt].

For, taking as their cause those two cognitions whose objects are the probandum and its absence, doubt is produced by the non-attainment of either one of the contradictory [alternatives] through the common [feature].
For a single sound cannot be pervaded by both eternality and non-eternality, which are mutually contradictory; indeed,
the coexistence of contradictory properties is observed only when based on a difference in the substrata (dharmin).
Just as space is eternal while a produced substance is non-eternal;

therefore, from this very contradiction of cognition (*pratītivyāghāta*), doubt is considered to arise through the common [reason]. And this same [contradiction] applies to the uncommon [reason] as well.

For even that [reason]— having established the absence of something in what is either permanent or impermanent— becomes a cause for doubt by way of demonstrating the contradiction between the existence of both [alternatives].
And this status of the uncommon [reason] as a cause of doubt is not accepted [by some],
because doubt arises only when both [alternatives] revolve in the mind without a fixed determination.
Furthermore, nothing at all is imparted to the intellect by means of what is unique (asādhāraṇa), because that [unique property] lacks any concomitance (anvaya) with anything else.
Moreover, doubt is observed only regarding things that are limited in scope.
If doubt were produced by way of exclusion (*nivṛtti*), then a "universal" doubt would be produced by an "exclusive" [reason] that is excluded from everything; however,
a doubt whose object is everything has never been observed before,
because it cannot enter into the intellect.
Nor can non-existence everywhere be understood merely by the absence [of a thing] in some particular place,
through which a doubt might arise;
for when positive concomitance (*anuvṛtti*) is not observed, negative exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is not established.

For smoke, which follows fire and is observed to have a negative concomitance (vyatireka), is understood to possess a nature invariably restricted to fire; thus, it is understood that it is excluded from those things where fire is not seen. However, how could the exclusion of that which is not associated with anything at all be cognized as being absent from everything that is capable of being perceived? Therefore, in this manner, a unique (asādhāraṇa) reason does not function as a cause for doubt.

If it is argued that, since entities possessing unique properties (*asādhāraṇadharma*) are observed to partake in both permanence and impermanence, one perceives the earth as having such a property and thus a doubt arises as to whether it is permanent or impermanent—then [we reply]:
in that case, the doubt arises precisely because of the possession of many common properties (*bahusādhāraṇa*), not from the unique property itself;
for the unique property is one thing, and the state of possessing that which is common to many is another.
Therefore, if that [inconclusive reason] has become a cause for doubt, what has been gained by the "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) [reason]?
Alas! In this way, it is established that only the "common" (sādhāraṇa) reason is accepted as the cause of doubt;
the uncommon reason does not possess the status of being a cause of doubt.

Another opinion is as follows: this [doubt] is indeed a cause for non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*). There is, it is said, a specific mode of cognition called "non-determination," and that is produced by this [doubt].
For one who perceives such non-dharma, there arises a cognition whose appearance is indeterminate, in the form "What kind of dharma is this?
And this [cognition] does not possess validity,
because its nature is that of non-ascertainment.
Nor is it a doubt, because it does not touch upon two alternative sides;
thus, this kind of non-determination is produced by the "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) [reason].
However, this is not tenable.
For there is no such mode of cognition as "non-determination" (anadhyavasāya) which it could produce; rather,
non-determination is simply the absence of determination (adhyavasāya).
And because it is of the nature of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), it is not something produced.
Alternatively, if the negative particle (*nañ*) is intended to denote "other than" (as in *abrāhmaṇa* and similar cases), then [the reason] is other than the object of determination;
and their status as having a doubtful cause is stated with respect to the object.

Since the status of being a reason for a conclusion is also observed in another case to be proven—having obtained both exclusion and positive concomitance, as in the case of "immateriality" [proving] "lack of action"]. (Msv 5.4.90)

In that case, it would be denotable by that word; and it has already been stated that its cause is not uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*). Now, suppose the negative particle (*nañ*) has a meaning contrary [to its usual sense], as in the case of *adharma* and so forth.
This being the case, the term "non-determination" (anadhyavasāya) would have to be understood as a negation (*viparyaya*);
however, a contrary apprehension (*viparītāvagraha*) is not produced by that which is non-common (*asādhāraṇa*).
But if "non-determination" is simply the ascertainment of the absence of determination, namely: "I have no determination regarding this object," then [it is not a cognition].
In that case, the absence of determination is understood precisely through the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*);
therefore, the logical reason (*hetu*) has no function there.
Consequently, it must be established that the uncommon [reason] is merely a cause for the desire to know (*jijñāsāmātra*).
For one who perceives that [object], there indeed arises the desire to know: "What kind of property (dharma) is this, such that from this property the entity (bhāva) would come to be?

Even though such a desire may sometimes arise even from the perception of the pure substratum (dharmī), it nevertheless certainly arises by way of the property as well; thus, its being the cause of that [desire] is not untenable.
And it is said:
"Therefore, from unestablished [reasons], there arises ignorance; from a non-exclusive [reason], the desire to know;
and from a general [reason], doubt is appropriate; likewise, [doubt arises] from a counter-argument."
As for what was stated here regarding the uncommon [reason] being a cause of doubt, that is the opinion of others;
for it is intended here to demonstrate the object to be excluded by the term "known relation" (*jñātasambandha*), and that is indeed consistent even if the uncommon [reason] is a cause of doubt.
Let it be that this [reason] may be the cause for anyone at all;
the intended meaning is that in any case, it is excluded by the term "known relation" (*jñātasambandha*).
However, the Śākyas consider the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason to be a cause of doubt.
And they cite "audibility" as a reason when the impermanence of sound is to be proven;
as it has been said:
"The Śākyas generally consider this very [reason] to be inconclusive."
Because it is withdrawn from both, it is like that which persists in both.
Thus;
and this very point was raised by the author of the Vārttika himself at another place and refuted by the aforementioned objections. //88//
Furthermore, is it the case that the things mentioned possess the status of being causes of doubt only by their very nature? No; he says: "The doubtful... (verse 89).
He states the reason with the words "of the determination" up to "having obtained [the end]";
where has this been seen? To this he says: "inactive.
For incorporeality, when permanence is to be proven, was a cause of doubt because it is common to both permanent and impermanent space and action.

That same [property], however, when "actionlessness" is the probandum, attains the status of a reason through positive and negative concomitance; likewise, the possession of fragrance attains the status of a reason for establishing that a certain portion of the earth possesses it.
Or, where the imperceptibility of air is to be proven by its being formless, [the same logic applies].
Either this perceptibility [of sound] is established through contact, or it is presented as being subject to "contradictory non-deviation" (viruddhāvyabhicāritā).
For intangibility is pervaded by the absence of action.
For neither the formless ether nor the self vibrates;
nor is it observed that chariots and the like, which possess those [qualities], are themselves formless. //90//
He demonstrates that the uncommon [reason] is the cause for ascertainment: "In the case of a portion of the earth," etc.
For one who perceives a specific odor and has recognized the pervasion (*vyāpti*), when a portion of the earth is established, there occurs an inferential ascertainment. //90 1/2//
It has been stated that two reasons connected to contradictory meanings constitute a cause for doubt regarding a single substratum.
Regarding this, he provides an example with the words "where... (yatra).
For in a case where one [proponent] establishes that "wind is not an object of direct perception because it is formless," [the other proponent may establish the opposite].
Others also state that from the perception [of one reason], there arises its opposite;
in that case, this constitutes a "non-erroneous contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicāritā*), as asserted by the Śākyas.
Therein, because of the convergence of two reasons of equal strength, doubt arises.
Because there is no difference between the two proofs in that their constituent parts are unestablished;
for the followers of Kaṇāda maintain that that which is formless and inherent in what is formless is imperceptible,
and such is the case with air.
Therefore, it is not perceptible.
They also declare that the intrinsic nature of action is visible because of its inherence in the same object as color;
likewise, touch is well known to belong to air as well.
And because its pervasion is well-established through direct perception,
the two [cognitions] possess equal strength;
consequently, there is doubt.
Because it is impossible for two contradictory things to occur in the same place, because their conjunction is untenable,
because no alternative is possible once a thing is established as real, and because the relationship between the sublated and the sublator would be of equal status.
Therefore, since both [alternatives] are subject to an infinite regress, doubt arises because of their identity;
however, regarding the specific distinction between their strength and weakness, the contradiction with inference has already been described.

When one person says, "The Buddha's word that 'an omniscient one exists' is correct because it was spoken by him, just like statements concerning momentary destruction and so forth," another replies, "The Buddha is not omniscient; my statement is correct because it was spoken by me, just as [it is true that] fire is hot and water is fluid.
In this case, the fact of being "spoken by me" is established for both parties.
However, the fact that [the Veda] was spoken by the Buddha is not unestablished;
therefore, because its constituent parts are unestablished, the former proof is sublated by one whose constituent parts are established by a powerful [means of knowledge].
As for what the Śākyas say—that a "non-erroneous contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārī) is a cause for doubt—[that is incorrect].
And a single [reason] cannot be a cause for doubt, because one or the other must be determined;
nor does the singular number intend to refer to a collection,
because such a collection cannot serve as the locus for the terms "contradictory" and "non-deviating."
For that [reason] indeed deviates by way of its two parts;
however, it should be stated that there are two types of non-deviating contradictory reasons (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*),
and not in the singular.
