If some describe this as a counter-reason (*pratihetu*), while others describe it as a different category of fault (*jātyantara*).

Whether [the reason] is common [to both sides] in part or in its entirety, or whether it is non-concomitant, each individual [reason] does not deviate from a contradictory object; thus it is called "the non-deviating contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*).
Let that be so.
However, it has been stated that a single [reason] is not a cause of doubt;

for this very reason, the author of the Vārttika demonstrated the status of being a cause of doubt by means of a name in the dual number itself: "two [reasons], connected with contradictory objects, are causes of doubt."
Here too, only this much has been stated: "the non-deviation of the contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicāritā*).
It has not been stated that "the non-deviating contradictory is the cause of doubt.
Therefore, in this context, it should be explained as "the non-deviation of these two [reasons] being contradictory," by virtue of their fitness [to produce doubt].
"Two non-erroneous contradictories," according to Yādava. //91½//
Some describe this "contradictory non-erroneousness" (*viruddhāvyabhicāritā*), which is a cause for doubt, as a distinct class from both the common (*sādhāraṇa*) and the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*).
Others, however, maintain that it is a sub-class of the common, because it consists of two parts of the aggregate.

Still others, on the other hand, hold that since this combined pair does not follow upon either [of the two] individually, it is simply the uncommon, characterized by a lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*).
Thus he says: "some.
And in another passage, the author of the Vārttika has demonstrated his adherence to the very point of commonality (*sādhāraṇya*).
As he says:
“And because it is common [to both], no one possesses this [knowledge] exclusively;
for the whole resides in the word ‘common’ through its two parts.
Thus [it is said].
Nor should it be said that because the two do not co-occur, this [reason] is merely "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa).

For if two things were employed by means of a single [term], then it might indeed be so; however, since each is seen to co-occur individually, when both are employed together, they cannot be said to be non-co-occurrent.
Moreover, if it were uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), its status as a cause for doubt would not be tenable,
because that [status] has already been refuted previously.
Therefore, this [reason] is indeed uncommon.

We, however, consider it far better to regard them as belonging to entirely different categories; for just as two things cannot be employed by one [agent] simultaneously and thus lack exclusivity (*asādhāraṇatva*),
so too would they lack commonality (*sādhāraṇatva*) as well.
What, indeed, is common here?
Because each [probans] is employed individually when pervading each [subject] respectively, and because the whole collection— which would be common only in part— is not employed.

For this very reason, the fact that the counter-reason (*pratihetu*) and the contradictory reason (*viruddha*) are causes of doubt has been stated here as distinct from the "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) reason; otherwise, since they would already be included by that [category], they would not be mentioned separately.
Furthermore, the manner in which they generate doubt is indeed different in these cases.

For the common [reason], being observed in both [classes], produces a cognition that is a cause of doubt; however, these two [types of reasons], by each presenting only one [of the two classes], are causes of doubt. Thus it was stated by the author of the Vārttika that they are included within the term "common" (*sādhāraṇa*). Indeed, it is not uncommon.
Thus it is. //92 1/2//
Wherever a thesis is contradicted by the means of proof previously stated [for that same person].
Therefore, a definitive conclusion should not be made [against him], because there is no sublation [of his position];
for those two causes of doubt which were characterized individually [in the previous verse]— // Msv_5.4.94 //
But how is there a determination (*nirṇaya*) regarding such a subject?

To this he says: "By the [five-membered syllogism] beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*) and ending with the conclusion (*nirṇaya*). For one who [is engaged in debate], by means of the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) which have been stated for the purpose of refuting the opponent's position (*pakṣabādha*).
The thesis (*pratijñā*), which is a member of the syllogistic proof (*sādhana-vākya*), is sublated; by that defeat, the determination of the other [position] must be made.

For instance, in this very example, while air is being experienced as immediate through the operation of the tactile sense-organ (*tvag-indriya*), the position of its being remote is sublated by that very experience.
Indeed, for us, the direct perception of air arising from the tactile sense-organ does not differ from the direct perception of water.
For here, it is not mere contact without a substratum that is experienced; rather, the substance which is the locus of that [contact] is also experienced.
Indeed, for one being struck by a powerful wind, there is no difference in consciousness whether water adheres [to the body] or not.

Therefore, following the result of the connection with the sense organ, it is determined that air is perceptible. In some cases, however, there is a sublation of the object by means of scripture, as for example: "The human skull is pure."
When Pāśupata stated, "Because it is a part of a living being,
like a fragment of a conch or mother-of-pearl," another person proves that [the bone] is impure, saying,
"Because it has originated from a living being, like excrement and so forth."
In that case, because the object of the prior proposition is sublated by scripture (āgama), the determination of the matter occurs by means of the subsequent one;
for when distinguishing between purity and its opposite, scripture alone is the refuge. While that [scripture] stands as an obstacle, the inference of purity does not find a footing.
For they remember:
"Having touched a human bone that is still moist, one should enter the water with one's clothes on.

And as for the statement, "Rudra indeed performed the Great Vow; he placed this human head upon himself," this is merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), not an injunction for the wearing of a corpse's head.
And here, it is perception and the other means of knowledge themselves that are called "means of proof" (*sādhana*) because they establish their respective objects.
But how can perception and the others alone be capable of subverting a thesis?
Since even in those cases, subversion might be suspected through the observation of commonality, he says: "because of the avoidance of subversion."
No sublation is observed in those cases; however, the mere possibility of future sublation does not remove their status as valid means of knowledge. //93 1/2//

In this context, by the monk [Dignāga] stating, "The reason is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) that is pervaded by a part of it," it is shown through the singular number that the reason is intended to be one and only one.
For this very reason, two reasons that are contradictory yet non-deviant do not possess the status of being valid reasons, because they are multiple;
however, this is not tenable.
For there is no determination from a combination of a counter-reason and a contradictory reason, like [the simultaneous presence of] height and the presence of a crow;
for neither individually nor even when combined are two non-contradictory reasons capable of producing certain cognition.
Therefore, two reasons with distinct and contradictory meanings have been shown here;
they say that contradiction is sixfold, fourfold, or even singlefold.
Multiplicity is not the cause of doubt;
rather, it is precisely the fact that they bring about two mutually contradictory objects.
For when two contradictory objects are presented together in one place by two [cognitions], people become doubtful regarding them.
It is not, however, because of the multiplicity of causes;
for even in the case of two causes of doubt, when each is individually understood, a definitive determination is observed in some instances precisely from the coexistence of both,
as in the case of "uprightness" and "being possessed of a crow."

For mere verticality alone is common to both a post and a person, and thus it is not capable of determining one or the other. However, when that same verticality is accompanied by the presence of a crow's roosting, it leads to the certain determination: "This is a post. Therefore, in this case, while a single factor serves as the cause of doubt, the determination arises from two factors together; thus, duality is not a necessary condition for being a cause of doubt.
The fact that multiple contradictory properties are established is itself the cause of doubt.

Just as a single common property existing in both the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) becomes a cause of doubt, so too, the very presence of two reasons with contradictory meanings in both parts [of the subject] is the cause for doubt. Therefore, it is not correct to deny the status of being a reason simply because there are two of them; thus he says: "In some cases... (*kvacid*).
Now, it may indeed be appropriate that doubt arises as to whether a tall object is a post or a person; however,
doubt has never before been observed to arise from the mere presence of a crow.
True.

However, for one who wishes to establish that a post exists merely by its resemblance to a crow, that [crow] alone is a cause of doubt; but when accompanied by verticality, it becomes a cause of certainty—it is only this much that is intended to be said, and thus there is no fault.
Moreover, it is observed that even non-contradictory factors, whether individually or combined, can function as a probans (*hetu*) for establishing a certain object;

for example, in the case of verbal cognition being an inference, the properties of "being produced from positive and negative concomitance" (*anvaya-vyatireka-jatva*) and "being a means of knowledge other than perception" (*pratyakṣānya-pramāṇatva*) can establish its inferential nature both individually and collectively.
Furthermore, if the cause for being a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) were simply plurality, then multiple reasons would not be employed for a single probandum (*sādhya*).
Yet, we observe that proponents do employ various means of proof to establish a single probandum, thinking, "This is one thing, and this is another.
Therefore, this doubt is based solely on contradiction.
However, with the intention that [the cognition] is not based on multiplicity, he says: "each individually.

Previously, it was stated that two things which are individually causes of doubt become causes of certainty when combined; here, however, it is demonstrated that even though they are individually indicative, they are also indicative when conjoined. //95//

Therefore, only those two [reasons] that have contradictory meanings should be shown as causes of doubt, and not merely by virtue of being different, as we have stated; thus he says, "Therefore," etc.
The threefold [classification] has been explained.
When there is a sublation of the meaning of the proposition stated by the scripture by means of the reason,
as in the case of "producedness" [as a reason] for "eternality," there is contradiction due to the sublation of the property (*dharma*).
But when there is such a restriction of a specific property, the form of the word would have a meaning even prior to the determination of its relationship [to that meaning]. (Msv 5.4.98)
He sets forth the various types of contradictory reasons (*viparītaprakāra*) for the cause of doubt, stating: "They say there are six kinds of contradiction.

The meaning is that some authorities declare six types of contradiction: those concerning the nature of the property (*dharma*), the nature of the subject (*dharmin*), the particularity of the property, the particularity of the subject, and both their natures and particularities.
However, others maintain a fourfold classification, because the contradictions regarding both [property and subject] do not exceed the individual cases; thus he says: "fourfold."
"But we," he says, "assert only one mode by the mere fact of subverting what is desired," namely: "or even in one way.
The word "or" (*vā*) signifies the exclusion of both the previously mentioned positions.

Alternatively, if it were the case that [the reason] would apply to those who partake of the remainder (*śeṣabhāj*), then the contradiction (*viruddhatva*) would simply be a sublation of the thesis (*pakṣabādha*); what is the point of introducing a further distinction?

He says "of that which is stated by the word" (*śrutyārthoktasya*) because they declare that in all three modes, there is contradiction when there is a sublation of the meaning of the proposition as presented by the word.
That is to say, the nature of the property (*dharma*), the locus (*dharmin*), or both is what is stated by the word.
Their specific particulars are for the most part already expressed by the meaning [of the thesis];
and these, together with their own essential nature and specific characteristics, are included by the term "the meaning of the proposition" (*pratijñārtha*),
for all of them are intended by the speaker.
However, specific attributes such as "dharma" and so forth are not explicitly included within the proposition (*pratijñā*).
Therefore, when that meaning of the proposition is sublated by the reason (*hetu*), the reason becomes contradictory (*viruddha*).
Yet, we consider this to be, as it were, a contradiction in terms.
For how can a reason be contradictory when it is sublated by the meaning of the proposition?
Indeed, that [reason] would be contradictory if it were sublated by the meaning of the proposition itself; for this [sublation] is well-established.
For the fact that a jar is produced is well-established.
It cannot be sublated by an eternality that is not established for [the opponent];

therefore, this should simply be called a "sublating [reason]. However, it should be understood that the author of the Vārttika stated it was "contradictory" merely on the basis of what is established for the other [party].

In that regard, he first illustrates the fallacy of contradiction (*viruddha*) by way of subverting the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the property (*dharma*), [stating]: "If [the subject] were eternal... (97).

He states that a sublation of a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣabādha*) occurs when the argument is formulated in this way, by saying "sublation" (*bādha*). He demonstrates that very formulation with the three quarters [of the verse] beginning "meaningful" (*arthavat*).
For those who maintain that the word denotes its own form (*svarūpābhidhānavādin*) say: "In the cognition 'this is a cow,' the object is understood as qualified by the form of the word."

And since it is impossible to denote a qualified object without first denoting its qualifier, the word must first express its own form (svarūpa) because it possesses grammatical inflection; thus, it is accepted that [the word] exists first by way of its own form.
Subsequently, however, the connection of the word with an external meaning is observed.
Therefore, even prior to the relation [of words], there would be the state of not having the thing itself as its referent;
because it is the cause of the cognition "it is here," [the universal] is distinct from substance and so forth.
Inherence (samavāya) denotes a specific connection, such as "here is this jar" and so forth;
furthermore,
the word "object" (artha) is subject to deviation.
Since the relationship [between word and object] is unknown when it is not yet cognized,
the essential nature (svarūpa) of the object never deviates from its own form, because it is cognized even prior to the determination of that relationship;
and it is logical that the meaning of a word is that which does not deviate.
Therefore, the own-form (*svarūpa*) of words must necessarily be denoted first; however, let it be granted that the denotation of specific qualities may occur at a time subsequent to that denotation.

Having thus established this, they state the formal argument (*prayoga*) at the end: "The own-form of a word possesses a meaning prior to the determination of its relation [to that meaning], because it is connected with case-endings (*vibhakti*)."

For even one who has not grasped the relationship [between word and meaning] understands words joined with case-endings such as *sva* and so forth; and when there is a connection with a case-ending, meaningfulness is observed, just as it is after the relationship has been grasped. But how, when used in this way, does the sublation of a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) occur? To this he says: "And because it is resorted to in its own form."

For when, first relying on the meaningfulness of the word's own form (*svarūpa*), one establishes that it is qualified by meaningfulness in general, then it is understood from the sense of the matter that its meaningfulness in terms of its own form is what is intended to be proven.
And thus, there occurs the sublation (*bādha*) of a specific property (*dharma-viśeṣa*) implied by the sense.
But how is it that when "in its own form" (*svarūpeṇa*) is accepted, the specific property of the dharma is sublated?
To this he says: "not in its own form" (*asvarūpa*).

For the state of possessing case-endings (*vibhaktimattva*), by virtue of its inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), makes known the meaningfulness of the word as something distinct from its own form, that is, as another object.

Because [the word] is perceived as a distinct entity after the apprehension of its relationship [with its meaning], it is therefore established by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*) as being that very same thing characterized by inflection (*vibhaktimat*). Consequently, this reason—that it possesses meaning in its own essential form (*svasvarūpārthavattva*)—contradicts the specific property [of the subject]; thus, there is a sublation of the specific property (*dharmaviśeṣabādha*). //99½//
He states an example of the sublation of the nature of the subject (*dharmin*) itself: "The cause of the cognition 'here' (*ihapratyaya*)," etc.

For when the substratum (*dharmin*) of inherence (*samavāya*) is established and its distinction from substance (*dravya*) and so forth is to be proven, the reason (*hetu*) stated is "being the cause of the cognition 'here'," as in the expression, "This jar is here."
The intended meaning is that since conjunction is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), there is a sublation of the very nature of the subject (*dharmisvarūpabādha*). //100//
In this case as well, the lack of inherence is established, just as it is for conjunction.
Therefore, because it contradicts the actual nature of the subject (*dharmin*), there is a contradiction (*viruddhatā*).
Furthermore, that unity which is imagined for inherence (*samavāya*) as being like existence (*sattā*)— [Msv 5.4.102]
In that case, because it differs from [the property of] being conjoined, there is a contradiction with the specific [property] of "being eternal";
this occurs when someone asserts the eternal existence of the self (ātman) against a Sautrāntika.
When that which is to be proven is invalidated because of the absence of its constituent parts, like space, then this invalidation of both specificities is established. (Msv 5.4.104)
The eyes and other sense organs exist for the sake of another because they are composite, like a bed and so forth;
in the case of a bed, the fact that it exists for the sake of another is due to the reasons of being composed of elements and being pervaded by them.
But how, then, is there a sublation of the nature of the subject (*dharmisvarūpabādha*) in this example?
To this he says: "In this case too.
In this example as well, because the nature of the subject—which consists of inherence—is brought to its opposite, the reason becomes contradictory (*viruddha*).

For it is observed that the state of being the cause of the cognition "here" belongs only to that which has the nature of inherence; therefore, [if the probans were applied otherwise], it would contradict that very nature, resulting in a sublation of the essential nature of the subject (*dharmisvarūpabādha*). //101 1/2//
And since the sublation of a specific property of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣabādha*) must also be demonstrated in this very case, he says: "And that which...
For the followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas) maintain that inherence (*samavāya*), like the universal "existence" (*sattāsāmānya*), is of a single nature.

Yet even that [inherence] of his is sublated because its particularity is undermined by the consequence of its becoming differentiated, just like conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Thus, the reason is one that contradicts a specific property of the subject. //102 1/2//
He provides an example regarding the sublation of both the nature [of the property and the subject]: "The self exists eternally.
When someone proves this to a Sautrāntika—namely, "The self is eternal because it is partless, like space"—then there occurs a sublation of both the property (dharma) and the subject (dharmin).

For the Sautrāntika, the absence of parts is intended to be connected with the absence [of parts] in space itself; thus, it would lead to the conclusion that the self (ātman) is likewise non-existent.
For the Buddhists maintain that space is merely the absence of obstruction, and not a separate ontological entity.
Therefore, because the self lacks parts, its own nature and its property of permanence are both sublated; thus, there is a sublation of both. //103 1/2//
He says "at that time" (tadā) because when this is being proven, there occurs a sublation of both specific qualifications.

For when it is argued that "the eyes and so forth are for the sake of another, because they are composite, like a bed and so forth," at that time there is a sublation of both specific qualifications; such is the meaning.
But how, then, is there a sublation of both specificities here? To this he says: "on the bed" (śayane), that is, on a couch.

The sublation [of the inference] is that its being for the sake of another is unestablished with respect to the self; furthermore, even though it is seen to be composite, it would have to be for the sake of another that is not composite. Msv 5.4.106.

Furthermore, it would follow that the eyes and other sense organs lack the nature of being for the sake of a self (anāhaṅkārikatva). Since the reason—"because of being a composite"—is seen to be pervaded by "being for the sake of another" in the case of a bed, a chair, and so forth, which are composites of the great elements forming a body, it would only establish that they are for the sake of another; whereas what is intended to be established is their being for the sake of the Self.
That [proposition] would not be established.
First of all, that specific property intended for the subject (*dharmin*) of being "for the sake of another"—namely, "being for the sake of the Self"—is sublated by this very reason.
Furthermore, even the specific property of the subjects such as the eye, namely "being composed of *ahaṅkāra*," is likewise sublated by this same reason.
For the state of being composed of a composite whole is observed to be pervaded by non-ahaṅkārika nature in the case of beds and such;
since those are material (bhautika), by that illustration, the eyes and other senses would also be material.

The followers of Kapila (the Sāṅkhyas) assert that the sense organs are derived from ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*); their argument is as follows: the logical reason [employed by the opponent] is pervaded by both "being for the sake of another" (*pārārthya*) and "being composed of material elements" (*bhautikatva*). Since the "being for the sake of another" in the case of the bed is not established as being for the sake of a self (*ātman*), there is first of all a sublation of the specific property (*dharmaviśeṣabādha*).

The sublation of the specific nature of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣabādha*) was already indicated by the pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding the composite nature of material things and will be explained immediately thereafter; thus, not only is the "being-for-the-sake-of-another" of the Self not established, but when one intends for the Self to be-for-the-sake-of-another while being non-composite, the force of the pervasion entails that the Self itself must be composite. To this he says: "non-composite... This reason does not establish that the Self is for the sake of something non-composite.
On the contrary, it would result in our very cohesion. //106//
He explains the sublation of the specific subject (*dharmiviśeṣabādha*) by stating "the state of not being derived from *ahaṅkāra*";
this has already been explained previously. //106 1/2//
Thus, the contradictory (*viruddha*) reason, which is to be excluded by the term "known relation" (*jñātasambandha*), has been explained at length.
Now, those very fallacies of the example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) that are excluded by that [term] must be shown;
for by means of them, the relation that constitutes a member of inference cannot be made known.
Therefore, they too are excluded by the very term "one who has cognized the relation" (jñātasambandha).
And this has already been stated by us previously.
As it is said elsewhere:

"By the statement 'the relationship is known,' the three [fallacies] beginning with the 'uncertain' (aniyata) regarding the reason and the example have been refuted by the author of the Bhāṣya. This was said in order to express that the pervasion (vyāpti) of one part of the indicator (gamaka) is the object to be indicated (gamya). (Msv 5.4.107)
The example based on similarity and dissimilarity with the probandum is established therein;
having indicated the meaning of the reason, the inclusion of the probandum is desired.
The property to be designated (uddeśya) is considered the pervaded (vyāpya), while the other is the pervader (vyāpaka).
The characteristics of the subject to be designated include its connection with the locative case, its being mentioned first, and so forth. (Msv 5.4.109)
"And its occurrence as well as the particle 'eva' would constitute the definition of the probans (upādeya-lakṣaṇa).
Therefore, in order to refute that [position], he first introduces the statement regarding the example with the words "of the indicator" (gamakasya).

To demonstrate pervasion (*vyāpti*), two kinds of examples must first be shown in the argumentative statement (*sādhana-vākya*). The meaning is that the example which, through similarity or dissimilarity with the probandum (*sādhya*)—namely the subject (*pakṣa*)—is presented, is what is being explained. //107½//
In that regard, he states the method of the example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*)—the word "therein" (*tatra*).
Its meaning is as follows: the statement that the logical mark (*liṅga*) establishes [the probandum] through its similarity to the example is the "reason" (*hetu*), as they say:
"The reason is that which establishes the probandum through its similarity to the example."
This means that it is the statement that makes known the probandum (*sādhya*). Its meaning is indeed the logical mark (*liṅga*).
And with reference to that [mark], the formulation of the probandum is intended as the similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

"Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire"—to what extent does this apply? To answer this, he says: "the subject" (*uddeśya*). It has been stated that the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is for the purpose of demonstrating pervasion (*vyāpti*).
And thus, when being taken up [as the subject], the object to be indicated, such as smoke, is stated as that which is pervaded;
whereas the other, the thing to be taken up, such as fire, becomes the pervader—this has been explained. //108 1/2//
But what is the nature of those two? To this he says: "yadvṛtta" (that which occurs in which).
By the terms "yadvṛtta" and "tadvṛtta," there is the inclusion of words such as "ya" and "tat" which have been fully established;
thus, this is the meaning that results.

Whatever is first employed in connection with a particular grammatical form (*vṛtta*) and is the primary object of reference (*uddeśya*), that very thing—when subsequently employed in connection with that same grammatical form and joined with the particle *eva* (only)—is the thing to be enjoined (*upādeya*). It should be understood that this same distinction between the object of reference and the thing to be enjoined applies to all cases, such as the cleansing of the cups (*graha*) and the threshing of the rice (*vrīhi*). //109 1/2//
And a word expresses its meaning according to its own capacity, independent of the speaker.
The status of things as probandum and probans arises from the conformity to the power of pervasion;
therein, when a speaker, due to ignorance, intends to express coexistence— Msv_5.4.111.
Or else, by way of the opposite, he does not intend to express pervasion in the reason;
or even if he intends to express it, he would not state the word [indicating] its connection. (Msv 5.4.112)
In a jar, perishability is pervaded by being produced, or [producedness] is pervaded by perishability;
therefore, that [perishability] would not be the cause of what is desired, nor would it be the cause of what is undesired.
But what, then, is the purpose of such a restriction on the application [of words]?
For words are dependent upon the speaker's intention;
whether they are employed in this way or that, they will certainly function according to the intended meaning.
Therefore, he says: "it speaks.
Words are not dependent upon the intention of the speaker;
rather, by their own inherent power, they function toward specific meanings in specific instances.

Therefore, since the desired conclusion cannot be established merely by following one's own intention, the manner of arranging the statement of the example must indeed be explicitly articulated. //110//

If, then, words were independent, the desired proof would follow the words even when the object is not established as such; therefore, he says: "The state of being the probandum and the reason. The intention is this: the power of the object does not proceed by conforming to the power of the word, nor does the power of the word [conform] to the power of the object.
Therefore, the power of a word does not follow the intended meaning of the speaker;
likewise, the determination of meaning does not follow the word.

Consequently, the relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the reason (*hetu*)—such as the producedness (*kṛtakatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*) of objects and so forth—occurs solely in accordance with the power of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and not in accordance with the word. //110 1/2//

He demonstrates what follows when words convey a meaning solely through their own power, independent of the speaker, by means of two and a half verses beginning with "tatrājñānāt" (In that case, due to ignorance).

For instance, when a speaker who is unskilled in providing an example intends merely to express the coexistence of the probandum and the reason—as in the formal argument: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced."
Just as [one might say] "producedness and perishability exist in a jar," or,
through a mistaken apprehension, one does not intend to express the pervasion of the reason;
or even when such an intention exists, due to some cause of error, one utters a word that is unfit for expressing pervasion.

However, one might assert— as before— either mere coexistence, or conversely, that there is a mistaken notion because non-existence is not pervaded by being produced; in that case, not only is the intended [proposition] not established, but rather the opposite of what is unintended follows from the reversal of the pervasion.
Therefore, that which is intended [to be proven] should be stated as the reason in the form of being pervaded;
for even when sentences are correctly employed, the meaning might not turn out accordingly. (Msv 5.4.114)
Because it is ultimately devoid of the pervasion of both the probandum and the reason,
[the argument] "sound is eternal because it is formless, like action or like an atom" is fallacious.
Even against one who asserts that [the subject] is non-existent— just like a jar or like space—
even if the locus (*dharmin*) is not established, there would likewise be the fallacy of the example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsatā*).

Furthermore, even though space is said to exist and to be endowed with both [properties], because one observes its lack of action and so forth, there is no pervasion of the reason; thus, it is excluded.

The property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) would not function as a logical reason (*hetu*), whereas perishability (*nāśitva*), which is precisely what is undesired [by the opponent], would instead be so; therefore, it is appropriate to establish a rule for the employment of examples in order to prevent such undesirable applications. He concludes this very point with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
The meaning is that [the reason] must be stated in the form of being pervaded by "being produced" (kṛtakatva) and so forth, which is recognized as the state of being a cause (hetutva). //113 1/2//
He demonstrates what occurs when meanings are dependent upon words with the following two lines beginning with "yadā hi.

The meaning of this is as follows: for when the status of things as probandum (*sādhya*) and reason (*hetu*) is established solely by virtue of their pervasion (*vyāpti*), then even if the speaker has not merely shown coexistence (*sahabhāva*), the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is nonetheless perfectly correct.

The meaning is as follows: since the entities [of the examples] do not abide in a relationship of pervader and pervaded that corresponds to that [intended relationship], there would be the status of a "pseudo-example" (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsatā*). This connects with what will be stated hereafter. For instance, in the formal argument (*prayoga*) "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal," regarding the examples—action (*karman*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), a pot (*ghaṭa*), and space (*vyoman*)—there is, respectively, a lack of the actual pervasion of both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the reason (*hetu*).
Indeed, action is impermanent; thus, it is devoid of the eternity that constitutes the probandum.
Since you claim that the reason is "immaterial," it indeed exists therein;
however, atoms are material, so the reason is absent in them,
whereas the property to be proven— eternality— does indeed exist in them.

In the case of the jar (*ghaṭa*), however, neither the probandum (*sādhya*)—eternality (*nityatva*)—nor the reason (*hetu*)—incorporeality (*amūrtatva*)—is present; thus, there is an absence of both. As for the ether (*vyoman*) as an example, the author himself will later explain its lack of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Furthermore, when this very argument is employed against the Sautrāntika, who denies the existence of ether, using the example "like ether," it fails due to the non-establishment of the locus (*dharmyasiddhi*).
He states that this constitutes a fallacy of the example (dṛṣṭāntābhāsatā), saying: "that [example] of one who speaks what is non-existent" (tadasadvādinam). //116//
He explains the absence of pervasion [in the following]: "Even when that exists.
And although similarity has been stated by way of pervasion, dissimilarity is not required.
But when, through the view that things arise together, one does not perceive the pervasion (vyāpti), [one should apply the counter-example].
When the speaker does not rely on an example of similar nature (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta),
or when he states its pure concomitance (sahabhāvitva) with that [reason].
Or even if the sequence is reversed, with the intention of establishing that [same point],
then the existence of space would follow;
and that [existence] is endowed with both the reason and the probandum, because of its eternity and its incorporeality.
Nevertheless, since the pervasion of the reason does not exist when considering non-material and impermanent things such as karma, even such an example must be rejected;
for this [example] also is not capable of establishing the probandum. //117//
The example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), along with its fallacies, has been explained.
Hereafter, he will explain the example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
In this regard, first of all, the following must be stated:
Should a statement of dissimilarity always be made alongside a statement of similarity, or not?

Regarding this, he addresses those who maintain that it must always be stated by those who prioritize negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), saying: "When similarity has been stated through pervasion (*vyāpti*).
He thinks as follows: the statement of an example is indeed for the purpose of making known the pervasion.
If that [pervasion] has already been made known by the statement of similarity, what is the purpose of the statement of dissimilarity?
Furthermore, similarity must necessarily be stated for the sake of making the positive concomitance (anvaya) known,
since inference has that as its primary basis.
Since the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is also established by means of that very [positive concomitance],
for otherwise it would be difficult to comprehend;
therefore, if the similarity accompanied by pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been stated, [the negative concomitance is likewise established].
"Enough with the statement of dissimilarity.
When, then, should the dissimilarity be stated? To this he replies with the three quarters [of the verse] beginning with "by the observation of coexistence":

when the speaker has correctly stated the example, but the opponent listener understands that by this mere mention of the coexistence of the reason and the probandum, pervasion (*vyāpti*) has not been established.

In that case, the phrase "establishing the desired [conclusion] by way of dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyeṇeṣṭasādhana*)—which will be mentioned later—is connected to the purpose of making known the absence of the reason (*hetu*) when the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent.

Indeed, when one who has practiced the method of dissimilarity relies on that alone and not on a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), then he says "establishing the desired [conclusion] by way of dissimilarity. Or, as for the phrase "or when he does not rely on it": this refers to when the speaker, being poorly trained in dissimilarity and ignorant of how to state similarity, expresses merely a coexistence with that similar instance, which is devoid of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Even then, he states that when questioned, one must establish the desired [conclusion] by means of that very same dissimilarity (vaidharmya): "Or the speaker," etc. (119).

Or when one who is confused demonstrates a reversed positive concomitance (*anvaya*), even then, with the desire to rectify that, by means of subverting the previous erroneous cognition through a negative concomitance (*vaidharmya*), he states that it establishes the desired [conclusion]: "a reversed positive concomitance. By subverting the previous cognition, it establishes the desired [conclusion] through a negative concomitance. (Msv 5.4.120)
Only the aforementioned linguistic convention is employed as the reason in that case;
for such is the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader (vyāpya-vyāpaka-bhāva) that is accepted between two entities.
Therefore, from the absence of those two, the opposite is perceived;
since the presence of smoke is pervaded by the presence of fire, non-fire is excluded from it.
"Smoke must exist only where there is fire"—thus it attains the state of being pervaded (vyāpyatva).
Likewise, since smoke is pervaded by the absence of fire in the case of non-fire, smoke is excluded from that [non-fire].

Because there is no other possibility, it is certainly pervaded by fire. [Objection: But if the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is absent, let that very point be demonstrated as it is; what is the use of stating the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*)?
[Reply: True, even so, the desired conclusion is indeed established.

However, this was stated by us under a misconception—that by the method of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) alone, one intends to establish the absence of the reason when the probandum is absent—and thus it would indeed serve as a proof for what is desired. As for that mere concomitance (sāhityamātra) mentioned previously, it is useful only in the context of dissimilarity; it functions as an aid to that very [method] which establishes the desired [conclusion]. Thus he says: "mere concomitance. //120 1/2//
Thus, the occasion for stating the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*) has been shown;
now he demonstrates the manner of stating it: "For the relation of the pervaded and the pervader... (121 1/2).
He states the reason for the contrapositive: "the presence of smoke" (*dhūmabhāva*).

For when the presence of smoke is pervaded by the presence of fire, then the absence of fire—that is, the non-existence of fire—being excluded from that smoke, results in the absence of smoke itself in what is not smoke; in this way, it is pervaded.
For when something exists only when another thing exists, and does not exist when that other thing is absent, it is said to be restricted to that [other] and pervaded by it;
just as smoke, existing only when fire is present, is pervaded by fire. Thus, the contrapositive of the pervasion between two absences is established. //122 1/2//

And because there is such a relationship of pervader and pervaded between two absences, it is for this very reason that the desired pervasion between two positive entities is established; thus he says: "In the same way, in the case of non-fire. When non-fire—that is, the absence of fire—is pervaded by the absence of smoke, smoke finds no room there due to the pervasion of its opposite and occurs only in fire; in this manner, its status as being pervaded by that [fire] is established. "In the same way" means: * **The pervasion of the positive entity:** Just as the absence of fire is pervaded by the absence of smoke, so too is fire pervaded by smoke. * **The establishment of the pervasion:** Since the absence of fire is pervaded by the absence of smoke, smoke cannot exist where fire is absent. Consequently, smoke exists only where fire is present, and thus its pervasion by fire is proven. This is the method for establishing the pervasion of a positive entity through the negation of its contradictory. This is the logical procedure for proving the pervasion of a positive entity. This concludes the discussion on the proof of pervasion. Now, the author will state the definition of the probans (*sādhana*). The definition of the probans is stated as follows: "The probans is that which possesses the three characteristics. What are these three characteristics? They are: (1) presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), (2) presence in the similar instance (*sapakṣasattva*), and (3) absolute absence from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣāsattva*). These three characteristics are explained in detail in the section on the definition of the probans. This concludes the section on the proof of pervasion. Now, the author will explain the refutation of the opponent's view regarding the nature of the probans. The opponent argues: "If the probans is defined merely by the three characteristics, then even a fallacious probans (*hetvābhāsa*) would become a valid probans, because it also possesses those three characteristics. To refute this, the author says: "The probans is that which possesses the three characteristics and is not sublated by a counter-argument. What is a counter-argument? It is an argument that establishes a conclusion contrary to the one intended by the proponent. An example is: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced. Here, "producedness" is the probans. Its three characteristics are as follows: (1) it exists in the subject (sound), (2) it exists in the similar instance (e.g., a pot), and (3) it is absent from the dissimilar instance (e.g., space). However, this probans is sublated by the counter-argument: "Sound is non-eternal, because it is produced. Since it is sublated, it is not a valid probans. Therefore, the definition of the probans must include the condition of being "not sublated. This concludes the refutation of the opponent's view. Now, the author will explain the classification of the probans. The probans is classified into two types: the essential probans (*svabhāvahetu*) and the causal probans (*kāryahetu*). The essential probans is, for example: "This is a tree, because it is a *śimśapā*. Here, "being a *śimśapā*" is the probans. Its three characteristics are: (1) it exists in the subject (this object), (2) it exists in the similar instance (trees), and (3) it is absent from the dissimilar instance (non-trees). The causal probans is, for example: "There is fire here, because there is smoke. Here, "smoke" is the probans. Its three characteristics are: (1) it exists in the subject (this place), (2) it exists in the similar instance (places with fire), and (3) it is absent from the dissimilar instance (places without fire). This concludes the classification of the probans. Now, the author will explain the fallacies of the probans (*hetvābhāsa*). The fallacies of the probans are fivefold: (1) the unestablished (*asiddha*), (2) the contradictory (*viruddha*), (3) the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), (4) the sublated (*bādhita*), and (5) the mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). (1) The unestablished probans is, for example: "Sound is visible, because it is a substance. Here, "being a substance" is the probans. Its first characteristic—existence in the subject—is unestablished, because sound is not a substance but a quality. (2) The contradictory probans is, for example: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced. Here, "being produced" is the probans. Its third characteristic—absence from the dissimilar instance—is established, but its second characteristic—presence in the similar instance—is contradictory, because nothing that is produced is eternal. (3) The inconclusive probans is, for example: "Sound is eternal, because it is knowable. Here, "knowability" is the probans. Its three characteristics are established, but it is inconclusive because it applies to both eternal things (like space) and non-eternal things (like a pot). (4) The sublated probans is, for example: "Fire is cold, because it is a substance. Here, "being a substance" is the probans. Its three characteristics are established, but it is sublated by the perception that fire is hot. (5) The mistimed probans is, for example: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced after effort. Here, "being produced after effort" is the probans. Its three characteristics are established, but it is mistimed because the effort was made before the sound was heard. This concludes the explanation of the fallacies of the probans. Now, the author will explain the types of inference. Inference is of two types: inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) and inference for others (*parārthānumāna*). Inference for oneself is the knowledge of the object derived from the three-characteristic probans. Inference for others consists of the statement of the three-characteristic probans. This concludes the explanation of the types of inference. Now, the author will explain the members of the syllogism (*avayava*). The members of the syllogism are five: (1) the proposition (*pratijñā*), (2) the reason (*hetu*), (3) the example (*udāharaṇa*), (4) the application (*upanaya*), and (5) the conclusion (*nigamana*). (1) The proposition is, for example: "Sound is non-eternal. (2) The reason is: "Because it is produced. (3) The example is: "Whatever is produced is non-eternal, like a pot. (4) The application is: "And sound is produced. (5) The conclusion is: "Therefore, sound is non-eternal. This concludes the explanation of the members of the syllogism. Now, the author will explain the purpose of the members of the syllogism. The purpose of the proposition is to state the object of the inference. The purpose of the reason is to show the pervasion. The purpose of the example is to show the existence of the pervasion. The purpose of the application is to show the presence of the probans in the subject. The purpose of the conclusion is to restate the proposition as something now proven. This concludes the explanation of the purpose of the members of the syllogism. Now, the author will explain the refutations of the members of the syllogism. The refutations of the members of the syllogism are: (1) the refutation of the proposition (*pratijñādoṣa*), (2) the refutation of the reason (*hetudoṣa*), (3) the refutation of the example (*udāharaṇadoṣa*), (4) the refutation of the application (*upanayadoṣa*), and (5) the refutation of the conclusion (*nigamanadoṣa*). (1) The refutation of the proposition is, for example: "Fire is cold. (2) The refutation of the reason is, for example: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced. (3) The refutation of the example is, for example: "Whatever is produced is eternal, like space. (4) The refutation of the application is, for example: "And sound is not produced. (5) The refutation of the conclusion is, for example: "Therefore, sound is eternal. This concludes the explanation of the refutations of the members of the syllogism. Now, the author will explain the types of debate (*vāda*). Debate is of two types: formal debate (*vāda*) and destructive debate (*jalpa*). Formal debate is a discussion between a proponent and an opponent who seek the truth. Destructive debate is a discussion where the parties seek victory over each other. This concludes the explanation of the types of debate. Now, the author will explain the rules of debate. The rules of debate are: (1) the presentation of the thesis, (2) the refutation of the opponent's

The meaning is that just as there is pervasion by non-existence (abhāvavyāpti) in dependence on pervasion by existence (bhāvavyāpti), so too there is pervasion by existence in dependence on pervasion by non-existence.
Nor does this result in mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayatā), because it is established as being beginningless, like the relationship between a seed and a sprout. //123 1/2//
But when existence and non-existence are both said to be pervasive, then from that [it follows].
In that case, there would be no mention of the exclusion of the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) from the pervaded;
therefore, when one seeks to establish fire by means of smoke, [the pervasion must be stated].
In that case, it must be stated that non-fire is pervaded by non-smoke, and not otherwise;
for if there were a coexistence of non-fire and non-smoke, the pervasion would be reversed.
There would be no benefit to the subject at hand, nor could anything else be established,
even in a case where the meaning is void of both or either one of the two.
But what is the purpose of resorting to the reversal of pervasion (*vyāpti*) between two absences? To this he says: "Because [the absence] is the pervader" (*vyāpakatvāt*).

For when a particular presence (*bhāva*) is the pervader, its very absence is stated as the instance of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) by virtue of being the pervader; in that case, there would be no mention of the non-deviation of the pervaded—such as smoke—from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), such as the absence of fire.
Furthermore, the statement of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-vacana) would have no purpose for the sake of that [demonstration].

For when it is stated that "where there is smoke, there is fire," just as one might say "where there is an absence of smoke, there is an absence of fire," the exclusion of the opposite case (vipakṣa)— namely, the absence of fire— from the pervaded (vyāpya), which is smoke, is not thereby demonstrated.

Therefore, by one who wishes to establish fire through smoke, the reversal of the pervasion between the absence of fire and the absence of smoke must be stated by means of a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Thus he says: "Therefore... [must be] stated" (ending with *anta*).

The meaning is that the relationship of the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*) must be shown by way of their non-occurrence—that is, by stating: "Wherever there is no fire, there is no smoke.
And when this non-fire is said to be pervaded by the absence of smoke, it must not be stated otherwise.

However, he states that it is only by means of the mode of the subject and the predicate as expressed through similarity—namely, "and not otherwise"—for the mode has just been explained immediately prior. 124, 125 1/2.
He states the fault in speaking otherwise [than the truth] with the words: "in the absence of concomitance between fire and smoke.

Just as it was stated that in the case of a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), the word expresses its meaning through its own power and does not depend on the power of the object—such that if one speaks merely of concomitance or if there is a reversal of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the desired conclusion is not established—so too it is here; this is the sense. //126 1/2//

Thus, in this case as well, the meaning does not depend on the word; therefore, where the meaning takes the form of an example and is devoid of either both the reason and the probandum or one of them,
there too no assistance toward the subject at hand is rendered, or rather, something undesirable follows.
Thus he says: "Even where...
The sense is that even when sentences are correctly employed, the desired goal is not achieved because the meaning does not depend upon them.
He provides an example for this:
That which is impermanent is indeed material, like an atom, like a cognition, or like space;
for here, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is stated in order to establish the pervasion with the probandum.
That which lacks this cause is not established by that probandum; therefore, even when concomitance is observed, it is not held that everything [possessing it] is necessarily understood.
Co-observation is not a [necessary] relation, nor is it pervasion (vyāpti) merely by that much;
for even though a jar is accepted as being endowed with both corporeality and impermanence.
Regarding the word "yat":

in the very same formal argument— "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal"— when such a dissimilarity (vaidharmya) is stated as "whatever is not eternal is also not incorporeal, like an atom," then the example is devoid of the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva-śūnya).
Because the atom is eternal, it is impossible to demonstrate its non-existence therein;
as for the example "like cognition," there is an absence of the reason [in the subject],
because cognition is formless, and thus its non-existence cannot be asserted.
The term *khavat* refers to the emptiness of the absence of both [existence and non-existence];
for since it is eternal and formless, the absence of both is difficult to comprehend therein. //127½//

In this way, just as with a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), one must demonstrate that [the reason] is fallacious even when it lacks pervasion (*vyāpti*). For it is precisely for the sake of establishing that [pervasion] that the exclusion of the reason from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is stated.
However, for that [reason] which lacks exclusion even from a portion of the dissimilar instances, [there is no pervasion].
With the intention that such a dissimilarity (vaidharmya) is useless because it is not pervaded by the probandum (sādhya) when there is no pervasion (vyāpti), he says: "By the probandum... [128 1/2].

And because such a thing is not pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*), he says "by that" (*tena*): even if the coexistence of two absences is observed in some instances, the relationship of the signifier and the signified (*gamya-gamakabhāva*) does not necessarily exist everywhere.
For example, although it may be the case that whatever is not eternal is also not incorporeal, as in the case of a jar or a wall...
In some cases, the coexistence of two absences can be demonstrated;
nevertheless, this does not apply to all [instances],
such as sound and so forth.
By this reason, it is intended that [the subject] is understood as being qualified by permanence;
for some incorporeal things, such as space (ākāśa) and so forth, are permanent, while others, such as karma and so forth, are impermanent—this is the sense. //129//
Why is this not accepted? To this he says: "because it is observed together.
For by the exclusion from only a portion of the counter-examples (*vipakṣa*), only mere coexistence (*sahabhāva*) of the reason is established;
and a relation consisting of that alone is not a constituent part of inference.
What then? It is pervasion (vyāpti). And this is not established by mere coexistence (sāhitya) alone.
He demonstrates this very point by means of an example: "even when [the property of] being corporeal is conjoined with impermanence."
This has already been explained previously. //130 1/2//

On this point, the Buddhists say: "Why is this? Because there is no pervasion (vyāpti) with respect to karma and so forth, it is not accepted as an example; and because it depends on everything without exception, and because it is easy [to find] yet remains unseen. (Msv 5.4.131)
Although negative concomitance (vyatireka) is accepted here as a means of proof for inference,
its lack of status as a constituent factor will nevertheless be explained in the *Yuktisastika* regarding verbal cognition.
It is said: "When positive concomitance (*sādharmya*) has been stated through pervasion (*vyāpti*), negative concomitance (*vaidharmya*) is not required.

For if there is even a hundredth part of doubt regarding the reason's exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), its capacity to produce knowledge (*gamakatva*) does not exist; thus, the entire counter-example must be required by the inferer to grasp that exclusion. And this [exclusion] is not difficult to ascertain.
Because it is easy to not see anything even when one is situated in only one place;
for while seeing all opposing factors is difficult, their absence is attained with ease.
Nor should it be said that this non-perception is incapable of establishing the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason due to the non-perception of what is unperceivable;
for we do not maintain that the necessity of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva-niyama*) arises from the mere non-perception of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*),
but rather that it is based on identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*).

However, when an opposing factor (*vipakṣa*) stands as an obstacle to the reason (*hetu*), the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) becomes impossible to grasp; and since that [invariable concomitance] does not exist even for one who stands in only a single part [of the field], the observation of its mere presence in the opposing factor is what functions [to establish it].

Therefore, as soon as it is understood that smoke is the effect of fire, it is simultaneously known that its acquisition of self-existence (*ātmalābha*) is dependent upon that [fire], and thus it does not occur in its absence.
Furthermore, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone is not the basis for the cognition of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*),
because that is impossible in the case of unique particulars (*asādhāraṇa*).
For there is no observation elsewhere of the specific characters (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire and smoke seen in the kitchen, once they have ceased to exist right there.
By what means could positive concomitance (anvaya) be experienced?
From where, then, could that [concomitance] arise, and from where, even more so, could negative concomitance (vyatireka), which is based upon it, arise?
Furthermore, among particulars (viśeṣa), there exists no such thing as a universal (sāmānya) that possesses a recurring intrinsic nature (svarūpa).
If it were to be determined through a relationship of the constrained and the constraint, that would be impossible because it is of the nature of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, certain particularities (*viśeṣa*) themselves, when characterized by some form of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), bring about the understanding of a specific [logical] property by way of its exclusion from heterogeneous instances (*vipakṣa*). For the purpose of demonstrating this, there is indeed the statement of dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-vacana*).
He replies to them with the passage ending in "aśeṣa-yukti":
this is the intended meaning— although negative concomitance (vyatireka) is a constituent of inference,
it is not established by mere non-observation alone.
Furthermore, its occurrence is established even by its arrival from that place;

nor does the determination of its being an effect imply its non-existence in the absence of a cause, because that very [non-existence] is difficult to ascertain in the absence of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
For that which exists when something else exists, and does not exist when it does not exist, is its effect;
therefore, the non-existence of difference [in the absence of consciousness] will not entail the consequence of non-consciousness, because there is no pervasion [between the two].
There exists a commonality among these things; let that pervasiveness be understood therein.
It must be understood that [the object] is the effect; however, if that [effect] were dependent upon it [the cognition],
there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayatā).
Or, let there be a distinction [of the subject] from mere perception, and let that be easy to establish; nevertheless, this much does not make reasoning a non-factor with respect to inference.
"Reasoning" (*yukti*), "yoga," "connection" (*sambandha*), and "concomitance" (*anvaya*) are synonymous.
This means that concomitance is not something that is not a constituent factor [of inference],
because for all cognizers, the arising of inference occurs precisely by way of that [concomitance].
Therefore, for the sake of explaining that, even a similar instance (sādharmyadṛṣṭānta) must indeed be stated;
it cannot be rejected absolutely. And this statement is made as a concession.
The established doctrine is exactly as stated: in a correct application based on similarity (*sādharmya*), dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) need not be required.
This is because positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone is primary, since negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) cannot be established without it.
For once the connection of smoke with fire is understood, the exclusion of non-fire is established by implication (*arthāt*).
Therefore, it should first be shown by way of affirmation (*vidhimukhena*), while its dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) may occasionally be mentioned on a later occasion.

As for those who read "anaṅgatvam" (non-membership), this is their explanation: for this constitutes the membership (*aṅgatva*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*) in inference, namely its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekau*).
For it is by means of those two that something becomes a constituent part (*aṅga*).
Therefore, just as being a constituent part consists in exclusion (*vyatireka*), why should reasoning (*yukti*), which is another name for inclusion (*anvaya*), not be the same?

Now, one might object that even in the case of a mark (*liṅga*) consisting of words, the subsequent connection (*anvaya*) occurring after the cognition is certainly not an auxiliary factor; therefore, he says: "In the verbal [cognition], it will be explained.
For it will be stated that in the case of verbal [cognition], which is distinct from inference, the reasoning (*yukti*) occurring after the cognition is not an auxiliary factor.
As he will say:
"This [positive] concomitance cannot be a constituent factor for cognitions of meaning";
however, in inference, positive concomitance is everywhere a constituent factor for comprehension.

As for those who explain that one must supply the phrase "the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not non-a constituent part [of inference] by that much alone," and claim that a logical justification for this very point will be stated in the section on verbal cognition (*śābda*), their first fault is the supplying of an unmentioned *anvaya*.
Furthermore, no logical justification for *anvaya* being a constituent part of inference will be stated in the section on verbal cognition.
For it has been stated in this very context by the phrase "whose relation is known" (*jñātasambandha*).
For this very reason, he will state that the dependence of inference upon positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is established.
Therefore, the explanation is exactly as stated. //132//

As for the objection that, in the case of inference, it is only particulars (*bheda*) that stand in the relation of the signified and the signifier, and that no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is possible among them, he replies with the words "the consequence of [universal] cognition" (*bodhaprasaṅga*).
There is no consequence of the relation of signified and signifier being restricted solely to particulars within inferential cognition.
Because they do not pervade all places and times, but are restricted to each individual instance;
nor, even when pervasion has been stated in a similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), is there anything [that remains unestablished] without that [pervasion].
They also accept the statement of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) out of a desire for the restriction of exclusion (vyāvṛtti).
When the reason has been ascertained through a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) by means of the probandum alone,
it is possible to experience the restriction (*niyama*) that another entity of that same kind exists;
and since that [restriction] is not possible when such an instance is absent, the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in those cases does not constitute a fault.
If there is no consequence of perceiving differences,
then for whom has this been shown?
There is no single, ultimate form whatsoever that follows after difference.
Because it has the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
And although at present inference arises only through the superimposition of a form known by convention as a pervasion (*vyāpti*), nevertheless,
since a precise investigation of that [form] is impossible, this is merely an error (*vibhrama*).
If this is so, then inference, which functions by superimposing a non-existent form, is simply not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
True;

however, by the force of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), a certain particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is apprehended through some conceptual form as a universal essence (*sāmānyātman*), and that very same particular characteristic, though merely delineated by another conceptual form, is thereby brought to realization.

That is designated as "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). For non-contradiction (*avisavāda*) is not the cause of validity; rather, the stability of purposeful action (*arthakriyāsthiti*) is non-contradiction. As they say: "Valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge; the stability of purposeful action [is its characteristic]."

"Non-deceptive" means that in the case of inference, there is the attainment of a real entity capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), preceded by the appearance of that entity; therefore, inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
As it has been said:
"Because of grasping at what is not that [the object], there is error; because it is not non-exclusive, it is not a valid means of knowledge.
Therefore, it is only among distinct things (*bheda*) that there can be the relationship of the signified and the signifier.
And since they do not constitute a basis for positive concomitance (*anvaya*), what has been said is indeed correct. To this he says: "It exists."
The meaning of this is as follows:
this would indeed be so if there were no such thing as a universal (*sāmānya*) that is distinct from the individual differences;
however, since it does exist, we shall establish its existence in the *Ākṛti* chapter by refuting all the objections raised by others.
And since its pervasion across multiple places and times is understood, it is not an unfit object for positive concomitance (*anvaya*);
nor is there a misapprehension of that [pervasion] as being in what is not that,
because it is ultimately real.
And thus, whatever pretext others may resort to for the sake of establishing the validity of inference, that too is merely a weak argument. //133//
Another opinion holds that even when a positive example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) has been stated by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*), a negative example (*vaidharmya*) must also be stated;
he introduces this view with the three quarters of the verse beginning with "some" (*kecit*).
As for the reason for such a desire, he says: "by the desire for a restriction of exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti-niyama-icchayā*). //134//
He explains this very point with the words "in the case of the reason" (*hetau*).
For they think as follows:
when indeed...
Exclusion from everything has been attained; it is restricted to the absence of the probandum.
But that is of little consequence, because it has been established in this way even for a fortnight;
for the mere absence of the pervader necessarily excludes the pervaded.
Therefore, just as when the whiteness of a cloth is mentioned, there is the exclusion of its opposites but not of its length and so forth, so it will be in this case as well.
However, a twofold [classification] is not tenable, just as in the case of fire and smoke. In this regard,

regarding the example of similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), when one points out "where there is smoke" and then applies the restrictive particle *eva* in the form "there is fire alone," if the reason is thus determined by the probandum— fire alone— then it follows that the reason is excluded from everything other than fire.
And this is not possible,

because it would entail the non-existence of even the locus of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), which would result in the fallacy of the reason not being a property of the subject (apakṣadharmatva),
and because it would entail the non-existence of the subject itself (pakṣābhāva).
Therefore, the statement of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) is always meaningful for the purpose of restricting the exclusion [of the reason] solely to the absence of the probandum;
for when that [statement] exists, it is made known that "in the absence of fire, smoke does not exist," whereas [without it] it would be understood as "it does exist. //135//
He refutes this as well, stating: "But that has little fruit.
The meaning is that this statement of dissimilarity (vaidharmya), when formulated in such a manner, yields little result.
To the question "How does it have little fruit?", he says: "Because..."
To explain what has been established, he says: "For it is merely the state of being a pervader.

This was established in the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*), "The mountain possesses fire," according to the principle: "The restriction [of the reason] is postulated from its counter-examples (*vipakṣa*), and not from that which is non-contradictory."

Therefore, even in the case of a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), one must demonstrate only the exclusion of the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka-abhāva-nivṛtti*) for the smoke and so forth that are the pervaded (*vyāpya*), and not the exclusion of anything else. //136//
Establishing this very point through an illustrative statement, he concludes with the words "Therefore":
"In this context, three [members] are recognized— namely, the proposition (pratijñā), the reason (hetu), and the example based on similarity (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta)."
In the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, the parts of a sentence are generally those of existent things.
And this has been demonstrated by the author of the Bhāṣya himself, because it is based on the three terms: the example, the reason, and the thesis.
Thus [ends verse 137].

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "That [inference] is of two kinds: that in which the connection is perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣato dṛṣṭasambandha*) and that in which the connection is perceived through general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭasambandha*).
Among these, an example of that in which the connection is perceived through direct observation is the cognition of the form of fire from seeing the form of smoke;

and an example of that in which the connection is perceived through general observation is the recollection of motion in the sun, having observed that Devadatta’s arrival at another location is preceded by motion."
By this, it is stated that because there are two kinds of objects of cognition (*prameya*), there are two kinds of inference (*anumāna*).

On this point, some who consider themselves experts in logic think that what is grasped through inference in some cases is merely a specific instance (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) already determined, but apprehended in a general way (*sāmānyataḥ*).
To dispel that misconception, the author of the Bhāṣya said this: "But that [inference] is of two kinds..."
"There is also inference whose object is a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that has not been perceived, as in the case of [the existence of] action (*kriyā*) and so forth.
But how can there be a perception of the relation with something whose particular characteristic has not been perceived?
[It is possible] because its effect, which possesses the property of arising, is perceived.
Even if the specific relationship with an object whose particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has not been ascertained is not understood in detail,
it is nevertheless observed in a general sense:
for every occasional effect is seen to arise from some adventitious cause that possesses the capacity for production.
Just as a cloth [arises] from the conjunction of threads, so too,
since Devadatta’s disjunctions from and conjunctions with his former and subsequent locations are occasionally perceived, some adventitious cause is inferred.
This is as follows:

They declare that inference based on a relationship perceived in general (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa-sambandha*) has as its object a specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) not previously perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

However, in the case of fire and such things, because their specific individuality was previously determined through direct perception, they call it inference based on a relationship perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣato-dṛṣṭa-sambandha*).
Furthermore, one should not say that substance alone is the cause of conjunction and disjunction.
Because [the effect] does not exist even when that [cause] is present;
nor can it be postulated that another substance has arrived, since that would be contradicted by the recognition of the previous substance.
Nor is it reasonable to claim that people do not perceive difference because they are deceived by the arising of successive moments that are similar [to one another];
for even when there is a difference in location and so forth, the failure to perceive that [similarity] does not result in error.
And it has been stated by the author of the *Vivaraṇa*: "The destruction of momentariness is indeed refuted by recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)."
Therefore, because a visible cause is impossible [in this case], some invisible cause of conjunction and disjunction is inferred;
and that is designated as "action" (*karman*).
For this very reason, it is stated in other passages that action is indeed imperceptible.
The author of the Bhāṣya demonstrates this: as he will state, "For these [qualities] are not perceptible," and "That which causes its substratum to reach another location is called action.

Thus, he clearly shows that action is inferred solely from the result of reaching another location; therefore, it is established that actions and the like are objects of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
To those who claim that "the two-fold nature of inference is established because the objects of cognition (prameya) are of two kinds," he replies: "The two-fold nature is not tenable.
The meaning is that this aforementioned two-fold nature is untenable.
To the question "In what way is it untenable? he says, with the three quarters of the verse beginning "Just as... (yathaiva).

Just as, indeed, the relationship between fire and smoke— which are both imperceptible— is perceived through their imperceptible forms, so too is it with regard to the forms of the goal to be attained and the means, since those two are also perceptible.
For in that very same way, there is a relationship between going and reaching that is directly perceived.
For we indeed perceive Devadatta as reaching another place and think, "He is going.
This conceptualization of action does not differ from the conceptualization of universals (*jāti*) and so forth;
for like those, it conforms to the presence and absence of the sense organs and possesses a non-mediated appearance.
Is it not the case that, in the instance of Devadatta, we perceive some other form of action distinct from the conjunctions and disjunctions with space?
That [action] is inferred solely by the observation of its effect; or [is it not distinct] from the universal, as the universal is distinct from the individual?
That which is experienced as form,
and which is determined as being the object of direct perception—
that very thing is the manifest individual (vyakti).
If it is asked, "What is the difference between this [karma] and its form?", then what about karma— is it formless? For even this does not differ from that at all.
But [this] is merely adventitious.

Therefore, just like the conceptualization of genus (*jāti*), we also include the conceptualization of action (*karman*) within the category of perception itself; thus, we divide determinate perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) into five types.
And it has been said:

"For one who is observing Devadatta as he has come into the range of vision, while reciting a poem composed by himself, does not perceive it as if it were something hidden, merely because of his own mental labeling.
Thus [it is said].
If the action were to be inferred from its result, there would be the undesirable consequence of it being perceived like Devadatta, as the sun is perceived;
yet it is not observed that one sees the sun moving or vibrating in the same way one sees Devadatta,
for its orb is always seen to be stationary.
Since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*) are indeed perceived even in that [action], they are equal;
therefore, from those two, there would be an inferential cognition (*ānumānika-pratyaya*) regarding both [the past and the future].

Furthermore, if action were inferred from its commencement as disjunction and its conclusion as conjunction, then the cognition appearing as "it goes"—which has the manifestation of the present—would not occur.
