For that [past object] is indeed past; how then could it be the objective domain of a cognition having the aspect of the present?
[The cognition] regarding fish in a steady stream of water is inferential, arising from the perception of the conjunctions and disjunctions of the incessantly produced parts of the water.
Cognition of motion would arise;
and even in a post from which a hawk has departed, action would be inferred as being like that of the hawk,
and consequently, that [post] too would become an object of the cognition "it moves."
If it is thought that the inference of action does not arise from mere disjunction, but rather from a conjunction preceded by disjunction,
then in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence [of inferring action] when a post already separated from one hawk is joined with another.
And when Devadatta has moved and come to rest,

if it is argued that there can be no inference of action in the hawk because the conjunction with another location produced by its flight cannot be brought about by an action inherent in a stationary post (sthāṇu),
then let action be postulated in the hawk as well.
In the case of a post (*sthāṇu*), however, there is simply no avoidance of the over-extension (*prasaṅga*).
For one whose vision is restricted and who has remembered the connection, there is necessarily a cognition of the obstructer (*pratibandhaka*).
And since there is the observation of an effect connected to its cause in the case of a post, it cannot be accepted as an instance of inference.
If it is argued that since conjunction and disjunction can occur in a post even through the action inherent in a hawk, there is no inference of an action residing in the post itself— that is not so;
for the determination of inference does not follow the dictates of practical necessity.
For a pervaded mark (liṅga), wherever it is perceived, brings to mind its pervader (vyāpaka).
Presumption (arthāpatti) is indeed set aside by the possibility of another explanation, but inference (anumāna) is not.
However, if uninterrupted productions of conjunctions and disjunctions are the cause for the inference of action, [then there is no need for presumption].
In that case, no motion whatsoever could be inferred,
because future conjunctions and disjunctions are not within the scope of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
and because only a few [conjunctions and disjunctions] are initially perceived.
Now, the inference of action is based on conjunction with and disjunction from one's own location.
Yet, it is not said that "the hawk is the location of the post.
Even so, there is still no escape from the over-extension [of the definition] to fish.
For them, water exists only in its own location. Furthermore, for those who maintain that space (*vyoman*) is imperceptible, the cognition of action— namely, "the bird is moving"— would be untenable,
because the conjunction with and disjunction from space are imperceptible, and thus inference based upon them is impossible.
Nor is the cognition "the bird moves" based on the apprehension of conjunctions and disjunctions of parts of the light spread through space, because it occurs even in total darkness;
and in your own system, there is no such thing as a substance called "darkness."

Since light consists merely of the absence [of darkness], it is impossible to establish that there is a determination of action (kriyā) caused by its conjunction and disjunction; thus, a twofold nature of action is not tenable in the case of perception.
As for the statement, "Indeed, those are not perceived," which expresses their imperceptibility—

We shall explain that very point differently right there. Furthermore, by the author of the Sūtras stating "the non-distinction of form and sound," it is established that perception itself constitutes the sequence.

And in the section concerning the *apūrva*, the statement "we perceive the form of the action" is intended precisely as a negation of perceiving the form of an action existing as a manifested state through a previously extended sequence of prior and posterior stages, as previously described.
Otherwise, if there were merely a negation of perception, the action would be eternally non-existent, like the horn of a hare.
For it is not merely the perception by direct observation (*pratyakṣopalabdhi*) that is denied there;
nor does the phrase "that which, having a substrate, causes it to reach another location" intend to suggest that [action] is inferable from its effect.

What then? It shows that action exists in the form of the *apūrva*, demonstrating that action does not exist as a substrate in its own essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), but rather as the substrate's capacity to cause it to reach another location.

"Even here, since the arrival of Devadatta at another location is preceded by motion, and since both [the cases of] Devadatta and the sun are such that their action is to be inferred, by what distinction is the inference of motion in the sun cited as an example of *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation), while for Devadatta the establishment of motion is likewise achieved through *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* alone?
Therefore, this [distinction] does not hold either according to the text or according to reason; thus it is well said that it is untenable."
For duality occurs when two counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) are mutually non-confused;
but here,
if there is non-perception of the sun, it would not [occur] even in the case of the present location.
If it is perceived in some cases there, let it be seen in Devadatta as well.
If there were dependence on another subject (dharmin) in that case, it would be a "general observation" (sāmānyadṛṣṭa);
such is the case for the collection of fire and smoke, and therefore they describe it thus.

Regarding the two specific instances where the relationship has been perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭasambandha*), that which is presented as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to the perception of the relationship is the case where the relationship is perceived only in a general sense (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭasambandha*). Even there, since the relationship between the movement and the attainment of a destination is indeed perceived through direct observation, there is no confusion between the two counter-correlates.

If, however, it is argued that even though perceptibility exists in the example, because the motion of the sun—which is the subject under consideration—is not perceptible, there is no relation perceived through direct perception, then first this objection is raised: "If [it is said] there is non-perception in the case of the sun.
Now, he refutes this: "No."
He states the reason: "even in a present place.
This means that even in a place being perceived at the present moment, there is simply no perception of its non-perceptibility.

If, however, it is maintained that the connection between fire and smoke is not perceived in some places, such as a kitchen, then [the opponent] says "in some place" (kvacit) to show that this [connection] exists in Devadatta as well, because it is not perceived when he has gone away. //139//
Thus far, it has been stated that what is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣato dṛṣṭatā*) is conflated with what is perceived through general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭatayā*).

Now, he states— by means of the three quarters beginning with "yadi"— that even what is perceived through general observation is conflated with the inference of the form of fire as it is intended to be perceived directly.
For if it is held that the inference of motion in the sun is a case of *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation) only because it depends upon another subject such as Devadatta,
then it would necessarily follow that fire and smoke— which exist in the relationship of the signified and the signifier— would also be so, depending upon another subject such as a kitchen hearth.
For this [inference] is understood in a general sense, without intending to specify distinctions of place and so forth, as "that which possesses smoke possesses fire."
Just as the locus of reaching another place is the locus of motion, so too this [locus] is devoid of being a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*). Therefore, they declare it thus.
The sense is that because the two-fold division as previously stated is impossible, the two-fold division must be described in the manner that will be explained hereafter. //140//
Therein, he first illustrates the relationship based on perception (pratyakṣa-sambandha) with the words ending in "budhyate": "When, indeed, between two specific instances of fire and smoke—
[such as] 'this fire has cow-dung for its fuel' (gomayendhana), meaning that cow-dung is its fuel..."
It was performed with cow-dung fuel and the specific qualities produced thereby.
When that very person, remaining in that same place, goes [to the fire] at another time,
Agni recognizes him again and again, according to his previous mode of cognition.
Its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) arises from the cognition of an object whose existence was previously doubted;
this is the "perception of particulars" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*), as described by Vindhyavāsin.
"Moreover, this establishment of the reason and the probandum is intended only between two general forms (ākṛti) through some exclusion; thus, no specific instance has been demonstrated."
Having first formed the cognition through perception that "this is a mountain" (a *bahuvrīhi* compound) and "this is a particular smoke produced by it," and then,
after some interval, having gone elsewhere, he perceives that very same particular fire by means of that very same particular smoke while standing in that [other] place.
The meaning is that at that time, inference becomes one whose connection has been perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭasambandha*).
By this, it is explained that only "inference based on the perception of particulars" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*) is expressed by the term "perceived through direct perception.
For, by the word *pratyakṣa*, the particular (*viśeṣa*) is indicated.
For it is by means of perception alone that such a specific internal distinction— consisting of the nature of the cow-dung fuel and its being produced from it— is capable of being understood,
and not by any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). However,

since even inference has such a specific distinction as its object through the mediation of that [perception], it is indeed appropriate to use the word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) as a figurative designation for this specific type [of knowledge].
The intention is that since *viśeṣadṛṣṭa* serves as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) to *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*, the twofold classification is justified.
[Objection: But surely *viśeṣadṛṣṭa* is not a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And this [inference] is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
because its object has already been apprehended.
For it is by means of smoke situated in that very place that the same fire produced from cow-dung fuel is inferred in that very place.
Therefore, because there is no difference in location, it would indeed lack authority;
hence he says, "of that," with three quarters [of a verse]:
for such a thing, which is perceived by direct perception, there is the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) due to its making known an object whose existence was being doubted.

Although there is no difference in location, because there is a difference in time, the validity [of the cognition] for one who is in doubt is unimpaired by way of cutting off that doubt. And this has also been cited as "perception of particulars" (viśeṣadṛṣṭa) by Vindhyavāsin; thus he says: "Perception of particulars. //143//
If this is an example of "perception of a particular" (viśeṣadṛṣṭa), how then is there mention of "grasping the form" (ākṛtigrahaṇa) in the Bhāṣya?
For in that case, only the particular should have been shown.
To this he says: "It is precisely of two forms... (ākṛtyoreva).

The meaning is this: when two forms are presented through some specific subordinate characteristic such as being fuel of cow-dung, and it is to be stated that there is a difference between the fire and the smoke within the general inference, the "inference from what is seen in general" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭam*) is here called "the solar [inference]" (*āditya*). Msv 5.4.145.
Furthermore, it has been established that the universal is an object of direct perception;
and here, "being a real entity" (vastutva) is stated as the reason for both [of these points].
In this case, there is the relationship of cause and effect.
For such is the cognition here:
"This very same form of smoke, which is a transformation of cow-dung fuel, is seen persisting until today."
Therefore, since fire continues to persist as having that fuel as its source, the apprehension of the generic form is not untenable. //144//
If that is so, then one should state only another instance of fire and smoke, without intending to specify any internal distinctions, as the example for *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*;
what is the purpose of the example of the sun? To this he says: "And even if it were another instance of fire and smoke... and so forth.

For just as the clearly manifest distinction between fire and smoke—arising from the kindling of grass, wood, cow-dung, and so forth—is perceptible to all cognizers, it is not so with the forms of motion and attainment.

Therefore, since the inference of the mere form of motion from the mere form of attainment in the case of the sun is based on a relationship perceived only in a general way (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), the example of the sun is indeed appropriate. //145//
Furthermore, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for grasping a relation in its general form?
For there can be no grasping of a relation between two relata that have not themselves been grasped;
nor is it possible for universals (*sāmānya*) to be grasped through perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Because that [perception] has only the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, inference is not [applicable], as it would lead to an infinite regress; therefore, he says: "the state of being an object of perception."
There would be an infinite regress if the apprehension of the universal were held to be through inference;

however, once it has been established that this [apprehension] is the object of perception by means of proving it to be conceptual (*savikalpaka*), it was concluded at the end: "Therefore, the perceptibility of the universal is established."
Now, one might object: "But for one who holds that there is no such thing as a universal at all, since neither difference nor non-difference can be established, [the author] says:
'And substantiality...'"
The fact that [the universal] is a real entity will also be established in detail in the section on *ākṛti* (form).
Furthermore, by establishing it as an object of perception, its status as a real entity is already effectively proven even within the context of perception itself.
And here, in order to demonstrate the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by stating "there exists a real entity that is a universal," the reality of the universal has indeed been introduced.

This, however, is a restatement for the purpose of explaining the reason. He says "here" [in verse 146] with the thought: "As for that person who is a rationalist (*haituka*) and does not respect the establishment of things through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) without a reason, we shall establish both [the existence of the self and its permanence] by means of reason alone."
The inference of fire from smoke must have a real entity as its objective support,
because it is a means of valid cognition other than non-apprehension, just like the cognitions of the ear and other senses regarding their own objects.
Furthermore, the universal possesses both substantial reality and perceptibility,
because it is an object of cognition other than non-existence, just like a unique particular entity.
In that regard, he first states the reason (*hetu*) for establishing [the object] as a real entity (*vastutva*): "of the inference of fire from smoke.

For the Buddhists declare that inference has a non-real universal (*sāmānya*) as its objective support (*ālambana*), because they admit that a universal is merely the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

For this very reason, they say that inference is indeed an error, yet it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it presents the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) by the force of the [invariable] relation.

To those very people, this is said: "Inference has a real entity as its objective support, because it is a valid cognition other than non-existence, just like the cognition of the auditory faculty and so forth regarding its own object."
For that cognition which is produced by the sense organs, such as the ear and so forth, with respect to their own respective objects, has only a real entity (vastu) as its objective support;
and whichever object a particular sense organ is in contact with, that is its own specific object, because the sense organs function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakāritva*).
Therefore, in this context, the qualification "with respect to its own object" is for the purpose of excluding cognitions such as those of a mirage.

If it were stated without such a qualification, the pervasion— that non-existence is not a separate means of valid cognition because [valid cognition] has a real entity as its objective support— would not have been stated,
since erroneous cognitions lack both [the aforementioned characteristics].
For these [mental factors] are not valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*),
nor do they have real entities as their objects;
for when an organ is associated with one [object], those [mental factors] arise with respect to a different object.
Such knowledge indeed has a non-entity as its object, yet it does not have an absolutely non-existent thing as its object.
Thus, once it has been established that inference has a real entity as its object, it follows by implication that the universal (*sāmānya*) is a real entity.
This [objection] has been refuted by the author of the *Bhāṣya* who employs the term "object" (*artha*) for inference on the grounds that it has a non-entity as its objective support (*ālambana*).
The Buddhists maintain that inference has a non-object (*anartha*) as its domain.

They argue that inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because, although it is an error proceeding by determining an object in what is merely its own internal reflection (*svapratibhāsa*), it does not deviate from the actual object since its activity is connected with that object.

To them, this is the reply: the object of inference is the universal (sāmānya) of the thing itself, which is indeed external; it is not merely the form of a conceptual construction (vikalpākāra). This will be established in detail in the section on the "Form" (ākṛti). //147//
Having thus established substantiality (*vastutva*) by implication, he now establishes it explicitly: "And the universal is a real entity.
This connects with what will be stated later: "The universal is a real entity because it is an object of cognition other than non-existence (*abhāva*), like a unique particular (*asādhāraṇavastu*).
He now demonstrates its status as an object of perception through a formal argument (*prayoga*) with the three quarters [of the verse] beginning with "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*).

That which is an object of cognition other than [the object of] non-existence is indeed apprehended by perception, just as, for the Buddhists themselves, the unique particular (*asādhāraṇa-vastu*) is so apprehended. //148//
That universal which is not cognized without inference does not exist,
and inference does not proceed without a logical mark (liṅga).
No one accepts that what is unique [to a single instance] can function as a logical mark (liṅga);
nor is there any unperceived mark that serves to reveal [its object]. (Msv 5.4.150)
Or else, there might be a further understanding of that [object] through another inference;
and its production would arise from a mark (liṅga) conjoined with the cognition of a universal (sāmānya).
And since that [knowledge] is also inferential, its arising must be through a logical mark (*liṅga*);
if one were to conceive it thus, [it would require] another inference [to know] that very knowledge.
Because signs, the possessor of signs, and inferences are infinite, even over many thousands of yugas, it is not possible [to know] a single possessor of signs.

Now, even if the inferential mark (liṅga) is common [to both the subject and its opposite], the cognition of the object possessing the mark (liṅgin) may arise from another means of knowledge, whether that means be valid or invalid. (Msv 5.4.154)

However, for the Buddhists alone—who consider the universal (*sāmānya*) to be the exclusive object of inference—an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) results; thus he says [in verses 149–153]: "The universal...
This passage is explained by its very wording (*nigadavyākhyāta*).
If, however, it is argued that there would be an infinite regress when inference is required for the purpose of grasping the universal that serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*),
yet inference is not required for the purpose of grasping that [universal] itself—
because it is cognizable through a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from the perception of the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of smoke and so forth— [then we reply:]...
And this [cognition] is not invalid,
because it results in the attainment of a thing capable of purposeful action;
nor is it a valid means of cognition, because its object is a non-entity.

Anticipating the objection that "therefore, because the probans is established through the alternative of being indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), there is no infinite regress," he says: "Now" (*atha*).

The intention is as follows: first of all, it is not possible for a cognition to be both valid (*pramāṇa*) and invalid (*apramāṇa*), because when two contradictory natures are negated in one place, the occurrence of one of them is unavoidable.

Furthermore, since that which is not a means of valid cognition lacks the capacity to establish an object of knowledge, it must necessarily be admitted that the cognition of such [an infinite regress] is itself a means of valid cognition;
and since perception and inference are not accepted [as its basis], it would consequently result in yet another distinct means of valid cognition.
Even so, it would follow that inference is eternally sublated;
rather, there would have to be another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that brings about the comprehension of the universal (sāmānya).
Or, whatever cognition arises regarding the possessor of a mark from a mark that has been incorrectly understood,
that too would always be false, like the cognition of fire produced from steam.

But surely, even though it is not a means of valid cognition, the recollection of the relationship is accepted as the cause for the comprehension of the probandum; in the same way, the comprehension of the probans would occur.
In that case, validity is attributed to the prior cognition;
its purpose is fulfilled merely by the arising of the memory based upon it.

Furthermore, just as another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is accepted as the means of cognizing that mark (*liṅga*), so too would it follow [that it is required] for the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*).
And in this way, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) to be mentioned later would arise.
By saying "either from a means of valid cognition or from what is not a means of valid cognition," he demonstrates that conceptual construction possesses an undetermined dual nature. //154//
"Let it be, then, that the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) is likewise understood; what is the fault?
To this he says: "Even so... (evamapi).
The intended meaning is as follows: even for us who are introducing the consequence of infinite regress, the aim is to bring about the destruction of inference.
Furthermore, the destruction of inference occurs even when another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is admitted;
for that very same means of valid cognition would then have to be the cognizer of every universal mark (liṅga) and marked (liṅgin). //155//

If, however, it is maintained that the cognition of the mark (liṅga) lacks validity precisely because it is admitted to have a single form, then the cognition of the marked object (liṅgin) derived from that mark— understood through an invalid means— would also be false,
just as the cognition of fire [is false] when derived from the perception of steam mistaken for smoke.
And thus, there would be no inference;
with the intention that this would be the perpetual abolition of inference itself, he says: "from what is not cognized by a means of valid knowledge" (apramāṇāvabuddhāt). //157//
Here he raises an objection: "But surely...

The meaning is that just as the recollection of a relationship, though itself not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), is accepted as a cause of valid cognition, so too will the knowledge of the logical mark (*liṅga*) be. //157//
He addresses this [objection] with the word "therein" (*tatra*).
For memory, arising from a prior cognition, is useful for inference by way of presenting that [object];
and since that [prior cognition] is indeed a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is logical that the resulting ascertainment follows it. //158//
However, no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is established regarding the attainment of the marks;
because of its absence, the traditional authority (smṛti) does not apply here in any way whatsoever.
If one were to say that this cognition is a memory by virtue of its non-difference [from the object],
then surely even the son of a barren woman would possess the capacity for recollection.
Furthermore, the unique nature of an object is not the cause of a cognition of a universal,
because its invariable concomitance with that [universal] has never been observed in any way whatsoever.
And since this mode is not possible in the case of the apprehension of a logical mark (liṅga), he says: "But not...

For in this case, even prior to the comprehension of the logical mark, no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is found to be applicable that could be presented by a cognition based on a means of valid cognition.

Nor should it be said that the cognition of the inferential mark (liṅga) is also merely memory; for he says "due to the absence of that" [in sūtra 1.1.4], meaning precisely because there is no prior means of valid cognition [for the mark]. //159//

[Objection: But surely, since the cognition of the inferential mark (liṅga) also leads to the apprehension of the particular (svalakṣaṇa) such as smoke that was previously grasped by non-conceptual [perception], it too is nothing but memory;
therefore, in this case as well, a definitive determination from another non-conceptual means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is indeed appropriate.
To this, he says: "It is mnemonic" (smārta).

Just as the present cognition of a relation is a form of recollection because it causes one to obtain what was previously grasped, so too this cognition of the logical mark (liṅga) is a form of recollection because it causes one to obtain what was grasped by non-conceptual [perception], being non-different from that. For one who asserts this, the capacity for recollection would be unavoidable even in the case of the son of a barren woman; for the established rule is that recollection has a previously grasped object as its domain.

Furthermore, the cognition of the general characteristic (*liṅgasāmānyajñāna*) does not have as its objective support (*ālambana*) the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) grasped by non-conceptual [perception]; how then could it be memory?
That which appears here was not previously grasped, and that which was grasped does not appear; therefore, it lacks the nature of memory.
But if memory were to have an ungrasped object, there would be the undesirable consequence of remembering even the son of a barren woman. //160//
Indeed, there would be an infinite regress in the cognition of the general character of the mark (*liṅga*) by means of inference;

for if the mark is itself of a general nature, it must be accepted that it is apprehended for the sake of [cognizing] that [general character], since that [general character] is to be known through inference.
The unique essence of the object itself will serve as the inferential mark (*liṅga*) in the cognition of the universal, and since that [essence] is indeed perceptible, there is no infinite regress.
Therefore, he says: "And not..."
What is the reason for this? He says: "Because... A mark (liṅga) is that whose invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) has been observed.
And its invariable concomitance with that universal (sāmānya) has not been observed in any way, whether spatially or temporally.
Because that which is unique cannot possibly persist through other entities, and because what is perceived in one place ceases right there. //161//
Or rather, through the perception of a relationship, this [entity] may be a universal, like "producedness";
for a unique particular object does not exist both previously and here [in the present].
Furthermore, for that which is inexpressible and free from conceptual construction,
the status of being a logical mark (liṅga) is not tenable without a prior mental connection (anusandhāna).
And those specific qualities that are conceptualized—those too lack a logical mark because they lack a concomitance;
for this very reason, even the cognition of them lacks the status of a logical mark.
Alternatively, if it were of a universal nature, there would likewise be no ascertainment [of its specific identity].

Furthermore, if one accepts the perception of a relation, it would result in the universal nature [of the sound] being established, just as in the case of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth; thus he says, "Or it might be...
He states the reason for this: "For not... (162).
Furthermore, he states that the unique (asādhāraṇa) entity is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) with the words "And not...
It is observed that smoke and the like, when made the object of conceptual constructions such as "this is smoke," serve as the logical mark for fire and so forth.
However, how could that which is unique and cannot be designated by any form whatsoever be a logical mark?
The phrase "the status of being a logical mark (liṅgatva) is not tenable" is to be connected with what is about to be said.

Now, one might object: "Since inference is observed even among animals who lack any verbal articulation (*śabdollekha*) and perceive only the unique particular (*asādhāraṇarūpa*), it is not the case that something is not a logical mark simply because it is inexpressible. To this, he replies with the three quarters of the verse beginning with "vikalpa":
the intention is as follows—let it be granted that animals lack verbal articulation; [nevertheless...]
However, even for them, there certainly exists a conceptual construction (*arthavikalpa*) consisting of the synthesis of what precedes and what follows.
Therefore, it is indeed logical that smoke—even when not yet designated as such—serves as the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for inference.
For smoke that has not ascended into the mind in the form "this is that [smoke]" does not become the inferential mark of fire.
And this is not possible in the case of the unique [specific property], because that [unique property] is not within the scope of connecting what precedes and what follows. //163//

In our view as well, those specific particulars such as smoke which are conceptualized as having an uncommon nature (*asādhāraṇātman*) are not a logical mark (*liṅga*) because of the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*);
how much more so, then, is the uncommon object-nature (*arthātman*) which is the exclusive domain of non-conceptual [perception]? Thus he says: "are conceptualized.

Precisely because of the absence of positive concomitance, even the cognition of an uncommon [particular] is not a logical mark for the cognition of the generality of the probandum (*liṅgisāmānya*); thus he says: "for this very reason. //164//

If, however, for the sake of establishing the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the unique particular is admitted to have a universal form, then—just as in the case of grasping the universal of the logical mark (*liṅga*)—there would follow the consequence of an infinite regress; thus, that [universal] too could not be determined. Therefore, he says: "Or else, if the relation were observed in some [particular], everything would be a signifier. (Msv 5.4.165)
Furthermore, the experience of the relationship [between the mark and the bearer of the mark] must necessarily be admitted for the possessor of the mark;
yet, prior to the operation of inference, no means of valid cognition exists for you regarding that [relationship].
Nor is it possible for the knowledge of the mark (liṅga) to arise from mere latent impressions (vāsanā);
and the knowledge of the bearer of the mark (liṅgin) would likewise [not arise] from that, for it does not come from a mark possessing the three characteristics (trirūpa).

Regarding the term "universal" (*sāmānya*): if, however, a relationship has been known through a universal with respect to some particular unique thing, and another person, upon seeing that [particular], infers the universal, then in that case,
everything would be a signifier for everyone.
He says that it is because there is no distinction: "In some cases... (165).
Thus, it has first been stated that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the determination of the logical mark (*liṅga*).

Now, he says— "the experience of the connection"— to show that at the time when the concomitance (*anvaya*) is not grasped, there is likewise no means of valid cognition for the knowledge of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*).
The meaning is as follows: when the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) has not been apprehended, its related mark (liṅga) cannot be understood.

Furthermore, prior to the operation of inference, there is no means of valid cognition for that [subject] in its nature as a universal—such as direct perception (pratyakṣa)—as we [Buddhists] maintain.
Therefore, even if the possessor of the mark were to be apprehended [by another inference], it would result in the fallacy of infinite regress (anavasthā). //166//
Surely, this conventional usage of the sign (liṅga) and the signified (liṅgin) is based solely on beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā);
what is the point of such excessive insistence here?
For a certain latent impression, having arisen, manifests a conceptual construction (vikalpa) in the form of some sign, and thereby initiates a specific conventional usage of inference.

As it has been said: "This very process of inference and the object of inference proceeds by means of the property (dharma) and the property-possessor (dharmin) as they are mounted upon the intellect; it does not depend on external existence or non-existence.
Therefore, he says: "Nor even..."
The cognition of a logical mark (*liṅga*) is not produced by mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
For a latent impression is a mental trace (*saṃskāra*) deposited by a prior experience;

it is not possible for such a thing to exist for a logical mark that is absolutely non-existent, like the horn of a hare. Therefore, how could the cognition of a logical mark arise from mere latent impressions?

If it is maintained that the cognition of the mark (liṅga) is based on that [cognition of the object], then the cognition of the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) would be established in exactly the same way; thus, the recourse to the authority of inference—defined as "the perception of the object from the three-featured mark"—would be useless. To this, he says: "And the cognition of the possessor of the mark... (verse 167).
Where non-existence functions as a logical mark (*liṅga*),
and that [non-existence] is not inferential because it is cognizable through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), no fault arises there.
For one who attains the cognition of the probandum from a probans already perceived through direct perception,
nothing further than this need be sought after.
Even where the apprehension of the probandum occurs through an inferred mark,
there too the fundamental mark is known from perception alone.
The status of being a logical mark (liṅgatva) belongs to [properties] such as "being produced" (kṛtakatva), or to an action or its causal factor (kāraka);
and since its perceptibility is accepted, one does not have to go far [to find it]. (Msv 5.4.171)
Surely this infinite regress is equally applicable to you as well when inferring the absence of rain from the absence of clouds,
since non-existence has non-perception as its logical mark (*liṅga*). If that [non-perception] were to depend on another similar mark, an infinite regress would result.
Therefore he says: "Where...
For where there is an absence of rain, the absence of clouds is not the inferable [object], because it is cognizable through another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called non-existence (abhāva).
Therefore, in this case, the fault of infinite regress (anavasthā), which arises based on the requirement of a similar class [of cause], does not occur. //168//
But for those who maintain that perception is self-evident, there is no infinite regress at all; thus he says: "from what is apprehended by perception.
This means "from perception itself. //169//
In that case, there would be an infinite regress in the inference of an inference;
therefore, he says: "Even where...
For the perception of reaching another location is the primary sign (*liṅga*), that which exists at the root.
The intention is that when motion is inferred from the sun as the means of establishing motion, there is no [temporal] duration involved. //170//

[Objection: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced; and its being produced is established by observing it [to arise] immediately after an action. If, in this way, one were to establish "being produced" based on its occurring immediately after an action, then that action itself would require inference from another cause, leading to an infinite regress. To this, he says: "The state of being a mark," [referring to the passage]:
"For some [hold that] in the inference of being produced, the action [is the mark], because it is observed there."
Thus, the mark has been stated as the state of occurring subsequent to the operation of the causal factors (*kāraka*).
In that regard, either the action unqualified by the causal factors, or the causal factor qualified by that [action], becomes the mark that qualifies the state of intermediate occurrence.
Both [possibilities apply].
In this way, since verbal testimony, analogy, and so forth depend upon universals (*sāmānya*),
it follows that because of the instability of those [universals], instability would result everywhere.
Therefore, it is maintained that other means of valid cognition are preceded by perception;
for if the object were a universal, there would be no other mode of apprehension [than perception].
And how could there be a direct perception of a particular (viśeṣa) when that which is called the "universal aspect" (sāmānyāṃśa) depends upon other entities?
For all [objects] such as visible form are common in relation to [their specific qualities] such as blue;
furthermore, the sameness of blue and so forth is in relation to their own particularities.
And that [action] is perceptible.
First, the perceptibility of action has just been established;
likewise, the causal factor (kāraka) is also indeed perceptible.
Potency, however, is imperceptible;
and it is neither a logical mark (liṅga) here,
nor is it an object of inference.
Therefore, since both the action and the agent are directly perceived, there is no infinite regress.
For even for those who maintain that the object is to be inferred, there is no infinite regress because it is established by the limit of the result;
this is all the more true for us. //171//

Thus, first, it has been stated that there is a difficulty regarding the universal's status as a real entity and its perceptibility if inference were non-existent; now, with the intention that the entire collection of means of valid cognition would likewise become untenable if the universal were untenable—since they too are based upon the universal—and that it cannot be considered invalid according to the reasoning to be stated later, he says: "In this way" (evam). //172//
Therefore, one must necessarily accept that other means of valid cognition are preceded by perception, as well as the perceptibility of the universal;
otherwise, an infinite regress would result. Thus he concludes with the words "therefore. //173//

Thus, the perceptibility and reality of the universal (sāmānya) have been established. Now, he addresses those who claim that only particulars (viśeṣa) are apprehended by perception, stating: "By perception... If the particular is intended to be a composite substance (avayavidravya), it is dependent upon other constituent substances; since we have already described its aspect as a universal, how can it be said to be perceived? //174//
If, however, it is maintained that the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) are simply the color and other attributes of the composite whole (*avayavin*), that too is incorrect.
For even those [color and so forth] are indeed universals (*sāmānya*) in relation to their own specific instances such as blue and the like; thus he says: "For color and the rest... and so on.
And those too are common as long as they remain atoms;
for even that form which belongs to a dyad is indeed common to both.
No one has any practical discourse regarding the ultimate particularity;
nor is there direct perception of it, whether in the aggregate or in isolation.
That which is not apprehended as distinct cannot attain the status of being apprehended as non-distinct;
nor is it possible for that which is apprehended by a cognition of non-difference to exist among things that are distinct.

If, however, it is held that blue and so forth are themselves the particulars, that is not correct; for even they possess the nature of a universal in relation to their own internal sub-varieties of blue and so on. Thus he says: "their own particulars" (svaviśeṣān). //175//

If, however, it is maintained that the specific quality is merely the blueness of a single bee or similar substance, that is not so; for even that possesses the nature of a generality (sāmānya) in relation to the specific blues residing in its own parts, such as its wings.
The blueness of a wing, too, is indeed a generality in relation to the blues of its constituent parts.
And thus, the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) regarding [the existence of] atoms must be demonstrated; therefore he says, "And those too...
Since atoms are partless, their form is indeed unique and non-common.
But he says that even before those [qualities], the nature of the dyad (dvyaṇuka) is also uncommon to both [the cause and the effect]—namely, "of the dyad as well" (dvyaṇukasyāpi). //176//
"Let it be that the atom itself is the particularity (*viśeṣa*); it will simply not be perceptible. To this he says: "And not by the ultimate [atom] (*antyena*).
For it is for the sake of practical activity (*vyavahāra*) that one follows after the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It is not due to addiction, nor does anyone have a practical transaction (*vyavahāra*) with the ultimate particularity (*antyaviśeṣa*); so what is the point of its being a matter of direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*)?
But surely even that which results in indifference (*upekṣā*) is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, he says: "And not...

[The form of the individual atoms] is not perceived when they reside in a gross object—like threads in a cloth—whether as combined or as distinct; thus, perception does not have particulars as its object in any way whatsoever. //177//
But surely, it is only the distinct, unaggregated atoms that are perceived, not a single composite substance;
therefore, how can it be said that there is a universal among those things which possess parts?

Furthermore, since it is only the aggregated atoms that, by virtue of their non-differentiated occurrence, are denoted by such terms as "particular" (*viśeṣa*) and "specific" (*asādhāraṇa*), they will thus be objects of direct perception.
Lest it be thought that a single atom might somehow fall within the range of perception, he says: "by way of distinction.
For it is always the whole that appears to everyone, not the distinctions of atoms.
Nor is it tenable to say that non-distinction is perceived when it is not perceived through its distinctions.
The meaning is that this is because it contradicts direct experience (*saṃvit*).
Now, is this very collection (*samudāya*) not something that exists for you [Buddhists] at all times? Nor does it exist.
For all [things], the arising of cognition is possible through the sense-object as a non-existent entity.
And there is no state of being an aggregate without the connection of a single genus;
moreover, even within an aggregate, their atomicity does not depart from them.

"Because it is a universal, even though [the object] is imperceptible, this cognition does not apply to the universal alone; rather, this cognition occurs as something distributed [over many objects], even without the conceptualization of a single [entity]."

Since this apprehension is of an undivided manifestation, what is the use of apprehending difference? To this he says: "Nor is there a difference..."—that is, difference is not cognizable by a cognition whose form is undivided.
The meaning is that the distinction between difference and non-difference is untenable. //178//
[Objection: "Even if there is no single [entity], this appearance of an undifferentiated mass might still occur by having a collection as its object. To this, he says: "The collection.
For how could those who deny even the universal (*sāmānya*)—which is universally recognized throughout the entire world—have a so-called "collection" that is a distinct entity?

When that which has such an object will have an undifferentiated appearance; moreover, since everyone at all times perceives it as a single substance, how could it be otherwise? To this he says: "And not at all times... (179).
Furthermore, this collection (*samudāya*) would not be possible without a single genus (*ekajāti*).
For there is no cognition of a "collection" regarding things of diverse genera, such as trees, jars, and clods of earth.
Therefore, he says "And not... [in the verse], implying that even if a collection is admitted, you would be forced to accept the existence of the universal "atom-ness" (*aṇutvasāmānya*).
And [the suffix -tva is used] in the sense of cause (hetau). //180//
Now, it might be argued that it is impossible to accept a substance whose nature is a universal without a synthesis of its existence in multiple parts;
nor is sensory cognition capable of this, because it is non-conceptual (avikalpaka).
Therefore, he says: "It is called 'the universal' (sāmānya).

Even though it is not apprehended by conceptualizing it as a substance that resides in various parts—on the grounds that a single unifying construction [is required] for the universal—nevertheless, its unitary nature is indeed apprehended even by non-conceptual [perception] (nirvikalpaka); thus, it cannot be denied. This is according to the principle of the universal as a whole (avayavin) that exists distributively (vyāsajyavṛtti).
It must be shown that even a universal such as "cowness," which resides in each individual, is perceived by a single sense-faculty.
Although that universal is not grasped in the form of the word "universal" itself, in reality it is indeed the universal that is grasped.

However, at a time subsequent to the recollection of words and so forth, it is grasped after being conceptually constructed as a "universal" through the reflective awareness of its persistence across multiple individuals.
And this has already been stated in the proof of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*).

Therefore, one should not say: "Let there be perception by the senses of the whole (*avayavin*)—which is synonymous with the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)—but not of that which resides in each individual instance. //181//
Just as a universal that exists by being distributed [over many instances] is perceived by the sense organs,
so too would it be for that which resides in each individual instance.
Furthermore, the Mīmāṃsakas do not necessarily assert the existence of atoms,
by virtue of which you might imagine that what is perceived is false.
He who denies that perception consists of an aggregate of invisible atoms would as well assert the non-existence of a rabbit's horn.
He states that "in both cases there is no difference in the cognition," namely by the word *vyāsajya*.
By this, the following is established: why is the perceptibility of the universal (*sāmānya*) not accepted in vain?
For even by those who desire particulars (*viśeṣa*) to be perceptible, the universal itself must necessarily be accepted as perceptible.
For when everything, such as form and so forth, is scrutinized with great precision, it is found to possess a generic nature;

and since a substance consists of various parts as its substratum, it too possesses that same nature; furthermore, because an aggregate of atoms alone is not perceived as having self-nature, and because the denial of substance would contradict direct perception.

Therefore, the intended meaning is that both the whole (avayavin) as a generality and all the generalities inherent within it, such as "cowness" (gotva), are indeed perceptible, and not merely the particularities (viśeṣas).

And because the purpose is precisely this, one should not charge the text with redundancy on account of its demonstration—through the discussion established in another section—that the whole as a generality is perceptible. //182//

Surely, you Mīmāṃsakas must necessarily admit atoms; therefore, since they are established for both parties, why postulate a substratum when it is sufficient to assume merely the capacity of those very atoms to produce a single uniform cognition?
What is the use of a further conceptualization of a possessor of attributes (dharmin)?
For the postulation of a property (dharma) is indeed simpler than the postulation of that [object];
therefore, he says, "by the Mīmāṃsakas.
This is the intended meaning.
For whatever is presented by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is what we accept;
and it is not the case that atoms alone, setting aside the gross [object], appear in a cognition born of the senses.
Since we disregard the gross [object] upon approaching it,
let atoms be postulated in accordance with that [perception].
Let them be.
We do not venture to deny the gross [element], which serves as the foundation, by means of that [subtle] power. //183//

But for one who denies the gross object of direct perception on the grounds of invisible atoms, even a rabbit would have to be denied by the notion that it possesses horns; thus he says: "In the form of an aggregate. (184)
If the reality of the aggregate were established, then the existence of atoms might indeed be understood as the cause for its proof. (Msv 5.4.185)
Therefore, whatever object is apprehended in whatever form at all times, that must be accepted as being exactly so— whether it be a universal or something else.
In dependence upon universals such as existence (*sattā*), everything—such as "cowness" (*gotva*)—attains its specific character;
therefore, one who speaks of the specific as being accessible to the senses would not be denying the universal.
If it is not apprehended in its general form, what then is this notion of "uncommon" [specificity] regarding it? Are atoms now like the horns of a hare?
No, he says: "[They are so called because they exist] as an aggregate."
For in this case, a subject (dharmin) established by perception cannot be abandoned on the grounds of parsimony of conceptualization (kalpanālāghava).
Once that [subject] is established, who would not accept that there are atoms (paramāṇu) consistent with it?
What is meant is that atoms are not necessarily accepted because there is no other means of establishing them. //185//
Therefore, whatever object is perceived directly as both a universal and a particular, it is impossible to deny that very same object as being directly perceived in that way;
for even universals such as "cowness" are unique (asādhāraṇa) when considered in relation to higher universals such as "existence."

Therefore, even if you maintain that perception is exclusively unique (particular), nevertheless, universals such as "cowness" cannot be denied as being perceptible; for they are established by the very capacity of perception. Thus he says: "Because of existence," etc. (187).

If, however, it is argued that even though the universal is apprehended by perception, it is not [considered] perception because it is not apprehended with the explicit mention of the universal— this is the doubt he anticipates with the words "sāmānya... (the universal...).
Or does it avoid [the fault]?
For in that case, even that which is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) would not be perception (*pratyakṣa*).
In that regard as well, [there are] non-conceptual [cognitions].
Whatever object is perceived in this world can indeed be described in two ways.
Thus ends the *Anumānavārttika*.
Now begins the *Śabdapariccheda* (The Examination of Verbal Testimony).
Among the means of valid cognition such as perception and the rest, that which must be stated here is the definition of verbal testimony alone.
What is the use of such extreme haste here? It is stated from the scripture: // Msv_5.5.1 //
In that state, because there is no conceptualization of the exclusion of others (*paravyāvṛtti*), there is indeed no unique mental image (*asādhāraṇollekha*).

However, if it is argued that even though it is not conceptually constructed as having that specific form, the conceptualizing [cognition] nevertheless perceives it in its own nature, and thus it is perception (*pratyakṣa*); [then we reply:]...

In that case, since the world perceives an object as a confused whole possessing two aspects, it can indeed be stated by investigators in both ways; thus it is established that the object, possessing two aspects, is apprehended by perception. And with the intention of establishing that the observation of the relationship [between word and object] occurs in a general sense, he says: "Whatever object the world perceives in this regard, that can indeed be stated in two ways."
"In this" means in perceptual cognition. //188//
Thus ends the chapter on inference (*anumāna-pariccheda*) in the *Kāśikā-ṭīkā* composed by the preceptor Sucarita Miśra.
Now begins the chapter on verbal testimony (*śabda-pariccheda*).

Since perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) have already been examined, the following *bhāṣya* is intended to demonstrate that the scripture (*śāstra*) as well is not to be further examined: “Scripture is the cognition of an object not present [to the senses] arising from the cognition of words.”

Now, it might be argued that according to the view of the author of the *Vṛtti*, it is not correct to state that "the means of knowledge need not be examined," because after stating that perception and the other means of knowledge are well-known (*prasiddha*) and that the scripture (*śāstra*) is included among them, one anticipates an objection regarding the possible deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of perception; having then stated its non-deviation, it would be logical to establish immediately thereafter that the scripture itself does not require examination.
For that is the subject under discussion;
why should it be interrupted by inference?
True, it is so.
This sequence, however, is based on another tantra;
for indeed, the Lokāyatikas maintain that perception is the only means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
They are awakened by the demonstration of the validity of inference immediately following perception, as maintained by the Vaiśeṣikas and others.
For thus the Vaiśeṣikas recite: "Valid cognition is twofold: that which follows from observation and that which follows from non-observation.
Likewise, others have described perception and inference.
Therefore, because it possesses a vast scope, is fundamental, and is conducive to the goals of human life, this is the [proper] treatise.
Immediately thereafter, wherever it was appropriate to mention something, that which is well-known among many was stated as the *upamāna* (analogy).
For in the *Nyāyavistara*, it is stated that analogy is the means of proving the probandum (*sādhya*) by means of a well-known similarity (*prasiddhasādharmya*).
Following that, the *arthāpatti* (presumption) was stated according to the opinion of Pārāśarya.
This is because it was stated by Kṛtakoṭi, who follows that very [Buddhist] school, immediately after that [statement].

Furthermore, since the nature of the means of valid cognition of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*) is simply the absence of the means of valid cognition of existence (*bhāvapramāṇa*), the subsequent discussion follows from that.
Moreover, by stating that "these means of valid cognition are well-known (*prasiddha*) in this way in other tantras," the strength of their established renown is expressed.
And by that respective witness, they are established as having emerged [from meditative absorption].
In this context, it is said "due to the cognition of sound"; how, then, is that to be analyzed?
Is it "consciousness from sound" (*śabdād vijñānam*) or "consciousness of sound" (*śabdasya vijñānam*)?
In the former case, the compound is untenable;
for the ablative case is compounded with [the word] *bhaya* ("fear").
But later on, there would be the undesirable consequence that even conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) would be scripture,
for conceptualizations of objects not in contact [with the senses], such as "this is a cow," arise solely from the cognition of words.
To this, it is replied:

This is indeed a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Nor does the [undesired] consequence apply to conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), for that does not arise from the means of valid cognition consisting of that word (*tacchabdapramāṇa*).
Rather, it is from the sense-faculty aided by sound.
For just as this sense-faculty, when assisted by odor, distinguishes melted ghee from oil,
so too [the mind], when assisted by sound, [distinguishes] genus and the other categories.

Thus, it has been stated at the conclusion of the discussion on perception that the result of the connection with the senses is an indirect manifestation (*parokṣāvabhāsitā*), and this exists in conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*). Therefore,
that very cognition which arises from the reflection upon the power of words and has as its object an entity not in contact [with the senses] is verbal (*śābda*).
For this very reason, the cognition of the mere object is not verbal.

For that [cognition] does not abandon the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), which has as its object an entity not in contact with the senses, in order to become the characteristic of a particular (*viśeṣa*) alone.
It is not possible to state it exclusively; for this reason as well, it is not something that can be expressed in words.
And as for what was said—that "knowledge of an object arises from the cognition of a word"—such a definition is not distinct; it is not the defining characteristic of a specialized treatise (śāstra).
That by which the engagement or the withdrawal of persons is taught— whether by means of that which is eternal or that which is produced— is designated as a "treatise" (śāstra).
Proceed; for he will say—"It is not deliberated upon because of the reminder.
What, then, is verbal [cognition]?
"We say that it is the knowledge of the sentence-meaning. [Objection: "But that arises from the knowledge of the word-meanings, not from the knowledge of the words. [Reply: "No."
Because the communication of word-meanings is an intermediate operation of words, just as the burning of wood is an intermediate operation of cooking;
for he will say:
"Just as the manifestation of objects occurs through the flame of burning wood," [it is said].
Therefore, nothing is untenable.
However, this must be addressed: why is a specific definition being formulated here at the occasion of the general definition?
For a treatise (*śāstra*) is indeed a specific kind of word.
If it is to be explained, [then proceed as follows]:
Even so, having stated the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), [the specific definition] would be indicated;
however, it is improper that the specific definition (*viśeṣa*) is indicated at this juncture of the general definition by one who is acting too hastily.
For here, the specific characteristics such as "being visual" (*cākṣuṣatva*) and so forth are not being defined for perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other means of knowledge.

Therefore, when perception and the other means of knowledge have begun to be discussed in general, it is appropriate to state the definition of verbal testimony (*śabda*) alone, and not that of scripture (*śāstra*).
This is what he says: "Among perception and the others... (Sūtra 1).
He states another objection: "sāmānya... etc.
For it is only that whose general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is already known that can be made to understand its particular (*viśeṣa*), and not otherwise;
for [a particular] cannot be understood when the substance (*dravya*) has not been characterized.
Therefore, earth and the other elements are defined by their specific qualities. //2//

Thus, it has been stated that the designation of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) as "the treatise" (*śāstra*) is untenable. Furthermore, he states that even the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), beginning with "from the cognition of words" (*śabdavijñānāt*), does not apply to the specific object to be defined—this being what was referred to by the phrase "and as for what was said. (3)
What, then, is the definition of a treatise? To this he says: "Engagement" and so forth. For in some [treatises], there is seen a statement regarding the nature of engagement and withdrawal.
By virtue of being a constituent part of that [Mahāyāna], its status as a scripture is also understood.
When the entire [process of] cultivation is complete, engagement or withdrawal arises from the sentence alone; therefore, that is scripture, not from the word and so forth.

Thus, that which provides instruction is called "eternal" (nitya), namely the Vedic statement; whereas the treatises such as the Dharmaśāstras are called "non-eternal" (anitya). It is not the case that [the term] "scripture" (śāstra) refers to sound alone. //4//
But surely, even sentences such as "kṣepiṣṭha" (the swiftest), which express only the essential nature [of a thing], are accepted as scripture;
why then is it said that scripture is that which serves as an auxiliary to engagement and desistance?
To this, he says: "The essential nature... and so forth.
"By way of being a constituent part of that" means by way of being a portion of the injunctive sentence;
for there too, there exists the injunctive statement: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu."
Therefore, passages such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest" constitute a single syntactical unit with it;
hence, it is appropriate that this too possesses the status of a scripture (śāstra). //5//
Now, it is argued that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) do not directly enjoin an action,
nor do they constitute a part thereof;
for the three parts [of an injunction] are the goal (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
And none of these [other types of words] are expressed by these [injunctions].
Therefore, we do not consider that words whose meanings are not actions possess syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with them.
Hence he says, ending with the words: "the scripture [is directed] toward the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)."
The intended meaning is this: although it does not convey an action,
nor anything related to an action such as a means (sādhana) and so forth,
nevertheless, these [words] form a single syntactical unit with the injunction, which is otherwise known by the name "word-efficient-force" (śabdabhāvanā).
For an injunction (*vidhi*) requires the knowledge that its object is praiseworthy in order to impel a person toward action;
and since the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are capable of producing this [knowledge], they are useful for instigating engagement or cessation when they perform this function.

Therefore, it is only when the entire *bhāvanā* (productive operation) is complete with all three components that a person engages in or desists from an action based on the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) together with its explanatory passages, and not from the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) alone; thus, it is precisely the injunctive statement accompanied by the explanatory passages that is effective.

"Speech is the scripture"—this we shall elaborate upon in the section concerning *arthavāda* (explanatory passages). Furthermore, something has already been shown in the exposition of injunction (*vidhi*). Therefore, enough of this excessive prolixity.
Precisely because knowledge of engagement and withdrawal arises from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*),

for this very reason, how could mere suffixes denoting injunction, or mere words such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) and the like, possess the status of scripture (*śāstra*) even when the injunctive hearing (*vidhi-śruti*) is present?

For where even a statement of the threefold productive operation (*bhāvanā*)— as a subordinate sentence— is incapable of inciting engagement when the explanatory passage is disregarded, [how much less so for other elements].
"How could there be an incapacity for words and their meanings in that regard? This is difficult to comprehend," he says: "Because [the meaning] does not arise from the word, etc. (v. 6).
Even when speaking of characteristics under the guise of not investigating,
he does not prattle on regardless of whether they are independently useful.
In that regard, whatever definition of words one might state based on worldly speech is of little use for one who desires to explain the Veda.
However, having considered that perception and the other means of knowledge are employed prior to even the mere letters,
their definition was formulated for the occasion of understanding the meaning of the treatise.
Thus, he justifies the Bhāṣya which has been criticized on the grounds that the definition and the object to be defined are untenable, by stating: "It is unexamined.

The intention is as follows: since the exegesis of the Veda is the subject at hand, only that which is useful for it should be stated; therefore, even by bypassing the general introduction, [the author] has defined the specific [subject] in this manner.
For here, the mere formulation of definitions is not intended as an end in itself;
rather, definitions are composed under the guise of critical examination.
Even therein, only that definition which is useful for the present treatise has been provided.
"The Veda is independent, because it is not dependent on a person. //7//

If he does not speak things that are independent and devoid of utility, then what follows? To this he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). For it is established that, unlike a mere chatterer, he does not utter what is useless.
In that regard, if he were to explain the definition of words as they exist in worldly speech, it would be useless for one who intends to expound upon this Veda. //8//

Now, if that which is not useful is not to be defined, why then are perception and the other means of knowledge defined? For their utility toward the Veda is not observed. To this he says: "Perception and the others.
The intention is as follows: first of all, there is great assistance for perception in the very determination of the nature of the Veda.

For without that [definition], it would not be possible to determine the mere phonemes (*varṇa*), measures (*mātrā*), and so forth at the very first moment of learning one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*);
and what has not been determined then would be of no use whatsoever at the time of understanding the meaning of the scripture, because it would not be remembered.

Therefore, having considered the utility of perception and other means of knowledge regarding the mere phonemes and so forth both before and after [the study of grammar], the definition of those was formulated.
Inference (*anumāna*) is also employed in the inference of the remainder of a mantra that has been applied to a specific ritual act (*pratīka*),
as in the case of "He offers [the oblation] with 'Of the god, thee'.
Analogy (*upamāna*) is likewise employed in identifying the specific archetype (*prakṛti*) for rituals such as the *saurya* sacrifice.
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is also [useful] in the postulation of a portion of an unuttered sentence.

Non-existence (*abhāva*) is also useful for the determination of words and sentences, as well as for the determination that rituals are characterized by unmanifest injunctions (*avyakta-codanā*) when there is an absence of substances, deities, and so forth; such is the meaning of the two initial terms. //9//
As for the definition of verbal communication found in sentences such as "Bring the cow," it has no utility here; therefore, that which pertains to the scriptures has been set forth.
And there is no particularity whatsoever that exists without a universal;
therefore, by citing a particular instance, one can easily define the universal.
Even this general form is specified by virtue of the context;
for "codanā," "upadeśa," and "śāstra" are cited as being synonymous.

And just as the word *codanā* applies exclusively to Vedic [injunctions], and there is no such utility for the definition of verbal testimony (*śābda*) as found in sentences like "bring the cow," he disregards that and formulates the definition only as it pertains to scripture (*śāstra*), saying: "As for...
He addresses the objection that "if the general [nature] is not defined, the particular cannot be defined," by stating: "And the particular..."
For a particular (viśeṣa) is not established by means of a general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa),

because of the possibility of deviation (vyabhicāra). However, since a particular does not deviate from the general, when that [particular] is characterized, the general included within it is characterized with ease.

For when it was stated that scripture (*śāstra*) is the cognition of an object not in contact [with the senses] arising from an injunction-cognition (*vidhāyaka-vijñāna*), then it can be understood that verbal knowledge (*śābda*) arises from the mere cognition of words devoid of a specific injunction;
thus, it is not mentioned separately. //11//
But was it not said that this is not a definition of a particular (viśeṣa), because there is no mention of a particular? To this he says: "The universal...
A qualifier is not necessarily something that has been explicitly mentioned.
However, even though it is obtainable through entitlement (*adhikāra*),

as will be explained in the case of the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices, so too here— despite the statement "from the cognition of the word" (*śabdavijñānāt*) following the section on "that which is characterized by injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇa*)— the qualification of the injunctive [word] will be understood.
Now, if it is argued that "codanā" is used because it is applicable to the subject at hand, the intention is that these are merely synonyms. //12//

And this acquisition of a specific distinction based on the governing context (adhikāra) is also accepted by Jaimini, who employs the term *codanā* without qualification in the second aphorism; thus he says: "And just as...
He thinks as follows: although the word *codanā* denotes any sentence that prompts action (*pravartaka-vākya*), nevertheless, in the first aphorism, by the word *atha*, the Veda...
In the treatise, the two terms "knowledge of words" (śabdajñāna) and "understanding of meaning" (arthavijñāna) are established in that manner.

By this very same reasoning, it has been stated that even the treatise (śāstra) need not be examined, because its validity is based on its inclusion within [the means of knowledge such as] direct perception and the rest.
Since the immediate sequence of meditation (*dhyāyanānantarya*) has been established, the word "injunction" (*codanā*)—by virtue of that very context—refers exclusively to Vedic injunction.

Likewise here as well, because the context concerns the authority of injunctions as defined by the scripture, the terms "cognition of words" (*śabdavijñāna*) and "cognition of meaning" (*arthajñāna*) refer to specific words and meanings;
specifically, the word "word" (*śabda*) refers to the injunctive [Vedic] expression, and the word "meaning" (*artha*) refers to that which is enjoined. //13//

Although the Commentator stated at the occasion of presenting the view of the Vṛttikāra that "the means of valid cognition such as perception and so forth are well-known, and the scripture (*śāstra*) is included within them," he shows that even there, the promise to examine the specific scriptures was made solely with the intention of relevance to the present subject— this is indicated by the words "perception and so forth."
But this must be considered:
if scripture (*śāstra*) is a cognition produced by an injunctive word, then are the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), Mīmāṃsā, and the manuals on ritual action (*karmānuśāsana*) not now scriptures?
And worldly sentences such as "Bring the cow" and so forth are also scriptures. If this were so, there would be a great contradiction with common worldly usage;
for ordinary people do not apply the term "scripture" to sentences such as "Bring the cow."
Furthermore, there is a contradiction with one's own words;
for they themselves assert that what is found in sentences such as "Bring the cow" possesses the characteristic of verbal testimony (*śābda*).
Moreover, in the Mīmāṃsā and other systems, we observe that even more than the Veda, it receives the metaphorical designation of the word "scripture" (*śāstra*) due to its excellence.
Moreover, this word "śāstra" may be either conventional (rūḍha) or etymological (yaugika); in either case,
it is entirely appropriate to apply it to the Vaidāṅgas and so forth.
For it has been described that within those [treatises] there is instruction on the meaning according to their respective subjects, and that their conventional usage is particularly excellent;
to this, it is replied:
This is a case of *yogarūḍhi* (a combination of etymological derivation and conventional usage), like the word *paṅkaja* ("mud-born") and others;

therefore, it does not over-extend [its application] to instances such as "bring the name" (*nāmānaya*). Even though the etymological connection (*yoga*) exists, ordinary people do not employ the term in those cases.
Ordinary people consider only those [treatises] which teach the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*) to be "śāstras.
Thus, because they possess auxiliary members (*aṅga*), these [Vedic texts] have the status of being *śāstra*.
Now, is it not the case that the definition of a *śāstra* is "that which prescribes" (*vidhāyaka*)?
And those [scriptures] do not effect anything at all.
This is not so;
for they are all intent upon the instruction for practice.
For in grammar, that which is spoken by the virtuous is taught as being [expressed] by these [correct words];
likewise, in Mīmāṃsā, in every section (adhikaraṇa), through the exposition of logic, there is everywhere only the instruction for performance.
Therefore, the rule is that whatever is a scripture is exclusively an instruction regarding engagement in and avoidance of [certain actions].
Furthermore, the worldly convention that "a treatise is merely that which instructs" has been restated here by the author of the Bhāṣya;
however, a definition of a treatise independent of that convention has not been formulated.
Therefore, that which [conveys] an object not [otherwise] proximate...

In this regard, the Buddhists have relied upon this inference, while the Vaiśeṣikas have accepted difference; however, the Sāṅkhyas and others have merely asserted difference without stating the cause of that difference.

The conceptualization of a sentence or the like as consisting of a final phoneme conjoined with preceding mental impressions, as well as the speaker's intention and so forth, do not exist in the case of smoke and such; by this, [the inference from smoke] is shown to be distinct.
That which has as its domain the human good (*puruṣaśreyas*) and is established in the world as "scripture" (*śāstra*) is indeed scripture.

On the other hand, that which has as its domain objects not in immediate proximity (*asannikṛṣṭārtha*), whether it be prescriptive (*vidhāyaka*) or non-prescriptive (*avidhāyaka*), is verbal cognition (*śābda*); such is the distinction.

And here, just as in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*), the various types of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-vikalpa*) regarding the word, its cognition, and so forth, should be demonstrated according to the speaker's intention.
One should not insist that cognition alone is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Rather, the distinction is as follows: with respect to the preceding means of knowledge, the subsequent cognition of the sentence-meaning is the fruit; and when that [cognition] is a valid means of knowledge, the resulting cognition of avoidance and so forth is the fruit. //14//
Those who maintain that there are only two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) consider this treatise to be non-different from inference;
in order to refute them, he sets forth their view with the words "In that regard" (*tatra*).
And this which has been stated by them is merely a formal proposition (*pratijñā*).
As for the presentation of reasons for their non-difference, that will be done on the occasion of refuting the reasons for difference stated by others.
But why exert oneself in presenting and refuting non-difference?
Is it not the case that this non-difference has already been refuted by the Sāṅkhyas and others who maintain the doctrine of difference?
Therefore he says: "Difference.
The meaning is that they have not stated an incorrect cause for difference. //15//

He sets forth the arguments to refute those very causes of difference mentioned therein, ending with the words "by the preceding mental impression" (*pūrvasaṃskāra*). For it has been stated by them as follows: "In verbal cognition, the final phoneme, conjoined with the preceding mental impressions, constitutes the sentence."
Or else, it is the first phoneme,
or all of them individually, or all of them together.
