It is either these very same sequential phonemes (*pada*), or the universal (*jāti*) of sentencehood itself, or the whole (*avayavin*), or the *sphoṭa*—with all distinctions such as individual phonemes removed—or it is the phonemes themselves that, when combined, express the meaning.
These same alternatives should also be shown to apply to the words (*pada*).
Likewise, the intention to speak, the effort, and so forth, are the causes for the production of the word-sound.
"Since all of this [characteristic] is not observed in smoke and the like, it is not an inference due to its dissimilarity (vaidharmya) to them.
To this, he states the refutation: "In that regard... (tatra).
When it is stated by the Buddhist that verbal cognition is non-different from inference because it arises through positive and negative concomitance— just like the inference of fire from smoke—
the opposition raised by means of the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) with smoke and so forth [is as follows]:
This is the fallacy known as *vaidharmyasama* (balancing the heterogeneity) or *vikalpasama* (balancing the alternative). What, then, is a "fallacy" (*jāti*)?

A *jāti* (futile rejoinder) is the counter-position established by means of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). For when a formal argument (*prayoga*) has been stated by the proponent, a consequential difficulty (*prasaṅga*) arises;
because it arises (*jāyate*), it is called a *jāti*.
And that *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) consists of an opposition based on similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
Regarding those [objections], it has been stated that they constitute the fallacies of "balancing the dissimilar" (*vaidharmyasama*) and "balancing the alternative" (*vikalpasama*);
for there is no difference [in the logical status of the examples] due to specific distinctions such as smoke, impermanence, or horns.
When the proponent has stated a reason based on similarity with the example (*udāharaṇasādharmya*), and the opponent offers a counter-argument based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*),
as for instance: when the proponent says, "The self possesses action because it is joined with qualities that are the causes of action, like a clod of earth."
The opponent's counter-argument by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is as follows: "Just as a substance possessing action is observed to be non-pervasive,
like a clod of earth,
so too is the self not [non-pervasive]."
Therefore, it is "devoid of action.
This is called the sophistical refutation (jāti) known as "balancing the heterogeneity" (vaidharmyasamā),
because of the alternative conceptualization of another property.
When a conceptual alternative is also applied to the probandum by means of a similar statement, this is called the fallacy known as *vikalpasama* (balancing the alternative).
For instance, in this very syllogism, the opponent says:
"Something endowed with the qualities that cause action is seen to be non-omnipresent, such as a clod of earth; something else is omnipresent, such as the self."
Thus, just as some things may possess activity while others lack it,

so too here, when an opponent has stated a proof by means of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), if one objects merely on the basis of its dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) to smoke and the like, the fallacy known as *vaidharmyasama* (balancing the heterogeneity) is incurred.
For the inference of fire from smoke is devoid of verbal constructions and the like.
And since verbal cognition is not like that,
it is therefore not inference.
In the same way, the "balancing of the alternative" (vikalpasama) should be demonstrated as follows.

It is observed that some [cognitions], such as verbal knowledge, arise solely from positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) and possess syntactical construction and conceptualization; however, others do not, such as the cognition of fire through smoke and the like.
Thus, some [cognitions] will be inference (*anumāna*) and some will be non-inference;
this is because two types of classes (*jāti*) have been established.
And it should not be said that there is a further means of accomplishment. //16 1/2//

But how is this [definition of] "birth" [established]? For the proof is as follows: verbal cognition is distinct from inference because it possesses a different characteristic (vaidharmya), just like perception. To this, he says: "smoke," etc. It is not [the case that the definition is unestablished].
To that extent, they have abandoned the three characteristics [of a valid reason] and stated a mere dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

However, since a mere qualification does not differentiate the dissimilarities of those inferences whose nature is the object (*arthātmaka*), there would have to be a distinction between those [inferences] and inference itself; yet such a distinction does not exist.
For smoke and the like do not cease to be inferential simply because they lack [the aforementioned] dissimilarity; rather,
it is by virtue of abandoning the three characteristics that "being produced" ceases to be a reason for "impermanence."
Even in the demonstration of the abandonment of the three characteristics [of a valid reason], a distinction from inference is established. //17//
As long as the abandonment of the three characteristics is not established,
for one who speaks merely of a particularity, there would be the fallacy of a futile rejoinder (jāti).

Even the cognition that arises from a word through its application according to one's will does not arise from smoke and the like; thus, here too, there is a deviation [from the rule] due to the functions of the constituent parts.

But for one who asserts a difference based merely on dissimilarity, the very statement of that dissimilarity would result in the production of a universal (jāti); thus he says: "By means of the three characteristics" (18).

Furthermore, this other distinction between verbal testimony and inference has been stated: for smoke and the like produce the cognition of the inferential mark through a connection that is indeed natural (svābhāvika),
whereas from a word, a comprehension of the object is observed even when it is employed according to one's own will.
Regarding the phrase "therefore, there is a difference," he says in response to that: "Just as...
The intended meaning is this: even here, if a difference were asserted merely on the basis of some dissimilarity, [it would be untenable].
Therefore, it is simply a [verbal] cognition.
Now, as for this argument: "Verbal cognition is distinct from inference because it brings about its object through the application of what is intended"—that is incorrect.

In that case as well, [the word] conveys its object such as form (*rūpa*) by means of its own inherent power (*svābhāvikī ātma-śakti*). Alternatively, if it is argued that the cause of conveyance is the application [of the word] to its own object according to one's will, then even an inferential mark (*liṅga*) is similar: when it is employed in an argument for the sake of another, it conveys that very person toward whom it is directed. Thus, the two cases are equal.

Now, if the convention of "employment according to one's wish" is what is being designated, then the meaning [of the statement] becomes this: it causes one to understand only that very thing for which it is conventionally established.
Consequently, there is an absence of an example;
for nothing other than sound makes an object known by following a convention. Thus, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For inference is a means of demonstration that does not conform to the application [of the object] according to one's desire,
and this [scriptural testimony] is not so; therefore, it is distinct [from inference].
That is not so;
for mere negative concomitance (vyatireka) alone is not indicative [of proof], since a logical reason (hetu) is required to possess both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
Furthermore, this reason is not understood anywhere as being pervaded by non-difference from inference.
Since nothing beyond the word itself is established through its arbitrary application,
if it is argued that there is a communication of hand gestures and the like according to convention,
then that must be either another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) or inference (anumāna).
It is not, first of all, a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because its defining characteristics are absent;
therefore, being known by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*), it is simply inference (*anumāna*).
This being the case, there is an inconsistency (vyabhicāra) due to that very [instance], and thus the exclusion of the reason (hetu) from the class of inference is not established.
This is what was stated: "There is inconsistency with those things that function as parts."
The functions of the limbs, such as the hands and so forth, consisting of contraction, extension, and the like, are called "limb-functions" (aṅgavṛttayaḥ). //19//

Even those things such as the notion of a horse, which have been established by convention for the purpose of conveying a certain meaning—they are considered its indicative mark; this is the settled rule.
And if [the Veda] were produced by a person, it would likewise be subject to error;
thus, the words of Vedic sentences would not possess universal truthfulness.
He explains this very point: "hasteti" (regarding the hand).

Those functions (*vṛtti*) residing in the hand and other limbs are called "hand-signs" (*hastasamjñā*) because they serve as auxiliary factors for the cognition of specific objects. But how, then, is this an inference?
For [the cognition] is not pervaded by objects such as the specific arrangement of the hands or specific numbers,
since it sometimes occurs even without them;

rather, when one understands an object from the particular arrangement of fingers and so forth, one understands it from the word itself through the recollection of the word that existed at the time of the convention.
That is not so;
for even without a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), a person who has not yet mastered the usage understands the actual object upon seeing the arrangement of the finger and so forth.
And there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) here;
for no deviation is observed in such an arrangement as that in which the pervasion (vyāpti) was understood.
This very point has been described in the passage beginning with "by that [reason], in other subjects (dharmyantareṣu)."
Therefore, this is indeed inference.
Thus it has been stated: "That [cognition] is established as having that as its mark.
Having followed all of this, the author of the Vārttika has provided a refutation.
For the comprehension of meaning from a word does not occur through an application [of meaning] according to one's own desire;
rather, words such as "cow" (*go*) and so forth convey their own objects solely in accordance with their innate power (*nija-śakti*).

However, arbitrary words (*yadṛcchā-śabda*), which are like hand gestures and the like, bring about the cognition of an object by following convention (*saṅketa*); since these are nothing other than inference (*anumāna*), what is the point of establishing a distinction for them? //20//
This is another cause of distinction: for while the determination of an object from a word depends upon a person, a word does not function in that manner; therefore, it is distinct [from inference].

He refutes this as well with the words "puruṣa" (person): a negative reason (vyatireka-hetu) establishes its object precisely by means of a negative concomitance (vyatireka), just as the vital breaths and so forth establish the self as distinct from the non-self body.
Moreover, dependence upon a person is observed to be a factor in the determination of meaning even in inference, as seen in the case of bodily gestures;
for whatever convention has been established by persons for the communication of a particular meaning,
that very same one is understood by others in reliance upon those persons.
Therefore, even here [the reason] is inconclusive. Furthermore, he states that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) because it is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), by saying "words" (*pada*).
For words convey their meaning through their own inherent power alone, not in dependence upon a person.
And this experience of a relationship is distinct from other cases:
in this instance, it depends on a person, whereas in the case of fire and smoke, it depends on place.
And others have stated that there is no difference [between scripture and inference] due to the dependence on time and other factors;
this is because, through the general absence of contradiction in the words of a reliable person, it is established by means of inference.
Even Vedic statements do not depend upon a person for the communication of their own meaning; they depend upon an authoritative source (āpta) merely for the determination of their own form. //21//
Surely, a word that has not had its relationship [to its meaning] grasped cannot convey a meaning;
nor is there an understanding of the relationship that is independent of persons.
Even Vedic sentences do not convey their own meaning unless the relationship between words and word-meanings has been grasped.
Therefore, this relationship between word and meaning depends solely upon human agency; thus, there is no lack of pervasiveness [in the definition].
For this reason, he says: "the relationship.
The intended meaning is as follows: in the communication of meaning, the word and the Vedic sentences are indeed independent.

And just as the experience of a relation here depends upon a person, so too in other forms of inference that very same [experience] is indeed seen to be distinct; he demonstrates this very distinction with the words "In this case... up to the end of the verse.
"In this case" refers to... [the rest of the sentence follows].
In the case of hand gestures and the like, there is dependence on a person, for such a convention is of human origin;
however, in the case of fire and smoke, there is dependence on place.
In the case of the rising of the moon and the swelling of the ocean, there is dependence on time. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), he indicates dependence on state.
By this, the following is meant: even in inference, the comprehension of the relationship is of many kinds, due to the distinctions based on place and other factors.
In the same way, here too [in the case of verbal testimony], there will be dependence upon a person;
for even in inference, the cognition of the relationship is seen to depend upon him.
Furthermore, they have not even refuted the reason for non-difference stated by the opponent; thus he says: "And it has been stated" (uktā ca). //22 1/2//
He presents that very reason for non-difference: "by the word of a reliable person" (*āptavāda*).

The meaning is this: just as in the case of smoke and so forth, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between two general properties is determined by setting aside their particular differences, so too in the case of verbal testimony, the pervasion between the general property of being the word of a reliable person and the general property of non-contradiction is understood.
And having understood it thus— that [the Veda] is non-contradictory because it is the word of the authoritative Lord (*īśvara*)— non-contradiction is inferred even in the case of the Veda;
therefore, this is indeed inference.

As long as non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*) is not inferred, a cognition that has arisen with respect to an object is indeed invalid (*apramāṇa*), because it lacks the quality of being determinative (*aniścāyakatva*).
The word "general" (*sāmānya*) is connected to each [term]. The ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of the elision of a suffix ending in *-lyap*.
Nor does a difference in all cases follow from the difference between words such as "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) and so forth;
nor is a distinction between those [words] perceived here from words such as "horse" (*aśva*).
Furthermore, no word reveals its meaning when its relationship [to that meaning] is unknown;
therefore, because the relationship has not been experienced, it would not be the case that [inference] is not inference.

In this case, even though sound, cognition, the object, and the cognition of that object possess identical forms, there is no distinction [between them] because such a distinction is not observed in the cases of fire and smoke; therefore, it is excluded by that very fact.

Thus, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is as follows: although a relationship cannot be apprehended due to the differences among the specific instances of the non-discrepancy of authoritative statements (*āptavāda*), nevertheless, their status as inference can be asserted on the basis of the cognition of their commonality (*sāmānya*), because a pervasion (*vyāpti*) is possible between two generalities. //23//
But surely this is a ground for differentiation:
inference is dependent upon the ascertainment of a relation,
whereas words such as "the unprecedented" (*apūrva*) convey their own meaning without depending on the knowledge of such a relation.
Therefore, because [the word] differs [from inference], he says: "And not...
Since words such as "cow" convey their meaning only when the relationship [between word and object] is already known, their status as inference is unavoidable;
however, if their difference [from inference] is asserted on the basis of examples such as the *apūrva* (the unseen force), then [the same would apply to words].
That is not so;

for the other [opponent] can also say that these [words] possess the nature of inference (*anumāna*), because they produce cognition dependent upon a relationship (*sambandha*), just like smoke and the like.
Furthermore, even words whose referents are previously unknown (*apūrva*) do not differ from words such as "horse" and the like.
He says "and not" because there is no difference in terms of being a word. //24//
What follows from this if it is so? To this he says: "And not...
Since these are indeed words, and a word whose relationship [to its meaning] is unknown is not a revealer [of meaning].
Therefore, even by these [words], the object must be cognized only when the relationship [between word and meaning] is already known, because they are words (*padatvāt*).

But how can a relationship with something like heaven (*svarga*), which has never been seen before through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is thus unprecedented (*apūrva*), be experienced?
It might not indeed be possible.

If [the relationship] were not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the unprecedented [relationship]—such as between the ritual action and its fruit—would be established by the means of valid cognition known as "presumption" (*arthāpatti*), since it could not otherwise be accounted for.

Furthermore, heaven is understood from the supplementary portions of Vedic statements to have the nature of unsurpassed bliss; thus, the apprehension of the relationship is possible through such cognitions.

Therefore, he states—beginning with "sambandha"—that what has been asserted by others, namely that "verbal testimony is not inference because it does not depend upon a [logical] relation, like the sense organs," is refuted due to the unestablished nature of that reason. //25//

Having introduced another reason for the distinction, he refutes it with the words "tulya" (equal) and so forth. [The compound] *śabdapratyāsattyā tajjñānam arthaś ca taddhīś ca* is to be analyzed as follows: "by means of the proximity of the word, there is the cognition of that [word], and the object and the cognition of that [object]. This too must be shown to be a non-conclusive (*avīta*) reason.
The refutation of that [objection] should be sought in the refutation of superimposition (*adhyāsa*);
therefore, the claim of having an identical form is unestablished. //26//

In the case of reflections, there is no lack of certainty; for whatever the original object is like, such is the face and so forth perceived in the mirror, and yet this is not a matter of non-inference.
Even in this case, direct perception is [the means of knowledge],
for when those who have gone [to another place] are inferred by their footprints and so forth, it is not subject to error by others.

Nor does it arise from a single sentence spoken only once, for there would be no distinction between this [type of cognition] and the understanding of multiple contradictory and non-contradictory things occurring at that same moment.
Furthermore, he states "in the case of reflections" because the reason [he has provided] is inconclusive due to the cessation of the speaker's intention; "ekānta" means certainty,
and that is its effect.
"It is not the case that it does not exist; thus, there is no lack of certainty.
To the question "In what way is there no lack of certainty?", he says: "The original object (bimba)."
For just as a reflection is perceived in a mirror, so too is the face and such understood;
therefore, there is a similarity between the object of cognition and the means of cognition here as well. Thus, the reason (hetu) existing in the case of reflections is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Now, one might object: "But this is not inference."

For it will be stated in the section on sound (*śabdādhikaraṇa*) that the face is understood through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself, being illuminated by the ocular light which has been reflected by the light of the mirror.
Therefore, he says: "And not...

The intention is as follows: when one has recognized the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between similarity and the reflection residing in the mirror with respect to fingers and other objects that are directly perceived, [then the inference occurs].
In that case, one would infer that even the face reflected in a mirror conforms to the actual object;
otherwise, one might suspect that even the contact with a finger, when perceived as having a different form, would cause it to appear as something else entirely.
Therefore, one should not determine that it is of such a nature. //27//
Let this be direct perception; why such fine scrutiny?
Let us demonstrate the inference itself even more clearly.
He says "perceptibility" (*pratyakṣatā*) because the dissimilarity between the object to be understood (*gamya*) and the means of understanding (*gamaka*) is apprehended therein.
By the word "of those that have gone," he demonstrates their imperceptibility (*apratyakṣatā*) for the purpose of establishing the scope of inference (*anumāna*). //28//
As for this which was said: "For in the case of verbal [cognition], a sentence uttered only once suddenly presents various meanings— both contradictory and non-contradictory—
just as in the cases of 'Dharma is an object characterized by Vedic injunction' and 'The white one runs.'"
It is not so in the case of inference;
for smoke, having its pervasion known by a certain [fire], produces a cognition only with respect to that one [locus].
Therefore, there is a difference between verbal testimony and inference.

And the formal argument is as follows: "Word is distinct from inference, because at one time it manifests multiple objects, like the sense-organ"; or else, the reason is not yet established, for the indicative mark (liṅga) is indeed one and the same.
For the indicative mark (liṅga) is also seen to possess that same nature [of being either a reason or a contradictory one].
If you argue that there is no inference due to contradiction, then for you, there would likewise be no scripture.
And where there is a single meaning within a sentence, there it would possess the nature of inference;
for when this [sentence] is uttered once, only a single intention is observed.
But that which arises from various flashes of intuition regarding objects not yet determined—
It is seen even when the characteristic mark is not distinct; therefore, it is not differentiated by this.
It illuminates,
like smoke and so forth; but sound does not do so.
"Therefore, it is distinct.
Having introduced that [objection], he refutes it with the words "from a single sentence.
The meaning is that even by this method, there is no distinction. //29//
"Why is there no difference?
To this he says: "Of the probans as well.
The meaning is that the reason (hetu) is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
For smoke as a reason simultaneously establishes fire-ness, heat, combustibility, and the state of being a transformation of fuel.
Likewise, in the case of the contradictory [reason] "sound is non-eternal because it is produced," it first establishes eternality according to the speaker's intention.
And because impermanence [is not established] by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the reason is therefore inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Now, one might object: "An inconclusive reason does not establish a single intended meaning, for a logical mark (*liṅga*) becomes a means of proof only through the force of pervasion."
Therefore, since being produced is pervaded by impermanence, it is that [quality] alone which causes [impermanence] to be known;
for a pervasion by a contradictory property is impossible for a single thing precisely because of the contradiction.
He raises that very doubt with the words: "Because of contradiction."
He states the answer: "It may be so" (*syāt*).
For it is understood that a word possesses the power to convey the intended meaning; therefore, even such a word conveys only one meaning at a time.
But in the case of a different meaning, this [reason] is likewise non-conclusive due to contradiction. //30//
And he says "wherever... because by this reason, the distinction between numerous sentences having a single meaning is not established;
for a word does not express only multiple contradictory things, but also non-contradictory ones.
This has been stated: "A word is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding that which is intended to be expressed.
And [it is argued that] once uttered, it produces a single cognition;
therefore, there is no presentation of multiple meanings anywhere, so the reason is unestablished (asiddha). To this, he says: "Once" (sakṛt) //31//
Granted that there is indeed a manifestation of multiple meanings from a word, yet let it be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to only one [of those meanings];
by this much alone, its difference from inference (*anumāna*) is established. Therefore, he says: "But as for... (*yastu*).
For indeed, the non-statement of an example is seen to be fallacious in the case of smoke and so forth;
yet even there, no example is stated because it is already well-known.
But when [the word] has not been practiced, one requires the recollection of its relata;
for in some cases, they understand it only after a long time, thinking, "It was used here."
Furthermore, the reasons stated by others here do not refute the non-difference [of verbal testimony from inference];
for there is identity between verbal testimony and inference, just as [the inference] of fire from smoke.
Because a single instance of perception is seen through positive and negative concomitance,
and because comprehension arises from this [perception] preceded by a [logical] connection.

Just as, prior to familiarity with the correct mode of expression, multiple meanings hover around a word, so too, when a mark such as smoke is not clearly understood, there is indeed the appearance of multiple objects;
for one who is doubting from a distance whether "this is smoke" or "is it a trail of dust," there arises an unsettled deliberation regarding either fire or a whirlwind. //32//

Likewise, he states that the failure to cite an example in the case of sound is not a cause for [its] distinction from smoke and so forth, because of deviation (vyabhicāra)—this is expressed by the words "dṛṣṭānta" etc. To the question "How is there deviation?", he replies: "Because it is well-known" (prasiddhatvāt). //33//
Now, it might be argued that while there is a requirement for an example when the subject is unfamiliar, in the case of sound, even that requirement does not exist; therefore, he says: "unpracticed.
He demonstrates this very requirement with the word: "here."

For where a doubt arises concerning the object of an unfamiliar word-meaning, as long as one does not understand— after reflecting for some time— that "this word has been used by the elders in this sense," one cannot ascertain that meaning.
Thus, it has been demonstrated that the proponents of difference have not correctly stated the causes of difference. //34//
He states that they have also failed to refute the reasons for non-difference asserted by the Buddhists, saying "paroktā" (stated by others).
He sets forth those very reasons for non-difference in two and a half verses beginning with "śabdānumānayor."
The meaning of this is as follows: just as the inference of fire from smoke arises from positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka),

and because a single instance of smoke is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and because direct perception is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) due to its capacity to bring about the cognition of an object not previously seen.
And because it has a general object as its domain, and because it relies upon objects belonging to the three times.
Some Mīmāṃsakas have stated that here there is a distinction from other objects:
for the scripture proceeds toward its meaning only when [the object] has been excluded by the two preceding [means of knowledge].
And it is preceded by a relation;
likewise, knowledge arising even from a word arises in this very manner.
And that other means of valid cognition [inference] is distinct from perception.
And verbal cognition makes known an object not perceived through direct perception, has a universal as its object, and pertains to all three periods of time.
Therefore, it is not distinct [from inference].
This is an explanation of the meaning of the proof-statement (*sādhana-vākya*).

The applications of the proof, however, should be shown as follows: "Verbal cognition is inference, because it is produced by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), like the inference of fire."
Because the arising of the perception of a single [object] occurs in that very same way, the reason is its being preceded by a [prior] connection;
those two alone are the probandum and the example.

Nor should it be said that [the case of verbal testimony] does not differ from [inference] in its being preceded by a relation, because it arises from positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*);
for the relation of inference consists precisely of positive and negative concomitance.
Previously, the reason was stated as "arising from a specific relation," whereas now, the reason is "being preceded by a general relation" without intending to specify the particularity.
In the same way, for the three subsequent [examples] as well, the application of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) should be performed as before.
In the fourth, however, the inference of fire is merely an illustration; [it concerns] that which is yet to be or has already occurred.
Inference must also be demonstrated. //35-37//

Now, he introduces the refutation of the reason for the difference [of objects] according to a certain school of Mīmāṃsakas with the words "by some. He shows a different perspective with the words "from the two preceding ones. The intended meaning is this: whatever functions with respect to that which is not delimited [as distinct from it] is different from that.
Just as inference [is distinct] from direct perception,
so too scripture functions regarding objects not determined by the former two;
therefore, it differs from them.
Furthermore, what is the purpose of establishing a distinction from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since no one maintains their non-distinction such that it would need to be refuted?
It is said:
there certainly is a misconception among some that this verbal cognition, which arises based on the operation of the auditory organ, is nothing other than auditory perception itself.
Because it follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [sound];
for this very reason, it does not occur for one who is deaf.
Thus, by demonstrating the difference through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), [the opponent's position] is refuted.
For he thinks as follows: it has been shown that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the apprehension of what is presently existing.
But this verbal cognition (*śābda*) has objects belonging to the three times; therefore, how could it be included within perception?
Furthermore, a deaf person does not know the object because of not hearing the word.
It is not because of the non-hearing of the object;
rather, there is the following formal argument: verbal cognition is distinct from perception, because its object is not determined by that [perception], just like inference. //38//

Even in that case, it would not possess the status of scripture if it were merely the speech of a person; if you say "let it be so," then what is the cause for confidence regarding the object, and how could there be such confidence regarding the speaker's intention?
Thus, having accepted this difference as a matter of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), he refutes the cause of that difference by means of inference, [saying] "in that case also" (*tatrāpi*).

For he thinks as follows: if the difference is asserted on the grounds that its object is not determined by inference, then human statements would lack the status of being authoritative scripture (*āgama*).

Because their objects are determined by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas Vedic sentences alone have as their objects things that are not the domain of other means of valid cognition; thus, the reason [you have provided] is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*).
What, then, is this undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭa*) that has been brought forward?
Indeed, it is precisely the non-scriptural nature of human statements that is sought after;
for scripture is the authoritative teaching (śāstra),
and a teaching is purposeful only when [the matter] has not been previously established.
He will say:
"Furthermore, these [statements] are merely restatements (*anuvāda*) that establish objects already established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
for this very reason, the Vedic sentence itself is treated as the distinct subject (*pakṣa*) in the treatise: 'The scripture functions with respect to its object.'"
The sense is that it is because of the utility [of the distinction] residing precisely in that difference.
He states this very point with the words "as follows" (yathā).
Regarding this, he states the refutation with the word "cognition" (pratyaya).
Thus, this proponent of the non-authoritativeness of the five types of speech should be asked:
"Is there for you a comprehension of meaning from them, or not?
It cannot be that there is none."
Because it would follow that all worldly conventions would be abolished, and because it is impossible for an existent thing to arise without a cause, a cause must be stated.

Since no cause other than the word itself is logically possible for this [knowledge], the cognition produced by human speech—which is born, unconfused, and unsublated by another cognition—is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, one should not accept the position that it is not based on scripture (*anāgama*).
Regarding the word "yukta" (it is logical):
the other [opponent], however, with the intention of including [verbal testimony] within inference, says—"of the speaker's cognition.
The intention here is this: for human statements are generally characterized by a high degree of non-correspondence [with reality].
Therefore, these [scriptural passages] do not determine their meaning merely by being heard;
nor does an undetermined meaning become known,
because knowledge is precisely that which is determined.
Therefore, prior to the arising of certainty, since there is simply an absence of knowledge, what is the point of an effort based on a cause? However,
when the speaker himself has ascertained the pervasion (vyāpti) in this way— "and he does not speak of what he has not understood"— then [the inference is valid].

Then, by means of that very statement—which is the effect of knowledge—one infers the cause, namely the knowledge; having inferred it, the object is ascertained through the non-deviation of the knowledge from the object.
And in that state, since the object is already understood through the mark (liṅga) of the knowledge, the statement is merely repetitive (anuvādaka). Therefore, it is not scripture (āgama).
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī), however, asks: "How indeed could this [cognition] exist?
The intention here is as follows: it is cognition that, once itself apprehended, determines the object;
and we shall explain later that there is no cause for its own apprehension. //39//
That [intention] is not the mark (liṅga) of the word’s meaning, nor is the word in any way [the mark] of it;
no distinction is perceived by means of those two, and thus it cannot be an object of inference.
Therefore, when the speaker's intention has not been determined by perception or other means of valid cognition,
even the words of a person attain the status of scripture for the listener.
Therefore, he says "no," meaning that what is not itself understood cannot be the mark (liṅga) of the object.
Now, it was argued that [the object] will be inferred from the word as an effect; to this he replies: "not the word."
Since there is no mark (liṅga) that serves as both [the probans and the probandum] in both respects,
he demonstrates this by saying "the particular" (viśeṣa).
For inference occurs by virtue of the power of pervasion (vyāpti).
And here, since the generality of speech is understood to be pervaded by the generality of cognition, that [particular speech] would be established from it;
and from mere cognition, mere objects [would be established],
but it is not so in this case.
This is because it is the specific cognition and its object that one desires to infer;
and since those two cannot be inferred due to the absence of a grasp of their relationship [with any other term], [one might object]:
"But surely, when a trustworthy person employs a statement, they employ it only after having known that very thing; thus, the relationship is indeed understood through the specific cognition itself."
Therefore, that very [word] itself shall be inferred.
If this is so, then the meaning is already understood prior to the sentence;
for otherwise, it would not be possible to point out where [the word] is employed.
Furthermore, no specific quality of cognition can arise—apart from the coloring by an object—which could then be inferred;
nor is mere cognition, devoid of an object, what is being inferred; and yet, from such [mere cognition], a specific object cannot be established.
Nor is knowledge uncertain, for the nature of cognition belonging to one characterized by doubt has already been demonstrated;
and such doubt does not arise from the words of human beings.
As for the suspicion of invalidity arising from occasional deviation, it has been stated that this is dispelled by [the speaker's] reliability (*āptatva*) and so forth.
If, however, it is argued that there is an understanding of a specific cognition such that one determines: "This person does not employ words whose meanings are unconnected," [then...]
Nor is it the case that the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not understood; therefore, it must certainly be that their concomitance with this [word] has been known by them.
Now, does a listener who has already ascertained the connection between words and word-meanings fail to understand the meaning from a human sentence altogether?

If this were so, then even if the intellect produced by the Veda were superior—being born as certain and non-erroneous—it would not be distinguished from the cognition produced by the words of a teacher.
For some degree of doubt may arise regarding the Veda as well, due to its being a composition of sentences and so forth; however, that alone does not constitute its lack of authority.
"By those two" means by cognition and by the word. //40//

Therefore, since perception and other means of valid cognition are impossible for apprehending the speaker’s intention, it cannot be claimed that the meaning of scripture is not inferable when that intention is not apprehended;
for the word itself functions as its logical mark (*liṅga*), just as smoke does for fire.
Nor, because it is not inferable, can it be apprehended by another means of valid cognition;
for it is not accepted that visible form is imperceptible simply because it is not audible.
This being the case, none of our own colleagues have, with sufficient care, recognized that this particular kind of inference is a means of cognizing such a property (dharma). Msv 5.44.

However, the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of a future object has been rejected in the case of *dharma*, because the inference of an object [from such a mark] is impossible. He says "by that" (*tena*)—meaning that the word of a person, which brings about for the listener an object never previously attained, is indeed scripture (*āgama*), just like the Veda. //41//

As for what is also said—that the Veda is indeed a distinct means of valid cognition because its object is different from that of other means—that too is a mere fantasy; thus he says: "Nor also... and so forth.
The intention is that it cannot be stated. Why can it not be stated?
To this he says: "Because it is a mark (liṅga)."

The sense is: when it has been stated that, by the previously mentioned reasons, all verbal cognition without exception is non-different from inference, then how could that which is its object (the word-meaning) be something not inferable? //42//

[Objection: But surely, since the Veda makes known an object not previously inferred by a mark (liṅga) consisting of the object’s own nature, it will be a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). To this, he says: "And not... For just as smoke-ness, producedness, and so forth—despite their internal differences—are considered forms of inference because they do not abandon the three characteristics (trailakṣaṇya), so it would be here as well.
However, if it is argued that those [characteristics] are simply absent here, [then...]
In that case, it should be asked:
what is the purpose of introducing these intermediate distinctions? //43//
Others, however, whose power [to refute] has been exhausted, take recourse in non-difference and stand as partial proponents (*ekadeśin*); he shows this with the words "it being thus established.
For this is their intention: the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) has indeed been asserted.
And that [Vedic authority] is indeed established even within the category of inference;

for just as the Veda is a means of valid knowledge among verbal cognitions, so too is the inference of the Veda from other inferences. Therefore, what is the point of such great effort in establishing the Veda?
Now, it was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya that "because it is yet to come into being, a dharma is not inferred";
therefore, if one were to accept its status as an inference, there would be a contradiction with that [statement].
To this, he says: "it will be."
The meaning is that this has been refuted with the intention of [addressing] the object, the form, and the inferential mark. //44 1/2//
But perception, inference, and desire do not incur fault even with respect to scripture.
If verbal testimony and inference were non-different by virtue of their definition,
then the knowledge of the Veda would not be a means of valid cognition, because it would lack that definition.
For human speech attains the status of valid cognition through the characteristic of being inference, because it shares the common quality of non-contradiction with the words of a reliable person.

Since there is an absence of trustworthy persons in the Veda, and since there is no experience of a [verbal] relationship [between word and object], it follows that there can be no definition of inference; thus, the consequence of its lack of validity arises.

But surely, if it were true in one part, it would possess the status of inference—because it is the Veda—just like the *agnihotra* section or the passage concerning Vāyu as the swiftest deity. (Msv 5.5.49)
He refutes this as well with the word "saṃjñā" (name/designation).
The meaning is: if its status as inference is due to its being a mental universal occurring subsequently, then let that be so; there is no fault in accepting that.

However, if non-difference is accepted on the grounds of the identity of their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇaikatva*), then because the defining characteristic of inference would be absent and no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is admitted, the Vedic words would result in being invalid. Thus he says: "By the defining characteristic... (verse 46).

[Objection: Was it not stated that "the identity of the definition [of verbal testimony] arises from the commonality of being non-contradictory with the speech of a reliable person"? To this, he says: "By the speech of a reliable person...
The point is that by this method, the validity of human statements is established because they are of the nature of inference, but this does not apply to Vedic words. //47//
"Why is it not established?
To this he says: "But in the case of the Veda...
Since there is no authoritative person [to compose it], it cannot be inferred as being non-contradictory on the grounds of being the speech of an authoritative person.
Furthermore, since the experience of a relationship between the Vedas and supersensuous objects cannot be established, they would be devoid of authority;
however, it will be stated in the *Vedādhikaraṇa* that the Vedas were indeed composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*). //48//

[The opponent objects: "But surely, having observed that certain portions of the Veda such as the sentences concerning the *kṣepiṣṭha* [oblation] have meanings consistent with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one may infer that other sentences as well—such as those concerning the *agnihotra*—possess true meaning because they are part of the Veda;
therefore, there is indeed the status of inference by way of this definition. To this, he says: "But surely... (verse 49).
Nor can there be figurative usage [in the case of the "sun-pillar"] because of the lack of pervasion (anaikāntyāt), just as in that [other] case;
therefore, such counter-inferences are not valid according to the direction previously stated.

Therefore, if the status of verbal testimony as a means of valid cognition is established as identical in both the world and the Veda by virtue of the distinction in their defining characteristics, then the authority of the Veda is proven.
Consequently, the defining characteristic of scripture—being the instruction of a reliable authority—would not exist;
for there is no possibility of a reliable authority in the Veda, nor, therefore, is it a means of valid cognition.
For this has already been explained previously: therefore, regarding that cognition which arises from a word, its intrinsic validity would not exist if a defect were perceived.
He refutes this as well with the words "not [the case] of the sun":
the reason "being Vedic" (*vedatva*) found in the sentence concerning the sun-pillar (*āditya-yūpa*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Now, one might object: "But this sentence does not have an unreal meaning."
For it will be stated in the *Tatsiddhisūtra* that the word "Āditya" applies figuratively (*gauṇa*) to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) due to similarity;
therefore, he says "in the same way. It follows that even the sentences concerning the connection between action and its fruit would likewise have to be taken figuratively.

Moreover, previously, by the power of the Veda’s own authority and the strength of its validity, the inferences of invalidity were refuted; yet, if one were to admit their status as inference, they would be difficult to ward off due to their equal force. Thus he says: "Not from this... (50).

Therefore, if one maintains that verbal testimony is a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) solely on the basis of a difference in its characteristics, then the Vedas would not be a valid means of knowledge;
furthermore, the status of being a valid means of knowledge would be established equally for both worldly speech and the Veda. Thus he says: "Therefore... (verse 51).

Just as others have relied upon [the definition] that "verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person" (*āptopadeśaḥ śabdaḥ*), even so, because there is no such thing as a reliable person (*āpta*) in the case of the Vedas, they cannot possess authority; therefore, one should not rely on that [definition]. He says this with the words "by that," meaning by the Vedānta.
Furthermore, he states that even in the world, being a reliable person is not the cause of authority, saying: "In the world... (v. 52).
He states the reason: "In what follows" (*purastāt*).
For, by virtue of being authoritative, there is merely the removal of the suspicion of invalidation;
however, the validity of all cognitions is indeed innate, as has been explained in the discussion on intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya-vāda*).
What, then, is the definition of scripture (āgama)? To this he says: "Therefore... [The verse continues: "Cognition produced by faultless words is a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). //53//
The validity of this [word] through inference is entirely equal [to that of other means of knowledge];
since others have already exerted effort regarding the word (*pada*), it is described here [in relation to the sentence].
First, the objects of the inferential mark (liṅga) and the word (śabda) are seen to be of a different nature;
moreover, he will establish that the word has a universal (sāmānya) as its object.
It has been established that the subject (dharmin) is qualified by its property (dharma), and that this is the possessor of the mark (liṅgin);
for as long as that [subject] is not the object of that [cognition], there is no inference.
However, that which exceeds the general sense is the domain of the sentence in verbal cognition;
this is established through the force of implication (*sāmarthya*), even when other words are not explicitly heard, because it is to be inferred.
He states that for a word of this kind, its validity is established by inference alone, and not by means of a formal definition: "by inference" (anumānena). //53 1/2//

Now, intending to state the distinction of the word (*pada*) from inference according to his own view, he states the reason for establishing that [distinction] with the words "The word... (*pada*...).

Although the demonstration of its distinction is not useful because the word is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the word-meaning (*padārtha*), nevertheless, since others have conducted an investigation by citing examples of words, we shall demonstrate its distinction precisely.
Regarding this: the meaning is "in the word. //54//
Now he states the cause of this distinction: "the object" (*viṣaya*).
He demonstrates the very difference in objects with the words: "the universal" (*sāmānya*), etc.
For, in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, [it was established that] the word...
It will be established that [the means of knowledge] has a universal as its object. //55//
He says "the subject" (*dharmī*), because it has been established in the section on inference (*anumānapariccheda*) that inference has as its object a subject qualified by a property (*dharma*).
That which possesses a mark (*liṅga*) is the "marked" (*liṅgin*);
there exists a mark that establishes that [subject] as qualified.
Now, since it might be argued that in inference a general property (*dharmasāmānya*) is inferred by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*), he says: "Not yet," and so forth.

As long as that inference does not have a specific object as its domain—that is, until it becomes an inference with a qualified object—it is not yet an inference at all; it is not [an inference of] the mere property (*dharmamātra*).
It has been stated that [the object] is not a separate domain because it is already established. //56//

But is it not observed that even a single word has a qualified object as its scope? For example, when asked, "Which king is going?", another person replies, "The King of Pañcāla. In that case, from the word "King of Pañcāla" alone, a person qualified by the action [of going] is understood.
Therefore, he says: "Because of the commonality.
If it is argued that a category such as number (saṅkhyā) and so forth exists [in all nouns], that is not the case for indeclinables (avyaya) and the like.
Even where they are perceived, there [the cognition] is a qualification of the manifestation.
And because that which is denoted by another word serves the purpose of the action-nature [of the sentence],
even in the case of a sentence-meaning, a word such as "gomat" (possessing cows) is employed where it is required.

Even though there is a distinction here, it does not constitute the status of being a thesis (pakṣatā) because it is already established; for in that case as well, the object is exactly the same as what was previously determined.
If something is understood from verbal cognition that exceeds the general sense, that is the specific domain of the sentence alone.
For it is the sentence itself—through the ellipsis of a word—that conveys [the meaning], such as "the King of Pañcāla goes.
Now, let there be an ellipsis of what was actually heard; however, [this does not apply here].
Even when another word is not heard, a qualified cognition is observed from a single word, as for example, when "the door" is said, [the meaning] "let it be opened" is understood;
to the question "how is this so?", he says: "by virtue of semantic competency (sāmarthya)."

For a grammatical factor (*kāraka*) has its pervasion (*vyāpti*) known through action; by the very power of that pervasion, it leads one to infer the verbal root (*kriyāpada*). And from the verbal root thus inferred, the cognition of the specific meaning arises from the sentence itself even in that case. //57//
Here he raises an objection: "Number," etc. He provides the reply: "Not at all," etc.
For how could it be so in a case where number and the like are perceived? To this he says: "Even where," etc.
For a qualifier is meaningful only when there is both possibility and deviation [of the qualified from it].

Now, the universal (ākṛti) does not deviate from oneness; however, since duality and so forth do not occur in oneness, numbers and the like are qualifiers only of the individual (vyakti) implied by that universal. //58//

Thus, it has been stated that the number and other factors qualify the individual manifestation (*vyakti*) by way of pleasing it; however, they qualify the action— that is, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*)— by being for its sake,
for it is to that [action] that they are applied through direct statement (*śruti*) and the other means of application.
He says "padāntara" (in another word) because he will explain [this] regarding the oneness of the animal and in the case of the "ruṇā" (red) and so forth;
by "padāntaratvena," he demonstrates that there is an absolute remoteness from being a qualifier. //58 1/2//

If it is argued that a word such as "gomat" (possessing cows), which has as its object a particular qualified by the function of a sentence-meaning, will therefore be an inference, he says: "The sentence-meaning.
Even though this [word] indeed has a qualified object as its domain, nevertheless, it does not possess the nature of inference.

For a subject (*dharmin*) that is already established as qualified by some unestablished property (*dharma*) becomes the thesis (*pakṣa*) when it is being proven. But in this case, nothing at all has been apprehended prior to the utterance of the word; yet once the word is uttered, it is indeed apprehended as qualified. Thus, what remains to be proven?
The very fact that [the meaning of the base] is already established constitutes the difference between the meanings of the base and the suffix; furthermore,
there is no apprehension of independence in the sense of the qualifier and the qualified.
In that case, the cognition would have the qualified object as its primary focus, whereas here it is the opposite;
furthermore, why is the position not conceived such that the word itself possesses the meaning?
For in that case, the reason would result in being merely a part of the meaning of the proposition;
yet, with respect to the specific smoke in the subject, it is the universal that is intended as the reason.
He demonstrates this with the words "tāvān" (only that much): one who has not grasped the relationship [between word and object] does not cognize a qualified [object] from a word;
however, one who has grasped the relationship, while cognizing it, does not cognize anything more than what was understood at the time of learning [the word]. Thus, how can this be inference? //60//

Moreover, in this case, it is established that there is a disparity: two distinct parts of a word, consisting of stem and suffix, are themselves distinct, yet they are understood as having distinct meanings and experience a relationship of qualifier and qualified.
Thus he says: "Because of the cognition of difference.
However, this [distinction] is appropriate to say in the case of words such as *pācaka* (cook).
For in that case, by means of the verbal root (*dhātu*),
only the agent is expressed through the suffix (*pratyaya*);
however, the specific [agent] is understood through the sense (*artha*).

But in cases such as *gomat* ("possessing cows"), since the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is traditionally taught to denote a qualified object—namely, "one who has that"—how can there be any disparity?
It was stated here [in the previous verse] that "only so much" means that the scope does not exceed what was understood at the time of etymological derivation;
however, this [present case] concerns the meaning of words such as *pācaka* ("cook").
It has been stated [as follows]:
moreover, in inference, a qualificandum such as a mountain, which is apprehended independently, is understood as qualified by a qualifier such as fire, which is remembered independently;
since both are apprehended independently by means of the word, he says: "by the qualifier," etc.
The mention [of perception] is for the purpose of illustration; the meaning is that recollection is also included. //61//
He states another point of disparity: "By means of the particularity," etc. (61 1/2).
Here he raises an objection with the word "atha" (now/if).
Even here, since it is the word itself—perceived as a textual sequence—that is the probandum (*sādhya*) as qualified by its meaning, there will be no violation of the logical order. //62//
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "The meaning of the proposition," etc.

The "proposition" (pratijñā) is the "subject" (pakṣa), which is the locus (dharmin) qualified by a property (dharma); with respect to that qualified whole, it is called a "part of the locus" (dharmyekadeśa).
That very same thing becomes the reason (*hetu*).
For sound (*śabda*), being taken as the subject (*dharmin*), is itself the reason.
Now, when from a distance the specific nature of the substratum of smoke is not perceived, then smoke is established as possessing fire (*agnimattā*).
And it serves as a reason; likewise, it will be so here as well. Therefore, he says: "the subject" (*pakṣa*).
For at present, it is a particular instance of smoke.
In this case, "sound-ness" (śabdatva) is the indicator, not "cow-word-ness" (gośabdatva), which will be refuted;
therefore, since the individual instance alone is the qualificand, it follows that there would be only a single logical reason.

If it is argued that [the difference] arises from a difference in the manifesters, it is not so, because there is no such cognition; or else, how could this [sound] be qualified? It cannot be by way of place or time.

If it is that which is qualified by the cognition of that [word] which is being inferred, then what else remains to be inferred? Nor is the power to cause cognition inferred as a property of the object to be made known.

The subject (*pakṣa*) is that which is currently being perceived; the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is that which was previously known; and the reason (*hetu*) is the universal (*sāmānya*) that follows upon them. Thus, the distinction between the subject, the similar instance, and the reason is logically established. //63//
"Now, one might argue that here too we shall take a particular sound as the subject (*pakṣa*) and state 'sound-ness' (*śabdatva*) as the reason (*hetu*);
therefore, he says: 'sound-ness. For it is a particular object that is intended to be inferred."

Nor is its nature as "sound" (śabdatva) a means of cognition, because it is inconclusive (anaikāntikatvāt). [Objection: In that case, the intermediate generality (avāntarasāmānya), namely "the state of being the word *go*," will be the logical reason (hetu). To this he replies: "the state of being the word *go*" (*gośabdatvam*). Therefore, in this case, there is only a single individual (vyakti) which must be qualified by the object and designated as the reason; thus, the fault of the thesis-meaning being a part of the reason (pratijñārthaikadeśatva) is unavoidable. With this intention, he says: "the individual" (*vyaktiḥ*). //64//

[The opponent] says, "Surely, a single individual instance (vyakti) differentiated by the differences among its manifesters (vyañjaka) will be made the subject of the thesis"—to which [the author] replies with the words "it might be so. He refutes this with "but not so":
a difference based on adventitious conditions (aupādhika-bheda) does not divide the real entity (vastu).
The sense is that [the cognition] does not depart from those conditions.
Furthermore, distinction occurs when there is a relation;
therefore, he asks "Or how? regarding what kind of relation exists here between the object and the word.
First of all, the object is not perceived at the location of the word, for the word is in the mouth while the object is on the ground;
nor is it perceived at the time of the word.
He says that in the Kali age there is an absence of the purpose of the Kṛta age: "Not yet," etc. (verse 65).
A specific word is established through the cognition of its meaning;
for that [cognition] exists at the time of the word. He raises this objection with the words "tatpratītiḥ" (the cognition of that). He refutes even this with the word "param" (furthermore).

When a specific [instance] is being inferred based on a general dependency, that [dependency] must first be apprehended as already established. If it is already known, what else remains to be inferred?

But surely, having taken the currently perceived specific qualities such as rapidity (*druta*) and so forth as the subject (*pakṣa*), one proves their possession of a specific power of communication; and the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is the time of learning [the word].
For there is no power in the particulars; that [power] resides in the universal alone, just as the genus "fire" resides in a single portion.
Thus, both the thesis and the reason are established in the same way.
Therefore, a word qualified by its object cannot be an inferable [property];
and how, in this case, can the property of being a predicate of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) be established for the word?
Nowhere is there a relationship apart from the connection between an action and its agent; because the king is the sustainer of the man, he is called "the man of the king."

"We shall take as the logical reason (hetu) the universal 'cow-word' (gośabda-sāmānya) which follows both [the slow and fast utterances], so that there will be no fallacy of the reason being a part of the thesis (pratijñārthaikadeśatā). To this he replies: "Not by means of communication. The intention here is that there exists no connection between the specific qualities such as speed (druta) and the object based on place and so forth.
Furthermore, it is not possible for them to possess the capacity to convey meaning. //66//
To the question "Why is this not possible?", he says: "Of the particulars (*viśeṣāṇām*).

Just as in the case of a large volume of smoke that has been made the subject (*pakṣīkṛta*), fire exists below in one part of it, and thus the smoke qualified by that [fire] becomes the probandum (*sādhya*);
it is not so with the particulars such as fluidity (*druta*) and the rest, for they lack the capacity to convey [the object].
"Because they are not indicative due to their deviation.

As for that universal which is the word "cow" qualified by the power of producing cognition, it has already been stated that in that case, the very same thing would be both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*); thus he says, "of the universal," etc. //67//
Concluding that a word qualified by its object is not to be inferred, he says: "Therefore... (verse 67½).
Thus, it has first been stated that sound is not the subject (*pakṣa*). However, if one were to take sound as the subject and state that "sound" is the reason (*hetu*),
that too is incorrect.
He states "because it is not a property of the subject" (apakṣadharmatvāt), asking "And how?"—the sense being: "And how is it ascertained? //68//
"Why is it not determined? To this he says: "It is not an action" (*na kriyā*).

Something connected as the agent (*kartṛ*) to some particular action becomes related to something else; for all other types of relations, such as those between owner and owned, are preceded by the relation between an action and its factors (*kāraka*).
In this regard, he states that the relationship between owner and owned is preceded by a relationship of action and its factors (kāraka), saying "the king":
for first, the king and the servant, having entered into the state of agent and object within the act of supporting, experience the relationship of owner and owned. //69//
"The tree stands in its branches" means "those [branches] belong to it";
in a location where there is fire, smoke possesses the agency of coming into being with respect to that fire.
In all cases, such as the relationship between cause and effect, action is present;
and it is understood that there is no relation whose form is not apprehended.
And when there is no relationship, neither the genitive compound nor the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* is possible;
therefore, it cannot be established that "this is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*).

Even those who, once the connection [of the word] with anything else has ceased, might assert that the word possesses the property of being a predicate of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) by virtue of having that [subject] as its object— just like the case of non-perception (anupalabdhi)— [are refuted].
Thus, he states that the relationship between part and whole is also centered on action— namely, "the tree":
for there is the cognition that "the tree, as the whole, resides in its parts," and sometimes there is the cognition that "the parts themselves, such as the branches, reside in it."
Thus, the relationship between part and whole is based on the causal agency of the action of subsistence (*sthitikriyā*).
Likewise, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) also has its core in action; thus he says: "In a location.
Smoke, being the agent in its coming into existence within a location containing fire, becomes conjoined with that location containing fire.
Thus, he states "the effect," etc., to show that even relations such as cause and effect are preceded by the relation between an action and its factors (kriyākāraka).
For *kiṇva* (ferment) is the seed of wine; being the agent in the transformation into the nature of wine, it is called the cause of wine.
The same applies to the relation between a whole (*samūha*) and its parts (*samūhin*).
An elephant is said to belong to an army because it performs a part of the army's function, namely, the conquest of the enemy;
however, no such form of relationship is perceived between a word and its meaning.
Furthermore, one cannot claim that a relationship exists whose form has not been determined; thus he says: "And not... (na ca).

Furthermore, without a relationship [between the two], neither the genitive case in the analytical statement (*vigraha*) "the property of the subject" (*pakṣasya dharmaḥ*), nor the *tatpuruṣa* compound "subject-property" (*pakṣadharmaḥ*), would be possible; thus he says: "And there is not...
He concludes that both the application (*vṛtti*) and the analysis (*vigraha*) are untenable, saying: "Therefore... (72)

Others, however, state that sound has the object as its domain, thus asserting it to be a property of that [object], just as non-apprehension will be described as a means of knowing non-existence. He introduces this point with the words: "When [the cognition] has ceased... (73).
They too must investigate this: how can sound have that [unconditioned] as its object?
For there is no existence of that place and so forth, nor is there any facing toward it or the like.
Therefore, because this [word] produces a cognition whose object is a thing,
the conceptualization of its nature as a property (dharma) is that "the word has that thing as its object."

And when that capacity to denote has been established, the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatā) would not serve as a factor for cognition; nor, in that case, would there be the status of inference.

If it were argued that something is a property because it indicates [the subject], and that it indicates [the subject] because it is a property, then there would indeed be the fallacy of mutual dependence; therefore, this hypothesis is also untenable.

And they do not recognize the word as distinct from its own form when the relationship [between the word and its referent] has not been grasped; by means of which there might arise here the cognition that it is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
He states that this too is not tenable: "By them also" (*tair api*).
The meaning is that the relationship of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) does not hold in any manner whatsoever.
He explains how it does not hold with the words: "Not that" (*na tat*) //74//

Since it is impossible for [the word] to be [the object] in any other way, its status as having that as its object must be stated by means of the method of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*) as being the generator of a cognition whose object is that [word].

And since this quality of generating a cognition whose object is that [word] is untenable without the relationship of denoter and denoted (*vācyavācakabhāva*), the acceptance of that [relationship] is necessary.
Once that is established, the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is not a factor for the cognition [of the conclusion].
And he states that a cognition produced by what is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) is not inference, by means of the two verses beginning with "Therefore" (vv. 75–76).

But if it is maintained that the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatā) alone is the cause for generating the cognition whose object is that [probandum], then, since the property of being a feature of the subject is itself impossible without that [cognition], there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayatva). Therefore, he says "because of its capacity to prove" (gamakatvāt), meaning that this conception also does not hold together. //77//
For this reason as well, there is no "property of the subject" (pakṣadharmatā); thus he says, "And not...

Those who have not apprehended the relationship between the signifier and the signified do not know the word as a property of anything other than its own essential nature (svarūpa), by which a cognition of the word as a property of the subject might arise. //78//
The property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) does not belong to smoke and the like by their mere intrinsic nature (*svarūpamātra*),
nor does it follow that this [property] depends upon a prior relation.
The cognition "this possesses smoke" arises even for one who has not previously [perceived the connection];
therefore, it would differ from the subsequent definition [of the reason].
But here, the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatā) is not something additional to the prior relationship;
nor is it prior to the cognition of the object. Therefore, this [property] would not be a non-member [of the syllogism].

Furthermore, the subject (dharmin) has not been apprehended here, such that it could possess that property (dharmatā), just as a location like a mountain is not established prior to the determination of its properties. (Msv 5.5.82)

And that which is stated here as the subject (dharmin) is not itself its object of cognition (prameya); for, as long as that [subject] is not determined, there can be no determination of the property of being a property of it (taddharmatva).

However, the cognition of the mere intrinsic nature [of the reason] is not the cause for the property-of-the-subject (pakṣadharmatā) in the case of smoke and so forth; rather, it is the connection with the subject (dharmin).
With the intention that this [connection] does not exist, he says: "And not... (na ca).

But surely, even here, the relationship with the meaning—that is, the subject (*dharmin*)—is already understood at the time of initial linguistic acquisition; to this he replies: "Nor even... (verse 79).
This connection of the property with the subject (pakṣadharma-sambandha) appears even to one who has not previously learned the relationship, being entirely independent of any prior connection;

yet it is not so in this case, as he says up to the words "the cognition that 'it possesses smoke'. Precisely because this connection of the property with the subject is independent of that [prior relationship], [it is not established].

For this very reason, it is distinguished from that which follows—namely, the characteristic of presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*); otherwise, there would be no distinction between them. Thus he says: "by that. The three characteristics of a logical reason (*hetu*) are: its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), its presence in the similar class (*sapakṣe sattā*), and its exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣād vyāvṛtti*).

And therein, he teaches that the subsequent [member] following the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatā) is characterized as the connection with similar instances (sapakṣasambandha). //80//
He states that this is not the case with the word itself by saying "but not here.
This [non-eternality] is understood subsequent to the comprehension of the meaning based on the prior relationship;
therefore, he says "nor is it" to indicate that it is not an integral part of the word.
For this reason as well, he states that [the probans] is not a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), saying "nor is the subject" (*na ca dharmī*).
The sense is that, for the time being, a subject distinct from the object (*artha*) is not established by valid cognition. //82//

Furthermore, if that object which is to be conceived as the subject (dharmin) and understood as possessing a property (dharmatā)— namely, the word— is already grasped as being a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) prior to [the formal statement], then what further remains?
By means of which, when the properties of the subject and so forth are known, there may be inference.
Nor is the word defined by its object of cognition;
for the state of being connected is perceived through the operation of all [words].
Wherever there is smoke, the positive concomitance (anvaya) with the existence of fire is clear;
however, there is no such certainty that wherever there is a word, its referent (artha) exists.
First of all, he is not perceived in this place or at that time; yet, if it be argued that [his cognition] exists due to his eternal omnipresence, then that would apply equally to all objects.
Because he has seen everything everywhere, and because there is no exclusion [of anything], it would follow that all words convey the understanding of every object without exception. (Msv 5.88)
Now, if it is thus conceived that [the word] lacks reality due to [particular] place and time,
someone might say that the expressive cognition is accompanied by the cognition of the object.
The property (dharma) remains exactly as it was to be measured even subsequently;
therefore, if its presence in the subject (pakṣadharmatva) is to be understood, it must first be understood at the very outset.

Then, since that [object] has already been apprehended, what is the use of a subsequent cognition of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth? Therefore, he says with the two verses beginning "And that which... (vv. 83–84) that it is not inference.
Now he refutes the positive concomitance (*anvaya*): "Regarding 'positive concomitance'...
Why is it not established?
To this he says: "By means of the operation" (*vyāpāreṇa*). //85//
He demonstrates this very point with the words "where" (yatra).
He states that it is not so here with the words "but not" (na tu). //86//
To the question "How is it not so?", he says: "Not at all," and adds that this has already been stated previously.
Now, one might object: since the word is pervasive and the meaning is eternal, the connection between word and meaning can indeed be demonstrated; to this, he says: "It might be."
He refutes [the objection] with the words: "In all objects" (sarvārtheṣu) //87//
If this is so, what follows from it? To this he says: "By that" (tena). //88//
He raises a doubt regarding the relationship by means of another alternative: "Now, if it is thus... (89).

Even so, it is not the case [that there is no such cognition]; for we observe that, even in the absence of a cognition of the object, there occurs in some instances a cognition of the expressive word with respect to persons who have not yet mastered the linguistic convention.
And in the case of a second or subsequent application, there might be the conceptualization of a positive concomitance;
yet even when applied a hundred times, the cognition of an object [previously] perceived never occurs anywhere.
Surely, for those who have already known the relationship, the positive concomitance (anvaya) is clearly perceived.
If this is so, then some kind of relationship must have been postulated prior to that positive concomitance.
This conceptualization of a positive concomitance (anvaya) cannot be a constituent part of the cognitions of the objects [of inference];
moreover, it is established that the very birth of inference is dependent upon such a positive concomitance.
When the capacity for cognition is already known, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) arises solely by its own force;
how, then, can this [concomitance] be said to be the cause?
