He refutes this as well with the words "not so," providing the reason up to the end of the passage beginning with "for it is seen by us."
Where has this been seen? To this he says: "avyutpanna... (unlearned...). //90//

One might object: "In the case of the second and subsequent utterances, the concomitance (*anvaya*) between the word, its meaning, and the cognition will be grasped. Anticipating this, he refutes it with the words "even a hundred times.
Even after a hundredfold usage, one who lacks the desire to know does not perceive the relationship.
And one who has not cognized the relationship does not comprehend the meaning. //91//
"Now, for one who has ascertained the relationship [between word and object], the cognition of the object through the cognition of the word does not deviate from it;
and it is precisely this that is intended to be inference," he says with "Now, [is it not so]? He answers: "If that were so..."
If there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) for one who has already known the relationship, then a different relationship between word and meaning must be admitted. //92//
To this, he says: "It is not a factor" (nāṅgam).
If it is not a factor, what follows? To this, he says: "Because of the positive concomitance" (anvaya).
The meaning is that when there is no connection with reality, cognition is not inference. //93//

But positive concomitance (anvaya), arising solely in accordance with the capacity of cognition previously understood, is not the cause for the apprehension of an object; thus he says: "jñāte" (when [the object] is known). //94//
From that alone, the power of the word is understood as being independent of it;
nor is its capacity [to signify] apprehended prior to the connection with smoke.
If the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the cognition of the word from an unknown object is also [adduced],
that too, by virtue of being established subsequently, is not a means for the cognition of the object.

Regarding the relationship that we shall explain, the causes for its determination are positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*atireka*); however, these two are not the means for the comprehension of the object itself.
Therefore, verbal testimony would not be inference, just like perception,
because it lacks the three characteristics [of a logical reason] and because it excludes such an object [as that of inference].
And if it were a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then the determination of its difference or non-difference would be appropriate;
however, in this case, the word-meaning is not cognized through the cognition of the word as a valid means of knowledge.
He summarizes: "Therefore...
In the case of inference, however, the capacity to convey knowledge is not established prior to the positive concomitance (*anvaya*); thus he says: "And not... (95)
Now he refutes the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "As for 'negative concomitance'...
For indeed, if the object is not apprehended, the knowledge of the word cannot occur without the knowledge of that [object]; thus, negative concomitance cannot be apprehended.
If the object is already apprehended, what is the use of resorting to negative concomitance? //96//
To the objection that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are now useless regarding the word, he says: "The relation" (*sambandham*).
The relation between the word and its object, consisting of the signifier and the signified, is the operation of the two [powers] in the manifestation of their capacity (*śakti*). //97//

And thus, having established that [verbal testimony] is not inference by way of abandoning the three characteristics [of a logical reason], he demonstrates this through a formal argument: "Therefore...
[The text continues: "Sound is not inference because it lacks the three forms [of a valid reason], just like perception."
Because of the avoidance of such objects;
and in that very same way, it is "such.
Furthermore, the avoidance of objects has already been described by the passage beginning with "for [the cognition] has generality as its object," and so forth. //98//
And this demonstration of the difference between the word and inference, which we have provided, is intended to display our proficiency;
it is not, however, that the word is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Thus he says: "satī" [verse 99].
For a word being employed is used in four ways:
regarding what is perceptible, what is imperceptible, what is already known, or even what was previously unknown.
In that regard, when [a statement] is applied to what was previously known, to what is perceptible, or to what has already been cognized,
it is a restatement (anuvāda), unless there is something additional.
But regarding what has never been seen before, there is either ignorance or even the cognition of a relation;
yet that relation is not its [the word's] object, for that object which is the referent is the domain of the senses.
Cognition does not arise regarding an object that is both imperceptible and unexperienced;
however, in the case of that which is imperceptible yet has been experienced, memory is held to occur.
Since it has already occurred with respect to what is already cognized, memory lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge;
for validity arises only from having the result of a definitive determination (*pariccheda*).
He demonstrates how it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with the word "pada" (word).
He then states those very four types with the words "perception" (*pratyakṣa*), etc. //100//
He states how there is no validity for one engaged in these matters: "In that case," [verse 101].
But regarding that which was never seen before and is now perceived directly, its invalidity is characterized precisely by non-origination; thus he says: "never seen before.
Or rather, it is the very cognition of the relationship that arises at that time; thus he says: "the relationship.
Nor should it be said that the relationship itself is the object of knowledge (*prameya*) for the word.
With the intention that this [relation] is to be known through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), he says: "the relation.
But since its meaning is understood from perception (*pratyakṣa*), he says: "of the two objects. //102//
He states that knowledge simply does not arise regarding what has never been experienced before and regarding what is beyond perception (*parokṣa*), saying: "beyond perception.
However, he states that there is recollection (*smṛti*) regarding what was previously experienced even if it is beyond perception, saying: "beyond perception" [in the second instance]. //103//
[Objection: But surely it will be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) by producing memory itself; to this he says: "when [the object] has already been cognized" (pramite).
For memory has as its object that which has already been cognized, and it is an established principle that a means of valid cognition has as its domain an object that is in immediate contact.
But how is it that what has an unmeasured object is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? To this he says: "Because [it lacks] determination" (*pariccheda*).
For a means of valid cognition has determination as its fruit;
and nothing at all is determined by memory.
Because it brings about the presence of nothing but the prior consciousness. //104//
Why is it not assumed that memory, like recognition, possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because its fruit is the determination of the object at that very time?
Only as much as was previously delimited is maintained;
by means of memory following that [delimitation], there is no cognition of its existence at that time.
The state [of Buddhahood], because it lacks any further excellence, does not differ from that which merely recalls;
whatever slight superiority there might be, that is not within the scope of that state.
Even if the means of valid cognition were only inference based on words,
there would be no fault for those who maintain the authority of scripture, because the meaning of a sentence is the object of scripture.
Here he raises an objection: "tādātvika" and so forth.

Even though that object was previously apprehended, why does memory—which makes known its existence at that [present] time—not become a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)? //105//
He refutes this with the words "as much as" (yāvān). Memory arises at another time, but unlike recognition, it does not at that moment determine the actual existence of the object.
Because it follows from previous cognition. //106//
But surely, memory arises solely from prior mental impressions (*saṃskāra*);
however, this cognition of the meaning of a word from the word itself has a presently existing cause and is merely a direct apprehension (*grahaṇa*).
How then can it be called memory?
Therefore, he says: "the word" (*padam*).
Let there be no recollection;
yet even this apprehension (*graha*) has no object beyond [that of the original perception], because there is no appearance of anything additional.
Therefore, the word is not distinguished from remembrancers such as similarity or prior perception; thus, it is not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
[Objection: But surely, when either the action or the agent is uttered, there necessarily occurs in the mind a connection between one and the other.
Therefore, how can it be said that no additional element is perceived? To this he says: "That which is additional... and so forth.
The meaning is that this clarity belongs to another word alone, not to a single word by itself. //107//

And this is told by us to our disciples out of mere friendship, not because the word is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, even if it were a means of valid cognition, the meaning of the sentence would not thereby fail to be the meaning of scripture (*āgama*).
For even by that means of valid cognition, you must necessarily arrive at the meaning of the word.
Therefore, a sentence that makes known an object not already apprehended by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is indeed a pramāṇa itself.
Thus, even though the word is included within inference, there is no deficiency;
for the meaning of a sentence is not something inferable. So he says: "It is a pramāṇa. //108//

But with respect to the meaning of a sentence, cognition arises from the word-meanings even without the experience of their relationship; therefore, it is distinct [from them], just like sensory perception.
Furthermore, this reason will be unestablished (*asiddha*) in the section concerning the sentence (*vākya-adhikaraṇa*);
and all [reasons] stated by others will be unestablished with respect to the cognition arising from a sentence.
He asks: "How is it that the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence is not inference?

For even that [knowledge] follows upon a prior observation; therefore, he says: 'the meaning of a sentence'—it is the word-meanings themselves, whose relation [to the sentence meaning] has not yet been grasped, that cause the understanding of the sentence meaning."
Therefore, the cognition of the meaning of a sentence is not inference.

And this should be demonstrated as follows: the cognition of the meaning of a sentence is distinct from inference because it arises without the experience of a [logical] relation, just like sensory perception. //109//
But how can that which is unconnected be a communicator of another object?
For if it were so, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished; to this he says: "In a sentence... (*vākya*...).

Regarding those many reasons for non-difference from the cognition of other objects that have been stated through inference, he says "of all" [sarveṣām], indicating that they are unestablished with respect to the cognition of the sentence-meaning;
for the cognition of the sentence-meaning is certainly not born of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
It is not so, because [the object] possesses a relation [to the particular];
furthermore, its having a universal as its object is unestablished, since its object is a qualified [particular].

As for the claim that it is a means of valid cognition other than perception, once analogy and the others have been established as cognizing objects not perceived [by the senses], they cannot be made inconclusive.
Furthermore, the cognition of an unseen object (*adṛṣṭārtha*) by means of fallacious inferences (*anumānābhāsa*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Likewise, even that which has the three times as its object is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the case of fallacious inferences;
for it has been stated in the determination of the power of words (*śabdaśaktinirdhāraṇa*) that "the operation of those two [word and inference] does not consist in the production of cognition."
If, however, "being preceded by a relation" is stated without qualification, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to perception itself,
for that too is indeed preceded by a relation between the sense faculty and its object.
If, on the other hand, it means "being preceded by a relation that is a constituent of inference," [then...]
That is unestablished, for pervasion (vyāpti) is a constituent factor of that [inference];
and pervasion is not the cause for the cognition of the meaning of a word from the word itself.

Furthermore, the state of having a general object (*sāmānyaviṣayatva*) is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) on account of mere appearance; for [the properties of] being produced by direct perception, being a means of valid cognition other than direct perception, and the cognition of objects not seen [by that perception] apply to analogy (*upamāna*) and the other [means of knowledge] as well. //110//

Since the cognition of the sentence-meaning arises in this way even from sentences whose constituent parts have never been seen before, for one who knows only the word-meanings, the Buddhists—perceiving its distinction from inference to be quite clear—desist from it; fearing that scripture (āgama) is not distinct from human [cognition], they labor only over the investigation of the knowledge of word-meanings.
For it is thus:
Having observed that even when sentences are not explicitly perceived, there is a cognition [of meaning] by virtue of being merely one who knows the word-meanings,
she— fearing a departure from inference— was not troubled in her investigation into the non-difference of words.
Thus ends the *Śabdavārtika*.
Now begins the section on Analogy (*Upamāna*).
Suppose a city-dweller, having been asked, "What is a gavaya like? [is given the following answer]:
The forest-dweller spoke these words: "As is the cow, so is the gavaya."
He thinks:

"Let it be granted for now that even the word (*pada*) is non-different from inference; yet, on this basis alone, the statement that 'word and inference are identical' proceeds. To this, he replies with a derisive remark: "In sentences" (*vākyeṣu*). //111//
Thus ends the section on words in the Kāśikā commentary composed by the preceptor Sucarita Miśra.
Now begins the section on Analogy (*Upamāna*).
Analogy also produces a cognition of an object not present [to the senses] based on similarity;
for example, as the sight of a *gavaya* produces a recollection of a cow—so says the Bhāṣya.

The intended meaning of this is as follows: even comparison (*upamāna*) need not be examined [as a separate means of knowledge], because it does not deviate from being of such a nature [as already included].

As for the meaning of the individual words: the similarity perceived in one thing produces, in an object that is not in contact with the senses, a cognition characterized by a similarity to a counter-correlative (the object seen elsewhere), in the form "this is qualified by similarity to that."

Regarding the phrase "with its object of comparison" (*sopamānam*), the words "that which" (*yat*) and "which" (*tat*) are to be supplied. Nor should it be argued: "Since no specific object is mentioned, how can a cognition qualified by similarity be understood?"
For here, non-investigation is established by restating well-known means of valid cognition;
and in the world, the status of analogy (upamāna) is well-established as having an object characterized by similarity, whereas according to Śabara...
Because it does not fall outside of that scripture, it has been described otherwise.
In that case, the object is understood precisely through the cognition of the person;
it is well known that "cognition" (buddhi) is the means of comparison (upamāna).
Therefore, there is no fault.
If it is argued that [the phrase] "because of seeing one part" is not included when stating "the perception of a specific visible object," we say no;
for it is included in the illustrative example.
For he says thus: "Just as the sight of a gavaya [leads to] the recollection of a cow."
The meaning of this is as follows: "darśana" (perception) is that in which something is seen; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
That which has the gavaya as its object of perception is "gavayadarśana" (the perception of a gavaya).
"Similarity" is the meaning of the other word (*anyapadārtha*).
What is meant is this: "the similarity perceived in the gavaya. Following the example here, the same applies to the defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*) as well.

It is understood that similarity is intended as that which is being perceived and being compared; and in the phrase "of the recollection of the cow," the suffix *lyu* is used in the sense of the agent according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*anidgṛhī-* etc.).

"Remember the cow, O non-measurer! Just as the similarity perceived in a gavaya produces the cognition 'this is similar to a cow,' so too does [the memory of the cow] produce [the cognition of similarity].
As for the connection [of the means of knowledge], it was already stated previously that because of its great prevalence, analogy (upamāna) follows immediately after verbal testimony (śabda).
Here, an objection is raised: "Since here an investigation is being set forth by way of restating well-known means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
it is appropriate to rely on the very definition of analogy (*upamāna*) as stated by the Naiyāyikas, just as one relies on analogy as a means of valid cognition as stated by them."
For they have stated thus: "Comparison (*upamāna*) is the means of establishing what is to be established (*sādhya*) by means of similarity with something well-known.

The meaning of this is as follows: it is the means of establishing—that is, the making known—of something not yet established, such as a *gavaya*, by means of its similarity to something well-known, such as a cow; for instance, the statement "As is a cow, so is a *gavaya*," addressed to someone who is ignorant [of the latter].
"Or, the cognition produced by that [comparison] is comparison.
To this he replies with the two verses beginning "Of what kind?"—stating the reason for formulating a different definition after setting aside that [previous one].
It is true that this was stated by the Naiyāyikas.
But this is not tenable,
because it is not outside the scripture just mentioned;
for this cognition of an object not in contact [with the senses] arises from the cognition of the word.
Therefore, in the Śābara-tantra, analogy is described in a completely different manner. //1.2//
He states that its status as scripture (*āgama*) is understood even according to the definition of scripture provided by the Naiyāyikas—beginning with the words "puruṣa" (person)—as follows:
for such is the Naiyāyikas’ definition of verbal testimony (*śabda*), namely, "the word is the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*).
And here too, it is precisely through the authority of a reliable person that there arises a cognition of similarity regarding the *gavaya* and so forth, which are not [otherwise] perceived.
It is not [known] from the correspondence of multiple authorities;
rather, considering that this statement belongs solely to an authoritative person (āpta) and is thus non-deviant, a certainty arises which is dependent upon that authority.
For them as well, it is simply scripture (āgama). //3//
Therefore, because it consists of his words, that [scripture] is indeed an authoritative tradition (āgama). //3//
If a cognition were to arise from a similar [object] regarding another similar [object],
how could it be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), given that it would be equivalent to the memory of meditation and so forth?
Just as an object of cognition is distinguished elsewhere by differences of place, time, and so forth,
it is not so here, in accordance with the situation in the city.
For some, the cognition that arises in the forest regarding a gavaya from having heard the sentence of extended application (atideśavākya) is analogy (upamāna), colored by the similarity to a cow.
But surely, even in the *Śābara-bhāṣya*, it is described that comparison (*upamāna*) is the cognition of a similar object arising from the perception of something unseen;
this too is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), because it does not fall outside the category of memory (*smaraṇa*).
For just as memory occurs when one is meditating upon something, [so too does this cognition].
Thus, even for one who perceives a similar object, there is recollection of another similar object;
therefore, there is no distinction between this [recollection] and that which arises from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and so forth.
Consequently, he states "from a similar [object]" to show that it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
The definition of the Naiyāyika, for its part, does not fall outside of the traditional scriptures;
however, the Śābara [definition] is indeed invalid, as it apprehends only a fragment. //4//
[Objection: Is it not observed that even a recognition (pratyabhijñāna) which is mixed with memory, arising through a difference of place and so forth, is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)?

Likewise here, for one who has seen a cow in the city and then sees a *gavaya* in the forest, the cognition of its similarity (*tadbhāna*) is a valid means of knowledge; therefore, [the author] says: "place, time, etc.
Indeed, the mere fact of a difference in place and so forth is not the cause for validity.
Rather, it is by way of being an object of cognition;

however, in this case, a cow qualified by another location and so forth is not being cognized, but rather that which was previously perceived in the city is remembered as existing right there even now. //5//

He sets forth the view of a certain school of Naiyāyikas, beginning with the words "śruta" (heard): "For one who has indeed heard the statement of analogy—'As is a cow, so is a gavaya'—and who, having reached the forest, possesses the cognition of the gavaya colored by similarity, namely 'This gavaya is similar to a cow,' this is analogy (upamāna). //6//

The gavaya is indeed perceived directly, but here it is the recollection of similarity [that functions]. Now, one might object: "In the case of an object characterized by similarity, there is neither recollection nor apprehension through the senses."
If there is no additional element in the gavaya due to the cognition of the meaning of the previous sentence, then,
because it is not distinct from remembrance, it does not possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
But if there should be some additional [cognition] by virtue of direct perception and so forth—
as long as it is connected with the sense faculties, it is remembered as "direct perception" (pratyakṣa).
He refutes this as well with the words "in perception" (*pratyakṣe*).

First, the gavaya is perceived through direct perception due to the contact of the sense organs; furthermore, the similarity to a cow, having been understood from the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*), is remembered. Thus, there is nothing that remains to be compared.
Here he raises an objection with the words "nanu" (but surely).
The intention is as follows: for here it is the gavaya, qualified by its similarity to a cow, that is understood;
and that [understanding] is not perception.
Because the cow is perceptible,
the gavaya qualified by it is the object of analogy;
for that [gavaya] is not determined by perception.
Because that [cognition] has only the gavaya as its object,
and because it is not remembered as having been understood from scripture,
since scripture has the universal (sāmānya) as its object.
And here, because there is the manifestation of a specific [object] as "this is that. //7//
He refutes this by means of the following half-verse and the preceding one, after having formulated the following dilemma:
"Is something more than what is understood from the analogical statement (atideśavākya) actually apprehended, or not?
If [the opponent] says "no," he replies:
Therefore, this connection, being no different from remembrance, is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).

Just as the knowledge of a word-meaning from a word is not additional because it arises from a presently existing cause, so too remembrance is not additional; therefore, it is not a means of valid cognition.
In the same way here as well, there is the cognition of the cow characterized by its similarity to the gavaya, which is understood through the sentence of analogical extension (*atideśavākya*).
If, then, this is obtained from perception alone, there is no room for another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). //8.1.2//

Now, it might be argued that since similarity to a cow is not perceptible when the cow is not present, a *gavaya* qualified by that similarity cannot be apprehended through perception; thus, there would be scope for another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*). To this, he says:
"For as long as... That which appears directly immediately after the operation of the sense organs is perception.
And thus, how could the gavaya, as qualified by similarity, fail to be perceptible?

Since similarity, like a universal (jāti), is fully present in its entirety within each individual species, it follows that even when the cow itself is not perceived, the perception of the gavaya as qualified by similarity to it is indeed possible; this is the intended meaning. //9//
There is no lack of authority in distinguishing a portion that is being remembered;
nor is the fact of having heard a statement of extended application (atideśa) of any particular utility.
For even those who have not heard the statement regarding that [similarity] develop this [cognition] when they see a gavaya in the forest after having directly perceived the nature of a cow.
Now, it might be argued that they lack the connection with names;
this is not so, for they nevertheless perceive the object in its true nature in every respect.
Furthermore, the relationship between word and meaning is not intended here as the object of cognition;
for that [relationship] is understood from the sentence once the sentence has been determined through similarity.

Nor is there a lack of validity due to the awareness of the recollection of words and so forth, because the distinction between the perceived and the recollected has already been established in the proof of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*); thus he says: "of the recollected.
The meaning is that when this distinction exists, there is no lack of validity.
He states that even the inclusion of the specific qualification of the scriptural statement of extended application (atideśavākya) yields no result, saying: "śruteti" //10//
How is it not applicable? [The author says: "Even those...

If the perception of a *gavaya* as qualified by its similarity to a cow is intended to be *upamāna*, then it certainly exists even for those who have not heard the corresponding sentence (*atideśavākya*), having seen a cow in the city and then seeing a *gavaya* in the forest; thus, the result of the qualification is trivial.
Now, one might object that for those who have not heard the sentence of comparison, there is no association of the name, such as "this is a *gavaya*."
He says, "There is this distinction: for others, it exists," using the word "atha" (now). He refutes this with "na nāma" (not indeed):
they too certainly know that which is intended as the object of knowledge (*prameya*) of analogy (*upamāna*).
Let the state of being a perceiver not be pursued by name. //12//
It might be thought: "The very relationship between a name and the named object is the domain of analogy (*upamāna*).

As it is stated in the *Nyāyavistara*: 'The purpose of analogy is the comprehension of the relationship between a designation and [its referent] (*samākhyā-sambandha-pratipatti*). And it has been explained: 'When it is said, "As a cow, so is a gavaya," one perceives through sense-contact that which is similar to a cow; one then understands that "gavaya" is the name for this [animal], [thereby establishing] the relationship between the name and the named object.'"
"One should practice [it].

Furthermore, for one who has not heard the extended application (atideśa) sentence and does not know the word, the comprehension of the relationship through conventional designation (samākhyā) is not possible; thus, there is no result, nor does recognition arise again in the forest.
Since the two potencies are beyond the reach of the senses, it is indeed memory that is accepted as their result.
Even in a cognition permeated by words, perception has been established;
therefore, let the object of knowledge, which is endowed with similarity, be called "the unprecedented" (*apūrva*).
To provide a qualification for this, he says: "And not...
He states the reason: "by similarity.

Since the referent of the word *gavaya* has already been determined through its similarity to a cow by means of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*) itself, the relationship between the word and its meaning is indeed understood, even though it has not been apprehended in the form of a specific individual instance (*vyaktirūpa*).
For it is understood at that time that the object resembling a cow is the denotation of the word "gavaya";
and this alone constitutes the essential nature of the relationship.
Therefore, it is well said that the qualification is redundant. //13//

[Objection: But surely, even for a relation that has already been known, its validity as a means of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) remains unimpaired; therefore, [the author] says: "And not... Here he states the reason: "Of the two capacities (*śakti*).
For the relation between word and meaning is indeed the restriction of the expressive capacity (*vācaka-śakti*) and the expressed capacity (*vācya-śakti*).
And because it is beyond the reach of the senses, it is not recognized here [in the present];
rather, that which was previously apprehended is remembered exactly as it was, neither diminished nor increased.
Is there then no recognition at all regarding that which is beyond the senses?
If this is so, how is it that fire and other objects previously experienced are recognized through inference?

And it has been said: "Even when [an object] previously grasped as distinct by place and so forth is again determined—as if by perception—through the inference of a valid means of knowledge, there is recognition.
And here too, he will say:
"By whatever means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) there is indeed the apprehension of the activity of the intellect"—
this is true.
We do not say that it is not recognized through indirect means;
rather, regarding this recognition— which arises from the senses and has a direct manifestation in the form "this is that gavaya, characterized by similarity to a cow"—
the relationship between word and object, in its nature as a potency (*śakti*), is not within its range.
But it is indeed the gavaya itself that was previously cognized through its similarity to a cow.
Thus,

for this very reason, he refutes the view that the relation [of similarity] is the object of recognition by stating, "And not of this... On the other hand, the *gavaya* has been previously cognized here through its similarity to a cow.
Thus, there is nothing inconsistent in the claim that [the self] is recognized. //14//

Now, it might be argued that the inclusion of the qualification [“not produced by perception”] is intended to exclude this from being perception; since this cognition of the *gavaya* is presented by the word “heard,” its object is not that of perception, and thus it will belong to analogy (*upamāna*). To this, he says: “By the word ‘sound’ (*śabda*)...”
For even in a cognition permeated by words, since the connection with the sense faculty is present and the nature of perception is held to be determinate,
why then is similarity not also perceived by it, just as genus and other such properties are?
But for those who maintain that [cognition] is non-conceptual, this is merely a semblance of direct perception;
and because of the absence of an object to be cognized, its status as a valid means of knowledge is not intended.

Since it has been described that knowledge following from a word is produced solely by the reflection upon the power of the word and is thus nothing but perception, one might argue that we do not perceive any additional object of cognition (*prameya*) for analogy (*upamāna*) in any of these definitions. To conclude that this [analogy] does indeed have a unique object of cognition, he says: "Therefore... (v. 15).
If, however, it is argued that the apprehension of similarity is dependent upon a counter-correlate (pratiyogin), and therefore it is not perception—
since perceptual cognition arises solely from the capacity of the object and the sense faculty,
and does not subsequently or previously reflect upon [other factors]— then [the following is said]:

Therefore, since similarity is indeed imperceptible even when the subject (*dharmin*) is perceptible, that which is qualified by it cannot be perceptible; thus, analogy (*upamāna*) has its scope. To this, he says: "by ascertainment" (*vyavasāya*).

This is the established doctrine of the Buddhists: that perception is non-conceptual and arises immediately upon contact. The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that perception consists of ascertainment (*vyavasāyātmaka*).
Therefore, why should similarity also not be cognized by perception, just like genus and the other [categories]? //16//

Even for those who maintain that [cognition] is non-conceptual, this is not a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is a semblance of perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*); thus he says: "perception," etc.

In this way, having first granted that similarity is a separate entity, it was stated that comparison (*upamāna*) lacks validity due to the absence of an object, since its object would have to be that perception [of similarity].
Now, he states the denial of similarity according to the Buddhist view: "The object of cognition" (*prameya*), etc.

Even for those who maintain that perception is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣavādin*), the status of comparison (*upamāna*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not accepted because of the absence of similarity as an object of cognition.
Therefore, while they are contending [with other schools], how can comparison be a means of valid cognition?
And this is their intention: for similarity is not indeed distinct from its substrata, because it is not perceived as such;
nor, if it were non-different from the substratum, would there be the consequence of it being merely that [substratum] itself. And how could it reside in the substrata?
It is not tenable that what exists in its entirety elsewhere should likewise exist in another place;
nor does it exist part by part, because such parts do not exist.
Furthermore, this similarity (*sādṛśya*) is not any one among substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), or action (*karman*),
because it has not been enumerated among them by those learned in the categories (*padārtha*).
Indeed, we do not perceive similarity as being included within the nine substances, the twenty-four qualities, or the five actions.
Furthermore, similarity is not merely a universal (sāmānya);
for that [universal] is the instrument in the cognition of that [object], whereas similarity is what is known by the cognition of "being like that" (tadvad-buddhi).
Furthermore, if it were similarity to that [the universal], then the same consequence would apply even to "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth.
If you argue that similarity consists in the commonalities of parts (*avayavasāmānya*), we say no; for even in those cases, the cognition of similarity arises only when considering them individually.

If it is argued that similarity consists in a plurality [of common features], we say no; for even when a plurality [of features] is combined in one place, the cognition of similarity arises independently of either the counter-correlate or the other [term].
Indeed, those objects may well be gathered together in one place,
yet they are not apprehended by means of a cognition of similarity;
for one does not recognize a cow as "similar" without having regard for the difference from its counter-correlate.
If it is argued that similarities exist in relation to what is applicable— that is, similarity is relative—
then is similarity now something merely relative? Indeed it is.
If it is manifested or produced by such dependence,
it is certainly not produced [by it],
just as duality is not produced by the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).
Because it is spontaneously established (*sahajasiddha*).
Since there exist manifestors such as light and the sense faculties, what else does it require?
Furthermore, if similarity consists in the commonality of parts, [then...]
Furthermore, because those two [the hands and head] do not exist in the twins, it would follow that [the universal] is non-existent there as well.
If one were to accept its existence even there, then upon the destruction of those [hands and head], the universal itself would be destroyed, which would result in the abandonment of your own tenet.
Moreover, in the case of a severed body and so forth, the transformational parts such as the hands and head are absent.
In the absence of generality (sāmānya), there is an absence of similarity (sādṛśya).
In the same way, this consequence should be shown regarding odor and the other [sensory objects] as well;
because the parts such as the ears lack further constituent parts, there is no similarity.
Now, it might be thought: "It is true that similarity is not the commonality of parts;
rather, this is a distinct entity (tattvāntara) altogether, different from substance, genus, quality, and action, or perhaps a specific kind of quality.
As the Guru has said: "Similarity is not a universal (sāmānya)."
What then? It is that very same thing, because "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth are not manifold.

And thus it becomes logically established that in that context, the meaning of the injunction is simply the conceptualization of similarity, which is the purpose of the injunction regarding the *śyena* sacrifice.

Because the specific individual hawk (*śyenavyakti*) and its genus (*jāti*)—as a composite whole (*avayavin*) composed of parts such as wings, skin, flesh, blood, bones, head, back, feet, belly, and so forth, produced by their own nature—cannot be accomplished with bricks;

and if similarity is intended to consist in the commonalities of these parts, then since those do not exist here [in the brick structure], similarity itself would be difficult to achieve. Thus, the proposed subject matter—"one should build the *śyenacit* altar"—would remain unestablished.
Furthermore, in this way, the cognition of similarity would also be possible even in the case of partless entities such as odors and the like.
But that is not the case;
for if similarity were a distinct reality (*tattvāntara*), one would cognize "the gavaya is similar" even without depending on the cow.
For in that case, that similarity would be entirely complete within it alone—what else, then, would it require?
If it is asked, "How can that which is qualified by similarity to a cow be understood when the cow is not perceived?"— if you say its relation to the cow is inherence (*samavāya*),
then that [inherence] must likewise be known through its similarity to the cow, just as the *gavaya* is.
Furthermore, as for this so-called "inherence" (*samavāya*), why should it be required even when perceiving the similarity residing in the *gavaya*?
For simply because "cowness" (*gotva*) does not inhere in a brindled cow (*śābaleya*) does not allow one to deny that similarity is also a real entity (*vastu*).
That [is] the connection with a greater number of common parts belonging to another class.
O Bāhuleya, even though that [similarity] is not cognized, dependence upon it is observed;
likewise, in the case of "this is the similarity of a gavaya to a cow," no cause for such dependence is perceived. Furthermore, let us grant that the cow indeed depends [on the gavaya].

For one who perceives a cow from a distance, even though they have not yet discerned the distinction between its specific parts and general characteristics, there would arise the cognition of a gavaya as being similar to that cow.
If it is argued that the general characteristics of the parts must also be required for that cognition [of similarity], [we reply:]...
The meaning of "dependence" must be stated.
If it is thought that its [the universal's] part-commonalities (*avayavasāmānya*) are the manifestors, then those residing in the *gavaya* must be the manifestors of that [universal].
And since those [parts] exist in the gavaya,
what is the use of perceiving them in the cow?
Therefore, once the cow is understood, even while its individual common parts remain unperceived, the cognition of similarity to a cow would arise.
For that similarity belongs to the two universals (jāti), and since those two are already cognized, what else remains to be expected?
As for this similarity consisting in the abundance of common parts, [it is likewise dependent on the cognition of the universals].
And this [distinction] would not exist if similarity were something other than the object itself, because similarity is present in equal measure everywhere.
It might be thought: "Those [particulars] are its manifestors;
and when there is an excellence in the manifestor, there is an excellence in the cognition of the manifested."
"Just as it is in the case of a jar and so forth, so it will be here too"—
that is not so;
for it is not mere cognition that is being excelled here.
Rather, we maintain that it is the very object itself that possesses excellence.
For this very reason, when the primary [object] is unavailable, something similar is sought out as a substitute, and not something only slightly similar; thus, your objection is trivial.
Therefore, similarity—which is merely imagined through conceptual construction and causes delusion like the double moon or a whirling firebrand—is not an object of valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*).

Since there is no corresponding object of knowledge (*prameya*), neither similarity nor any other means of knowledge can serve as a factor for analogy (*upamāna*); thus, it is dependent [on something else]. //17//
Regarding this, he states the solution: "of similarity.
The intended meaning is this: this is not merely imagined through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), because the two causes for its being false are impossible.
For cognitions such as that of two moons, arising from some defect, are sublated when there is a change in time and other conditions;
however, similarity—just like genus and so forth—is real. Thus, since even similarity exists, why should it be denied?
This very similarity is understood, free from doubt, and uncontradicted even in other places and so on; therefore, similarity certainly exists.
It should be conceived in such a way that it is logically consistent with the force of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
for indeed, there is nothing whatsoever that is impossible regarding what is directly perceived.
Regarding that which was first asked—namely, "What is its essential nature?"—the answer is stated:
"By many constituent parts," and so forth.
Its meaning is as follows: similarity is that connection with another class [of things] by means of many common constituent parts (*avayava-sāmānya*).
The mention of the apprehension of the commonality of parts belonging to different classes (*jātyantara*) is for the sake of illustration;
for even the similarity of individuals (*vyaktisādṛśya*) is indeed observed in the case of the Yamas and others.
Likewise, similarity is indeed observed even without commonalities of parts, through the connection with commonalities of qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and so forth.
As in the case of paintings and the like;
by this, the objection raised as to how there can be similarity in paintings and such is answered.
In the same way, one should demonstrate the commonality of shape and dimension even in the case of fire.
As for the objection raised regarding the impossibility [of similarity] when the acceptance of similarity of parts between the two twins is maintained,
that will indeed be refuted.
However, even in the absence of similarity of parts, the similarity of the qualities of the whole is simply the similarity of the qualities of its constituent parts.
This is because the commonality of the parts serves as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, for those who maintain that [the whole] is a distinct reality (*tattvāntara*), this [commonality] must be admitted as being included among the qualities (*guṇa*) due to its dependence on a substratum;
it cannot be a fifth category, because such a thing is not observed in the world.
It is established in the world that the categories of existence (*padārtha*) are genus (*jāti*), substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*).
Therefore, since this [word] is itself a quality, its inherence (*samavāya*) in both quality and action is logically untenable.
Now, if it is argued that [the word] causes both quality and action—which are themselves inherent in a substance—to be understood as similar [to that substance], [we reply:]...
Because of inherence in the same object;
if one says "because of inherence in that which is inherent in the same object," we say no,
because there is no means of valid cognition for its inherence in a substance.
For the commonalities of parts, such as the ears and so forth, which are inherent in individuals, are perceived by direct perception;
however, similarity must be grasped by means of a cognition of resemblance.
Since there is no substance that is "similar to odor" and so on, similarity is therefore nothing other than the commonality of parts.
But was it not stated that the cognition of similarity would necessarily follow because many common parts are perceived in one and the same object?
This has been answered by the statement "of another class" (*jātyantarasya*).
Similarity arises from the inherence in one class of those [parts] which inhere in another class.
It is neither the mere intrinsic nature,
nor is it a multiplicity;
this indeed will be explained further below.
Therefore, the apprehension of another universal must be admitted.
As for the objection that "it is not produced by that [universal]," that is true.
But it is manifested;
as it has been said:
"And there are many universals (sāmānya) of qualities, parts, and actions."
Similarity is said to be that which manifests as a commonality distinct from the primary [individual].
Thus:
for whatever is the cause for the perception of something, that is its manifestor.
Therefore, even in each individual case, universals are indeed perceived by their own nature alone;
however, the state of having similar parts due to the inherence of another universal occurs only where there is a resemblance such as that of "lotus-petal eyes."
That will come about for them through the abundance of the commonalities among their own constituent parts.
Thus, by virtue of their own nature as genus, quality, substance, action, power, and so forth,

these [entities] constitute similarity; and since that which consists of inherence (*samavāya*) is not manifested in another genus unless it has been previously perceived, its dependence on that [perception] is indeed logical.
Nor does that which appears in dependence upon another object become a non-entity;
for instance, Devadatta’s status as a father is perceived in dependence upon his son, yet it is not therefore a non-entity.
Therefore, such relative things cannot be subverted.
For this very reason, the cognition of "very similar" and so forth is possible based on the accumulation or non-accumulation of commonalities among parts.
Therefore, it is established that similarity consists of the commonalities of qualities, parts, and so on, as delimited by a different universal (jāti) and a different individual (vyakti). //18//
Now, in the phrase "this woman has eyes like lotus petals," the eye of the woman is compared to the petal, which is a part of the lotus;
and if similarity consists in the commonality of parts, that is not possible here.
Because it is itself a constituent part;
for there is no other constituent part, such as another eye, belonging to the eye.
Therefore, he says: "similar," etc.
It is not necessarily the case that the generality (*sāmānya*) belonging to a part of a large whole is similarity (*sādṛśya*).
Rather, it has been stated that similarity consists in the commonalities among parts;
and this [similarity] exists even among the parts themselves, such as the eyes and so forth.
He says that because it is possible through the abundance of commonalities among its own constituent parts, the cognition of similar parts in women and so forth is indeed logical. //19//

Granted that similarity may exist in parts due to their connection with intermediate commonalities of parts, how is it accounted for when a cognition of similarity is observed in various instances even without such [intermediate] parts? To this he says: "In this way."
This grasping of commonality among parts is not the governing factor.
Rather, whatever commonality of qualities and so forth produces a cognition of similarity, that alone constitutes similarity; therefore, there is no single uniform nature here.
The diversity of similarity must be accepted according to what is observed.
For example: "The Brahmin is indeed fire" (*agnir vai brāhmaṇaḥ*)—this means he is similar to fire.
What is the similarity between these two?
The meaning is that the birth of the [four] castes (*jāti*) is from the single mouth of Brahmā.
This will be stated in the *Tatsiddhi-sūtra*.
But how, then, is it understood that these two possess the same origin?
In the Śruti it is indeed said: "Prajāpati fashioned from his mouth the Trivṛt [stoma], among the meters; Agni, among the deities; and the Brāhmaṇa, among human beings.
And in the world, this [distinction] is to be observed between those of equal birth.
The commonality of qualities, however, is clearly evident in the world in works such as paintings, and in the Veda in the statement "the sacrificial post is the sun.
Its variety arises from the distinctions of being single, double, triple, or the totality [of these].
Neither the dharmas themselves nor their abundance constitutes similarity;
for it is the genus and so forth, which possess abundance, that are perceived as being similar.
Similarity of substance is seen in the world between two people wearing identical ornaments, and in the Veda, in the passage: "The priests proceed wearing red turbans.
Similarity of action is seen in the world through common activities such as study and so forth.
And in the Veda, [the term *śyena*] is used because of the commonality of swooping down and seizing, as it says: “Just as a hawk swoops down and seizes,
so does this [sacrifice] swoop down and seize the hateful enemy.”
Similarity of capacity, however, is understood in the world from such expressions as "Bhīma is a wrestler," and in the Veda from the case of *soma* and *pūtīka* plants;
for the capacity of the *pūtīkas* to function as *soma* is indeed understood from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
Because it is understood as being the effect of that [cause], and because an effect possesses a capacity that conforms to its cause;
and as it has been said: "That portion of the Soma which fell became the Pūtīka."

Some have a similarity of their own specific duties (*svadharma-sādṛśya*); for instance, in the world there is mutual similarity among those with three tufts of hair (*triśikha*) and others, such as those with five tufts (*pañcaśikha*), and in the Veda, for Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and others, Narāśaṃsa is the second *prayāja*.
For in those cases, the similarity consists precisely in the restriction of duty (*dharmaniyama*).
It has already been stated that similarity consists precisely in the commonality of attributes (*dharma-sāmānya*) between the original material (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*).
Furthermore, these factors—genus (*jāti*) and so forth—whether occurring singly, in pairs, in groups of three, or collectively, produce the manifold variety of similarity. //20//
Now, surely that in which similarity inheres is apprehended by the cognition of "similarity.
And if the commonalities of parts constitute similarity, then since those [commonalities] inhere in the parts, they should produce the cognition of similarity in those [parts] alone.
Now, since those [properties] are more numerous for them, and they reside in the commonalities of parts, it would follow that those very [commonalities] are what constitute similarity.
To the question, "How then can there be a cognition of similarity regarding things belonging to different classes? he says: "Not [mere] properties."
True.
For this very reason, similarity is neither the commonality of parts called *dharmas* nor their abundance,
because the cognition of similarity does not arise with respect to them.

For it is precisely that other genus, such as the *gavaya*, or another individual, such as the *āgneya* or *saurya* sacrifice, which is possessed of a greater degree of those [common] features that is grasped by the cognition of similarity.
Therefore, similarity consists in nothing other than the inherence of those [features] in another genus.
In their own nature, however, each of those universals individually is merely the basis for the cognition of oneness, just like the universal of "giving.

But when they are combined and endowed with the inherence of another genus, they constitute similarity; and this [similarity] is precisely what is meant by the phrase "the greater number of commonalities among parts."
"Conceptual proliferation," thus [it is said]. //21//
The Yamakas ask: "How is this so? Since it has been seen, why is this said here?
For in some cases this occurs among many, while in others it occurs even among very few."
The reality of that [entity] is not lost by such a distinction;
moreover, even these universals are imperishable except through the destruction of their substratum.
And because it is conjoined with an infinite substratum, no destruction occurs elsewhere;
therefore, not everything is postulated as a universal by virtue of its permanence.

Here he raises an objection: "Of the twins," etc. This is an objection from one who grasps only what is explicitly stated: "If similarity belongs to a different genus (*jātyantara*) due to the connection with many common parts, how can there be similarity between the two individual instances (*vyakti*) of the twins?
But the other [responds]: "The mention of a different genus is merely illustrative; why this insistence on that point alone?"
Therefore, he mocks [the opponent], saying "this poor child," by stating "because it is observed":
wherever such similarity is observed— whether in the universal (*jāti*) or in the individual (*vyakti*)— there alone should it be resorted to.
"Why do you bind [the relation] only to one [of the two]?
It might be argued:
"For entities such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth possess a single nature."
This similarity as well is logically consistent in the same way:
if its nature is to reside in few things, it is appropriate only for two individuals; if, however, its nature is to reside in many things, then it belongs only to two universals.
But [an opponent might argue that] partial destruction (ardhavaiśasa) renders [the object] non-existent;
therefore, he says: "For in some cases...
The meaning is that both [existence and non-existence] are established because there is no contradiction with experience (pratītyavisaṃvāda). //22//

Now, it might be argued that universals (*sāmānya*) are similarity, and these would perish with the destruction of the individual instances (*vyakti*); therefore, the doctrine that the universal is eternal would be abandoned. To this, he says: "Universals... [and so forth].
Let these, for their part, be non-eternal; however, since other universals such as "cowness" (gotva) and so forth are indeed eternal, there is no contradiction with common worldly experience. //23//
What, then, is the distinction among other generalities?
To this he says: "infinite.
For the substrata of "cowness" and so forth are indeed infinite.
Thus, even upon the destruction of one [individual], because there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in another substratum, destruction is not absolute.
He states "by that" (*tena*) to show that the doctrine of an eternal universal (*nityasāmānyavāda*) is also not non-universal:
"Or rather, the destruction of a universal is not admitted anywhere."
For everything has some basis in other locations and so forth.
Because of their great number, this similarity might even exceed [the original];
for those [features], though scattered, are likewise present here and there even in a direct perception.
As for the perception of similarity in parts,
that too must belong to the parts themselves by virtue of their similarity to other constituent parts.
Thus, first of all, since there is no conceptualization of a difference from another,
that which follows must be a universal devoid of similarity.
But where a single generality of the primary [parts] is perceived, or rather, even for the generalities of the constituent parts, there is no absolute destruction—as he says: "of the generality.
He states the reason: "of all" [parts]. //25//
If it is argued that there must also be a cognition of similarity in those cases, he says: "Of these.
Their similarity is present in an exceeding degree;
it is not, however, that it does not exist in each individual instance.
It is not only in cases such as [the movement of] the universal soul (sāmānyamanas) to another location that the existence of a substratum is postulated;
rather, those very [faculties] are indeed perceived in some objects even through direct perception (pratyakṣa). Thus he says: "Those... (tāni) //26//
But surely, it has already been stated that the eyes and so forth possess similarity due to the abundance of their own constituent parts;
however, how will there be similarity among those very parts? To this, he says: "Otherwise.
For non-occurrence is of two kinds: some things are simply unestablished, such that they cannot be established in any way whatsoever.
Furthermore, when something is not possible given a certain assumption, it is untenable;
in that case, what is absolutely untenable is simply disregarded.
However, when something is possible under a certain assumption but impossible otherwise, the possibility of that [assumption] is determined by means of another assumption.
For in this very way all worldly investigators understand;
and no contradiction is observed in other regions and so forth.
Therefore, this is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Just as in inference a logical mark (*liṅga*) that has an ascertained form is the means of cognition, so too here, [the object] is understood through some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its conceptualization is aroused by another means of valid cognition;
and there is no doubt regarding the validity of either one of these.
However, when two [alternatives] are both established as having certain validity, there is merely a requirement for reconciliation, such as: "How can these two be made consistent?
This is like the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, where there is a scriptural injunction regarding its taking and not taking;
in that case, it is not possible to establish one by means of abandoning the other.

Therefore, just as in that case, when it is asked how both [of these] may be established, both are established by means of different applications (*prayoga*), so too here, both— which are established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and whose existence is certain— are [established] through the postulation of another object (*arthāntara-parikalpanā*).
And in this case, the state of inseparable connection (avinābhāvitā) is conceived only at that very moment;
it was not previously ascertained. Thus, in another way, this [connection] is not the cause.
Neither his absence from home nor his being outside are necessarily observed;
furthermore, there is no other means of knowledge for their coexistence.
For it is solely through the impossibility of [the effect] occurring otherwise that one thing is understood by means of another;
if that concomitance is not perceived, it cannot be so postulated.
It is sought after because it appears precisely in that form;
for indeed, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are distinct, as they possess distinct causal complexes (*sāmagrī*).
For this very reason, they are distinguished from one another.
Furthermore, the causes of invalidity are doubt, error, or ignorance;
since these do not exist even in the case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), how could it lack validity?
If it is asked, "How can there be valid cognition (*pramā*) from a relation that is not known? [we reply:
No, the relation is not the cause of validity; rather, it is the absence of sublation (*bādhaviraha*).
And since this [point] is no different here as well, no fault whatsoever appears to us regarding the presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). //29//
[Objection: Surely the absence from the house is not possible without [the person's] presence outside; therefore, it is an invariable concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*).
And that cognition of another object which arises from an invariable concomitant is inference.
Therefore, this cognition of presence outside is indeed inference. To this, he says: "without" (*avinā*).
The intended meaning is as follows: some read [the definition] as "the perception of an inseparable object by one who knows it is inference";
even for them, what is intended by "inference" is the perception of the inseparable [object] by one who knows its inseparability—that is, by one who knows the very fact of being inseparable.
And it was not previously understood here that the absence from the house occurs without [the person's] being outside.
For at that very moment, having postulated external existence through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), the state of invariable concomitance—that "this does not exist without that"—is postulated.
Therefore, although it is real in its own nature, because it was not previously cognized, it is not the cause for the arising of [the subsequent] cognition. //30//

[Objection: In that case, for one who has already apprehended the relationship [between the two], there would be inference; therefore, he says [the words] ending with "gṛhābhāve" (in the absence from the house).

The intention is that, first of all, the coexistence of the two is not apprehended by everyone as a rule; thus, for one who does not know their coexistence, this is established as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
Even for one who has understood the concomitance (*sāhitya*) of those two, it is not possible to grasp that concomitance unless those two have been grasped;
nor is the perception of one of them possible through the apprehension of the other without presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*).
However, by the very principle of "inexplicability otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*), through that single absence from the house,
the other correlate must necessarily be understood at the time of establishing the relationship by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); [this occurs] subsequently.
The nature of inference.
He who stands at the door of a house and conceives of an external existence— when he is in one place, he is not then found elsewhere.
Even then, its non-existence is not perceived everywhere;
nor will there be pervasion of the reason simply because of its absence in one location.
Indeed, in this case, non-existence is understood through non-perception;
and since that is accomplished without effort, it is established for one who remains in a single place.

Or else, one of those two must be cognized as being external [to the other]. If this is not postulated, then because one of the two related members would remain unperceived, there could be no cognition of their coexistence (sāhitya) at all. Therefore, for the sake of establishing coexistence, presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) must be sought; thus, with the intention of proving it to be a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), he says "and the means of valid cognition" up to the end of the verse.
He clarifies the intended meaning with the words "by that" (tena). //31-32//
Now, one might object: "It is not necessarily the case that one of the two related terms must be apprehended through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
For it is possible for someone standing at the door of a house to perceive both [the absence and the person] through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and thereby experience the relation;

and from such a known relation, the inference of being outside can be derived from the absence in the house. Thus he raises this doubt with the words: "gṛhadvārī" (standing at the door of the house). // 34 //
To this, he states the following reply: "Even then," etc.

The intention is as follows: while it is indeed established that the existence of a person outside [the house] is inferred from his absence from the house, nevertheless, all [objects] are not understood in this very same way.
For cognition occurs even for those who have not grasped the relationship [between words and their referents].
Furthermore, this mode [of inference] is not possible when one's presence in one place leads to the understanding of one's absence everywhere;
indeed, it is impossible to understand that something exists in one place by means of its non-existence in the entire world.
The intention is that the non-existence of the world cannot be cognized.
[Objection: But in this way, it is understood that when this [object] exists in one place, it does not exist elsewhere in its vicinity;
and thus, once the pervasion is known, there will be an inference of non-existence everywhere upon the perception of a single location.
Therefore, he says: "And not...
For the pervasion of the reason by the non-existence of the three worlds cannot be established merely through the non-existence of one part. //35//

If it is argued that "the relation is not understood because of the non-existence of the world, and because of its [the world's] non-understanding," then surely non-perception is the cause for the understanding of non-existence.
And just as Devadatta, being present in one place, is not perceived in another location, this non-perception does not establish the absence of the entity there;
for that [non-perception] occurs even when things exist at a distance, due to the failure to reach that place.
Having gone again and again to those regions, if the object is not obtained,
then, due to the absence of any other cause, it is understood to be non-existent.
But surely, even in the absence of fire and so forth, since those things distinct from smoke and the like do not go to that place, the clear negative concomitance (vyatireka) is not established.
When something is not perceived, it is determined to be non-existent.
Likewise, when that which exists in one place is not perceived anywhere else, it can be understood to be non-existent everywhere.
For non-perception, unlike perception, does not require effort.
For perception, as an effect, depends upon its own causes—such as the sense-organ and the contact with the object—and thus occurs only in one place, not everywhere;
however, the absence of perception does not depend on anything at all. Thus he objects: "But here...
The word "here" refers to a specific location.
In this case, indeed, non-existence is understood from non-perception in one particular location;
and that [principle] is the same everywhere as well. //36//
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "Not by this.
Why is it not perceived? To this he says: "Because of that place," etc.
For it is the non-perception of that which is capable of being perceived that establishes its non-existence.

However, in the case of objects situated at a distance, non-perception is possible precisely because of their unsuitability [as objects of perception], even though they exist; therefore, there is no certainty regarding their absence. //37//

If, however, all villages, cities, rivers, deserts, and other locations were not reached, then Caitra’s absence from them could be known; but this is not possible to accomplish. With this intention, he says: "Having gone, having gone... (38).
Here he raises an objection: "But surely...
The intention is this: first of all, a reason that does not exclude the counter-example (vipakṣa) is not a prover; yet it is not possible to go to and perceive all counter-examples.
Therefore, the exclusion of the reason from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) must necessarily be apprehended through non-perception of that which is situated in only one part;
it will be the same here as well.
And those things such as smoke, being excluded [from the counter-example], are "those that have smoke and so forth as their exclusion" (*dhūmādivyatirekiṇaḥ*).

In the absence of fire and so forth, those [reasons] such as smoke which are negative instances fail to establish their negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), because they do not reach the location where fire and so forth are absent. //39//
For one for whom the non-existence of another entity is the object of cognition, there is a fault;
but for me, the concomitant [reason] is a prover by the mere fact of its not being perceived.
But surely, in other cases as well, the connection [of non-perception] with the absence [of the object] is established,
since the absence of Caitra is observed through his presence elsewhere.
Because [the concomitance] is limited in scope within literary works, and because the absence of fire is not observed in the presence of smoke, the status of smoke as an indicator is postulated.
He refutes this with the words "of which" (*yasya*).

For according to the Buddhist, who maintains that exclusion (*vyatireka*) is primary, a reason does not become a means of cognition if there is no apprehension of its exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*),
since for him the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is the absence of other entities.
It means the non-existence of anything other than the entity such as fire, that is to say, anything that is not non-fire;
for that [non-existence] is not possible without the exclusion of all non-fire.
For me, however, the reason that establishes concomitance is the indicator [of the probandum] by means of the restriction of mere positive concomitance (anvaya-mātra-niyama).
And that [restriction] is established by merely not observing [the reason] in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) through just two or three observations. // 40 //

Surely, even for one who maintains the theory of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), it is equally difficult to perceive smoke that is accompanied by fire that is unarisen, past, present, or located in infinite places.
If it is argued that fires not yet perceived as accompanying [the smoke] are nonetheless inferred simply from seeing the accompaniment of a few fires,
then in this case as well, the relation of the absence of Caitra— who does not exist in the entire world— to his presence in a single location is indeed established.
For even here, in the case of Caitra, the absence of that [property] is indeed observed in some instances while it is present in others;
yet, on that basis alone, its absence is inferred everywhere. To this, he says: "But if it were so... (41).
Regarding this, he states the rebuttal: "Because of concomitance" (*sāhityāt*).
The intended meaning is this: our inference does not have the individual (*vyakti*) as its object, but rather has the generic form (*ākṛti*) as its object.
Furthermore, because a universal (ākṛti) inheres in its entirety within each individual instance, the perception of their coexistence is easily obtained;
for the coexistence of universals is understood through a single observation alone.
For this very reason, even the observation of two or three instances is required when there is a suspicion of deviation, in order to establish a rule of necessity.
For once the concomitance (*sāhitya*) is understood, a doubt arises: "Is this connection of smoke with fire merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), or is it innate (*sahaja*)?

In that regard, through repeated observation and the non-deviation of the positive concomitance (*anvaya-avyabhicāra*), and because there is no cause for the introduction of any other limiting condition (*upādhi*), the conviction arises: "This [smoke's] connection with fire is essential (*svābhāvika*).

However, in the case of fire, even though its relation has been initially understood, upon seeing it again in another instance where it deviates from smoke, a limiting condition such as "moist fuel" (*ārdrendhana*) enters into the picture.
Nor should there be any suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to differences in place and so forth;

for while deviation has indeed been observed in the case of two things whose concomitance was determined by a single observation— such as fire [and smoke]— in this case, this very coexistence belongs to one thing that exists simultaneously with the other.
Because it exists in infinite locations, it is first of all not tenable [to be a single entity].
But surely, another place is perceived by Caitra as empty, because it is distinct from that [occupied] place, just like a place situated nearby. Msv 5.7.44.
For the state of being a contradictory non-erroneous reason (*viruddhāvyabhicāritva*) is understood in exactly the same way:
because of being distinct from the proximate location, like the location occupied by Caitra.

However, when a person perceives [something] in its entirety in one place through the very act of seeing it twice, three times, or more— if even smoke were to deviate from fire in such a case, [it would be untenable].
For even in this case, deviation would be observed after only two, three, or four observations,
yet it is not so observed;
therefore, it is determined that this [substance] has the nature of being accompanied by fire.
But for one who lacks confidence even in this way,
there would be a lack of confidence in all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alike, because of observing deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in some instances.
Furthermore, the exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣavyatireka*) is established by implication alone in such a case.
For one who first seeks [the negative concomitance], it is difficult to obtain because the locations of the counter-examples (vipakṣa) are infinite.
However, once the restriction of the essential nature (svabhāva-niyama) is known, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is easily obtained because the essential nature is never deviant.
Indeed, no one would ever suspect that fire could exist anywhere at any time without having heat as its essential nature.
"Because it occupies a limited space" means because it has a delimited location. //42//
But in the case of the existence in one place and the non-existence in the world, such a cognition of concomitance (*sāhityajñāna*) does not occur; thus he says: "here" (*iha*).
For here, the single non-existence is co-present with everything and resides in infinite locations, rather than being limited to a specific location like the forms of fire and smoke.
Therefore, in this case, the notion of co-occurrence (sāhitya) is difficult to apprehend. //43//
Here he raises an objection: "But surely," etc. The absence of Caitra in another location is apprehended through inference;
for it is inferred in this manner:

All hidden levels [of reality] are connected with the absence of Caitra, because they are distinct from the location occupied by Caitra, just like the vicinity of a place where Caitra is known to be present. //44//
He refutes [the objection] with the word "contradictory" (*viruddha*).
For how could there be the state of being a non-deviant contradictory (*viruddhāvyabhicāritva*)? To this he says: "like that," meaning "and like Caitra, to another place."
"Therefore, in all cases, non-existence is to be understood through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) alone;
there is no other way. //45//
If that [non-existence] is accepted as an inference preceded by the apprehension of concomitance (*sāhityagrahaṇa*), then it must be preceded by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*);

and by this much, the validity of presumptive testimony is established. With this intention, he says: "Otherwise, its [the person's] establishment would not be possible; therefore, his non-existence is known through others. (Msv 5.7.46)
Therefore, in this case, as well as in any cause where the existence of a capacity is understood from the observation of its effect, it is preceded by presumptive reasoning (arthāpatti).
By the words "of this [self]" up to the end [of the sentence].

As for the one who says: "First, a connection is observed between one's own self, which exists in one place, and its absence everywhere; therefore, one infers it for another as well"—he should be asked: "How is the non-existence of one's own self in all places understood?"
If it is by means of non-existence, it must be stated for what [non-existence];
for first of all, the non-existence of perception in distant places cannot be understood through its cessation.
Because of their very distance, they are simply unfit for perception; therefore, one cannot conclude that they are non-existent in relation to oneself.
Furthermore, if they were actually present there, they would not be distant at all;
consequently, one's own body would simultaneously become perceptible in another location.
Furthermore, it would be perceived due to its suitability;
for whatever exists in a certain place becomes suitable for the perception of its own self together with its substratum,
and this is not the case here.
Therefore, it does not exist in other places;
thus, the non-existence in other places must be apprehended through inference,
not through the non-apprehension of perception.
