And in that case, the "incompatible non-erroneous" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) has already been explained: "The other locations are possessed of Caitra, because they are locations distinct from those near the location where Caitra is, like the location where Caitra is.

And wherever doubt is produced by a counter-reason (*pratihetu*), there [the reason] is everywhere capable [of proving its conclusion] through another stronger factor, namely non-existence (*abhāva*). For it functions in this way:
This perception of Caitra in its entirety in one place would not be possible if Caitra were present in another location;
for entities are of two kinds: localized or all-pervading.
Non-existence (*vibhava*) is also twofold:
all-pervading and that which pervades its own substratum;
the former includes space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.
Birth and the other [characteristics] exist in the future.
For that which is connected by all future conjoined things, yet remains unarrived,
is established as being omnipresent.
And by that [extension], the self, space, and so forth are called "pervasive" (*vibhu*).
However, the self is not like space;
for that which is spherical is understood to be fully contained within a single location.
Furthermore, just as a whole does not exist in its own parts, so it cannot exist in another location.
For if it were to have parts elsewhere, it would not be perceived here in its entirety;
or, if it were to exist there, it would be something other [than what is here] due to the interruption in the interval between them.
Nor can it function like a genus (*jāti*);
for a genus is formless,
and this [universal] is not such a genus in one respect.
Conjunction is its connection with another location; and that is not possible for one who has not come [to that place],
for it is observed that one becomes conjoined with other locations only after having gone there.
For this very reason, [the Self] is not all-pervading.
Now, is it not the case that an effect serves as a logical mark (liṅga)? No, because it does not depend on a relationship.
Having observed its state of being related, this capacity can be understood, and not otherwise.

And since perception and the other means of knowledge are impossible at the time of seeing that [object], the validity of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) would exist even without the three characteristics [of a logical mark]. (Msv 5.7.49)
Therefore, since it is impossible for that which exists in one place to exist elsewhere, the comprehension of the whole is established by including its non-existence elsewhere;
but what here is the impossibility?
For no obstruction to the comprehension of the whole is observed here by anyone.
Indeed, it is only when the cause of obstruction is weak that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) establishes itself by not contradicting the inference from existence (*bhāvānumāna*).
And here, the inference from existence is weak because it is contradicted by a counter-reason (*pratihetu*).
However, where both [reasons] occur together with equal force, [the situation is different].
"In that case, since the justification [of the fact] occurs through the postulation of another fact, nothing is untenable.
Thus, the distinction between presumption based on non-existence (*abhāvapūrvikā arthāpatti*) and inference has been stated;
now, in order to demonstrate the distinction from perception (*pratyakṣapūrvikā*), he first states its formal proposition: "And where... and so forth.
Even in cases where the power of a cause such as fire is postulated because the effect such as burning is observed, there too, presumption (*arthāpatti*) itself is primary.
If, however, an inference (*anumāna*) occurs subsequently, let it be so;
for since it was cited in the *Bhāṣya*, the distinction of presumption based on non-existence (*abhāvapūrvikā*) from inference has been described as being primary. //46,47//
In this context, the proponent of inference (anumānavādin) presents the logical mark (liṅga), stating "of the effect" (kāryasya).

For they think as follows: inference is of two kinds—that which has for its object a perceived particular characteristic (dṛṣṭasvalakṣaṇa-viṣaya) and that which has for its object an unperceived particular characteristic (adṛṣṭasvalakṣaṇa-viṣaya)—such as the inference of motion from conjunction, disjunction, and so forth.
Since an effect is known in a general way to have a relationship with its cause, the cognition of it [the cause] from that [the effect] is indeed a form of inference. Thus, this is inference.
He refutes this as well with the words "not a relation" (*na saṃbandha*).

For one who has previously seen a sprout from a seed, yet does not perceive it again at another time despite the presence of such a [seed], infers by means of an inference based on essential nature (*svabhāvānumāna*) that "this [seed] must produce a sprout," and while thus inferring, he suspects:
"Why is the sprout not produced?"
Then one might postulate: "There exists some specific difference in potency inherent in the seed, by virtue of which the effect existed previously but does not exist today.

But how can this be considered inference, when the knowledge arises simply from the investigation of the presence and absence of the previous and current sprouts, without any apprehension of a relation?
Furthermore, all inference is dependent upon the grasping of a relation; it is impossible for there to be inference between two related things when that relation has not been grasped.
Nor, in this case,
are victory and defeat— the relationship of slayer and slain found among snakes, mongooses, and the like— not mentioned, because their supersensuous power (*śakti*) is not distinct from inference.
And upon hearing such statements as, "He is fat, yet he does not eat during the day," [one infers his nocturnal eating]. (Msv 5.7.51)

Some conceive of it as having the objective referent as its domain, while others conceive of it as having the word as its domain; and on the basis of scripture, they declare it to be non-different from that [referent].
It cannot be experienced by means of another instrument of valid cognition; for this very reason, even the apprehension of that which possesses it is not possible.
Therefore, how [could there be cognition] from a relation that has not been apprehended?
"The power and its possessor are not established through the effect"—
this is what he states with the words "by seeing," etc.
Now, it has indeed been understood that the generality of the effect is pervaded by the generality of the cause.
Therefore, that [capacity] will be inferred. True; however, without the postulation of capacity (*śakti*), the very notion of "cause" does not cease.

For a sprout is understood to have the seed as its cause because it exists when the seed exists and because its existence is not deviant from other states; yet, when it fails to arise even though the seed is present, it deviates from that [seed] as well, and thus the very cognition of causality collapses.
One supports that [relation] by postulating a capacity (*śakti*).

And once a capacity inherent in the cause has been postulated, if the relation is understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), let it be so; for when the capacity is established, presumptive testimony is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just as in the established doctrine.
He concludes that presumptive testimony, arising even without the characteristics of inference, is a distinct means of valid cognition: "of presumptive testimony" (*arthāpatter iti*) //49//
He refutes the example cited by another commentator with the words "from inference" (anumānāt).
For victory is known through its pervasion (vyāpti) with defeat; thus, having seen that [victory] in a single instance—such as a mongoose that kills snakes—one understands the defeat of the opponent.
And by seeing the defeat, one understands the victory of the opponent.
This is not to be cited as an example of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). //50//
It was stated that "presumption based on what is heard" (śrutārthāpatti) will be explained;
he now provides an example of it: "Fat... //51//

And regarding its object, there is a dispute; he sets forth [the following] in order to determine it definitively, ending with the words "they conceive of it as being for the sake of an object. He says "and from scripture" because all [schools] maintain that it is not outside of scripture. //52//
Furthermore, the practical application of this [method] is generally established in the Veda;
it would follow that it is non-Vedic if it were to differ from that. (Msv 5.7.53)
Some maintain that even that [meaning] belongs to the very word that was heard;
others, however, hold it to belong to another sentence whose meaning has been corrupted by that [first one].

First of all, this meaning is not intended for the words as they are being heard; for it is not logical that a single sentence should have multiple meanings, nor that its expressive power should function in such a way.
For the meaning of a sentence is indeed understood through the connection of the meanings of its constituent words;
however, the meaning of the word "night" and so forth is not conveyed by the sentence concerning the day.
The eating at night is neither a combination of the meanings of the words "day" and so forth, nor is it their exclusion;
therefore, that sentence cannot be the means of conveying it.
He states his intention regarding the acceptance of the non-differentiation of the scriptures with the words "for the most part" (*prāyaśaḥ*).
Its utility in the Veda is great for establishing the results, the unseen force (*apūrva*), the specific ritual details (*vidhyanta*), and so forth;
otherwise, everything would be non-Vedic due to the absence of scriptural authority. //53//
Even though [the Veda] is based on scripture (*āgamika*), he introduces a further point of contention with the words "of the statement" (*vacanasya*).
Here he shows the essential conclusion with "not indeed" (*na tāvat*).
He states the reason with "for not" (*na hi*).
To begin with, a sentence cannot express even a single meaning, let alone many meanings. //55//
If [the sentence] is not expressive, how can there be comprehension of the meaning from the sentence? To this he says: "padārtha... (from the word-meanings).

And this will be explained in the section on *tadabhūta* (that which is not present). Now, if the meaning of the sentence regarding the night is not expressed by the sentence regarding the day, it will nevertheless be understood through its own meaning, in the form of the connection of word-meanings (*padārthānvaya*).
Therefore, he says: "not night, etc.
For indeed, the referents of words such as "night" do not exist in the sentence concerning the day; how then could there be their syntactic connection (*anvaya*) therein? //56//
[Objection: But surely the meaning of the sentence regarding night and so forth will be understood simply from the connection with the meanings of the words "day" and so forth;
therefore, he says: "Not day and so forth. //57//
Furthermore, because it is occupied with another meaning, there is no assumption of a second meaning;
therefore, this [meaning] is understood through another sentence present in the mind.

And even if that [scripture] is based on tradition (āgamika), one must state which among the means of valid cognition— such as direct perception (pratyakṣa) and the rest— that sentence upon which it relies is authoritative.
For when a sentence has not been uttered, perception is certainly not admitted;
nor is there inference, because this [sentence] has never been seen in association with that [object].
If, however, the status of being a logical mark (liṅga) is admitted even when the relationship [between word and object] is unperceived,
then by the mere utterance [of a word], there would be cognition of every sentence.

Nor can all words be understood through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), for not all words are perceived as being connected [to their meanings], such that an inference could be made regarding them.
He explains what was stated—that there is no multiplicity of meanings—with the words "of another meaning" (*anyārtha*).
Therefore, he says "consequently" (*tasmāt*) to show that this is the meaning of a different sentence altogether, and not of the sentence concerning the day. //58//
Thus, this is not the meaning of the root scripture (*mūlāgama*) itself;

rather, one must determine which among the means of valid cognition—such as perception and the rest—is the authority for that other statement present in the mind by which this meaning is understood. To this effect, he says: "Of that" (*tasya*). //59//
Regarding this, he states that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing that [the Veda], saying "for not" (*na hi*).

He further states that inference (*anumāna*) is also impossible because the sentence regarding the day (*divāvākya*), which would have to be connected with it, is not observed, saying "not inference" (*nānumānam*). //60//

But if one were to seek an inferential mark (*liṅga*) in the sentence regarding the day when the relationship [between word and meaning] is unknown, there would be a lack of restriction; thus he says: "If, however... (verse 61).

If, however, it is argued that one first grasps the very relationship between the daytime sentence and the nighttime sentence, and then infers [the latter] from that, this would indeed be established; yet, not all worldly and Vedic sentences cognizable through *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard) are understood as being related to all [other] expressive sentences.
Therefore, he asks how those [causes] can be inferred from them, and says: "And not... (verse 62).
Nor is a specific [meaning] inferred by means of an inference from existence;
rather, in this case, only the very existence of the specific sentence is understood.
In this context, a subject that is already established independently and is qualified by an independent property—
a subject thus distinguished by its attribute— is not recognized as the object of inference.
If, however, the qualification of that [subject] is measured by means of a statement that has been heard,
then the thesis would be one whose qualification is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, if this [word] were a logical mark (liṅga) merely because no other mark exists,
it would follow— just as in the case of a word— that it is a part of the meaning of the proposition itself (pratijñārthaikadeśatva).
In that very same way, the relationship of property and property-bearer between two words must be rejected;
for if it has not been apprehended, it cannot be its property, and if it has been apprehended, it cannot be an object of inference.
For this reason as well, inference is not [possible]; thus he says: "And not...
For something qualified by a relation known through some universal nature (*sāmānyātman*) is what is inferred, not the mere existence of a thing. And it is not [the case that] the qualified...
Because the relationship [of the word] is unknown, whereas here both of those are the reverse. //63//

And since in this case the very nature of the sentence is the object of cognition (*prameya*), it is not—as in the case of a mountain or similar locus—a previously established, independent substratum (*dharmin*) that is qualified by some property (*dharma*), such as fire, which is itself independent and unrelated [to the subject].
Thus he says: "previously established" (*pūrvasiddha*). //64//

Now, if one takes the very sentence that has been heard as the subject (*dharmin*) and proves its being qualified by a sentence not heard, then, because that [unheard sentence] is unestablished, the thesis would have an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*). Thus he says: "Now... (verse 65).

Furthermore, when a sentence that is already heard is being established as qualified by a sentence not yet heard, no probans (*liṅga*) is perceived at all; nor does an inference occur without a probans.
If that very [sentence] is again desired to be the probans, then it would constitute a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*).
He states "moreover" (kiñca) to explain that when the word, as qualified by its meaning, is made the subject of the thesis, it has already been stated [that this leads to a fault]. //66//

The relationship between property and its substratum (*dharmadharmibhāva*)—as in the case of the sentence regarding "day" and the sentence regarding "night"—must likewise be rejected, just as in the case of word and meaning; thus he says: "tadvadeva" (in the same way).

Just as it was stated there that if the referent, the substratum (*dharmin*), is not apprehended, then [the other term] cannot be its property (*dharma*), so too here, if the sentence regarding "night" is not apprehended, [the sentence regarding "day"] cannot be its property.
Apart from the relationship between action and its factors, there is no such thing as "dharmatā";
and because it is inexpressible, this dharma does not exist by way of being an object.
If it is argued that the capacity to denote arises from conventional understanding, then the consequence would be an infinite number of expressive powers;
furthermore, the status of being a property (dharma) arising from the object of inference would be rendered fruitless.
Nor can that sentence be understood even through its constituent word-meanings, because they lack a necessary connection;
for it is universals, being established otherwise, that lead to the understanding of a particular.
The sentence is understood.

However, if it is argued that it is first apprehended for the purpose of establishing the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatā), then the intention is that there would be an absence of the object of inference (anumeya). This is the intended meaning.
He explains [this] with the words: "not unperceived" (nāgṛhīte) //67//
Moreover, it is described in that very same passage: "No relation exists apart from the connection between an action and its factors (kāraka).
Therefore, just as a word has no connection with an object based on an action, it is said that [the universal] is not a property of it.
Thus, he states "action" (*kriyā*) to show that the properties of the sentence concerning the day must likewise be rejected in the case of the sentence concerning the night.

Furthermore, there is no relation between these two sentences—whether in the form of the object-and-subject relationship (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) as exists between a word and its meaning—as it is said that "meaning is expressed by a word," but one sentence is not the designator (*vācaka*) of another sentence; thus he says "non-designative" (*avācaka*).
In the case of a word (*pada*), since it generates the cognition of an object, its status as an object [of inference] is accepted, and thus the absence of an inferable [object] has been shown.
Here, however, because a sentence (*vākya*) is not denotative, it is impossible even to conceive of it as having that [object] as its referent; this is the distinction. //68//

If, however, it is argued that the sentence concerning the night is indeed understood from the sentence concerning the day, and therefore that [sentence] also possesses the capacity to denote it— such that there exists a relationship characterized by the object and the subject of cognition— then it would follow that a single sentence has multiple meanings.
For even the sentence concerning the night conveys its own meaning, and this is not tenable; with this intention, he says "because of [the nature of] cognition.
Now, it might be argued: "Let it not be that [the sentence] has that as its object due to being non-expressive..."
However, that sentence is inferred from it;
therefore, as the mark (liṅga) is the object of inference, the "daytime sentence" is itself designated as the mark by virtue of being its property (taddharma).

Regarding the claim that its status as a property arises because it is the object of inference, [the author] says "anumā" (inference), meaning that since the inference is already established beforehand, [that status] is redundant. //69//

Thus, it has been stated that the sentence as a whole lacks indicative power (*aliṅga*); now he says, "by the word-meanings," [intending] that the indicative power of the individual word-meanings contained therein must likewise be refuted.
[An objection: But surely the word-meanings themselves have not yet grasped the relationship [with the sentence]?
Yet nothing among these is established without another statement;
nor is there any other way for them to be connected with that statement.

Now, if it were to be argued that another sentence is to be supplied in this case, and likewise in that one as well, then even though they are far apart, one cannot escape the consequence [of their connection], for there is no lack of relationship.
Therefore, it is better to know [the truth] from the very first through what is unconnected [to the object];
and positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) should be rejected, just as in the case of a word.
Just as [the words] convey the meaning of a sentence, why do they not likewise convey the meaning of the "night" passage?
To this, he says: "The general," and so forth.

The general action or the general agent, once apprehended, cannot be established otherwise unless it attains a mutual interconnection; therefore, it leads to the understanding of that specific detail, and that very specific detail is what is called the meaning of the sentence. //70//
And this method is not possible for the presentation of the statement regarding night; thus he says: "But not...
Although the statement regarding day is not the expressive word for the statement regarding night, nevertheless we shall infer it.
And therefore, it will be understood from that [context]. First, he raises this doubt with the words ending in "athaitadvācītyanyat";
here he states the refutation with the words "tathaiva."
In this regard, since there is no evidence whatsoever for postulating such a separate sentence, one should disregard it and first demonstrate the resulting infinite regress:
even that postulated sentence is not capable of making known the *rātri* [sacrifice] injunction;
nor is it reasonable to claim that something entirely unrelated can be its indicator.
Furthermore, if one were to postulate yet another sentence, that same fault would recur;
thus, whatever sentence one might wish to postulate would itself be incoherent and incapable of conveying meaning, resulting in an infinite regress. //72//

If, however, it is postulated that only the final [word] is the indicator despite being unrelated [to the others], then it would be better to simply postulate that the first word of that same kind is the indicator;
what is the point of postulating another sentence?
And with the intention that this is not tenable, he says: "Consequently" (*tataśca*).

Thus, first of all, the status of the opponent's statement as an object of inference has been refuted by the impossibility of its possessing the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth;
now he says: "Of the positive and negative concomitances" (*anvaya*), showing that their negation is to be demonstrated just as in the case of the words themselves.
For when the statement regarding the night exists, the statement regarding the day has no similarity whatsoever with that which is not heard;
therefore, by this same reasoning, the object [of comparison] also lacks the status of being an object of comparison (anupamāna).

When the [intended] meaning is precluded from being applied to the sentence by the mark of its being a simile, it would likewise be so for the [individual] words; therefore, there is no possibility [of such a function] in the preceding cases.
Therefore, the communication of the meaning of an unheard statement would be its very acquisition of selfhood; it is held that this cannot occur without [the hearing]. Msv 5.7.76.
Why is it not assumed that this [scripture] does not exist without this meaning?
And why is this not understood as the meaning of the scripture, just like the meaning of a sentence?
The positive and negative concomitances do not exist [in this case],
because there is an absence of a relationship with that place, time, and so forth;

nor is there a positive concomitance with cognition, since even in the absence of the cognition of the sentence regarding the night, one who is proficient [in the language] [attains it] from the cognition of the sentence regarding the day.

The intention is that it should be demonstrated—like the word "ādi" (and so forth)—that positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), which occur subsequent to consciousness, are of no use [for establishing the nature of the object]. //73//
Thus, it has first been stated that the sentence concerning the night is not cognized through perception, inference, or scripture;
now he shows that analogy (*upamāna*) is also not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this case, by the verse ending with "śrutavākye" (v.
74ab). Furthermore, he states that the sentence concerning the night is not analogized even on the basis of its meaning, just like the sentence concerning the day, by saying "arthasya" (v. 74c).

And just as the comparison of the sentence concerning the night with the sentence concerning the day and its respective meaning has already been refuted, so too must the meaning of the sentence concerning the night be refuted by those two; thus he says, concluding with the words "upamānatve" [in verse 75]: "Therefore... //75//

Therefore, since there is an absence of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says "therefore" [in the verse], meaning that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) alone is the refuge for understanding the sentence regarding the night.
The corpulence perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is contradicted by the prohibition of eating; and by that corpulence, daytime non-eating [is inferred].

Therefore, because of their mutual contradiction, the statement regarding the day, being unable to convey its own meaning, necessitates the inclusion of the statement regarding the night; thus, that statement regarding the night is inferred. //76//
He now introduces [the following] to refute what was stated—that [the inference] has the object as its domain—by saying: "apart from this object.
The intention is as follows: for indeed, either the fatness or the prohibition of eating mutually sublate one another, and both obtain their existence only through the postulation of an object.
For when [eating] during the day is prohibited for the fat person...
In conceptual cognitions, the word is perceived first;
once the purpose of the sentence has been achieved, there is no further [cognition] that is scriptural.

In the case of eating, corpulence arises from eating at night itself, not from the mere statement regarding the night; therefore, it is logical that this is indeed an *arthakalpanā* (inference based on the sense).

Furthermore, just as the meaning of a sentence, though not explicitly stated by others, becomes the intended meaning of the scripture when it is understood through the inconsistency of the literal word-meanings.

He asks: "Why, then, does even an object that is to be understood through the inconsistency of the sentence-meaning not fall within the scope of scripture (āgama)? To this he says: "vākyārtha... [verse 77].
First, he addresses the initial objection with the words "savikalpaka" (conceptual).
For the cognition resulting from presumptive testimony (*śrutārthāpatti*) is conceptual, and conceptual cognitions are preceded by verbal expression.
Therefore, since the presumption culminates in the word, the object established through that very word is not the domain of presumptive testimony.
But surely, this [objection] applies equally to all conceptual constructions involving means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):

even through the senses (*indriya*) or inferential marks (*liṅga*), fire is cognized only preceded by the word; therefore, even in those two cases, the word alone would be the ultimate basis, and thus it would be the word residing in memory that is the conveyor of meaning.
This is the same here as well:

for just as the organ of action, being in direct contact with the object itself, illuminates that very object, and a logical mark (*liṅga*), being connected with the object, makes that [object] known and not the word; so it is here too.
In the same way here as well, that which is otherwise untenable is established by the fact itself (*artha*), not by the word (*śabda*).
Thus, in the cases of presumption based on what is seen (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*), they have only the object (*artha*) as their domain.
To this, it is replied:
It is true that a sentence, like a word, requires another sentence as its means to convey the meaning;
for when "he cooks" is said, the expectancy is not satisfied merely by the direct perception of rice.
Rather, by means of the word "rice," the sentence— being understood as itself incoherent— requires another sentence,
and not that meaning in its own form.

For this very reason, when the *nirvāpa* mantra has been transferred to a modified (*vikṛti*) rite, since the original deity is absent, the word denoting that deity is removed; in its place, the word "to Sūrya" (*sūryāya*) is substituted.
In the mantra for cutting (*chedana*), however, in the phrase "for strength, for thee" (*iṣe tvā*), the word "I cut" (*chinadmi*) is supplied.
In the passage "He cuts from the heart, O Agni, then from the tongue, then from the breast," the word "cuts" (*avadyati*) is supplied as a connective (*anuṣaṅga*).

Furthermore, it is not the case that the meaning alone is attached; for "attachment" (*anuṣaṅga*) is understood as the completion of a sentence, which is grasped even by the mention of a word, yet only in the form of its meaning.
One conceptualizes that meaning, while the word itself may indeed exist merely as pure being (*sanmātratayā*).

If, however, even there the word were required, animals would have no conceptualization of meaning; yet that is not the case, for their effort toward the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful is clearly observed.
For thirsty cows go to ponds.

Indeed, if there were no relationship between rain and heat, or if it were not ascertained, this sentence would result in a cognition of what is to be understood that lacks a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇaka*). (Msv 5.7.79)
And living beings [seek] a place capable of remedying that [suffering].
Therefore, since even those who lack knowledge of words are seen to possess conceptual cognitions such as inference and so forth, it is certain that there is no dependence on words in those cases.
Furthermore, the cognition resulting from the presumption based on what was heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) simply does not exist for animals.
For this [cognition] arises from the derivation of words, and as has been explained even in the context of perception, such derivation does not exist for them;
furthermore, it is observed that even for others who are unlearned and lack knowledge of words, there is no cognition of the meaning of what is heard through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
How much more so, then, for animals?
Furthermore, it is understood through positive and negative concomitance that there is a dependence on words in the case of presumptive testimony based on what has been heard (*śrutārthāpatti*).
However, in the case of inference and the other means of knowledge, let there indeed be a recollection of words by virtue of the awakening of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), as this is unavoidable.
But there is no dependence on the word itself.
Therefore, in this case, it is another sentence that possesses meaning which serves as the justification for an untenable sentence, rather than a mere meaning or a mere word.

For this very reason, even when the justifying sentence is heard by one who has not grasped the relationship [between words and meanings] and does not know the meaning, the "untenability" regarding the cognition of the sentence-meaning is not pacified.
Even for one who has understood the meaning, there may still be a conceptualization regarding the intention [of the speaker];
therefore, one who has heard the sentence does not have the notion that it is deficient, because its purpose has been attained.
For as long as a word has not accomplished its function, so long is its cognition understood [to be incomplete].
That becomes its meaning;
for the word *artha* signifies purpose.
For this very reason, the meaning of a sentence is the meaning of the scripture.

However, since a sentence has fulfilled its purpose through the connection between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka-saṃsarga*), that which is subsequently understood as a further meaning does not cease to be scriptural (*āgamika*).

For it is not logical to claim that what is understood through the necessity of making sense of the meaning already grasped as the purpose [of the sentence] is not attained; thus, the previously understood meaning of the sentence remains the scriptural meaning.
What, then, is the distinction? It is said:

If the meaning of what has been heard and transmitted is lost through negligence, then there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the occasion of losing what was prescribed in the *Yajurveda* and other such texts; otherwise, however, it is an expiation for the occasion of an unknown loss. Thus, he teaches the expiation by collecting the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*), namely "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā," whenever [the Veda] is unknown. For it is precisely that portion of the Veda which is to be understood through the presumption of the meaning of what has been heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) that is called "unknown."
For it is not known as being any one of the *ṛc* verses and so forth. //78//
Here he raises an objection: "But surely...
[The opponent says: First of all, there is no connection between the sentence concerning the day and the sentence concerning the night;
or even if it exists, it is not known.

Furthermore, how could the validity of a perception whose connection [to its object] is unknown be established merely by seeing another instance of a connection? Moreover, how could perception possess the status of a means of valid cognition without a [logical] connection?
If it is argued that there is a connection between the sense faculty and its object, we say no, because [the cognition] is independent;
for at the very moment of perception, this [connection] is not discerned by anyone.
However, that [object] which might be determined later through experience would not at all be a factor of valid cognition; it is indeed equivalent to what is non-existent.
Just as those for whom the eye and the ear do not act by reaching [their objects] accept the validity of the cognition thereof, so it will be in this case.
Therefore, whether the relation exists or does not exist,
that cognition alone which arises as non-perishing shall possess the status of valid knowledge.
The assumption of something else is not tenable,
because it would lead to an over-extension;
for a nature that is necessarily connected brings about the obstructer precisely through the force of that connection.
However, since there is no obstruction [to its being so], there is no reason for a restriction when imagining it to be something else;
therefore, this cognition of the "night statement" is indeed invalid. //79//
He refutes [the objection] with the words "of the relation" (*sambandhasya*).

The meaning is that "being a means of valid cognition" (*prāmāṇyam*) is "being an instrument of valid cognition" (*pramākaraṇatvam*); and the word *pramāṇa* is derived by means of the instrumental case (*karaṇasādhana*).
He demonstrates that the relationship [between word and object] has no causal role in regard to validity with the words: "of perception" (pratyakṣasya) //80//

Now, one might object: "Since perception is produced solely by the contact of the sense organs with their objects, the relationship [between word and object] cannot be a cause for its validity. This is the objection raised up to the words "if it exists" (*asti cet*).
The author refutes this with the words "no, because of independence" (*nānapekṣaṇāt*). He demonstrates this very independence with the words "for not... (*na hi*).
For it has been established that a relationship is the cause for the arising of valid cognition in inference, and such is not the case here. //81//
But he says that investigation occurring after the time of direct perception is not a factor of valid cognition: "By which [investigation] also... (verse 82).
Moreover, in the view of those who maintain that the sense-faculties do not function by reaching their objects (*aprāpyakārin*), even the existence of the relationship itself is absent;
therefore, just as they accept the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of perceptual cognition, so it will be here as well. To this, he says: "not having reached" (*aprāpya*). //83//

Therefore, disregarding [the aforementioned objections], one must accept that a cognition which is connected, arisen, non-doubtful, and non-erroneous is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), even when there is a difference in place and so forth; thus he says: "Therefore... By the word "is born" (*jāyate*), he rejects invalidity characterized by non-arising; by the word "unfailing" (*abhaṅgura*), he rejects doubt and error. //84//
Furthermore, no one disputes its status as a means of valid cognition;
rather, there is disagreement regarding its difference or non-difference from it, and the determination in that matter has already been made.
And where cognition does not arise even without a [logical] connection, what can be done there? That too is certainly not a cause for validity.

In that [Vedic corpus], there is no perception of any connection whatsoever regarding the *śruti* (direct statement) which is merely imagined through *smṛti* (tradition), nor regarding the application (*viniyojikā*) by means of indicative marks (*liṅga*) and so forth, nor regarding the completion (*paripūraṇa*) by means of results (*phala*) and so forth.
Furthermore, the claim that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is not a valid means of knowledge is an unconventional dispute;
for the practical activity of those who proceed on its basis is never frustrated,
and the capacity for successful activity is precisely what constitutes validity.
"There is a dispute regarding difference and non-difference based on inference, and we have provided a resolution to that"; thus he says: "Nor even... (85).
If this were so, then even in inference the relationship would not constitute a factor at all; therefore, he says "tat" (therein).
For in that case, since cognition itself does not arise when there is no knowledge of the relationship, the cause for its production is indeed relied upon.
However, as for its validity, even there it depends solely on the absence of sublation. //86//
He demonstrates the utility of the Veda through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) with the words "by memory" (*smṛtyā*).
Indeed, a vast portion of the Veda is established by the means of knowledge known as presumptive testimony; it would not be established without that [presumption].
For just as the revealed scripture (*śruti*) gains its own identity through being manifested by recitation, so too does this [portion of the Veda] gain its identity through presumption.
Thus, those for whom the means of valid cognition consists of what is heard and presumptive testimony (śrutārthāpatti) have said:
"Just as the literal reading is a means of comprehension, so too is the inherent capacity (sāmarthya) of the Vedic texts."

"And they do not recite even one [verse] of that very [Veda], yet they might recite a thousandth part. Just as, for instance, having encountered the Smṛti of Manu and others concerning the Aṣṭakā and other rites, and while searching for their source and finding error,
deception, experience, or the words of another person to be impossible, one postulates the Śruti itself as the source because the Smṛti would otherwise be inexplicable without a basis.

In this way, through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and other means, the direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*) that assigns its own application is inferred—as follows: first, when a mantra recited in a particular context (*prakaraṇa*) has been taught by the rule for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*), it is not logically sustainable without a purpose; thus, there arises a general requirement for assistance to the sacrifice.

When a specific requirement is sought, and having observed the power (*śakti*) of the mantra, [the injunction] is applied according to the principle "whatever it may be able to do" (*yac chaknuyāt*), based on the meaning it is capable of expressing.
"All that" and so forth would be inconsistent if this [cognition] were not distinct from inference;
even if it possesses such a nature, it would not receive the name "inference" if it exists as one desires.
Thus ends the *Arthāpatti-vārttika*.
Direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is postulated as the applicator of a mantra to its object;
for example, in the case of the *barhis*-mantra, [the statement] "one should cut with this" constitutes its application based on indicative power (*liṅga*).

As for application by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*), for example: in that very same mantra, because the word *dāmī* is capable of denoting the act of cutting, it alone is applied through *liṅga* (indicative power), whereas the other words are applied through *vākya* itself, in the form of their co-occurrence with that word.
As for application by context (*prakaraṇa*), however, this refers to the *samidh* and other such mantras recited within the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
For they (the subsidiaries) require a purpose,
and the sacrifice requires assistance;
thus, when there is this mutual requirement, an implied scriptural statement (*śruti*) is inferred to the effect that "by these [subsidiaries], one should assist the sacrifice."

As for the displacement from its position (*sthānavinoyoga*), it is as follows: regarding the mantra "O you named Dabdhi... which is studied within the sequence of the *upāṃśuyāja* in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) themselves;
there is a scriptural injunction that one should perform the *upāṃśuyāja* with this [mantra], and [another] that the *adhvaryu* priest should perform these [rites].

And in the case of rituals for which the fruit and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) have not been heard—such as the Viśvajit, the Saurya, and others—a scriptural injunction capable of completing them is inferred: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," and "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer the Saurya oblation"; and the procedure is [inferred] to be like that of the Āgneya sacrifice.
The utility of the Veda through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on what has been heard is indeed much greater than this.
Nor is this established by inference alone;
for in this case, no relationship between that which is unaccountable and the postulated [explanation] has ever been observed.
And inference does not occur without a perceived relationship; therefore, in this case, presumption (*arthāpatti*) alone is the recourse.
[This refers to the phrase] "one who perceives the relationship."

"The state of being a Buddha is metaphorical; the state of being [an ordinary] vision is [literal]. He says, "All that," because if one does not rely on presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), all of this would be inconsistent.
However, if it is intended that, although distinct by definition, it is subsequently wished to be expressed by the word "inference" due to its commonality with inference, let it be so.
He states that [this] is established as not being a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) with the words "In this way."
Thus ends the chapter on Presumption (arthāpatti) in the Kāśikā commentary composed by the preceptor Sucarita Miśra.
Now begins the chapter on Non-existence (abhāva).
Regarding this, the commentary states: "Even in the case of non-existence, there is the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this object which is not in contact [with the senses].
What, then, is indicated by this? It is certainly not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It is not logical that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is defined by the absence of a means of valid cognition.
If it is argued that the absence of the previously mentioned means of valid cognition is the definition,
then this would apply equally to all means of valid cognition.

For indeed, all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) can be called "the absence of a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇābhāva*), since they consist of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*). Furthermore, there is no single definition common to all means of valid cognition by whose absence a sixth [category] could be characterized.
Moreover—valid cognition (pramāṇa) is that which establishes some object of cognition (prameya).
We do not know what it is that is established by this [non-apprehension].
But was it not said: "of this object, namely 'it does not exist,' which is not in contact [with the senses]"?
What is meant [by this]?
That "that which is not an object of perception and so forth does not exist" is the object of cognition (*prameya*) of non-existence (*abhāva*).
This is incorrect.
The meaning of "it does not exist" is that this is not cognized here.
Furthermore, it cannot be understood that there is "knowability" for that which is not being cognized.
And of which means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would this be the object of knowledge (*prameya*)?
If [it is argued that it refers] to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*),
that is not so;
for the absence of a means of valid cognition is simply the non-arising of a valid cognition.
And that [cognition] is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); this appears almost as something extraordinary.
If it is thought: "The cognition that 'it exists' or 'it does not exist' is established without dispute among all worldly people and investigators;
and it has already been explained in the Vijñānavāda that cognition cannot be without an object, nor can its object be merely its own part."
Therefore, it is for the sake of the firmness of this very cognition that the object of knowledge (prameya) is postulated;
that [object] is the domain of non-existence (abhāva).
They consider this cognition "it does not exist" to be the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), while the non-existence of the jar and so forth is the object of knowledge (prameya).
For this very reason, they divide non-existence into four kinds according to the distinctions of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth;
for a division of a non-entity is not possible.
However, if non-existence is not accepted as a distinct category of reality (*tattvāntara*), [then the following applies].
What then is the absence of curd in milk,
which is called prior non-existence?
And for this reason, this is the absence of milk in curd.
It must be stated what its objective support (*ālambana*) is.
If it were the bare ground itself, that would not be the case,
because it would follow [absurdly] that it exists even where there is a jar.

If it is argued that the mere surface of the earth (*bhūtalatva*) alone is the objective support (*ālambana*), then what other reality (*tattvāntara*) could there be? Thus, the distinction between objects of cognition (*prameya-bheda*) is established;
and from that distinction follows the distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-bheda*).

For that [non-existence] is not a contact with forms by way of their existence, nor by way of their non-existence; yet, even in the absence of such an operation, the arising of the cognition "it is not" is observed,

just as when someone who has seen only the intrinsic nature of a house or similar object goes elsewhere and, upon being questioned about the absence of something, determines its absence at that very moment.
Thus, this cognition that "it does not exist," which arises even in the absence of sense-object contact, is not sensory;
nor does it have any inferential mark (liṅga) as its producer.
If it is argued that non-apprehension is the logical mark (*liṅga*), we say no; because it is not cognized.
For a logical mark whose form is not cognized does not lead one to infer the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*).

Nor is it the case that [non-apprehension] reveals the absence of an object when its relation [to that object] is unknown; for non-apprehension does not manifest the absence of existence while remaining itself unapprehended.
Since non-apprehension is itself of the nature of an absence, if it were to require another of its own kind [to establish its own existence], there would be the fallacy of infinite regress.
Therefore, this must be accepted as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) for the sake of establishing the non-confusion of entities.
Furthermore, there is a well-known tradition among the Mīmāṃsakas that "this is indeed a sixth means of valid cognition.
Consequently, this treatise is intended for the purpose of defining that [sixth means].
That is incorrect; for by this [statement], there is no proof (*pramāṇa*).
Indeed, from the text itself, it is determined that there is simply an absence of proof, not a proof.
Even when it is said "it does not exist," worldly people understand this only as the absence of an object of cognition (*prameyābhāva*), and not as some [positive] object of cognition;
therefore, such a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) is neither consistent with the text nor compatible with reason.
For it is only when knowledge has been established that an inquiry as to whether it is valid or invalid is appropriate;
yet there exists no cognition other than the perception of the bare ground.
That very [cognition] indeed manifests in two ways.
That [space] is both associated with objects and dissociated from them.

When it is perceived as associated with a jar or the like, then the conventional usage "the jar exists" proceeds; but when there is cognition of that [space] alone, [the usage] "it does not exist" occurs.
Nor should it be said that because a cognition of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) is observed even when subtle entities exist,
it follows that they do not exist there either, yet they manifest;
for that very [consciousness] manifests in two ways.
For the cognition of that alone (tanmātra-bodha) is twofold:
when the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is perceptible or when it is imperceptible.
Among these, the cognition of that alone which occurs when the counter-correlate is perceptible is itself the non-existence of the jar and so forth.

Even for those for whom non-existence (*abhāva*) is an object of cognition (*prameya*), it is precisely through the non-perception of what is perceptible that non-existence is determined as "it does not exist.
Therefore, this very cognition of "that-only" (*tanmātra-buddhi*), which is established for all disputants, is designated as "it does not exist.
Furthermore, whatever is sought as the cause of non-existence, let that be accepted as the cause of this very cognition of "that-only," which is established for both disputants.

Therefore, precisely where there was previously a cognition of a jar, when a distinct cause occurs, only a cognition of that [cause] alone arises, and not a cognition of the absence of the jar and so forth.
This must necessarily be admitted;
otherwise, indeed, the absence could not be apprehended.
For in that case, the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) is itself the means of valid cognition; yet it cannot be established by one who has not apprehended it.
For even in the state of deep sleep, there is indeed the absence of a means of valid cognition... [the word *abhāva* is missing from the source].
Nor is there a certainty that [it] does not exist;
therefore, non-perception, when not itself apprehended, cannot determine non-existence.
Furthermore, since that non-apprehension is also of the nature of non-existence, it would require another non-perception to establish it, leading thus to an infinite regress.

And if non-perception were to determine only the mere existence [of an object], then even when that non-perception has ceased, Devadatta would [still be known] in that form of the thing where the five means of valid cognition had previously not arisen.
Otherwise, there would be no certainty that "it did not exist.
For this sometimes occurs:

when someone who was not seen in a certain place is later seen again, even though there was no prior perception [of him], there arises the cognition of his previous absence; that [cognition] would not occur if there were no subsequent perception.
Therefore, it must be said that this cognition arises solely from the reflection upon non-perception;
and in this way, it reveals the absence of that [object] precisely as it is being apprehended.
Furthermore, if there were a further apprehension [of that non-perception], it would entail the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If it is maintained that the perception of the object consists solely in the cognition of that [object] itself, nothing is faulty;
for that cognition, being self-luminous as a result, does not depend on another illumination.
Therefore, the experience of that [object] alone is designated as the non-existence of that [other].
Therefore, non-existence (abhāva) is not a separate object of cognition (prameya);
nor do we understand what is being characterized here by the claim that the cognition "it does not exist" is a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), since it would be like an error.
Here he says: What is not understood here?
According to what you have stated, it is determined from the text that there is indeed an absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
for some, it is said, do indeed maintain that non-existence (*abhāva*) is a means of valid cognition.
This very effort of the author of the Bhāṣya is for the purpose of refuting that [view].
How is it refuted by this?
Listen.

As for what some say— that "non-existence" is the meaning of the term "that which is not in contact [with the senses]," and that the non-existence of that which is not an object of perception and so forth is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— that is not correct.

For this "absence of a means of valid cognition" (pramāṇābhāva) means that it is not a means of valid cognition; and the reason for its being a non-means of valid cognition has already been stated. This too is untenable.
If this meaning were explained in accordance with the text, then there would be a clear contradiction with the Bhāṣya in another section;
for it is not appropriate to refute an opposing view by a mere assertion such as "the number residing in the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) divides the linguistic usage.
Therefore, this must be explained.
Here he says: "By 'means of valid cognition' (*pramāṇa*) etc.
The meaning is this:
this is indeed the definition of the means of valid cognition.
As for what was said— that "how can that be characterized by its absence"—
that is true; however,
the word "pramāṇa" is not intended here in the sense of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in general, but rather, what is being stated is this:
"The absence of the five aforementioned means of valid cognition" [is the definition].
And there is one commonality among the five,
namely that they are all positive means of valid cognition (*bhāvapramāṇa*).

Therefore, for the purpose of understanding the existence of a thing, the means of valid cognition regarding non-existence (abhāvapramāṇa) applies there as a means of valid cognition regarding existence (bhāvapramāṇa).

"Existence is the means of valid cognition for non-existence. This will be explained in two ways further on: either as the cognition of existence consisting in the non-modification of the self, or as the cognition that "there is no other [object] than the mere perception of the bare ground."
"Very well.
What is its object?
It is the fourfold arrayed absence of an object of cognition."

For if that [non-existence] did not exist, even the conventional usage of "walking on foot" and so forth— which is preceded by the ascertainment of the absence of thorns and the like— would not occur, since non-existence would lack the status of being an object of cognition (*prameya*).

If only the bare ground were perceived here, and not the exclusion of thorns and such, then even when those [thorns] are present, they would be grasped by the cognition "it does not exist," because [the bare ground] is perceived.
But the denial of cognition is indeed contrary to experience;
for there is no difference in the non-manifestation of existence and non-existence.
As for what was said—that it is simply the cognition of that [bare ground] which is designated as "the jar does not exist"—[that is incorrect].
In this regard, we do not know what is excluded by the word "mātra.
If it excludes nothing, then it is meaningless.
Now, [the opponent] objects: "In that case, there must be an exclusion as an object;
otherwise, if one were to exclude something while it is actually existent, the conventional usage would be impossible."
This alone is the distinction between those whose cognition is of a mixed nature and those whose cognition is of that [object] alone: namely,
that this [latter cognition] has a distinct object,
and the distinction from other objects is non-existence.

If it is argued that the object is nothing other than cognition itself, then even when there is the perception of a relation [between subject and object], that [cognition] exists; therefore, it would manifest as "it does not exist.
Furthermore, if something is negated here—
It is said that "it does not exist there.
It is not the cognition "there is no jar here" that is being negated when it is said that "it does not exist there";
rather, it is the cognition "there is no jar here" that is being negated.
For if the word "non-existent" were within the domain of cognition, there would be an absence of cognition itself.
Now, if it is argued that the meaning of "the jar is not non-existent" is simply that "only the bare ground is perceived," ordinary people do not understand it in this way.

Moreover, there would be no desire to investigate whether a subtle object exists or does not exist if non-existence were nothing at all; for if that were so, what other doubt could there be regarding a perceived object concerning subtle things such as hair or a fiber?

For the non-existence of other entities is simply the perception of that [object] alone; and since that [non-existence] is already known and must be free from doubt due to the self-luminosity of consciousness (*saṃvid*), what else remains to be sought?
If it is argued that non-existence is the cognition of that alone when the counter-positive is perceptible, and not when it is imperceptible, then what is the point of its being imperceptible,
since non-existence is not distinct from cognition?
If non-existence were a distinct category of reality (*tattvāntara*), then the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyādarśana*) would be required for its ascertainment;
for the contact of the self, the sense organ, the mind, and the object is indeed the cause for the production of cognition.

Thus, when an object sought through inquiry is not perceived despite the presence of unimpaired sense organs and other conditions, and despite being sought with effort, it is then postulated that its non-perception is due to its absence.
In this way, a subtle inquiry is justified for the sake of establishing perceptibility.
However, if there were non-existence upon the perception of that [object] alone, then the qualification "perceptible" would become superfluous for the purpose of defining non-existence.
As for what was said— that "the cause of the non-existence of something should be understood as the cognition of that thing alone, because of the parsimony of conceptualization"—
that is incorrect. For one cannot disregard what has been established by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) simply because it results in a parsimony of conceptualization.
Nor is it logical to say that whatever is the cause of an absence is the cognition of that [object] alone;
for the striking of a hammer and so forth is the cause of the absence,
yet by that, the cognition of "that alone" is not produced.
For the manifestation of the nature of an object such as the ground has the sense organs and so forth as its causes;
it does not depend on the removal or the striking away of a jar or the like.
As for that which is the non-perception of what is capable of being defined, it determines non-existence.
The argument that this follows as a consequence in the state of deep sleep is incorrect; for indeed,
when an object has not been apprehended, its absence cannot manifest without a substratum.
For in some cases, the non-existence of something appears [to the mind], but not as an independent entity.
Therefore, he says:
"it does not arise in the form of a real thing."
Furthermore, nothing at all is manifested to one who is in deep sleep;
and where [is there an object] for which non-existence could be delimited?
Moreover, it is the non-arising of a competent means of valid cognition that determines non-existence.

Furthermore, for one who is in deep sleep, there is no object capable of being apprehended by a means of valid cognition that does not manifest; thus, how could a certainty regarding its non-existence arise?
Therefore, since non-perception is itself ungrasped, the non-existence of the object in deep sleep does not manifest.
However, this is not a valid perception;
furthermore, it is incorrect to designate something as having previously been non-existent even when its non-perception has ceased, as is the case with that which is currently being perceived.
That is not so.

For in that case, when many things capable of being perceived in the same manner are being remembered, if one among them is not remembered, its non-existence is cognized through the cessation of memory—
which is functionally equivalent to the cessation of perception— just as the existence of other entities is known through memory. At that time,
both the non-existence and the cessation of memory are indeed present.
Nor is it understood [as such];
rather, it causes one to understand the prior absence of the jar itself, so there is no infinite regress.
Therefore, the cognition "it does not exist" is a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
And it is now established that non-existence (*abhāva*), divided into categories such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth, is an object of valid cognition (*prameya*).
This is the meaning:

where the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which are capable of producing comprehension, do not arise to make known the existence of an entity such as a cloth according to their respective functions, [that is non-existence].

In that regard, the status of non-existence as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is possible; by this, it is shown that the word "means of valid cognition" is used here in reference to the fivefold set of means of valid cognition due to the context.
Furthermore, by the phrase "it does not arise with respect to the nature of a real entity," he shows that a cognition consisting merely of independent non-existence is not a means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, from the statement of the definition of worldly means of valid cognition (*laukikapramāṇa*), it follows that wherever the capacity of the means of valid cognition is possible, it is precisely there that their non-arising constitutes the means of valid cognition for the determination of absence (*abhāva*).
For it is by such a means alone that worldly people understand "it does not exist.
The meaning of the *Bhāṣya* is also this: even through the absence [of other means], worldly people understand "it does not exist."
Because it is non-deviant:

for when an object that is not in contact with the senses—namely, that which is called "absence"—is manifested in the form "it does not exist," the cognition that arises is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) known as absence (abhāva).
Furthermore, the establishment of the non-confusion of entities depends upon the validity of that [cognition].
That which does not exist in milk, such as curd and so forth, is called prior non-existence (prāgabhāva).
The non-existence of milk in curd is held to be the non-existence by way of destruction;
whereas the absence of a horse and so forth in a cow is called mutual non-existence.
The parts of a head that are devoid of production, growth, and solidity—
such as those in the form of a hare's horn— are called absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva).
Just as curd would exist in milk, or milk in curd, or a cloth in a jar,
or a horn in a hare, so too would consciousness exist in the earth and other elements, and corporeality in the self.
And for such a [logical] type, no deviation (vyabhicāra) is possible;
thus, it should be connected [to the preceding context] by supplying: "even that which is separated [in space], if it produces a cognition by virtue of expectancy (ākāṅkṣā).
As it is said: "Whatever is related to something else, even if it stands at a distance, by that [relation] it is [connected]."
According to this principle. //1//

It has been stated that where there is a non-arising of the appropriate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the purpose of cognizing the actual existence of an object, there is the means of valid cognition consisting of non-existence (*abhāva*).
But what, then, is cognized by this [means] therein? Non-existence is, first of all, understood by its own respective means of valid cognition.
Therefore, he says: "Because there is no confusion of entities. (1.1/2)
He explains the very non-confusion of entities with two and a half verses beginning with "curd in milk":
this fourfold mutual distinction between cause and effect and so forth that has been shown is designated as the "non-confusion of entities" (*vastvasaṅkara*).
It is cognized through non-existence (*abhāva*).
"In the form of a rabbit's horn, etc.
means that when those parts on the head of a rabbit are perceived in that form, they are non-existent;
however, in their own nature, they are indeed existent. //2-4//
But if non-existence were not an authoritative means of knowledge, everything would be confused with everything else; thus he says in the two verses beginning with "In milk":
"In this way.
This means that just as curd is in milk, so too milk would be in curd.
The objection beginning with "the horn in a rabbit" is a charge of error raised regarding the non-establishment of absolute non-existence;
for indeed, the absolute non-existence of horns and the like in rabbits and such is not established without recourse to the means of valid cognition consisting of non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*).
Furthermore, the proponents of the doctrine that consciousness is an emergent property of the elements (*bhūtacaitanyavādins*) cannot be refuted;
for among the great elements such as air and the rest,
fragrance exists in water, taste in fire, and both of these together with form exist in air.
And they are not touched by the sky, nor is there a measurement of the body.
Furthermore, this conventional discourse based on the distinction between causes and so forth would not exist if non-existence did not occur through the various types such as prior non-existence.
These [distinctions] cannot belong to a non-entity; therefore, this [entity] possesses substantiality.
What is the non-existence of effects and so forth, other than the existence of causes and so forth?
Otherwise, the absolute absence of smell and so forth would not be established;
for it is an established principle that each of the four great elements is devoid of one quality respectively. //5,6//
He states the fault in universal confusion with the words "And not...
This worldly transaction of ordinary people which is observed through the distinction of cause and so forth would not exist if there were universal confusion.

When commanded, "Bring milk," one brings only milk and not curd; if curd were brought instead of milk, this would not be possible if there were no mutual distinction between cause and effect and so forth. //7//
Now, it may be objected that so-called "non-existence" (abhāva) is not perceived as a distinct category of reality;
for we apprehend the ground through its own means of valid cognition,
whereas we do not perceive a jar when there is no means of valid cognition [for it].
But there is no other thing called "the absence of a jar" that arises in the cognition;
even when one says "the jar does not exist," the meaning is that the jar is not cognized, not that the absence of the jar is cognized.
Therefore, since non-existence is characterized solely by the absence of all defining descriptions and is not some distinct reality, he says: "And not...
As for the claim that it is not perceived by the means of valid cognition for positive entities, that is true.
For this very reason, non-existence (abhāva) is a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Even in the case of the statement "the jar does not exist," the meaning is not that "the jar is not cognized"; for even though the jar exists, one says that it is not cognized.
Therefore, when asked whether a jar exists or not, one who has not ascertained its absence designates it as "non-existent," but this is merely non-apprehension;
thus, the cognition "this jar does not exist" is indeed a valid means of cognizing absence (*abhāvapramiti*).

Furthermore, this fourfold division that has been described is not established in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*), which is characterized by the absence of all designations (*sarvopākhyāviraha*).
And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: [Non-existence] is a real entity (*vastu*), because it possesses a fourfold division.
"As with substance and so forth.
As for what they also say: "Non-existence is not some kind of reality;
for blue and other [colors] are distinguished from one another by their own nature, which is restricted to each respective object."

Since non-existence (*abhāva*) does not possess any differentiator whatsoever in this way, we do not perceive it as excluded [from existence]. Therefore, how could we establish it as a distinct reality?
However, its conventional usage—which consists in the application of conceptual terms such as "it does not exist"—must somehow be explained as being based solely on existence itself.
But it is not the case that non-existence is something other than the absence of association with others, which is restricted to a single form;
that [position] has already been refuted by the very refutation of the "partialist" (ekadeśin).
Furthermore, it must be explained how the conceptual construction (vikalpa) that "there is no object" is itself cognized;
for the object of conceptual construction is a form (rūpa) touched by words,
and such a thing does not exist here.
Furthermore, the self is not capable of association with verbal expression through conceptualization,
because it is unique (asādhāraṇa).
Precisely for this reason, since there is no conceptualization regarding the self, conceptual construction [is said to] state that self-awareness is perception.
As it has been said: "This [mind] does not conjoin this [object] with verbal expression, because such an activity would be contradictory to its nature as a self.
If it is thought that even conceptualizations of non-existence, like those of genus and so forth, have only superimposed objects as their domain;
"It is not by this that the conceptualization of non-existence is corrupted"—
that is not so;
for whatever is superimposed, being of the nature of a genus, is distinct from its corresponding conceptualization and is itself diverse.
How could there be a single word as a cognitive object? For among those things that possess distinct imagined forms, there exists no unifier whatsoever who,
through the determination of a superimposed identity between the preceding and succeeding [moments], would employ a single word.

Conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), however, are momentary and restricted to their own respective objects; they do not engage with the objects of one another. How, then, could they be joined together? Furthermore, in the absence of such a connection, to speak of them having "superimposed objects" would be entirely false. Therefore, one must necessarily accept that there exists some unstable form called "non-existence" (*abhāva*), just like "existence" (*bhāva*), which is associated with the word "not" (*na*).
Therefore, when it is asked, "What, then, is reality? those who know reality have resorted to a twofold reality alone: namely, the existence of the existent and the non-existence of the non-existent.
Furthermore, if it is argued that the non-perception of a struck jar is due to its having been destroyed, provided there were no [prior] existence of the non-existent; [we reply: no.
What is destruction?
If it is nothing at all, then there would follow the consequence of its being perceived as before.

For we do not perceive any cause for the non-perception of a jar that has not lost its prior capacity for causal efficiency, provided that destruction is not accepted as some distinct entity (*tattvāntara*). Thus, it is established that [destruction] is a distinct entity.
And this was stated in order to refute the notion that non-existence (*abhāva*) is indefinable; however, non-existence is not a real thing (*vastu*).
Because it contradicts worldly convention;
for just as "the hare-marked one is not the moon" contradicts worldly convention, so too does the claim that "non-existence is a real entity."
For existence is substantiality (*vastutva*),
and this [existence] is not asserted as substantiality in a primary sense with respect to non-existence;
for non-existence is indeed capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
Because it is observed that [non-existence] generates knowledge;

and because, when a prescribed act is not performed, it is precisely prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)—functioning as a qualifier of another action—that serves as the cause of demerit (*pratyavāya*).
Thus, the establishment of its status as a real entity (*vastutā*) should be understood to apply to subsequent cases as well.
Furthermore,
its existence is established because it is apprehended by cognitions of both inclusion and exclusion;
therefore, like a cow or other such things, it is understood to be a real entity because it is an object of cognition.
Nor does it arise as merely figurative or as an error by chance;
therefore, the nature of being both universal and particular is not false.
Regarding the statement "the entity," it refers to the body and so forth.
The established tenet is that the entity itself consists of both existence and non-existence.
In that case, how can there be a lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) for that very absence which has the form of an entity?
Is there now absolute non-difference between existence and non-existence?
We say:

no; for even though they are distinct, there is indeed some degree of difference between them by virtue of their relationship as property (dharma) and substrate (dharmin), just as in the case of color-form and other qualities.
What, then, is the relation between these two— is it conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*)?
It cannot be conjunction first of all.
Because it is a property of a substance;
nor is it inherence,
because that would entail the consequence of both existence and non-existence.
For if there were an inherence in non-existence, existence itself would not exist at all.
It is not through inherence in non-existence that something becomes non-existent;
for a jar does not become non-existent simply because it inheres in non-existence.
Because inherence is untenable when [the substratum] does not exist;
rather, the non-existence of the jar arises from the blow itself.
As for that other entity which is unstruck and not removable, and which is perceived in the form of non-existence—how could that be non-existent?

Therefore, since everything arising from its own causes—whether eternal or otherwise—is born with an unmixed nature, it is established that this [nature] is a property of the entity (*bhāvadharma*), just like genus (*jāti*) and so forth;
and from that, its status as a real thing (*vastutva*) follows. //8//
For this reason as well, he states that non-existence (*abhāva*) is a real entity (*vastu*), using the passage from "or else" (*yadvā*) up to "the entity" (*vastu*).

Non-existence, when apprehended in its general form—as well as through its specific divisions such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth—and in its nature as exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), consists of both generality and particularity;
therefore, for the purpose of employing it as a real object, [it is said]: "Non-existence is a real entity."
"Because it consists of both the universal and the particular, like a cow and so forth.
To prove that same thesis, he states another reason: "because it is an object of valid cognition" (prameyatvāt). //9//
Is this not an unestablished reason?
For the relationship between universal and particular is merely figurative in the case of a non-entity;
for a form that is a universal, denotable by a single word, is observed in things such as cows.
Furthermore, the particular forms such as the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) are denoted by various distinct words;
therefore, even here, for one who possesses discriminative knowledge, the relationship between universal and particular is merely figurative.
However, in the absence of such discrimination, this is nothing but an error based on a single word—the notion that "non-existence" is the nature of both the universal and the particular.
Therefore, he says: "And not...
The sense is that when there is a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), either an error (*bhrānti*) or a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is postulated; but such is not the case here. //10//
The non-arising of perception and the other [means of knowledge] is called the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāva);
it is either the non-modification (apariṇāma) of the self, or consciousness directed toward another object.
In an entity that is eternally of the nature of both being and non-being through its own form and the form of others,
some perceive a particular form at a particular time.
Whenever and wherever a desire to grasp or an experience arises for someone, that person perceives it, and by means of that [perception], they are designated.

Thus, first, that which was stated in the Bhāṣya—namely, "of this object [which is] non-proximate, [expressed as] 'it exists'"—has been explained. Now, he explains the term *pramāṇābhāva* (absence of means of valid cognition): "the non-arising of perception and so forth.
