If it is asked, "What is this non-arising? he says: "It is of the self."
For the self has a modification consisting of cognition.

When the self does not undergo such a modification in the form of the cognition of a jar or other objects upon the ground or elsewhere, that non-arising of perception and the rest is called its abiding in its own nature, which is termed the "absence of a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇābhāva*).
And when that [absence] is the means of valid cognition, the resulting fruit is the cognition that "it does not exist."
Alternatively, the cognition of the non-existence of an entity is said to be the non-arising of perception and other means of knowledge;
therefore, that [non-arising] itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while the cognition of negation (*abhāva*) and so forth is its result—this is the distinction. //11//
Now, if an object consists of two natures, then it should appear as such all at once; what need is there for another means of knowledge? To this he says: "By its own nature," etc.
By its own nature, that object—such as a cow—is existent, while by the nature of a horse or other [animal], it is non-existent.
Therefore, within this very twofold nature, only a certain aspect is perceived at a certain time; there is no rule that the entire essence must be grasped. //12//

But what is the reason that, although [an object] consists of two natures, only one form is perceived and not the other? To this he says: "Of whichever, wherever. For that which is manifest is perceived, not that which is unmanifest; just as at night the form of fire is not perceived, but its touch is.
Or rather, it is generally that which is intended to be grasped;
therefore, cognition and designation occur precisely through that which has arisen from both the existent and the non-existent.
What is this [that is said to be] "cognized" or "experienced"?
For experience itself is not what is experienced; that [experience] is consciousness (cetanā), whereas the object is what is experienced.
True;
for experience also [is established] precisely because the attainment of the object would otherwise be impossible.
Thus, by this method, it demonstrates the very manifestation of the object, and so there is no fault. //13//
The other part exists as a support for that [part];
for in the cognition of both, there is indeed the inclusion of both.
For this determination that "it is precisely this" which arises with respect to an entity does not occur without being accompanied by the cognition of the absence of other things.
Even the cognition that "it does not exist" does not occur without following upon a real entity;
no knowledge whatsoever arises devoid of a supporting basis.
When the aspect of existence is apprehended through the operation of perception and the other means of knowledge,
the non-arising of that [operation] constitutes the apprehension of the aspect of non-existence.
First of all, the cognition "this does not exist" does not arise through the sense faculties,
for the sense faculty is indeed connected only with the aspect of existence due to its functional capacity.
When one [of two objects] that has become manifest is apprehended with the desire to grasp it, the other remains dissolved by virtue of its being a subordinate quality.
Just as in the case of the apprehension of one between a universal and a particular, so too is it here; thus he says, "of that" (*tasya*).
And this has been stated by us as a statement made on the basis of a concession (*anvāruhyavacanena*).
However, there is indeed a persistence of one or the other in the cognition of existence and non-existence; thus he says: "Of both," [verse 14].
He demonstrates the very same conformity by means of the two [verses] beginning with "this very [one]. "This very [one]" means that it is unmixed with any other entity.
For indeed, when another entity has not been excluded, a mixed nature cannot be determined.
Furthermore, no cognition whatsoever arises that is devoid of the support provided by the negation of a negandum—even the word "non-existent" [implies this].
By the word "whatsoever," it is meant that there certainly exists a cognition that is empty of following after the non-existence of an entity.
But he shows that it is certainly not the case for non-existence. //15,16//

It has already been shown that an object consists of both existence and non-existence, and that something is experienced at some time or another. Now, he demonstrates the division of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for these two aspects: "Perception and so forth" (verse 17).
But how, again, is this understood:
that for one whose eyes are wide open, there suddenly arises the cognition of the ground as qualified by absence— such as "there is no jar here" or "the ground is devoid of a jar"?
Like the perception of one carrying a staff,
it is not possible for that absence to be imperceptible;
for when the qualifier is itself imperceptible, the qualified object cannot be perceived.
Just as one who possesses a staff is called "staff-bearer," it cannot be said that a distinguished cognition does not exist at all,
because there is no experience of the absence of its substratum.
Moreover, the self is the non-existence of an entity;
how could it be experienced as independent?
For the properties of entities, such as form and so forth, are never apprehended as being independent.
The doctrine of independent non-existence (*svatantrābhāvavāda*), however, is indeed independence itself;
for it demonstrates that an entity consists of both existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, by stating "the aspect of existence" and "the aspect of non-existence," it clearly asserts that the apprehension is characterized by that non-existence.
Furthermore, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its independence? For it is never perceived in that way.
Is it then the case that non-existence is not perceived at all?
Or it is understood as being independent;
first of all, the former alternative is not tenable,
because there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its comprehension, which would result in the consequence of eternal non-cognition.
Furthermore, when conjunction is negated, there is no determination of an independent absence;

for absence consists precisely in the negation of conjunction with a counter-positive, and that [absence] is dependent upon a substratum. Thus, through the proximity characterized by being a qualifier of the conjoined, when there is contact with the sense organ, it indeed becomes the object of sensory cognition.
For this one distinguished cognition must have either non-existence as its object or the sense faculty as its object;
if it were non-existence, then it would also have existence as its domain.
And this is not accepted [by you].

Therefore, when something is being perceived, that which is not perceived at that very time does not exist; thus, we do not see any distinction between the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for what exists and for what does not exist.
To this, he says: "Not yet," and so forth.
This is said with reference to the *śadola* mark;
and that will be refuted later on.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "the aspect of existence" (*bhāvāṃśa*).

For capacity is to be understood through the observation of its effect, and that [capacity] of the sense organs is perceived only in the apprehension of positive entities (bhāva), not in the case of non-existence (abhāva) either;
however, we shall explain later that it is indeed apprehended even without that [positive entity].
In this context, however, the intended meaning is that the relation between the sense organ and its object is "attainment" (prāpti) accompanied by "fitness" (yogyatā).
As for the claim that two things associated with a single cognition possess a single means of valid cognition (ekapramāṇatva),
that is not correct.
Because even a single cognition is seen to have multiple causes,

we shall explain that this recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) arises from the conjunction of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), the sense faculty (*indriya*), and [other factors]. Furthermore, it has been stated that there is a distinction between the perceived and the remembered, even when both appear within a single cognition.
"For those objects are indeed isolated. For a person named *Ḍittha*, when distinguished by a name established through memory, is not non-perceptual;
yet the name itself is not perceptual, because it is being remembered.
For when its qualifier has not been apprehended, the qualified object is not understood; nor is it understood if [the qualifier] is not perceived.
Likewise here as well, when a real entity is being perceived as qualified by an absence brought forward by the lack of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāva), nothing is untenable.

Even in the case of "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*), insofar as it is a verbal cognition, the referent of the cognition is precisely that which is qualified by the qualifier brought forward by the word "staff," and not the staff itself.
Perception may indeed function in both cases by virtue of its capacity;
however, the sense organs do not possess such capacity in both cases,
since in the cognition of absence there is no dependence upon them.
But surely, since it is non-different from the entity, there is contact with it;
for there is no absolute non-difference here either, as in the case of form and so forth. (Msv 5.8.19)
For even when there is no difference in the substratum (dharmin), a distinction between two properties (dharmas) is indeed accepted;
because they consist of emergence and suppression, their apprehension remains established.
Because it will be explained later.
Now, is there also in inference a specific cognition produced from the combination of perception and inference? No;
because inference arises depending upon positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
And because the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is followed precisely by the qualified [subject];
for the pervasion (*vyāpti*) "that which possesses smoke possesses fire" is understood.
And it has been said:
"It is not so, for here there is no assumption of an infinite capacity in the inferential mark (liṅga).
Even here, in the cognition of a specific instance such as "this possesses fire," there is indeed a dependence upon perception.
This very [process] is the mode of apprehension of non-existence (abhāva).
There is nothing inconsistent in the claim that [the sense organ] qualifies a locus already apprehended by another means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, the statement that there is sensory contact with non-existence (abhāva) by way of its being a qualifier of a [substantive] conjoined [with the sense organ] is incorrect.
Because that which is unrelated cannot logically function as a qualifier, as this would lead to over-extension;

otherwise, since contact could be established simply by one who desires the meaning of a qualifier, there would be no point at all in resorting to the notion of "the qualifier of what is conjoined. Enough of this. //18//
Not understanding the intended meaning, he objects with "But surely" (*nanu*).
For the contact (*sannikarṣa*) between an object and a sense faculty is merely reaching (*prāpti*);
and since non-existence (*abhāva*), being non-different from existence (*bhāva*), has reaching by the sense faculty just like existence itself.
And here, the reply should have been given simply by disclosing the [logical] compatibility (*yogyatā*); yet, disregarding that, he has asserted an absolute non-difference (*atyantābheda*).
Therefore, I shall first refute this very point.
With this intention, he says: "Not so.

For if there were absolute non-difference between existence and non-existence, then upon the contact of the sense organ with an existent thing, there would also be [contact] with its non-different non-existence;
but such is not the case.
Because even non-existence lacks absolute non-difference from form and so forth, just as [form lacks it] from itself. //19//
He demonstrates that non-existence (*abhāva*) is indeed identical to form (*rūpa*) and so forth by saying "of two dharmas.
The meaning is that even though the substratum (*dharmin*) remains undivided, a distinction between the two dharmas—which consist of existence and non-existence—is also accepted.
He states the reason for this distinction as "emergence" (*udbhava*).
Furthermore, the distinction between apprehension and non-apprehension is observed even in the case of existence and non-existence when they are respectively manifest and suppressed;
yet this [distinction] would not be possible if unity were postulated.
For it is not the case that a single reality is perceived as both manifest and suppressed. //20//
And this very sign of solitude is perceived:
the non-connection of the cognitions of existence and non-existence with the senses, and the independence from the senses.
Furthermore, some describe the differentiation of form and so forth as being due to the difference in the perceiving subjects,
just as one and the same man appears in the form of a son and so on [to different people].
For the distinction among form and so forth is always produced by the mind alone;
nor is there any conception of a "collection" for those things that are not distinct in terms of location and other such factors.
And he states that this is the cause for distinguishing between these two with the words "this very [thing]":
the independence from the sense organs (akṣa) regarding the cognition of absence will be explained later. //21//
And some maintain that this distinction among form and the other [objects] is based on the distinction between their perceivers;
they say that this can be understood even in the case of these two [space and time], stating "of form and so forth.
For some speak thus: "Just as a single face appears as if divided due to the difference in conditions such as emerald or ruby,"

And just as a single person appears as if divided due to differences in perspective, so too here there will be a distinction between existence and non-existence based on limiting conditions (*aupādhika*).
[Objection: But if the distinction is merely conditional, does it not follow that their unity is ultimate (*tāttvika*)?
Let it be so according to this view; nevertheless, the established order of form and the other [sensory objects] is indeed proven. //22//
And this has been stated by us using the term "following after" (anvārudhya),
for the distinction among form and the other [sensory objects] is not based on a difference in their perceivers, but rather is based solely on a difference in cognitions.
For it is logical that a single form, which is understood through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), appears differentiated due to the diversity of its limiting conditions (*upādhi*).

However, since there is no cause for the differentiation of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth in their unity, and because this [reason] is equally applicable to both existence and non-existence, he says "merely by cognition" with this intention.
But what is this substratum (*dharmin*) consisting of existence and non-existence?
As for the two properties of existence and non-existence,
neither is perceived as distinct from the collection of form and so forth,
because it is incapable of withstanding conceptual analysis such as [the inquiry into] its mode of subsistence.
Therefore, the subject (*dharmin*) is the collection of form and so forth that are non-differentiated by location and other factors, and not some other ontological entity; thus he says, "And not...
The intended meaning is that there is no subverting cognition here, as there is in the case of a forest.

And although this was already stated in the proof of determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*), it is mentioned here for the purpose of establishing the basis of non-existence (*abhāva*); thus, there is no tautology. //23//
Form and the other [sensory objects] are held to be one insofar as they consist of the substance of the six qualities;
yet, with respect to their own specific natures, they are mutually distinct.
If there were no such dependence here as there is there, then indeed no distinction would exist;
for the nature of being existent or non-existent could not belong to one or the other of the two cognitions.
When there is a connection with "existent," the nature of being existent is thus perceived;
however, the notion that "this is not here" is caused by its non-connection with that.
Having grasped the actual existence of an object and having recollected its counter-correlate,
a mental cognition of non-existence arises, independent of the sense faculties.

Thus, the difference and non-difference of non-existence from existence have first been demonstrated. He confirms those very points by means of the example of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, with the words: "substance possessing qualities" (*sadguṇadravya*).

For it cannot be denied that color-form and the rest are distinct even in relation to their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), on the grounds that they do not differ from the nature of existence and so forth.
Or rather, by that [distinction], it is not the case that non-difference in the form of existence and so forth is rejected.
Likewise, even non-existence, although distinct from existence as a property (*dharma*), is accepted as non-distinct with respect to its own nature (*svarūpa*).
This is said "in the form of a substance" (*dravyarūpeṇa*).

The meaning is that form and the other [sensory objects] are non-different from substance, and since that [substance] is non-different [from them], they are non-different by virtue of its nature. //24//

He says "That which... (verse 25) to show that, if one does not rely on the distinction [between existence and non-existence] as with form and so forth, but considers only the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), then the character of being existent or non-existent could not belong to either of the two—existence or non-existence—in the cognition.
However, he states that this difference in cognition is caused by the connection or non-connection with the sense faculties: "tatsambandha" (due to its connection).
By this, the claim made by some—that "we do not perceive a nature of non-existence that distinguishes it from existence"—is refuted.
"Because of the discrimination between the forms of existence and non-existence":
that which is in contact with the sense organ, such as the ground, is cognized as "it exists"; that which is not connected, such as a jar and so forth, is cognized as "it does not exist. //26//
But surely, immediately following the operation of the sense organ, the cognition "there is no jar here" arises;

so why this distinction that the cognition of absence is not produced by the sense organ? For we do not observe the cognition of absence arising when the operation of that [organ] is absent, as we do with the cognition of presence.
Although non-existence differs from existence,

nevertheless— just like color and other qualities— it is perceived either through inherence in a conjoined object or as a qualifier thereof; thus, even after merely seeing the form of the sense organ itself, one may subsequently remember something [of that non-existence].
In that case, when questioned about the non-existence of other things, he understands it at that very moment.
Contact certainly exists;
therefore, that cognition would be sensory (aindriyaka). To this, he says: "because it has already been apprehended.

The intention is this: since absence cannot be apprehended when its locus is manifold, there is a requirement for the sense organ here solely for the purpose of apprehending the locus, not for the apprehension of the absence itself.

Just as an absence cannot be apprehended without its counter-positive being remembered— and thus, for the sake of that recollection, the awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by prior cognition is required—
so too is the sense-faculty required for the apprehension of the locus.
Moreover, mere contact is not the sole cause for the production of sensory cognition.
Rather, it has been explained in the section on perception that [knowledge] is an attainment accompanied by capability;
and it will be stated later that the sense organs do not possess the capability to produce the cognition of absence, because that cognition occurs even when those organs are absent.
What is the meaning of "mental" (mānasa)? Does it mean that it is produced by the mind (*manas*), like the cognition of pleasure and so forth?
If that is the case, then it is nonetheless nothing other than perception (*pratyakṣa*).
And it is true that the mind does not possess independence with respect to what is immediately preceding or external;
however, what is stated here is the operation of the mind as it is common to all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It is thus stated that the cognition of absence is produced solely from the contact of the self and the mind, independent of the external sense organs, due to the absence of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, the expression "having perceived and having remembered" indicates a common agent for both actions because of the non-difference between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*). //27//
But how is it understood that this apprehension of existence depends upon the sense-faculties, whereas the apprehension of non-existence does not?
For the presence [of cognition] when that [object] is present is common to both.
To this he says: "by its own nature" (svarūpa).

For when someone who has ascertained the very nature of a house goes elsewhere and is asked, "Is Caitra there or not?", that person, being thus questioned, understands at that very moment that he is not there.
If, however, the cognition of absence were dependent upon the sense organs, it would not arise in the absence of their operation.
Nor should it be said that this is merely the recollection of a previously apprehended absence;
for an absence is not perceived when there is no recollection of the counter-positive (pratiyogin),
nor does the recollection of the counter-positive exist at the time of perceiving the locus (āśraya).
For indeed, when asked about many things, non-existence is stated; yet, it is not on that account that there is no recollection of them at present, nor is it specifically remembered—
thus, that [objection] is incorrect.
For it is not logical that a universal called "non-existence," having been cognized elsewhere, should be remembered in connection with a particular;
for that memory arises from the seed of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) deposited by a prior experience, and it is not capable of taking even a slight degree of non-difference as its object.
It is indeed captivating that at that very moment, following the recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), a cognition of non-existence arises independently of the sense organs;
this is what is meant by the statement "it is apprehended at that very time.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that this is effectively a case of non-occurrence of perception, because the result of perception—namely, memory—is absent. //28//
Nor is inferential status perceived here due to the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
But surely the positive aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*) would be the mark; [we reply] that it was not grasped at that time.
For birth arises from the cognition of non-existence only when the aspect of existence is not intended to be grasped;
however, when that [existence] is being perceived, no cognition of non-existence arises.
Furthermore, this [reason] does not establish the property of being a predicate of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) as a word does;
for existence is considered to be inconclusive (anaikāntika) with respect to all non-existences.
When the existence of a certain thing has been known at some time,
its non-existence is also understood in that very same place at another time.
Thus, the view that the cognition of non-existence is produced by the senses has been refuted.
Now, he refutes its inferential nature with the words "nor even here.
To this, he raises an objection with the words "the positive aspect," etc.
He refutes this with the passage ending in "matir antena":
here there are two entities to be negated—the object of negation and the locus of negation;
of these, the object of negation is certainly not the logical mark (*liṅga*).
For the indicator (liṅga) must indeed be cognized;
yet at that time, the jar is not perceived,
for while it is being perceived, its absence cannot be apprehended.
But when the proposition is established, that which is non-existent and unperceived cannot function as a logical mark (liṅga).
Therefore, non-existence—specifically the absence of the object to be negated—is not the logical mark for what is intended to be grasped. //29,30//
"Let it be, then, that the non-existence of the substratum of the negation is the logical mark (liṅga). To this, he says: "And not this...
Here, "this" (eṣa) refers to the entity (bhāva) presented by the opponent as being perceptible.
Just as it was stated that when the object is made the subject (pakṣa), the word is not a reason because it does not possess that property (ataddharmatayā).
In the same way, this existence of the ground is not a property of the absence of a jar or other objects.
Furthermore, inferential cognition acquires its own nature by depending upon positive concomitance (anvaya),
and yet no connection of the existence of the ground with all absences is known.
To the question, "How then will they have faith in that?", he says: "Together" (saha). //31//
Let it be granted for now that there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of non-existence with some existent thing, such as a floor;
however, even in the case of something like a jar whose existence has been known at some time, its non-existence is also apprehended in that place. Thus he says: "In some [place]" (*kvacid*). //32//
Wherever there is the state of not having previously perceived something, and where there is the cognition of its absence,
that cognition of its absence is observed to occur in relation to that [object] without depending on the senses.
If there were a perception of a relationship between some entity and some non-entity, then it would follow that every means of valid cognition [would apply] therein.
Even when the aspect of existence is apprehended, there is no certainty regarding non-existence;
since everyone possesses such a cognition, it lacks the status of a logical mark due to its deviation.
And when a relation is being apprehended, the apprehension of the related terms is certain;
by what means of valid cognition, then, does the notion of non-existence arise therein?
At that time, there can be no apprehension of the relationship through the inferential mark (liṅga);
therefore, the cognition of non-existence must necessarily arise from another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
It is not only the case that the absence of something is understood in a place where it has never been seen before;
rather, the absence of even that which has never previously been observed in a certain location is understood there. Thus he says: "Wherever... (verse 33).

But if it is maintained that the inference of one absence from another absence occurs because a relationship has been apprehended with respect to some single absence by means of [the perception of] a presence, then there would be an over-extension; thus he says: "of something" (kasyacit) //34//

And he demonstrates by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that this is not the case, with the passage ending: "Even when the positive aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*) is apprehended, there is no cognition of everyone regarding the non-existence of another thing.
Furthermore, this positive entity (*bhāva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it is related even to other absences (*abhāva*).

Therefore, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), this [reasoning] lacks the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*) for establishing the non-existence of things such as a jar; thus he says: "In this way, due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it is not a logical mark. (35)
Furthermore, the apprehension of a relation depends upon the apprehension of the relata.

Therefore, it must be stated what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is employed here when the relatum called "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is to be apprehended; thus he says: "The relation... (verse 36).

A cognition known through a logical mark (liṅga) is not a means of valid knowledge for the ascertainment of that [connection], for in that case there would be a mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya); with this intention, he says: "at that time.
Therefore, he says: "there," meaning that another means of valid knowledge must necessarily be sought for its apprehension. //37//
The non-arising of the subsequent [cognition] cannot be the inferential mark (liṅga);
nor can there be a connection with a qualifier for it, since that occurs only in a general sense.
Now, he states the objection of the Buddhist who maintains that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is the logical mark (*liṅga*): "of perception and so forth.
For reasons are divided by the Buddhists into two kinds: effect (*kārya*) and essential nature (*svabhāva*).
And non-apprehension is simply the apprehension of one [of two things] when they are conjoined within a single cognition.
And since its own nature as well as the nature of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) shines forth, it has the nature of both knowledge and the object of knowledge;
for it does not deviate from the existence of the object of knowledge any more than it deviates from its own nature.

Furthermore, its "essential identity" (*tādātmya*)—which is the necessary connection (*pratibandha*)—is with its own effect, namely the conventional usage consisting of conceptual thought and words such as "it does not exist," or else with the fitness (*yogyatā*) for such usage.
For this [non-perception] does not deviate from the conventional usage "it is not," just as a *śiṃśapā* tree does not deviate from being a tree.

Thus, for one who—due to ignorance of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*)—is deluded and still entertains the possibility of a jar even when a location devoid of it is perceived, [the non-perception] leads him to infer either the conventional usage "it is not" or its fitness (*yogyatā*).

And so, the formal application (*prayoga*) of the non-perception of the absence of a jar and the like is as follows: whatever is perceptible and is not perceived in a certain place, that does not exist there.
Furthermore, when a location is being perceived, the visible jar is not perceived;
this [position] he also refutes with the words: "There is no connection of that [non-perception] with a qualifier.

For the very absence of the jar—which one intends to infer through non-perception, or the linguistic usage "it does not exist," or the fitness for such usage—is not understood as having a connection with even a single qualifier while the non-perception itself remains unconnected.

How, then, can there be an inference of a specific [absence] from that? For that is simply the perception of the ground; and since no such linguistic usage is observed as "there is no manifold variety of objects such as pots, cloths, and so forth," how could one employ the specific linguistic usage "the pot does not exist"?
If it is argued that this is the non-apprehension of the jar, and therefore it establishes either the absence of the jar or the conventional usage regarding its absence—
then what is the relationship between that [non-apprehension] and the jar?
For that [perception] is indeed the perception of the location;
its very nature as the non-perception of the jar lasts only so long.
And since that is indistinguishable for everyone, how can it be designated by one person alone as "the absence of a jar," as if it were some distinct entity?
And why is it that, even when a jar exists, the linguistic convention "the jar does not exist" does not occur?
If you say it is because it contradicts the convention of existence, then how can there be a convention of existence when the jar is not perceived?
For even at that time, there is indeed the perception of the location;
for the perception of the empty space is the non-perception of the jar,
and this does not occur when the jar is present— if you say this.

What is the meaning of "separation" (viveka)? Is it not simply non-existence? If that were the case, the statement regarding being "separated" would be purposeless in the absence of such [non-existence].
Therefore, this distinction as well—

that the conventional usage "it does not exist" applies when a jar is absent, but not when it is present— is indeed difficult to establish. Furthermore, we do not understand by what specific distinction this inference of the conventional usage "it does not exist," which stands apart from the mere absence of the jar, is established.
"Even that [capacity] is not perceived as anything distinct from the entity itself;
since its fitness is not distinct from it, when that [entity] is cognized, the fitness is also cognized— thus we see nothing here that remains to be inferred," says the author of the *Vārttika*.
However, setting this aside for now, another refutation has been stated. //38//
Furthermore, no means of valid cognition arises with respect to the generality of non-existence;
since there would be deviation, how could specific instances be cognized by it?
And if it is argued that a logical mark (liṅga) cannot be apprehended unless it is itself understood, then that [mark] too,
being a non-entity (abhāva), would have to be apprehended by another non-entity as its cause.
And that [inference] must be apprehended by another [inference], for without being apprehended, it cannot function as a logical mark (liṅga).
For the apprehension of that [mark] would itself have to occur through yet another mark; thus, there would be an infinite regress.
If there were no such indicative mark (liṅga), then just as before, this would lead to an infinite regress;
therefore, it must certainly possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) somewhere, even without being an indicative mark.
The cognition "it does not exist" is the fruit of this [non-arising] of perception and the other means of knowledge;
and its status as a valid means of knowledge is understood immediately from that very [fruit].

However, while the absence of a relation is indeed established by the non-apprehension of a general absence (*abhāvasāmānya*), no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arises regarding that general absence itself; thus he says "sāmānyeti.
Furthermore, because particulars (*viśeṣa*) are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), they cannot be made known through non-apprehension; thus he says "vyabhicārāditi" //39//
Moreover, a mark whose form is not cognized cannot serve as a mark in inference; therefore, this non-arising of perception and so forth, being itself an absence, must be cognized by another mark.
For they say thus:
"Whatever negation there may be, all of it arises from non-apprehension alone.
And thus, since an infinite regress would result in each case by following a series of similar subsequent marks, he says with the two verses beginning with "na ca":
this was stated by way of a reductio ad absurdum, namely that non-apprehension is the absence of apprehension.
However, the claim that "non-apprehension is an object distinct from other things" has already been refuted. //40,41//

In this way, even that which is the absence of the form of a mark (liṅga) must necessarily be understood first for the sake of grasping the relationship [between the probans and the probandum]. Even when that is understood, because one would have to admit another mark of that same nature, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā).
Therefore, since in some cases inference would necessarily be absent, he says "the mark" (liṅga), etc., implying that another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) must be admitted. //42//
If it is argued that the very cognition "it does not exist" is the inferential mark (liṅga), that is not so;
for that [cognition] is the result.
How can the non-arising of perception and the other means of knowledge be its inferential mark?
For it is precisely for the sake of establishing that [object] that the logical mark (liṅga) is sought;
that cognition which is produced by means of the three characteristics is what is intended as inference. And there is never any dependence upon a cause for that which is of the nature of non-arising.
If non-existence is [the object] of pride, how can it be so? And what would its object of cognition be like?
For just as the object of cognition is indeed non-existence, so too should the means of cognition be accepted as such.
Likewise, when the object of cognition consists of existence, non-existence does not have the status of a means of valid cognition;
similarly, even when the object of cognition consists of non-existence, existence does not have the status of a means of valid cognition.
But once the cognition has been established, what is the use of an inferential mark (*liṅga*)?
To this he says: "No.
If that [cognition] is the result, then what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? He says: "Of that very [cognition]."

That very [cognition] for which that result exists is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because the result follows immediately after it, given that perception and other [means of knowledge] have not yet arisen. //43//

Furthermore, even according to the texts defining inference as established in the Buddhist tradition (*saugatasamaya*), that which does not arise from perception and the other [means of knowledge] cannot be considered inference; thus he says: "possessing the three characteristics" (*trilakṣaṇa*).
For they recite as follows:
"Inference is the cognition of an object based on a mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three forms."
Furthermore, non-arising— the prior absence of arising— is not produced by anything at all,
much less by a cause possessing the three characteristics.
But surely, it is maintained that the non-perception [of a cause] as a cause constitutes inference?
But it is not the case that "inference" (*anumāna*) refers to the result of inference (*anumiti*), because [the term] is derived by way of denoting the action (*bhāvasādhana*).
Therefore, what is the point of refuting that?
True; however, its status as inference has already been refuted on the grounds that it lacks the nature of a cause (*ahetutā*).
But by this, the inclusion of infinite characteristics is described. //44//

Here he raises an objection: [the word] "means of valid cognition" (*māna*)—for validity (*pramāṇatā*) is understood in the case of perception and so forth to be pervaded by the nature of an existent entity;
thus, it follows that upon the cessation of that [existence], [validity] is also ceased. This is the sense.
But the other [author] says: "The fourfold non-confusion of the mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) has already been described by us.
Nor is any difference perceived between the cognition of that [negation] and the cognition of a positive entity, because they share the commonality of being free from sublation (*bādhaviraha*)."
And that [absence] is the cause for validity; it is not the positive nature of the thing itself.
That [positive nature], however, is in no way a causal factor for validity, even if it happens to be somehow associated with them.
Therefore, invalidity does not arise from being an absence.
With the intention that [a cognition] is indeed non-authoritative when the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is a non-existence (*abhāva*), he says "the object of knowledge" (*prameyam*).
It is entirely appropriate that he states "non-existence is the means of valid cognition regarding non-existence," as he says "the object" (*meyo*). //45//

Just as the means of knowledge "non-existence" (abhāva-pramāṇa) is not appropriate when the object of cognition consists of existence, so too [the means of knowledge "existence"] is not appropriate when that [object] consists of non-existence; thus he says: "consisting of existence" (bhāvātmaka). //46//
The status of being a means of valid cognition does not rest upon the command of a king;
for validity belongs to both [perception and inference] because their fruit is the definitive determination [of the object].
And if its status as a means of valid cognition is not accepted because it is a non-entity,
then there is the conceit that a real entity is indeed observed to be the cause [of cognition].
In that same manner, [the properties of] being a logical mark (liṅgatva) and being an object of cognition (prameyatva) would not exist;
and if that were the case, the aforementioned conventional usage would not be established.
Since the means of valid cognition do not arise, non-existence cannot be a property;
where non-existence exists, there can be no connection with it whatsoever.
For that which is not present there, this would be its property;
yet it cannot be an object of cognition, because it lacks both the status of a property and a subject.
It is not a royal decree that valid cognition (pramāṇa) must consist solely of a positive entity;

rather, whatever has the fruit of determination (pariccheda) as its result is indeed valid cognition, and that [quality] is the same even for that which does not arise from perception and the like. Thus he says: "of that which consists of a positive entity."

It might be argued: "Since validity is observed only in the case of a real entity (*vastu*), non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), being a non-entity, cannot possess the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And this being the case, for the Buddhists as well, the logical mark (*liṅga*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) would not exist, for they too do not observe these in a non-entity. To this he replies with the verse beginning "If" (*yadi*), consisting of one and a half lines.

He states the fault in [granting] permission: "If that were so," etc. The meaning is that this worldly transaction (vyavahāra) would not exist; that is, the transaction described through the distinction of cause and so forth would not occur. //48,49//

He states that the non-arising of perception and the other means of knowledge is not a logical mark (liṅga) even because it does not possess the property of the subject (apakṣadharmatva)— namely, "of the means of knowledge" (*pramāṇānām*).
The intention is that when non-existence (*abhāva*) is taken as the subject, the non-arising of perception and so forth cannot be understood as a property thereof,
because there is no relationship [between them] with non-existence.

[Objection: "But we shall establish that the ground is qualified by the absence [of the jar], and since that [ground] was previously cognized, it will be the locus (dharmin) of that [absence]. To this he says: "Where...
For there is no non-arising of perception with respect to the ground itself.
Because it is that which is being known. //50//
"In that case, it will be a property of the jar, because perception and the other means of knowledge do not arise with respect to its object. To this he says: "That which...
This is true;
although it might somehow be a property of that [object] with respect to which perception and the others do not arise, [it is not so].
But this [subject] is not being cognized here,
because of the absence of both the property and the property-bearer;
for indeed...
But the connection [of the cognition] would exist through non-existence, because it has that as its object;
and since the state of being an object arises from the cognition of it, the object of measurement does not exist within the cognition itself.
No relation such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*) exists;
for if [the property] has not been apprehended, it cannot be a property (*dharmatva*), and if it has been apprehended, the proof is already established.
Because it is denotable by the word "non-existence," and because it is not [itself] perception and so forth,
the non-existence of the means of valid cognition is distinct from them, just as the non-existence of objects of cognition is distinct from those objects.
Non-existence, too, is measured by a means of valid cognition corresponding to its own nature;
because it is an object of knowledge, just like existence, it is distinct from that which has the nature of existence.

For all ritual actions, together with their entire collection of constituent parts, causes, and fruits, do not indeed coalesce here with one another; therefore, this [sacrificial system] is not the source of true rites.
Having taken that locus (the ground) as the subject, its being qualified by non-existence is what is to be proven, because [the ground] is not perceived [as qualified by the jar at that time];
nor is the ground qualified by that [jar], because at that moment the jar is absent there. //51//
However, it will have similarity with non-existence because that [non-existence] is its object;
for when non-existence is the object of knowledge (*prameya*), it certainly becomes a logical mark (*liṅga*). But an entity that has not been perceived will not be its object.
And he says that when [the object] is known, there is an absence of anything further to be cognized: "by means of non-existence" (abhāvena) //52//

But there exists no other mode of relation with non-existence (*abhāva*) due to its non-arising, by virtue of which one could follow its being a property [of the subject] and thus have an inference; thus he says: "Conjunction," etc.
Furthermore, he says: "Not when unperceived," etc., to show that [non-existence] is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*).
For when the mountain has not been apprehended, smoke cannot be understood as having that [mountain] as its property (*dharmatā*).
If it is argued that, just like that, non-existence is also perceived beforehand, then what was already established is being proven. //53//
Thus, having established difference through both perception and inference, he demonstrates it by means of a formal argument: "The word 'non-existence'... (verse 54).

He states another argument, ending with "abhāvo 'pi" up to "bhāvāt": "Even non-existence... Therefore, he concludes that non-existence is distinct from the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) which consists of existence, saying "tasmāt" (therefore). //55//
He demonstrates the utility of non-existence (*abhāva*) [in the Veda] with the words "the ritual acts" (*karmāṇi*).
That which consists in the non-confusion of the fruits of all ritual acts, their mutual non-confusion, and the absence of a mutual relationship of principal and subordinate among them—
this is not possible without the authority of non-existence (*abhāva-prāmāṇya*).

Having analyzed the six means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in this commentary by means of both reasoning and scripture, it is also established that there is no distinction between what is accepted here and that which is desired by others as being two additional [means]. Msv 5.8.57.
In this world, a cognition arising from hundreds and so forth up to thousands, provided it is free from contradiction, is not distinct from inference.
Much that is handed down by tradition in the world is not true; however, if it is true, it does not differ from scripture (āgama).
"It is accomplished without exception" means:
"as," "to the extent that," and "accordingly"; "here" means in this context.
This is a restatement of the Veda. //56//

Now, one might object: "Has not a follower of Vyāsa’s opinion described two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in addition to comparison (*upamāna*), and has the Sage [Gautama] also accepted the validity of probability (*sambhava*) and tradition (*aitihya*)? Therefore, the reason for rejecting those must be stated. To this, he says: "Because of reasoning" (*yukti*).
For it is precisely the six means of valid cognition that are logically consistent and accord with scripture; and scripture here refers to the Mīmāṃsā system.

Therefore, by means of both reasoning and scripture, the sixfold system of valid cognition alone has been analyzed and deliberated upon here in this *Śābara-bhāṣya*. As for those two additional [means of knowledge] that were accepted [by others], they are already included within these very [six]. //57//
But where, then, is its inclusion? To this he says: "It occurs here.
That cognition which is held to be the means of valid knowledge called *sambhavā*—namely, that there are one hundred from a thousand—is not distinct from inference (*anumāna*).
One hundred is understood from a thousand because of their state of non-separation (*aviyutibhāva*), that is, because of their invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
Therefore, it does not differ from inference.
As for the authority of tradition (*aitihya*), it has already been stated to be entirely false,
such as [claims regarding] the discovery of hidden treasures, the subjugation of asura maidens, and so forth.

Regarding the statement "Draupadī had five husbands" and so forth: if that is true, then it does not contradict authoritative scripture (*āgama*), for this is indeed the teaching of a reliable authority (*āpta*).
And it has been said: "Even the statement of a person attains the status of scripture for a listener.
Therefore, since they are included within inference and scripture, the separate presentation of *sambhava* (probability) and *aitihya* (tradition) is not established.
Thus ends the "Examination of Non-existence" in the *Kāśikā* commentary composed by the preceptor Sucarita Miśra. *** Now begins the "Refutation of Diversity. ***
Previously, the injunctions that project results in the next world were explained by others;
now, the author of the Sūtra states the projection of results in this life.
The reading of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) should be examined;
here the commentary says: "Now, let other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exist, but why is verbal testimony (*śabda*) not a means of valid cognition?"
"Because the signless (animitta) is an apprehension of what exists.

The meaning of this is as follows: although, due to the non-deviation from all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), sound is not a means of valid cognition by virtue of a property common to all means of valid cognition, it is nonetheless not a means of valid cognition by virtue of its own specific inherent property.
For instance, since cattle are produced by the *citrayā* sacrifice, the meaning of the injunction "one should sacrifice with the *citrayā*" is that cattle result from it.

Yet, even for a sacrificer who has performed the *citrayā*, cattle are not seen immediately thereafter, despite his possessing all his sense faculties intact. Therefore, the thought arises: "Surely this *iṣṭi* does not have cattle as its fruit."
This is what was stated: "It is without a basis (animitta), because it is the perception of something that exists.
What is meant by this? For animals are perceived through the instruments of perception such as the eyes;
yet, animals are not perceived immediately following the sacrifice intended for those desiring cattle.
Therefore, because of the aforementioned contradiction, the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
Furthermore, this objection is seen to have its meaning already established;
for in the *Codanā-sūtra*, the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) has stated the objection and its refutation with the words, "But surely [the Veda] is not thus," and so forth.
Anticipating the objection that this is therefore redundant, he says: "In the other world.

The meaning of this is as follows: there, injunctions such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," which have the other world as their fruit, were already refuted according to the views of outsiders to the Veda, such as the Buddhists and others.
Now, injunctions concerning rites like the *citrayajña* which have results in this life (*aihika*) are being refuted.
Surely, the reasons such as "being a sentence" (*vākyatva*) and so forth can indeed be used to challenge both types of injunction (*codanā*).
Those very reasons were implicitly included there by the author of the *Bhāṣya* when he showed that "whatever is worldly speech is [subject to doubt].
The author of the *Vārttika* also explained this: "Or rather, all injunctions have their authority dependent upon persons."

Therefore, this claim that only those [actions] whose fruits belong to the next world are implied therein is incorrect. Furthermore, as for what was said regarding the "implication of worldly [results]," that too is improper;
for here also, a total implication has been made when it is stated: "Since the Veda is thus seen to have transgressed [its own rules], we consider that even its fruits such as heaven do not exist."
And the author of the Vārttika also says: "This being the case, even sentences such as those concerning the Agnihotra sacrifice would have a false meaning."
Therefore, they consider it logical that in both cases there must be an implication of both.
What is this systematic arrangement?
To this it is said:
It is true that in both cases there is an implication of the absence of fear; nevertheless, there is no tautology because the reasons are different.
For instance, in that [first] case, the reasons for the implication stated by others are "being a sentence" (*vākyatva*) and so forth.
Injunctions concerning such matters as the fruit of the Citrā sacrifice are false,
because even when they fall within the scope of perception and other means of knowledge, they lack consistency with the actual facts.
But now, by means of reflecting on the power of the word "tu," internal reasons alone will be established.
And so it has been said:
"If immediate succession (*ānantarya*) were not stated, it would [still be understood] because of the comprehension of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*)."
Thus [it is said].
For capacity (*sāmarthya*) is the auxiliary factor for all verbal roots when they express their meaning;
therefore, even though there is no scriptural statement (*śruti*) that "the sacrifice has infinite fruit," [the result is understood through capacity].

Nevertheless, it is understood through the force of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*); for otherwise, how could it be that "when she was present, she did not give the fruit, yet at another time, being absent, she will give it"? Nor is it the case that animals possess an infinite capacity for mental cultivation (*anantasamabhūtabhāvanā*).
For heaven (*svarga*) cannot possibly exist without the acquisition of a specific body, sense organs, and so forth, which are projected by various [karmas];
therefore, let it not be immediately [after death].

However, these "animals" can indeed come into existence for the sacrificer right here [in this world], since they are not perceived immediately after their own cause, and because there are other perceived causes such as acceptance of gifts, while the fruits of the *Citra* sacrifice and others have not been heard of [in this context].
These [objections] can indeed be understood.

However, this very reflection on the power of words (*śabdaśakti*) was demonstrated by the author of the Vārttika through arguments such as "or rather, not in the case of the fruit of cattle-sacrifice" (*na vā paśuphale*), while following the method of the logicians (*tārkika*).

Thus, when the injunctions regarding the *citrā* sacrifice—which have fruits in this life—have been addressed, the same principle applies to other [injunctions] due to their commonality; consequently, the objection once again stands against the injunctions for the *agnihotra* and so forth.
And this [objection] is stated even by way of an objection regarding the present life (*aihikākṣepadvāreṇa*).
For this very reason, it is called "an objection regarding the present life.

What is meant is this: for those things whose fruits pertain both to the present life and to future lives, this objection is made precisely by means of prioritizing the objection regarding the present life.
One might argue: "Granted that results such as heaven in the next world may not be perceived immediately after the action; however, why are visible fruits such as cattle not perceived?

Since these are not perceived, they surely cannot be the fruit [of the action]. By this deviation of the injunctions regarding actions with visible fruits, there arises an implication (ākṣepa) against other actions whose fruits belong to the next world, based on their similarity to those cases.

Previously, however, those [objections] were raised by relying on extrinsic validity (*parataḥ prāmāṇya*) using reasons such as "being a sentence" (*vākyatva*) and so forth, which were stated by others.
Thus it was said, "stated by others.
He states another resolution: "In the Sūtra," etc.

The intention is as follows: in the *Codanāsūtra*, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakṛt), by looking ahead to the objections and their refutations that were yet to be stated by the Author of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra), described them for the purpose of supporting the initial thesis.

Now, however, since the Author of the Sūtras himself states [the objection] directly, he has declared that this very point is the field for all objections against the Vedic injunctions (*codanā*). //1//

In this refutation, the very same reason for the objection previously stated is presented—up to the words "citraiḥ... phalāni"—with the following meaning: the injunctions (codanā) which have as their objects such things as the Citrā sacrifice yielding cattle as its fruit are the subjects (dharmin).
If such a thing is seen to be false, like the words of one wishing to deceive, as when it is said, "There are fruits on the riverbank," yet they are not found there; Msv_5.9.3 //
Or else, the *citriṇī* sacrifice does not have cattle as its fruit because it does not bestow them at the proper time;
or rather, like bathing, eating, and so forth, those [cattle] are not even things to be accomplished by that [sacrifice].
Because it does not exist at the time of its production, like the pleasure of satisfaction in heaven and so forth;
by way of dissimilarity, both [pleasure and pain] would likewise exist during the crushing [of the body].

If it is argued that "immediacy" (*ānantarya*) has not been stated [as a reason], it is not so, because it is understood through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*). "Falsehood" (*mṛṣā*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*),
with respect to those objects which, despite being suitable for engagement, are not cognized by perception and the other means of knowledge.
If such [a thing] is false— just like the speech of one who wishes to deceive—
the word "etcetera" (ādi) includes injunctions (*codanā*) concerning the *agnihotra* and other rites as well.
Now, is not the speech of one wishing to deceive the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) here?
Nor is it necessarily the case that [the object] is unreal because it is not connected with perception and so forth;
therefore, the example is devoid of both [properties].
Hence he says: "In that regard... (tatra).
In this context, the statement "nadītīra" (riverbank) and so forth, which is employed when no such object exists, is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
And since one who intends to deceive generally employs such a type of statement, it is said [in the sūtra] "by one who intends to deceive" (*vipralipsuḥ*). //2,3//
Now, he explains what was stated as "the objection regarding this world" by means of the phrase "or not":
the subject (*dharmin*) is the *citriṣṭi* (the sacrifice for desired objects), and the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is that it does not have cattle as its fruit.
"Because they give cattle at the proper time, like bathing and so forth.
He states another formal argument (prayoga): "Those too," and so on.
Those animals are not to be accomplished by means of a citrā sacrifice,
because they do not exist at the time of the citrā's production, just like the bliss of satisfaction in heaven;
by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) here, the satisfaction produced by eating is intended.
These two applications should be understood as stated in the Bhāṣya: "The sacrifice does not have cattle as its fruit" and "at the time of the action, there must be a fruit of the action.
Immediately following this, the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "For at whatever time the crushing occurs, at that very time the pleasure of the crushing [occurs]."
He applies that as a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) to the two types of formal argument (*prayoga*), stating "by way of dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyeṇa*).

In both arguments—namely, "the *citrayajña* does not have cattle as its fruit" and "cattle are not produced by that [sacrifice]"—there may be ease in crushing [the opponent's position] by way of dissimilarity;
and such is the arrangement of the dissimilar examples here.

Whatever is to be accomplished is produced at its proper time, just as pleasure [is produced] from massage; and whatever is to be accomplished becomes a source of pleasure upon its production, just as pleasure arises from the production of massage. //4,5//
Now, it was argued that [the Veda] lacks authority because of contradiction with what has been stated;
yet there is no contradiction here at all,
for the Word does not declare that as soon as an action has been performed, the fruit must arise immediately.
However,
this [meaning] was expressed by him through that which constitutes a single part of his word.
Because there is no assumption of an intervening period of time and because of the inherent nature of karma,
the immediate succession of the painting and other such acts is a qualifying characteristic when they are being enjoined.
In this case, there is first of all a lack of correspondence, and furthermore, a contradiction;
for here the state of being reduced to ashes is seen, which is indeed contrary to the journey to heaven.
Regarding the phrase "the fruit":
since the matter concludes with this much,
it will therefore bestow the fruit at another time.
This has been stated: "If it is argued that [the action] will yield its fruit at a later time," and this is what he says: "immediacy. He refutes this: "not by capacity."
Although immediate succession has not been explicitly stated, it is nevertheless understood here by implication;
for when it is said that "this is its fruit," it is understood from the very sense of the matter that it must occur immediately after this [action].
Otherwise, how could it bestow its fruit at a different time?

[Objection: Even so, let the immediate succession obtained through presumptive force (*sāmarthya*) be sublated by the non-perception of an immediate fruit; but how can an injunction (*codanā*) that operates without distinction be sublated? To this, he says: "By the word... For presumptive force (*sāmarthya*) is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nevertheless, since the capacity (*śakti*) is the auxiliary factor for all verbs expressing their meaning, it is indeed a part of the word itself.

Therefore, just like the *sruva*-ladle offering, even in the case of non-substantial [meanings], the result is determined immediately after the object; thus, even in the cognition of that [capacity], there is certainly a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). //6//
He says "kālāntara... [etc. to show that immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is understood from this as well:
for if he had heard the *liṅ* suffix in the sense "it will give its fruit at another time," then some kind of conceptualization might have occurred on the strength of that.
But now, since the statement concludes with "this is the fruit of this action," and because the fruits of all actions are perceived as being immediate, [the action must be immediate].
Even in the case of Vedic rites such as the Citrā sacrifice, although they are enjoined, immediate succession remains as a qualification due to the inherent nature of that action. //7//

Immediately following this, another commentary states: "There is even some Vedic statement that contradicts what is perceived, namely: 'This sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes directly to the heavenly world.
He states the specific reason why that [statement] was mentioned with the word 'here' (*atra*).
For here, in the case of sentences such as those concerning the *citrā* sacrifice, lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) was asserted due to the discrepancy between the statement and reality."
In the subsequent passage concerning the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*), he demonstrates the contradiction by stating "in the journey to heaven" (*svargayāne*).

For the sacrificer, whose self is of the nature of unsurpassed bliss, a state of being reduced to ashes—vastly removed from heaven—is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); such is the case with the injunctions for the *Citrā* sacrifice and others.
The statement regarding the sacrificial implements is false because it contradicts direct perception;
the statement regarding the stone is [false] by way of similarity, while the speech of a trustworthy person is [true] by way of dissimilarity.
If he were other than the body, he would not be the possessor of the sacrificial implements;
nor would he possess the status of a sacrificer, and his very existence would be difficult to establish.

However, while there might be a postulation of a result at a later time on the grounds that no contrary perception exists—merely because the immediate result is not perceived—it is impossible for a body that has been reduced to ashes to go to the heavenly world even at a later time; this constitutes the distinction from the previous case. //8//

Furthermore, the commentary states: "Moreover, any statement of this kind that contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not authoritative—just as, for example, 'gourds sink in water' or 'stones float.
He explains that [commentary] with the sentence ending in "yajñeti."

The property to be proven (sādhya-dharma) is that the statement regarding the sacrificial implements possesses the nature of dharma, [which is] false, because it contradicts direct perception (pratyakṣa-virodhāt).
"That which contradicts direct perception is false, just as the statement 'stones float,' which refers to rocks; this is to be shown by way of similarity (*sādharmyeṇa yathā*).
He states the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) with the words "by way of dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyeṇa*).
"That which is non-erroneous is not contradicted by perception, as is the case with the speech of a trustworthy person.

However, because the stone-example was previously presented as an instance of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) between the pleasure of pressing and [actual] pleasure, there might be the misconception that the author of the *Bhāṣya* stated the "stone-sentence" also as a case of dissimilarity. To dispel this confusion, the author of the *Vārttika* has demonstrated the distinction between similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). //9//
But is it not the case that the reason—"because of contradiction with perception"—is already established?
For there exists a conscious being who is the enjoyer of the fruits of the next world and the agent of actions;
he will go to the heavenly world.
It is with reference to that very point that it was stated, "he will go to the heavenly world.
Therefore, what is the contradiction? To this he says: "from the body.
For if the conscious being were indeed other than the body, [then there would be no contradiction].
There could be no manner of connection whatsoever for him with the sacrificial implements;
rather, it is the body alone that has a connection with the sacrificial implements such as the *sruk* and *kapāla*.

It is with this intention that the connection expressing possession (*matvartha-saṃyoga*)—namely, "the sacrificer is the possessor of the sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudhī yajamānaḥ*)—is logically consistent.
Furthermore, the direct reference "this very [is he]" is appropriate only because the body is perceptible, not because the self is;
for this reason as well, the Commentator has stated: "He points to the embodied one."
Furthermore, the term "sacrificer" (yajamāna) is indeed inappropriate when applied to the self; for the sacrificer is defined as the agent of the sacrifice,
and it is not possible for the self to be the agent of a ritual action consisting of many sequential moments of activity, as previously described and enjoined.
O Lord, because there is no non-inherent causality (asamavāya) for actions that result from the conjunctions and disjunctions of spatial divisions in preceding and succeeding locations;
regarding this, he says: "If it were not so, then even through non-perception, the term 'positive injunction' (vidhi-śabda) would not exist here."
Because it possesses this distinction, this [object] would not have been included by way of differentiation.

For if one were to assume that the fruit [of an action] exists in the future when it is expressed by an injunctive word, then there might be a resolution of the contradiction; however, even if [the action] is present, such a resolution does not exist.
In this way, there would be no fruit even in the case of a ritual because of its reduction to ashes;
therefore, he refutes those conceptual constructions [of efficacy] by means of that [very fact].
And so: we have stated this while provisionally accepting the existence of a self;

however, in the ultimate sense, even the existence of a self distinct from the body and the senses is difficult to establish due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Thus he says: "existence."
And this will be elaborated upon in the *Ātmavāda* [chapter]; therefore, it is not expanded upon here. //10//
Furthermore—the Bhāṣya states: "And this [sentence] 'he goes' is not an injunctive word.
He explains its intended meaning with the words "If...
The meaning of this is: "If indeed here..."

If there were an injunctive word (*vidhiśabda*) in the passage concerning the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudhivākya*), then, since no immediate fruit is observed for the *citrā* sacrifice and others, the citation of the passage on the sacrificial implements for the purpose of presenting a contradiction through distinction would be untenable.
Therefore, the refutation of the injunctive word is intended to justify the adoption of the distinction [of time] established by oneself. //11//
"What is the distinction regarding the word of injunction (*vidhiśabda*)? To this he says: "Injunction," etc.

For since no specific time is mentioned in the word of injunction, one may—by the very power of the injunction itself—postulate that the fruit occurs at another time, thereby avoiding the contradiction with non-existence, as is the case with injunctions for the *Citrā* sacrifice and others.

But here, because the statement "he goes" (yāti) is a description of the present, the contradiction with direct perception cannot be avoided; thus, there is a distinction due to non-perception. //12//

We have stated this with the intention of [the example of] the *citrā* sacrifice and other such cases—that by postulating the future occurrence of the result when the word is injunctive (*vidhi*), the contradiction can be resolved.

However, in the present case, because the reduction to ashes is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is not possible to postulate that the result is the attainment of heaven by virtue of its occurring at another time.
For even by a thousand injunctions, a matter that is inherently impossible cannot be made intelligible.
This is what he says: "And the result.

What, then, is the result of refuting the status of [the Veda] as an injunctive word? To this he replies: "By its power. For an injunction, which consists in the impelling of a conscious being, cannot exist without one who experiences the results in another world.
Furthermore, this kind of nature is commonly observed in the *arthavādas* and in the *mantras*; therefore, all of them should be diligently included within the scope of the argument.
If this were so, then even sentences concerning the Agnihotra and other such rites would have a false meaning,
because they are part of the same Vedic corpus as sentences concerning the Citrā sacrifice and the like.

Thus ends the discussion on the refutation of the manifold [theories]. Even if [the existence of the self] were logically untenable, one might still postulate a self distinct from the aggregate of the body and its instruments;
and even the departure for the heavenly world (svargaloka) could be metaphorically attributed to that [self] as residing in the body.
Or rather, the refutation of the injunctive word is for the purpose of negating such conceptualizations as that its status as perception is merely figurative with respect to the self. //13//
Furthermore, this portion of the Veda consisting of *mantras* and *arthavādas* is more frequently contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as:
"Aditi is the heaven, Aditi is the mid-region," and "The sacrificer is the single-potherd cake" (*ekakapāla*), and so forth.
All of this must be diligently and primarily included as the subject (*pakṣa*) under the charge of falsity regarding worldly matters.

With the intention that, because that [Vedic injunction] is false, the falsity of others will follow as a necessary consequence, he says "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*). Regarding the *Bhāṣya* passage, "Because of that similarity, there would be a lack of confidence even in the injunctions for the Agnihotra and so forth," he states its intended meaning with the words "this being so" (*evaṃ sati*).

For when the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) in [texts such as] the *Citrapaṭa* and similar works has been established, then, by virtue of being a single part of the Vedic corpus, the falsity of sentences concerning the *agnihotra* and so forth can also be inferred;
therefore, since the entire Veda lacks authority, dharma cannot have the nature of being characterized by injunction (*codanā*). This is the objection.
Thus ends the "Refutation of the Citrā Sacrifice" in the *Kāśikā-ṭīkā* composed by the Preceptor Sucarita Miśra.
Now begins the "Refutation of the Relation."

First, the proof of our own position is as follows: Vedic speech is non-false regarding its own meaning, because it does not depend upon a speaker with respect to that meaning, just like the cognition of a word-meaning arising from a word. (1)

Immediately following this, the Commentator introduced a refutation of the objection by means of the eternity of the relationship, stating: "But the relationship of a word with its meaning is innate; its cognition [arises from that].
This, however, is incorrect.

Indeed, it is appropriate to point out defects such as contradiction (*viruddha*) or unestablishedness (*asiddhi*) immediately after the opponent’s objection and its grounds; however, to state something else without having refuted that [objection] is entirely irrelevant. Therefore, he says: "In one's own position" (*svapakṣe*).

The intention is this: for as long as the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) possesses the characteristic of being independent due to the inherent nature of the relationship [between word and meaning], [the objection does not apply].
Validity is not established so long as the means of proof has been refuted; thus, even if the proof is undermined, the thesis that "dharma is characterized by Vedic injunction" is not proven.

Furthermore, it is his intention to explain many other matters through this sequence, such as the investigation into the relationship between word and meaning; otherwise, [the work] would be rendered incomplete.
That would become as if fallen into space;
and this will be explained on the occasion of defining the nature of sound.
Nor does this fail to connect with the objection.
Because it is observed that there is opposition in both ways,
as it has been said:
"Opposition occurs in both ways because of the subversion of the opponent's reason."
"Or, by means of stating one's own proof, that which is one's own is here stated.

And it is not the case that the refutation of another's proof will not be performed here; rather, [the point] that "the reason is unestablished (asiddha) there" will be stated in the section on the refutation of the *citrā* sacrifice.
It was said "for the time being" (*tāvat*) because [the refutation] must be carried out according to this sequence.
And he states that proof of his own position by way of a formal syllogism (prayoga) in order to please the minds of the logicians: "Not false," etc.
The subject (dharmin) is the Vedic word;
"it is true in its own referent" is the probandum (sādhya).
The word *dharma* [is used] in its own primary sense (*svārthe*), because it does not depend on a speaker;
that which does not depend on a speaker for its own meaning is true,
just as the cognition of an object derived from a word [is independent].

For a word is connected with its own object by its very nature and does not depend upon a speaker for its communication; this will be explained in the section on the refutation of the [need for] a connection (*sambandhaparihāra*).
The term "its own object" (*svārtha*) should be understood here as qualifying both [the word and the object] according to the system of the treatise.
For if it were merely stated that "Vedic speech is non-false," it would follow that the meaning is trivial, as it would result in the establishment of the correctness of the opponent's position.
For the sentence "one who desires heaven should sacrifice" (yajeta) is not correctly accepted as having the meaning "one who desires heaven should perform a sacrifice" (yāgaṃ kuryāt),
because that would contradict the established conclusion of the sixth [chapter] and others;
for it will be settled there that "one should bring about heaven by means of sacrifice."
Furthermore, the reason stated as "because it does not depend on a speaker" would be equally unestablished (*asiddha*) for Vedic sentences as well;
for those too possess their own intrinsic nature, which produces a correct cognition because they arise from eternal sentences.
In this context, the sentence, the intellect, and the Veda, as well as the horses mentioned previously, are the reasons. //2//
Relying on the eternality of words, meanings, and their relationship, the opponent asserted falsity on the grounds that [the Veda] arises from a lack of relationship;
whereas it was stated [by us] that the relationship exists and is eternal by means of the passage beginning with "autpattika" (inherent). (4)
There is a dependence on a speaker for the sake of manifestation; however, with respect to their own meaning— the object to be communicated— they do not depend on a speaker,
because they are not of human origin.

Furthermore, because the relationship between word and meaning is eternal, even the speech of a reliable person (*āptavacana*), which is human in origin and concerns objects cognized through other means of knowledge, depends upon the speaker’s own authority.
As it has been said: "In the case of the utterances of reliable persons, there is dependence on humans. (1)
He states another proof, ending with the words "tatkṛta" (produced by that):
