"The cognition produced by Vedic sentences is valid," this is the thesis to be proven,
because it arises from eternal sentences.
Just as the cognition whose object is the nature of that sentence [arises],
for that too arises from the sentence,
since a cognition without an object does not arise.
And the eternity of the Vedic statements will be established in the section concerning the Vedas (*vedādhikaraṇa*).

Regarding this very point to be proven, it was stated during the occasion of explaining the previously mentioned commentary (*bhāṣya*)— namely, "because it is not otherwise"— that [the Veda] is produced by causes free from defects and is generated by utterances not composed by untrustworthy persons.

He says "here" [in verse 2] to show that the reasons—namely, "because there is an absence of sublation despite differences in place and so forth"—must be demonstrated even when there are differences in place and so forth.
Regarding this, the commentary states: "It might be argued:
'There is no connection at all between a word and its meaning; how then can it be either human-made or not human-made?'"
He states his intention [for the following verse] with the words "by the end of [the discussion on] the eternal and non-eternal.

Its meaning is as follows: Having refuted the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the Vedic injunctions (*codanā*) by means of the reason stated by the author of the Sūtras—that they are independent because they rely on the eternality of words, meanings, and their relationship—another, such as a Buddhist, has now asserted their falsity on the grounds that [the relationship] lacks origination (*udbhava*).
And thus, at that time, the author of the Vārttika demonstrated by means of the Vṛttikāra’s view that intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) is to be established right here.

Accordingly, in order to avoid the charge of redundancy with the statement "and it is stated by the author of the Sūtras," the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) was presented using precisely those reasons for objection that were set forth in the context of extrinsic invalidity (*parataḥaprāmāṇya*).
And here too, the author of the Bhāṣya says "it speaks"—that is, it causes one to understand and becomes the instrumental cause for the one who is understanding.
Thus, the very cause for intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) has been stated as that which was declared in the *Codanāsūtra*. //3.1.2//
In order to eliminate false views, those devoted to that [truth] do not accept these two [positions]:
either that there is no connection here at all, or that it is something created; this will be explained [later]. //5//

By the impossibility [of other relations], the connection (*saṃśleṣa*) of the remaining [words] is what remains; and in that very relation, the conventional understanding (*laukikī pratītiḥ*) is certainly established. (6)
He explains this very point with the words ending in "sambandha" (the relationship), which will be stated later.
For the purpose of refuting the falsity of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*), the existence of a relationship and its eternity were stated as the two reasons;
yet both of these are not accepted by our opponents.
In this regard, the absence of a relationship has already been stated by this very commentary;

however, the fact that [the property of] being produced does not convey [the meaning] when first heard will be stated by the words: "If it does not cause cognition when first heard, then how can it be something produced?"
Thus, it has been stated here that the reason— "because of independence due to the absence of a relationship"— is unestablished; furthermore,
it has been shown that in the absence of a relationship, the cognition of a meaning asserted by another does not arise.

For it is by the power of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) that knowledge of one thing arises even for one who perceives another thing. However, if one were to disregard the necessary connection, then anyone who knows something would know everything, which leads to the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). //4,5//

In this context, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), having stated that relations such as cause-and-effect are untenable for the word, demonstrated that only the relation of conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*) is possible;
the Author of the Vārttika demonstrates this with the words "by impossibility" (*asambhavena*).
Relations such as that of the efficient cause and its effect, or the locus and the located, are absolutely impossible between a word and its meaning.
The relationship of cause and effect is indeed accepted by the grammarians who follow the Buddha;
they too have said:
"Although meanings and words are clearly perceived through direct perception,"
The signifier and the signified, however, are forms of cognition; nevertheless, [they are not identical].
Thus it is said.
For they think as follows: "The phonemes (*varṇa*) are not the word, because each one individually does not convey the meaning."
Furthermore, because it is impossible for a collection of parts (*avayava-samudāya*) to originate from [phonemes] that do not exist simultaneously,

and precisely for this reason, since universals such as "cowness" (*gośabdatva*) are impossible, and since the specific instances of the elements (*bhūta*) and so forth cannot be denotative due to their difference in every individual usage,

and since the phoneme-cognitions, memories, and latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) have been rejected just like the phonemes themselves— even in the case of the final phoneme accompanied by the latent impressions produced by the preceding phonemes— [the word as a whole cannot be established].

Since each individual phoneme, like any unprecedented phoneme, lacks denotative power by virtue of its nature as a mere sound, and since no final phoneme of the nature of *sphoṭa* is apprehended through the process of synthesizing all preceding phonemes and words, the word is nothing other than a cognition consisting of the simultaneous presence of the forms of multiple phonemes.

Likewise, the meaning— whether it be a genus or an individual, a part or a whole, a quality or a qualified— is devoid of any determinable form, as it is far removed from conceptual constructions such as their difference or non-difference.

Since it is impossible for [the word] to exist externally, it consists merely of a cognition whose nature is the perception of external universals (*jāti*) and so forth, arising immediately after the experience of the word which is essentially knowledge.

To refute that [external existence], he says: "The word is not connected with the object, because it is not perceived in the location immediately following that [object], just as the Vindhya [mountain is not perceived in the location of the] Himavat. (7)
In this way, either the [single] object or both are to be established as being unconnected;
furthermore, the statement beginning with "kṣura" was spoken for the purpose of establishing the reason. //8//

If it is said that the connection [of the probans] is precluded by grasping it as having the nature of a capacity (*śakti*), then [the argument] would be proving what is already established; if, on the other hand, it refers to mere relation (*sambandhamātra*), then [the same fault follows]. //9//

And since this very object, being of such a nature, is indeed produced by the word, they maintain that the relationship between word and meaning is precisely one of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). But this is utterly remote from the truth; for if this were so, the cognition of an object would arise even for those who do not know the true nature or the power of words.

For it is indeed observed that even rice grains, though covered by earth and water, begin the causal process of sprouting and so forth despite their powers being unknown; thus it is well said: "because of the impossibility [of such powers] in the remaining [elements].
But how is conjunction (saṃśleṣa) left as the only possibility?
It is because it is both perceived and accepted.
For ordinary people are observed to apprehend an object as connected with a word through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such as "this is a cow.
Furthermore, some have accepted that the very non-connection between word and object is their relationship;
and this theory of superimposition (*adhyāsavāda*) has been explained at length.
Since worldly people generally consider conjunction alone to be a relation, that very relation is what must be refuted as it has been proposed; thus he says: "In that [place]," etc.

That which exists by means of a substratum is perceived in that very location, like a rope in a jar, or in the location immediately adjacent to it, like the middle finger in relation to the index finger.
Furthermore, neither of the two is perceived in the location of the other;
therefore, there is no relationship between these two, just as there is none between the Himālaya and the Vindhya mountains. //6,7//
Alternatively, he says "thus" (*evam*) to indicate that the object (*artha*) itself should be made the subject of the proposition (*pakṣīkārya*).

Or else, he says "the two" (*dvayam*) to indicate that the two things, being mutually unrelated, are the probandum (*sādhya*) when they are not perceived either in each other's location or in the location immediately adjacent to them.

Regarding this, the author of the *Bhāṣya* stated: "If there were a connection with the object, then upon the utterance of the words 'razor' (*kṣura*) and 'sweetmeat' (*modaka*), the primary effects of cutting and filling would occur [respectively]."
He states his intention [in the verse] ending with the word "kṣura":

"The meaning of this is as follows: here, the author of the Bhāṣya has implicitly included the reason 'because it is not perceived immediately after that location' for the sake of establishing the relationship between word and object.

And regarding that [reason], someone might consider it unestablished (*asiddha*) due to the delusion of the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the form 'this is a cow'."

He is thus addressed: "If it follows that the connection between word and meaning is rendered inconclusive by relations such as those between father and son, then the example [of the lamp and its light] lacks the probandum due to its own connection with a single substratum, such as the floor. (10)
If the relationship between the signified and the signifier were denied, there would be contradiction with worldly experience;
furthermore, there would be a contradiction with one's own statement, for [words] are not devoid of a relationship. //11//
If there were a connection with the [phonetic] characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*),

the object (*artha*) would also have to be located at the very place of the word; and since the mouth is the location of that [word], then upon the utterance of the words "razor" (*kṣura*) and "sweetmeat" (*modaka*), the mouth would undergo cutting and filling.

And those [two] do not exist; therefore, because the causal efficiency (arthakriyā) of things such as sweetmeats is not perceived, and because [the object] is not seen immediately after that location in the location of the word, the reason is established.
Furthermore, there is no cognition of coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the word and its object;
for we do not perceive an object colored by the word in the same way that a blue lotus is perceived as colored by its own blueness.
For in those two cases, there arises a cognition whose form consists of a dewlap and so forth, as well as a cow and so forth.
Regarding this, the Siddhāntabhāṣya states: "The relation which is to be designated here, that very one you do not designate," and so on.
He states his intention with the words beginning with "atha" and ending with "hīnatā":

"The intention here is this—the relationship between word and meaning intended is not one consisting of the capacity of the signifier and the signified; therefore, if the absence of a relationship characterized by physical conjunction were being proven..."
In that case, there is the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
However, if [the reason] refers merely to the absence of a relationship, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to [other types of] relationships such as those based on kinship.

Furthermore, because even the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains share a connection through a common ground and so forth, the example would be devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyahīna*). //8.10//

But if it is intended that the relation between the signified and the signifier itself is what is meant, and it is thus established that "the word is not connected with the object," then there is a contradiction with common worldly experience; thus he says, "The signified...
He states another refutation: "Contradiction...
Here he provides the reason: "For not... up to the end of the section.

The intended meaning is as follows: for there are four types of persons—the one who has understood (*pratipanna*), the one who has not understood (*apratipanna*), the one who is doubtful (*sandigdha*), and the one who is mistaken (*viparyasta*).
Among these, the one who has understood is the one who causes [others] to understand.
The others are dependent [upon one another] for their demonstration, and the thesis (*pratijñā*) exists for the purpose of demonstrating them; therefore,

whichever among those [factors] is intended by the opponent to be demonstrated, that very thing cannot be demonstrated by means of words whose scope is the meaning of the thesis and which are devoid of the relationship between the signified and the signifier.

Therefore, for those who employ a formal proposition (*pratijñā*), it is accepted that there exists between the word and its object a relationship characterized as that of the signifier and the signified; thus, in refuting that [relationship], one faces a contradiction with one's own words (*svavāgvirodha*). This contradiction with one's own words regarding denotation (*abhidhā*) is fivefold.
By means of utterance, naming, the property, the substratum, and the expression of both. //11 1/2//
The meaning of the proposition cannot be established for another by means of words;
for in the act of expression, the status of being an object resides in that which is to be expressed. //12//
The status of words as either instruments or agents has been established, because they are adopted for the purpose of cognition and because their joint operation is intended to be expressed. (13)
Now he elucidates the essential nature of the relationship between the signified and the signifier—beginning with the words "abhidhāna" (denotation) and so forth.

Its meaning is as follows: in a single act of denotation, the word is either the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the agent (*kartṛ*), since the application of grammatical factors (*kāraka*) depends upon the speaker's intention.
But the meaning is simply action;
therefore, when this method [is applied], it is either the state of being a non-agent of action or the state of being an agent.
The phrase "the relation has been defined" connects with what is to be said later.

Alternatively, he says "in the cognition" [of the object] to mean that when the cognition of a single object such as a cow is being produced, the word and its meaning—which are intended to be co-present like the Soma-cup (aruṇa) and the one-year-old cow (ekahāyanī) taken up by a single speaker—are restricted; that [restriction] is the relation between these two.
The phrase "because of being grasped" (*upādānāt*) indicates the intention to specify [the object] by way of its being grasped.

For it is the qualifier of that which is to be grasped (*upādeya*) that is intended to be specified—just as in the case of the singularity [of the sacrificer] in the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*).
However, the qualifier of the subject (*uddeśya*) is not intended to be specified.
Just as oneness is a qualification of the cups,
for the cups are the objects to be designated (uddeśya),
since the act of wiping is prescribed with respect to them.
And here, in the comprehension of the meaning, both the word and the object are to be accepted together, as in the case of the sacrificial animal in the *yoga* [of the injunction].

Therefore, their inseparability (*sāhitya*), which is most intended to be expressed, serves as a qualifier; thus, there is a restrictive relationship (*niyama-sambandha*) between these two, just as between the red color (*aruṇā*) and the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*).

But it is not reasonable to assume an intention to express concomitance (*sāhitya*) between the red cow (*aruṇā*) and the one-year-old female calf (*ekahāyanī*) when they are not heard [in the text] as such; for in that case, the sentence is completed with respect to the aggregate.
As for the word and its meaning...
Since [the word] is not heard as a qualifier for the act of cognition itself, how can there be an intended expression of their non-simultaneity?
The state of being currently heard is not the cause for the intention to express a qualification;
rather, it is also for the sake of practical linguistic usage (*arthasaṃvyavahāra*).
For instance, in the case of cooking and so forth, when [the action] concerns the rice-porridge and the like, or the pot and the like...

By observing linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), one understands even a meaning that has not been explicitly stated; at that time, one conceives of the intended concomitance (*sāhitya*) of the pot and other items.
Thinking thus, and desiring to cook himself, he brings all those things together.

Similarly, here too, a child, by observing the specific linguistic usage of an elder who is the agent of the action, infers the cognition directed toward that object; and because that cognition occurs immediately after the word, he determines that the word is its cause.

Furthermore, since the perception of the elder (the person being instructed) by the speaker in this context is for the sake of another and is thus the primary factor, the coexistence (*sāhitya*) of word and meaning as they are employed is intended to be expressed.
Having understood this, one should likewise, when employing [language] for the sake of others, take up word and meaning as they enter the heart in their combined state.

And since one brings about the understanding of another by uttering a sound, it is well said that there is an intention to express a collection [of sounds], just as there is an intention to express a collection of phonemes. //12-13 1/2 //
In that case, the connection between the meaning and the word is restricted to a single [sentence].
Even though there is no mutual connection between the constituent factors (*kārakas*) therein, [the sentence-meaning is established]. (14)

Nevertheless, when there is an action [of one] toward that [other], and there exists a relationship of beneficiary and benefactor in that action, the relation between those two is subsequently proclaimed as "conjunction" (sambandha). //15//
Surely, by saying this, you have shown that there is a connection between the word and the object only through action,
not directly with each other,
since a connection is impossible without a relationship of subordinate and principal.
For it will be said: "And because the qualities (guṇas) exist for the sake of another, there is no [direct] connection [between them], owing to their equality.
This might be so;
since all connections are preceded by the connection between an action and its factors (kāraka), it is precisely the connection between action and factor that has been demonstrated here.
Let that be for now; however, it must be stated what the relationship between these two is that occurs at a time subsequent to that.
Having restated all of this, he provides the rebuttal: "In that case" (*tatra*), meaning within that aforementioned context.
The meaning of this is as follows: although there is no mutual relationship between the factors (*kārakas*) because they exist for the sake of the primary object, [the following applies].

Nevertheless, whatever action is apprehended in the process of comprehension or expression, there exists between the word and its object a relationship characterized by mutual assistance, which arises subsequent to the connection between the action and its factors (kāraka).

Furthermore, this [position] is internally contradictory and contradicts other passages. For instance: on the one hand, it is stated here that the relationship between word and meaning consists in their being the beneficiary and the benefactor (*upakāryopakārakatva*) within a single action, based on the phrase "because it is employed for comprehension" (*pratipattāv upādānāt*), which implies that the relationship is essentially a mutual restriction (*parasparaniyama*) consisting in the word being a member of the inference of the action. On the other hand, elsewhere it is stated that the relationship is a causal capacity (*śakti*). Thus, there is a contradiction. Moreover, it is said that the relationship is the fitness (*yogyatā*) of the word to denote the object, and that the relationship is the non-existence of the denoted object in the locus of the denoter; yet, in another place, it is said that the relationship is the non-existence of the denoter in the locus of the denoted. Consequently, the relationship is not established as having a single nature. Furthermore, it is stated that the relationship is the cognition of the denoted object through the denoter, and that the relationship is the cognition of the denoter through the denoted. In another place, he will state that the relation is indeed capacity (*śakti*).

And in some instances, he speaks of the restriction of the word's capacity itself as the relation, saying: "The restriction of the capacities of the signified and the signifier is characterized by the result."
It is also stated elsewhere:
"That which constitutes the state of being the object and the agent through a single denotation,
or that which is the restriction of the instrument and the sequence by means of a single expression."
"Therefore, there is no relation between the word and its object.
Consequently, this must be examined: what kind of relation between word and object is intended here by the author of the Vārttika?

To this it is replied: Just as in the case of a substance and a quality grasped by a single act of purchase, there exists a relationship characterized by mutual assistance through the fulfillment of their mutual requirements—
since a quality that is not supported does not bring about the act of purchase,
nor is a substance capable of accomplishing the act of purchase unless it is delimited by specific qualities.
Moreover, even when a substance serving as the substratum is being taken up by means of a quality through its own power, it is not included in the purchase,
because [the substance] is already secured by [one's own] cow;
[for] in the case of the substance, there is only the quality.
Because it excludes others, even when its own quality is being employed, the act of purchase does not accept it, due to the obstruction by its own quality of redness (*aruṇima*).
This very fact constitutes a restriction (*niyama*).

Thus, in this case as well, for the sake of accomplishing the act of denoting the comprehension of a single object, there exists—between the word and the meaning, which are employed with an intended concomitance (*sāhitya*) following the relationship between the action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*)—that which [arises].
That itself is the relationship.
But what is this mutual assistance between these two?
Listen: for an object cannot be made known without a means of making it known.
A word is not a signifier without that which is to be signified;
therefore, existing as signifier and signified, they become mutually benefactor and beneficiary.
Since this nature of theirs is fixed, the designation of a "relation" occurs when there is a restriction [of their function] through mere extreme proximity.
But restriction alone is not the relation;
for this very reason, there is also the theory of the relation of capacity (*śakti*).
For it is only when the capacities of the signified and the signifier exist that the relationship of the benefactor and the benefited arises.
However, power (*śakti*) itself is not the relation; rather,
in this context, by means of a metaphorical identification with proximity (*pratyāsatti*), "power" is called the "relation," and "restriction" (*niyama*) is called the "relation."
Such discourses as "agency" or "instrumentality" are merely verbal designations;
in reality, however, a relationship is nothing other than the state of being the benefactor and the beneficiary.
But how is it said that this nature of theirs is fixed? It is explained as follows: [text continues]
For when a word has not been uttered, there is no relationship of mutual assistance between the word and its object;
yet at that time, the two do not cease to exist, because they are eternal.
Therefore, this [position] is untenable.
That is not so;
for it exists in the form of a potentiality,
and it has already been established that inseparable connection (avinābhāva) is of no use here.
If it is argued that "designation" (saṃjñā) constitutes the quality of being intelligible, then this [designation] would not be a factor [of that intelligibility].
Having observed that the Veda brings about understanding through conventional usage, it is postulated [as a means of knowledge];
yet this [Veda] does not convey its meaning as long as the relationship [between word and object] has not been determined.

For even when a word has not been uttered, there exists a power to convey [the meaning] in the word, and a power to be conveyed in the object; for this very reason, the relationship is said to be eternal.

But even so, when many words such as *kara*, *hasta*, and others convey a single object, and when a single word such as *go* expresses multiple meanings, how can non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) be understood?

Therefore, since context and the other factors are also necessary for the determination of word-meanings, it has been established through the method of inclusion and exclusion (*āvāpoddhāra*) in the linguistic usage of elders—

that when a word is employed with the intention of conveying a particular meaning, that is its meaning. Furthermore, this intention (*vivakṣā*) is to be inferred from the force of the meaning, context, and so forth.
When it is said, "Bring the cow to milk," it is understood by implication that what is intended is an animal possessing a dewlap and so forth;
when it is said, "I shall fight," a cognition of the chest arises by implication.

Thus, since words—distinguished by differences such as meaning and context—are each endowed with distinct capacities and serve as the designators of various objects, there is no deviation of the word [from its referent].

Furthermore, the object itself—such as a hand or other things, which are distinguished by different states capable of being denoted by specific words—is the respective denotatum of words like "hand" and so on; thus, the word does not deviate [from its referent].
Moreover, this rule has been stated to apply within the context of a single action.
Furthermore, when both word and meaning are employed within a single practice or expression, there is no mutual deviation between them;
for this very reason it was said: "When they are restricted to a single [practice]," etc. (14, 15).

Now, if it is argued that when the relation between word and meaning is said to be a restriction based on a single causal operation (*ekakriyānimittaka*), then the inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)—which is a factor of inference—would necessarily be relied upon; consequently, the cognition of an object arising from a word would, by virtue of that [concomitance], become an inference, just like the cognition of fire from smoke. To this, he says: "And yet not...
He further states: "It has been established," referring to what has already been proven regarding verbal cognition (*śābda*).
Now, if inseparable connection (avinābhāva) is not useful, what then is useful?
The Commentator has stated: "The relationship between the name and the named."
But surely this relationship too is useless? He anticipates this objection with the words "the name" (*saṃjñā*).
The meaning is that it is a constituent part of that [word], being a factor for its denotative capacity (*gamakatva*). //16//
How is it that [the word] is not a constituent part (*anaṅga*)? He says: "because they cause one to understand" (*gamayanti*).

Through the observation of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), there arises from that [word] the capacity to cause understanding (*gamakatā*), just as [the capacity to cause understanding] subsequently arises in the case of smoke and so forth.
In that same way, she would be bodiless; she is not comparable to smoke and the like.
For when the invariable concomitance has been ascertained, it is that [concomitance] which effects the cognition;
yet, at the time of the initial cognition, that [concomitance] has not yet arisen as the means of proof.

In this world, prior to the capacity for denotation, there is no cognition of invariable concomitance; and it is only when the relationship is here communicated from the elders that [the word's meaning is understood].
At that very moment, they do not indicate "this is its signifier" by means of another's own nature; rather, in some cases they declare, "This person is to be understood from this [sign]."

In some cases, it is said that "this is the denoter" and "this is the denoted"; in other cases, having observed an action directed toward an object upon hearing a word uttered, [one understands the relationship].

The state of being a name consists precisely in its capacity to convey meaning; it does not exist apart from that [conventional] relationship. //17//
And since this is so, it follows that the capacity to indicate, as in the case of smoke and the like, is preceded by another relation; thus he says, "Therefore.
He states the fault in [assuming] their equality: "That is not a factor.

Just as in the case of smoke and so forth, it is the very state of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) that is the factor for cognition, and not the capacity to indicate which arises at a subsequent time.
Thinking that "the same would apply there as well," he now states the rebuttal by way of the dissimilarity with smoke and so forth: "This is not [the case]. //18//
He demonstrates this very distinction: "nirūpita" (ascertained).

For in that case, regarding smoke and the like in a location such as a kitchen, after the ascertainment of the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with fire, it is precisely that [concomitance] which makes it a signifier (*gamaka*).
Furthermore, he says "by way of being a signifier" because the status of smoke as a signifier is not apprehended at first. //19//
But regarding sound, he states the opposite in the following half-verse and the next: "In this case... (20 1/2).

It has been stated that the initial acquisition of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) regarding a word occurs precisely through its capacity to convey meaning; this is now explained by the triad beginning with "they communicate" (*kathayanti*).

The meaning is as follows: the acquisition of linguistic usage regarding a word occurs in three ways—either from the instruction of elders, from their actual usage, or from the co-occurrence of other words.
And in all such cases, it is first understood that [the word] possesses the capacity to convey meaning.

As it has been said: "In the instruction of elders, one first perceives that 'this is the denoted' and 'this is the denoter'; therein, the status of being a cognizer is understood by means of inference."
By this, from whatever word this meaning has been determined, [it is established].

Therefore, these two are certainly established in this world as possessing the power of denotation; thus, the status of being a denoter is established, even though it remains intermingled. Furthermore, beyond that: Msv_5,9.24.
When the meaning has been determined through positive and negative concomitance as something abstracted [from its adjuncts],
it relies upon the distinctions of many universals, qualities, substances, and actions.

He does not wish to definitively determine the conditions that have suddenly arisen— whether they consist of what is heard from scripture or what is characterized by logic— because the world lacks such a cause for determination.
Thus, it is precisely the relationship of indicator and indicated (*gamyagamakabhāva*) that is understood.

Even in cases where, upon seeing the activity directed toward an object by the elder who was prompted after a certain sentence has been uttered, one infers through his behavior that he has understood the meaning of "cow" and so forth,
there too [the understanding arises] because from this word this meaning was understood by him.
Therefore, it is understood that the very capacity of a word to convey meaning (*gamakatā*) is what is apprehended first, such that "this is its meaning.
Even in cases where it is co-occurrent with other well-known words— as in examples such as "the *pika* sings sweetly in the mango tree" (*sahakāratarau madhuraṃ piko rauti*)—
for one who knows the meaning of "mango tree" (*sahakāra*) and so forth but does not know the meaning of "pika," the word *pika* [is understood] as that which sings in the mango tree.

Since one understands that "it is an indicator" (*gamaka*) precisely as its state of being an indicator (*gamakatva*), it is established that in all cases there is the state of being an indicator, not [mere] linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). //21–23½//
Now, is it not the established conclusion that the word-meaning is the form (ākṛti)?
And its status as the denotable meaning cannot be understood without recourse to positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
Therefore, it would follow that the cognition produced by the word must have that [form] as its primary object.
Therefore, he says: "In this way.
The meaning is as follows: here, the function of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) consists merely in establishing the restriction of the extracted meaning;
however, the capacity to denote (*vācakatā*), which has as its object meanings intermingled with various universals (*jāti*) and so forth, is already established. //24 1/2//
Indeed, the linguistic usage of words and their meanings is observed even among cowherds;
yet they do not extract the meaning through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Nor is it reasonable to say that words are "unexpressive" (*avācaka*) with respect to them.
When things are perceived as being equal,

those who know the Vedic sentences distinguish between them for the purpose of determining the meaning of words such as "pika" based on the usage of Mlecchas and others, and for the sake of establishing their relative strength or weakness.
For [the rule] is weak regarding general and particular cases that are separated by an intervening category.
A word that expresses a general meaning arises through the power of indication (lakṣaṇā);
therefore, one must necessarily distinguish by means of that word how much is actually expressed.
Since this will be explained later, he says [the following] in one and a half verses beginning with "bahujāti":
the intention is as follows—worldly people seek merely the practical transactions of rejection, acquisition, and so forth;
and their transaction is not necessarily accomplished solely by a confused understanding of the meaning arising at the very moment the word is uttered.
They are thus indifferent toward the distinction between words used according to Vedic revelation (śrauta) and those based on conventional definition (lākṣaṇika), and so forth. //25,26//
If that is so, for what purpose then do they analyze? To this he says: "strength and weakness, etc.

For those who abide by the scriptures are unable to perform the meaning of the scriptures if their capacities have not been determined; therefore, since the discrimination of the power of words is useful for their rejection and adoption, they perform such analysis. //26 1/2//
He elaborates on this very point with the two verses beginning with "separated by a degree" (*kakṣyāntarita*).
The meaning of this is as follows: generality (*sāmānya*) is of two kinds, the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*). The higher is called "Being" (*sattā*); the others are the lower.
Substantiality and the like are also universals;
because they are also causes for the cognition of exclusion, they receive the designation of "particulars" as well.

These are designated by the term "particulars of the universal" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*); and therein, the "particulars of the universal" are separated from the own-meaning (*svārtha*) of the word for the universal by an intermediate level (*kakṣyā*).

For example, when the word "existent" (*sat*) denotes existence (*sattā*), the "particulars of the universal" such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth are separated from it by that [existence].
And when that [word] functions toward those [secondary meanings] by the power of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it becomes weak;
however, since it functions toward its own primary meaning by means of direct denotation (*śruti*), it is strong therein.
What, then, is this so-called indication? It is the cognition [of a meaning] through the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the expressed meaning.
As it has been said:
"The cognition of the inseparable connection with the denoted meaning is held to be the definition [of indication].

It is appropriate for those established in the treatises to make a distinction as to how much is indicated through the inseparable connection with the denoted meaning, and how much is expressed by the word through its own power, for the sake of specific practical application.
And since that indication (*lakṣaṇā*) generally arises from a permanent relationship, it is said to arise "from a permanent relationship.
However, the mere existence of a relationship is the seed of indication.
He asks: what, then, is the utility of distinguishing between the literal (*śrauta*) and the indicated (*lākṣaṇika*) in the performance [of the ritual]?
Listen: In the world, first of all, how much of the Vedic [language] is indicated by its connection with the denotable meaning through constant association?
In that regard, due to the abundance of usage, it is understood even when its specific [Vedic] forms are absent. (Msv 5.9.29)

In the Vedic injunction, "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, and buttermilk to the Kauṇḍinya," the Vedic statement regarding Brāhmaṇas in general— being weaker as it descends to that specific individual, Kauṇḍinya— is set aside by the statement regarding Kauṇḍinya, which resides in the immediately proximate particular. It is exactly the same in the Veda as well.

It should be shown that the general scriptural injunction, "The *yajus* and *sāman* are performed in a low voice" (*upāṃśu-yajuṣā*), is sublated by the specific scriptural injunction, "The *nigada* is performed loudly" (*uccair-nigadena*).
By using the word "general" (*sāmānya*) here to qualify the particulars, [the author] shows that there are no particulars existing apart from the general.
For there is the view of some who hold that "particulars" (*viśeṣa*) are ultimate entities residing in eternal substances.
And since they are the very causes of the cognition of exclusion, they are indeed particulars (*viśeṣas*).
For the followers of Kaṇāda maintain that the creation of the world proceeds from atoms through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth.
And it is not possible to produce a world of unmixed forms by means of atoms that, being atomic in nature, possess no mutual distinction from one another.
Therefore, some maintain that there exist so-called "particularities" (*viśeṣas*) inherent in atoms which differentiate them from one another;
and they claim that these are indeed perceived directly by those whose every impurity has been shaken off.
To them, the following is said:
First of all, among entities that are dependent on the senses, we do not perceive particulars that exceed the intermediate universals (avāntara-sāmānya).

For instance, earth and the other [elements] are distinguished from qualities and actions by their being substances (*dravyatva*); and earth is distinguished from other substances such as water by its being earth (*pṛthivītva*).
By way of being a tree, a tree [is distinguished] from other earthen things;

by way of being a *śiṃśapā*, a *śiṃśapā* [is distinguished] from other trees. In this manner, this discourse on particularities (*viśeṣa*) should be carried out down to the level of atoms. What is the use here of another particularity?

However, even among atoms of the same kind, we shall infer that their form itself is distinct based on the distinction between their effects; for indeed, a prior entity whose form is undivided is not capable of producing an effect whose form is divided.
Alternatively, there will be a quality called "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*) which serves as their "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) because it differentiates them from one another.
If it is argued that this very [entity] does not establish itself because it does not depend on any further particularity,
then how will the particulars themselves be established without depending on further particularities? Or else, there would be an infinite regress.
Therefore, this admission of further distinctions is indeed feeble.

As for the statement that "yogins perceive them," those who possess faith understand it thus: "We, however, lack such faith, as we seek logical reasoning. Thus, it is well said regarding universals and particulars. //27-28½//

Because it is employed [to denote] the highest generality (*parasāmānya*), and because it is not employed [for anything else], it denotes the mere "cow-ness" (*gotvamātra*) which is related to a single object, such as the dewlap and so forth. (Msv 5.9.30)
The cognition "this is the word *go*" arises from positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*);
therefore, its capacity to convey meaning (*gamakatā*) comes first, while its status as a signifier (*abhidhāyakatā*) follows.
The connection [expressed by] "having that as its cause" (tannimitta) is characterized by the relationship between signifier and signified;
however, this restriction of the relationship is what is called "inseparable concomitance" (avinābhāvitā).
Because it does not cause comprehension prior to the apprehension of the relationship,
the word "cow" and so forth lacks expressive power, just like the word "Devadatta."
It has been stated: "Those who know sentences distinguish [the meaning] through the presence and absence of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
He demonstrates that positive and negative concomitance with the following two verses, beginning with the word *tatra* ("therein").
Therein, in the case of universals such as "cow" and so forth—

Because the word "cow" (go-śabda) is used extensively, and because it is observed to be applied to Bāhuleyas and others even when specific individuals such as Śābaleyas are absent, and because it is not applied to other entities despite the presence of higher universals such as "existence" (sattā), it is known through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the word "cow" denotes the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) alone, which is connected to a single composite object (*ekāvayavin*) along with the dewlap and other features; and this is understood through the inseparable connection (*avinābhāvin*) with those [features] that share a single objective referent.
"One characterizes 'cowness' by means of a mark.

Therefore, it is established that the relationship between word and meaning is first understood as the very relation of the signifier and the signified (*gamya-gamakabhāva*), and not as invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). //29-30½//
He concludes: "Therefore...

Now, one might object: the relationship between the name and the named has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya; however, people in the world do not consider a name to be that which makes [the meaning] understood.
For smoke is not called the "name" (saṃjñā) of fire;
therefore, he says: "it is the designator" (abhidhāyakatā).
The intention is this: when it is known that "this is the signifier of this object."
Since it is not logical for that which is not functioning to be a cause for comprehension, its operation is inferred;
and the operation of the word is called "denotation" (abhidhā).

Therefore, in this case, due to its connection with the act of denoting, the specific quality of being a signifier (abhidhāyakatā) is recognized in the word as a particularization of its capacity to convey meaning.

Since being a designator (*abhidhāyaka*) is precisely what constitutes being a name (*saṃjñātva*), it is established that the relationship between the name and the named (*saṃjñāsaṃjñisambandha*) [is one of denotation]. However, he states "the relationship" (*sambandha*) to show that while inseparability (*avinābhāvitā*) is a restriction of the relationship, it is not the relationship itself.
And this was stated by us in the passage, "It is restricted to the extracted meaning.
Therefore, understand that [the conclusion] is summarized by supplying the word "tasmāt" (therefore), just as a word that conveys meaning is understood through linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).
In the same way, the cognition of capacity is understood to be the means for that [attainment].
And just as the apprehension of its own form functions toward the result, so too does the cognition of the relationship; it cannot be said to be ineffective.
The words "absence of positive concomitance" (anvaya) and "absence of negative concomitance" (vyatireka) are synonyms; therefore, one should not suspect a difference in their meaning. //31,32//
The author of the Bhāṣya has implicitly included the usage "if it is a signifier" (pratyāyaka); he states this with the words "sambandha... (beginning with "sambandha").
For proper names such as Devadatta and the like signify only that very object for which they have been conventionally established.
Nor do these [words] possess any inherent power whatsoever. Therefore, the formulation of the argument is as follows: the subject (*dharmin*) is the word "cow" and so forth;
it is to be proven that it lacks the power of denotation (*abhidhā-śakti*).
The reason is "because it depends on another means.
Whatever depends on another means is not capable [of its function] by its own nature, just as the word "Devadatta" and so forth depend upon the apprehension of a convention. //33//

In this regard, the Commentator, having raised the objection—"If a word is expressive, why does it not express its meaning when heard for the first time?"—offers a solution by stating, "In all cases, our observation is the authority," and so forth, explaining that a word conveys its meaning once its power has been grasped through the force of observation;
he demonstrates this with the words "Just as... (yathaiva).
First of all, why is it accepted that a word possesses the capacity to convey meaning?
If you say it is by the force of observing linguistic usage, this is equally true in the case of perceiving the innate power (*śakti*).
For it is not observed that people who do not know the power [of words] comprehend meaning from them. //34//

It might be argued as follows: illuminators such as lamps are seen to illuminate their own objects even when their relationship [to those objects] is unknown; and since the word is of a different nature than that, it is therefore not an illuminator.
And that is not so,
because of the diversity of capacities;
for entities indeed possess diverse capacities.
Granted that a lamp, by virtue of its being perceived directly, may indeed illuminate even that with which it has not grasped a relationship;
however, for this reason alone, it does not follow that sound must also possess that same property.
Therefore, this objection is untenable.
Moreover, since rice and other such things indeed initiate their effects even when their own forms have not been perceived, why is that property not attributed to the word?
For rice and the like are productive causes (*kāraka-hetu*),
whereas the word is an indicative cause (*jñāpaka-hetu*).

If it is argued that, for this reason, the apprehension of its own form (*svarūpa*) is required, then by what authority has it been commanded— by what means of cognition— that the apprehension of the own form must be expected, but not the apprehension of the relation?
If it is replied that this is by the force of observation (*darśana*), [we respond as follows:]
This is the same regarding the apprehension of a relationship:
when something is designated as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for something else,
its dependence on auxiliary factors does not impair its own inherent capacity.
For there is nothing in this world or in the Veda that,
when accomplished through a specific procedure, does not desire assistance from such [an authority].
And because it is restricted to each individual, it may function as an instrument;
it may exist either through the distinction between external and internal, or according to the speaker’s intention.
For someone distressed by darkness might even say this:
"What is seen by me with this eye of mine has been seen by the lamp."
Even in the case of inference, it is solely by the power of perception that specific indicators such as logical marks (*liṅga*) and words depend upon the apprehension of a relationship;
the eyes and other [senses] do not. For in all cases, perception is our primary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

We do not accept that the eyes and so forth are the agents [of cognition], because only that which is the cause of knowledge is a cognizer; this is what he states with the words "its own nature" (svarūpa) and so on. //35//
But surely, even before the apprehension of the relationship, is the word capable of denotation or not? If it is capable, what is the need for dependence upon the apprehension of the relationship?
If it is not, [then it can never denote].
For it would be the apprehension of the relationship itself that, according to the logic of the authoritative tradition (*sadāgama*), would constitute the cause;
therefore, he says: "that which is the most effective means" (*yatsādhakatamam*).
We certainly do not perceive the word as being incapable prior to the apprehension of the relationship.
And that which is capable does not abandon its own power by depending on an auxiliary cause. //36//
Why, then, would it not destroy [its own power]? To this he says: "For not... (na hi).
For if the dependence on an auxiliary were to destroy its own power, then every worldly or Vedic instrument (karaṇa) would lose its status as an instrument;
for every instrument indeed requires the assistance produced by the procedure (itikartavyatā). //37//

Furthermore—let it be granted for now that the requirement of a procedure (*itikartavyatā*) does not destroy the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*); on the contrary, by that very [requirement], the status of being an instrument does not even exist, because there is a rule of dependence upon it for every individual nature of an instrument. Thus he says: "with respect to each self" (*pratyātma*).

[Objection: "In that case, since the effect cannot be produced without the conjunction of both [the means and the procedure], how can the distinction between the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) be demonstrated?

To this, he says: "External and internal... Since even an external factor may, in some cases, be intended as the instrument when there is an activity of the causal factors (*kāraka*) based on the speaker's intention, he says: "...in some cases it may be so. (38)
But in the case of constant functioning, even with hundreds of lamps, the blind have no vision for the perception of forms and so forth; therefore, the eye is the illuminator.
Due to the conjunction of the body, the self, and the mind; by virtue of its unique power;
and because of the presence of consciousness, the eye is held to be the instrument.
Likewise here too, the knowledge of the relationship is an auxiliary factor because it is well-established;
if it is considered an instrument due to its being more weighty, who can prevent that?
The statement "just as the eye" is used to express the possibility of deviation;
moreover, they maintain by means of reasoning that even in Devadatta, the capacity [of the sense organs] is unmanifest.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "udvigna" (distressed).

Even though the eye is an internal factor for the arising of knowledge, it is not considered the instrument; rather, due to a certain specific degree of mental intensity, he intends to designate the external lamp alone as the instrument. //39//
And this state of being an instrument, which is based on the desire to speak, is occasional.
However, when [the function] is eternal, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is understood to be the instrument for the constant accomplishment of the effect; thus he says: "in its eternal operation.
The meaning is that for the blind, there is no vision—that is, no seeing. //40//

Now, it may be granted that the eye possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) in relation to the lamp and so forth, because of the qualification of the non-existence of its effect [in their absence];

however, since the contact between the self and the mind (*ātmamanas-saṃyoga*) is extremely proximate to the production of cognition, how can the eye have the status of an instrument in relation to that? To this, he says: "the body... and so forth.
The intended meaning is this: proximity alone is not the cause for being an instrument;
rather, there is proximity relative to external factors such as a lamp, whereas there is uniqueness (asādhāraṇya) relative to the internal conjunction of the self and the mind.
For the conjunction of the self and the mind is common to the cognition of taste and so forth; thus, it cannot be understood as the cause for the perception of color by virtue of being non-deviant.

However, the eye’s causality with respect to the cognition of color is established precisely through its uniqueness. This has been stated in the passage beginning, "But the distinction between the eye, color, and so forth. //41//

Thus, having demonstrated in the example the distinction between the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—which are produced by the specificities of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) and proximity (*sannikarṣa*)—he applies this to the subject at hand with the words "in the same way" (*tathaiva*).

By this, it is shown that even that which was stated—that the apprehension of the relationship (*sambandhagrahaṇa*) alone must be the cause according to the logic of scripture (*āgama-nyāya*)—may also occur by virtue of a specific intention. //42//

Furthermore, regarding the explanatory passage in the *Bhāṣya* which begins with "Just as the eye, without an external light, [cannot see]," he states its intended meaning with the word "yathā" (just as):
for the eye [requires] other means such as a lamp, etc.
When external light is present, form is not perceived by the blind;
furthermore, because the result follows immediately [from its presence], the eye is accepted as the instrument.

If that relationship between a name and the named— which depends on human cognition and was not established prior to those [names]— is indeed intended [to be real], then it must certainly have been created [by someone].
Just as in the case of a rope, a jar, and so forth, there is no commonality because they are based on different locations and so on;
therefore, their lack of connection is intrinsic.

He states—“Devadatta”—to show that the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since even that which is dependent is by its very nature capable of manifesting form; furthermore, the example is also deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikala*). //43//

It has been explained in the *Adhyāsa* [section] that even for arbitrary words (*yadṛcchāśabda*), the capacity for cognition already exists and is merely manifested by grammatical injunction (*niyoga*).

Here, regarding the statement "as in the case of the word *cakṣus*" in the Bhāṣya, he provides the justification for the fact that the eye is an instrument (*karaṇa*) with the words "illumination" (*prakāśa*). Furthermore, although this was already stated under the rule *nityavṛttau*, it is mentioned here again for the purpose of supporting the Bhāṣya; thus, there is no tautology. // 44 //

Thus, having established that the relationship between a name and the named is produced, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) has raised the objection: "If it does not convey meaning when heard for the first time, then it must be a product.
The author of the Vārttika demonstrates this with the words "puruṣa... and so on.
And thus, the formal argument here is as follows: whatever is the relationship between a name and the named is a product.
Because it depends upon a person, like the conjunction between a rope and a jar. //45//
Furthermore, regarding the commentary beginning with "For these two, word and meaning, are by nature unconnected," he states its intended meaning as follows: "distinct," etc.

The meaning is this: just as in the case of a rope-snake and the like, which occupy different locations and times, there is no commonality whatsoever such as place and so forth; [yet they appear as one].
Thus it is with both sound and meaning;

therefore, just like that [previous case], those two as well are inherently unrelated. And the formulation of the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: "Sound and meaning are inherently unconnected."
Because they do not occupy the same place and time,
like a rope and so forth;
those two [the self and the body] are indeed not of the same place and time.
Because it is perceived as having a substratum in a different location and so forth, it is exactly like that [the self]. //46//
Thus ends the "Refutation of the Objection Concerning the Connection" composed by the Preceptor Sucarita Miśra.
